title: ‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Conversations are supposed to be two-sided – but all too often we come up against someone who’s passionately, exclusively in love with the sound of their own voice. Time to fight back …
Author: Anita Chaudhuri
Headline: Conversations are supposed to be two-sided – but all too often we come up against someone who’s passionately, exclusively in love with the sound of their own voice. Time to fight back …
Content: Illustration: Michael Parkin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Michael Parkin/The GuardianSocial etiquette‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpersConversations are supposed to be two-sided – but all too often we come up against someone who’s passionately, exclusively in love with the sound of their own voice. Time to fight back …Anita ChaudhuriSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was in my early teens, I was often invited round to a schoolfriend’s house for dinner. Her family struck me as wildly progressive: they were Danish and indulged in all sorts of “out-there” activities – fondues, candle-making and, most terrifying of all, the talking stick.Before the meal was served, someone would retrieve the sacred broom handle and it would be passed around the table. You could speak only if you had possession of the stick. Despite it being the most stressful thing ever (it meant being in the spotlight, and then remembering to keep quiet the rest of the time), I now frequently yearn for a more convenient version of that stick.For example, I met a friend recently who I see infrequently but keep up with via voice notes. No sooner had we sat down than he launched into a long discourse about his new marathon training food plan. He only broke the flow to order an omelette: “Four egg whites, two yolks, is that possible?” (We were in my local greasy spoon, so the request was greeted with mirth.) When we left, 90 minutes later, he finally had the grace to turn to me and ask: “And how are things with you?”Walking home, I felt a mixture of disappointment and irritation. Had he always been so self-absorbed? So uninterested in anyone else? I couldn’t help wondering if our one-sided virtual updates had played a part in the problem.There is a name for this type of egocentric behaviour – “conversational narcissism”. Although it was coined by the sociologist Charles Derber in his 1979 book The Pursuit of Attention, the term seems more relevant than ever. “WhatsApp communication and voice notes are really a series of monologues,” says Charlotte Fox Weber, a psychotherapist. “In face-to-face situations, people are forgetting how to pause naturally, to make space to hear and listen. And people are chatting on the phone – an activity that at least requires turn-taking in a defined way – much less often.”A lot of our communication online can feel weirdly transactional, focused on logistics or niche WhatsApp groups. According to Tamu Thomas, a life coach and author, this has damaged the art of improvised conversation. “People have less capacity for meandering conversations that don’t have a purpose,” she says. “A good dialogue is a back-and-forth between two people discovering new things about each other, even if they have known each other for years. Because there are now so many different channels available to stay in touch, some people are confusing communication with connection.”Knowledge is power, though. If you can recognise the five types of common conversation hogger, it will be much easier to handle them.The serial monologuistView image in fullscreenWill he ever stop talking?Photograph: Posed by models; skynesher/Getty ImagesWe have all come across this one – the person who, likethe Ariston washing machine in the 90s advert, just goes on and on and on. “It’s not only that these people feel the need to dominate the conversation; they often select topics that are not necessarily meaningful for anyone else. For example, it might be cathartic for someone to share the granular detail of their lost luggage or their dishwasher leak, but it has no value for anyone else,” says Fox Weber.For Jane and her partner, Ian, dinner parties at his best friend’s home have become an ordeal. “It’s his wife,” groans Jane. “We don’t have children; they have three. We have to brace ourselves for her monologues that cover everything from school trips to football trophies and, worst of all, their various ailments. I sit there with a fixed grin, wondering how long I can reasonably pretend to be fascinated by someone else’s child’s orthodontic treatment. It’s even worse when they invite other couples, usually fellow parents. Then it becomes a game of monologue ping-pong. It’s not easy finding a gap in the conversation when I can mention that I have had a perfectly interesting time lately – going to films or the theatre, and reading great books.”Sarah Rozenthuler is a psychologist and dialogue coach, and the author of Now We’re Talking and several other books focused on how to have meaningful conversations. She suggests taking a counterintuitive approach. “Try time-boxing them. Tell yourself you are going to give the person your full attention for a certain amount of time, say five minutes, or 10 if you can stand it. Abandon all expectations about having your own say. Allowing the other person to feel fully heard usually helps them to settle down a bit.”When the time is up, she suggests deliberately redirecting the chat, without shutting the other person down. “So you might say something like: ‘Well, that’s really interesting, and it reminds me of …’ and then share something from your own experience, or change the topic altogether.” She believes this strategy works on two levels. It lets you speak, and it’s a reminder that each of us needs to take responsibility for maintaining a two-way conversation, rather than sitting there seething like a helpless bystander.The trauma dumperView image in fullscreen‘Have I told you about my latest one-night stand?’Photograph: Posed by models; NicolasMcComber/Getty ImagesThe trauma dumper loves nothing better than a session of oversharing with no boundaries and no thought for how it might land with others.Phoebe’s friend Andrew falls into this category. “I’ve seen other people blossom and grow through therapy – but for Andrew, it’s given him licence to overshare and not listen to others. His booming voice is always the loudest in the room. Nothing is off limits, from lurid details of his one-night stands to the long-running feud he has been having with his mother since the age of four.“For me, the lowest point was in a restaurant when he shared the intimate details of his vasectomy. As if that wasn’t bad enough, he repeated the story at a dinner party I attended with several of our friends, including his ex. I didn’t know where to look. I have no idea how to rein him in, because I feel that if I tackle him about the oversharing directly, he might turn that into a trauma drama to share with others as well.”Thomas suggests interrogating what is really bothering you about such a dynamic. Are you feeling used? What do you want from the relationship, if anything? She says: “I had a friend like this and I realised that what I wanted was her to contact me during the good times, not only the crises. I asked her to phone me when things were going really well, for example sharing the funny thing that happened at work that day. It was scary, but saying, ‘I really want to be part of your joy as well as your struggle,’ was a lot more productive than angrily accusing her of dumping all her problems at my door. Eventually, we were able to have a more constructive relationship.”The boomeraskerView image in fullscreen‘Let me tell you all about my weekend.’Photograph: Posed by models; skynesher/Getty ImagesFor those unfamiliar with the term, boomerasking is posing a question so you can talk next. My friend Emma often complains about a colleague at work who falls into this category. She says: “Every Monday morning, without fail, he will ask me: ‘Good weekend? What did you get up to?’ But his fake question is a ruse to allow him to boast about all the amazing things he did. It makes me feel boring, and at the same time manipulated – not a great combo.”Boomerasking was first identified in a study co-authored by Michael Yeomans, associate professor of behavioural science at Imperial College. “A boomerask is a question that boomerangs right back to you,” he says. “There are three types of boomerask. The first is the ‘ask-brag’, where I have something exciting I want to tell you, such as: ‘I went to France for the weekend.’ Then there’s the ‘ask-complaint’. That’s when I might ask: ‘How was your journey into work?’ You might answer, only for me to go into great detail about how the tube was packed, there was an accident, someone spilled coffee on my shoe. And then there’s the ‘ask-share’, where I ask for your opinion about something, but I’m not listening – I’m waiting for a break so I can jump in and share my opinion. In all three cases, the perceived sincerity of the question hooks people in.”How can we take back control? “Our research shows that boomeraskers think they are being helpful and inclusive. So, if the other person is important to you, know that there will be plenty of time to have your say later. You may feel their interest in you is only superficial, but their interest in communicating something with you is certainly genuine. That’s worth celebrating.“The other thing our research has shown is that ‘mirror questions’ take the sting out of the exchange. Next time a boomerasker enquires about your commute, mumble something vague and then ask with great enthusiasm about their journey.”So it takes the sting out of it because if you don’t give them a real answer, then you haven’t wasted your energy on someone who isn’t interested? “Yeah, and also crucially, they can’t cut you off.” It won’t necessarily shut the boomerasker up, but if you feel more in control, you will find them less annoying.If none of this helps? “If you want to have some fun, boomerask them back, and see how they react,” suggests Yeomans.The interrupterView image in fullscreen‘What you need to do now …’Photograph: Posed by model; Milky Way/Getty ImagesInterrupters are easy to spot but difficult to confront. When Jo was made redundant, she started meeting up for coffee with a former colleague. “I thought she could give me a bit of moral support and, crucially, a reason to get out of the house.” However, these sessions soon proved unsatisfying.“What I really wanted was someone to confide in about the unfairness of my job loss, and my fears about being 55 and unemployed.” But the friend proved to be an unexpectedly aggressive listener, cutting Jo off at every turn with: “Have you thought about retraining? My friend is earning a fortune now.” Or: “The thing you need to do now is find out about how to outwit the applicant tracking systems. If I lost my job, what I would do is blah blah blah.” But Jo didn’t want advice, and the constant interruptions made her feel belittled. She just wanted someone to listen.How can we get an interrupter to mend their ways? “It depends on how much you like the person,” says Fox Weber. “It’s not always a bad trait: it can come from a kind of skittishness, a desire for the conversation not to go meandering off-piste. But it can create chaos, because the interrupter is imposing their will on what should be a collaborative dialogue, and breaking the flow.”Fox Weber says the interrupter is much easier to handle in a group setting. “That allows you to advocate for other people. If you see it happening, don’t leave it to the interrupted person to defend their space. If another person jumps in to Person A’s story and steers the chat in another direction, you can be the one who stops it. You might say: ‘Wait – she’s telling a story. Let her finish it.’ You can say it nicely.”What if it’s a one-on-one situation? “It’s harder, but you can still insist the other person step back, by saying: ‘Hey, I’m still telling my story.’ Then get back to what you were saying, even if you’ve lost the flow.”The care bearView image in fullscreen‘How are you? And I have I told you about my latest campaign against world poverty?’Photograph: Posed by models; Sanja Radin/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe care bear’s idea of small talk is to launch into a mini Ted Talk about how they are campaigning against AI datacentres, sewage pollution or world hunger. What they are definitely not here for is a bit of banter.“I’ve got a neighbour like this, and I’m not proud of it but I have been known to dive into the corner shop to avoid them if I see them coming,” says Lauren. “She will approach me with a tilt of the head, look deep into my eyes and ask: ‘Howareyou, really?’ If I don’t have anything deep and meaningful to share, which I never do, that will be her cue to start on one of her important causes – the state of social care in the borough, food banks, homeless people. This is going to make me sound like a bad person but … she issoboring. Not to mention hard to escap once she’s in full flow.”Boomerasking: the sneaky, insincere way egotistical people dominate conversationRead moreThis type is particularly maddening because they occupy the moral high ground. What’s the best way to deal with them? “Try saying, as genuinely and sincerely as possible, something like: ‘I can understand your concern about XYZ, and I, too, really hope there’s going to be some change or improvement,’” says Rozenthuler. “Then change the subject. It’s not about being brutal and brisk. It’s about being kind, acknowledging the person but then moving on. This type of person is often stuck in a groove and it’s going to take a lot more than you or I have capacity for to help them get out of it.” Actually, I think I may have a solution. Where did I leave that broomstick?Names and identifying details have been changedDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of pop | Kylie Minogue | The Guardian
description: Rejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: Rejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …
Content: La la land … Kylie MinoguePhotograph: Vincent Peters/Trunk ArchiveView image in fullscreenLa la land … Kylie MinoguePhotograph: Vincent Peters/Trunk ArchiveKylie Minogue‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of popRejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …Michael CraggSun 13 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAround the release of Pet Shop Boys’ 1988 album Introspective, Neil Tennant coined the term “imperial phase” to describe an era when he felt the duo “understood the essence of pop music and so we felt we could do what we liked”. For his less flowery partner in pop excellence, Chris Lowe, this was typically followed “by disappearing up your backside!”.In 2010, critic Tom Ewing fleshed out Tennant’s term byimposing three criteria: “command, permission, and self-definition”. Command related to an artist’s willingness and ability to push boundaries in a way that would reverberate through what followed. Permission, meanwhile, connected to the public and their goodwill towards an artist as they pushed things forward. Finally, self-definition, Ewing said, is the way the imperial phase defines the rest of the artist’s career. All future work will be compared with, or mentioned alongside, the output from the imperial phase.By the time Kylie’s album Fever dropped, everything in its subsequent era represented her very own imperial phase. Everything she did in 2001 and 2002 seemed to click perfectly: every video, every choice of single, the tour, the press attention, the fashion, the cohesiveness of the vision, the way she reshaped pop and nudged it forward. And it was all led by the hypnotic weightlessness of the downright oddCan’t Get You Out of My Head.The song was born one autumn weekend in 2000 in a garage studio in Surrey belonging to former Mud guitarist Rob Davis, who had been encouraged by manager and impresario Simon Fuller to write some songs with the excellent pop star turned songwriter Cathy Dennis.double quotation markI don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with itCathy DennisOn the Sunday, using Cubase on a Mac computer to create a drum loop before adding some guitar, the seed of Can’t Get You Out of My Head was planted. While Dennis came up with the title hook – the song, as she noted, doesn’t really conform to a typical verse-chorus structure, with each line almost acting as its own chorus melody – it was Davis who added the “‘la la la” section. The demo was finished in three hours, while Dennis’s vocals were laid down by 7pm that same day.The demo was played to Fuller down the phone. He later played it for S Club 7, but they passed on it. The song was also presented to Sophie Ellis-Bextor, but again it was deemed unsuitable. It was Fuller’s idea to send it to Kylie. “And I was thinking: ‘But this song isn’t what Kylie does,’” remembered Dennis. “Obviously, now, none of us knows what Kylie’s going to come out with next, because she can’t be compartmentalised.” Kylie, meanwhile, “knew a few bars in that this was for me”, she wrote in 2002. “By the end of the track I wanted to know how quickly I could get into the studio.”View image in fullscreenNavel academy … Kylie’s famous and influential dress in the Can’t Get You Out of My Head video.Photograph: Parlophone Records/Warner Music GroupAs promised, though much to Davis’s surprise given he’d convinced himself she wouldn’t turn up, Kylie arrived in Surrey to record Can’t Get You Out of My Head. In between some fancy salmon salad and other treats, the song was finished in a few hours. The mysterious pop alchemy of adding Kylie to a song took them all by surprise. “Even though Kylie wasn’t the first artist to be offered the song, I don’t believe it was meant to go to anyone other than Kylie,” said Dennis,“and I don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with it, with the video, looking super-hot!”Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just “good, for a pop song”, as joyless people were wont to say, keen to use the caveat in case their muso credentials be tarnished. As pop began to absorb the outre production styles of R&B experimentalists such as the Neptunes and Timbaland – Britney’s career-restructuring I’m a Slave 4 U, produced by the former, would arrive in the same month as Can’t Get You Out of My Head – audiences were becoming more attuned to pop that was looking to push the boundaries. This felt like dance-pop beamed in from the future, where the first time you hear it you’re like, “Huh?” then the second you’re like, “Wait!” and then the 35th time you start to worry you may never listen to anything else.Its title becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s sexy futurism would also dictate the visual feel of the era: sleek lines, icy-cool silhouettes and just a hint of something darker lurking underneath. For the album’s cover, shot by Vincent Peters, Kylie’s stylist and creative director William Baker was inspired by the French artist Jean-Paul Goude’sphotos of Grace Jones, which highlighted both her sexuality and her power. Baker also wanted Kylie to be attached to the tools of her trade, so on both the album cover and artwork for Can’t Get You Out of My Head, a microphone’s black power cord winds its way round Kylie’s body.Less overt than the buttock-hugging, Carry On vibes of Kylie’s previous album, Light Years, and its lead single, Spinning Around, the Fever look was leaning more into an artful sexiness. This was highlighted in Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s video, directed by Dawn Shadforth, in which the utopia promised by the millennium was laid out in front of us via forensically manicured cityscapes and futuristic fashion: we see her dance on what looks like a rooftop garden centre and in a clean white dome, and losing herself in a dress made of purple-silver Post-it notes.It also gave Kylie yet another iconic fashion moment, one that would be replicated at gigs and fancy-dress parties for decades to come, in the shape of the white hooded dress, split to the navel.While the dress grabbed the attention, it was the all-in-red dancers behind Kylie, sporting matching face-covering visors, who caused a problem for Top of the Pops producer Chris Cowey. As Can’t Get You Out of My Head started to dominate, the show’s lighting department began to complain that their red gels were going missing at the show’s on-set afterparty “because everyone was taking [them] and wrapping them around their heads and doing the dance”, Cowey says. “Just kind of drunkenly doing Kylie impersonations.”By the early 2000s, after Oasis v Blur, the UK had become mildly obsessed with chart battles, ideally those featuring attractive women. On 17 September 2001, the same day as Can’t Get You Out of My Head, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was set to release Not Such an Innocent Girl, the lead single from her self-titled debut solo album.Posh had already been beaten, the previous year, by actually-quite-posh Sophie Ellis-Bextor, whose Rob Davis-assisted Groovejet (If This Ain’t Love) had left Beckham’s banger Out of Your Mind at No 2. This time, Victoria roared on to the battlefield with a ropey single and mildly scathing bons mots for her Australian rival. “When I first heard [Can’t Get You Out of My Head], if I’m being totally honest, I didn’t like it,” Posh mused. “And I’m being completely honest.”For Posh, “an old-fashioned type songwriter”, Kylie’s single, while having “a very catchy melody”, didn’t resonate with her because she enjoys “a song that has a bit of emotion”. Posh was also retroactively blaming Kylie for criticisms of Out of Your Mind: “And I have to say that last year when I brought out a dance record, and I had effects on my voice, like she has on her voice, I am still getting a caning for it now.”In the end, on the UK chart of 23 September, Can’t Get You Out of My Head crashed in at No 1, shifting an eye-watering 306,000 copies, holding off emerging talent Bob the Builder’s cover of Mambo No 5 in the process. It would stay at No 1 in the UK for a month, a feat matched in Australia. Posh’s Not Such an Innocent Girl would have to make do with a No 6 entry in the UK and sales of 35,000. The clash was such a hot topic that the BBC ran anews storywith the headline: Kylie trounces Posh in chart battle. “Victoria is pleased to have a Top 10 hit,” a Posh spokeswoman was quoted as saying.double quotation markI think it came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriouslyLarry Flick, journalistThis particular pop star chart battle also served a specific escapist aim. Both singles were released shortly after 9/11, as the western world tried to recalibrate itself following a terrorist attack. The horrors seemed so overwhelming that any hint of normality was gripped tightly with both hands, and Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s futuristic escapism became a hypnotic balm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor some journalists, the mere existence of Kylie was proof that Osama bin Laden and the Taliban could never win the “war on terror”. “Two people dominated the cultural landscape of this country in the last quarter of the year: Osama bin Laden and Kylie Minogue,”wrote Julie Burchillin the Guardian as 2001 came to an end. “I really do believe that Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”Kylie was suddenly being held up as an emblem of western ideals – the literal face (and body) of the UK’s reaction to the global threat from a terrorist organisation. The Daily Mail printed a list of reasons to be cheerful, post-9/11, topped by Kylie. The picture they used alongside the piece was captioned “Fungirl Kylie, scourge of the Taliban”. Watching from the outside as this narrative unfolded, Kylie was “dumbfounded. I understand the way they’re seeing it as a positive thing, but no! Don’t write things like that!”Actual human Kylie, not the projected superhero being pushed to the frontlines, was being interviewed live on local radio when the attacks took place. One of the DJs asked her on air, “So how does it feel to be a pop star in this situation?” “A two-second silence on live radio seems for ever,” Kylie remembered in the Face magazine. “I said: ‘I can’t believe you just asked me that.’ I think they swiftly cut to a record.”View image in fullscreenKylie contagious … Minogue performs her Can’t Get You Out of My Head/Blue Monday mash-up at the 2002 Brit.Photograph: JMEnternational/GettyAmericans, at first, clung to a very different kind of superstar and song. Enrique Iglesias’s windswept ballad Hero, released on 3 September 2001, was one of the few songs played by New York City DJs after the attacks, but by the time Can’t Get You Out of My Head made its debut on the US charts in January 2002, a shift was happening. People needed something to dance to. “It was definitely at a time when people were gingerly going back [out],” remembers NYC music journalist Larry Flick. “I think [Can’t Get You Out of My Head] came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriously. There were a few things, in New York, that got us through 9/11: there was the return of Friends, the return of David Letterman, and the Kylie record.”double quotation markIan McKellen sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching herDavid Russell, Kylie fanFlick remembers the second time he heard it, in the Roxy, New York’s disco roller rink turned hip nightclub, which was famed as a venue that tested out new records. “I ran to the booth and I was like: ‘How about you playing Kylie?’ And the DJ goes: ‘Baby, this is the shit.’ He played it for about 20 minutes and the crowd lost their minds.”Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just a hit; it was a smash. It didn’t just peak in all the usual places Kylie tended to, but also in places such as Belgium and Romania and Switzerland and Hungary. In the US, it quickly started to climb not just the Dance Club charts, where Kylie had been a regular, but also the main Billboard Hot 100, a chart she hadn’t been in since 1988.“Can’t Get You Out of My Head was inescapable,” remembers US Kylie fan David Russell. “It started to get played on the radio, and then suddenly the video was on MTV. Kylie did Saturday Night Live with Ian McKellen hosting. I begged the publicist and she got me in. McKellen said: ‘You lucky, lucky people, it’s Kylie Minogue!’ He then sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching her.”Back in the UK, Kylie won twice at the 2002 Brit awards, scooping best international female and best international album for Fever. But it was her award-show performance that would gain instant notoriety, later becoming a mainstay of any homosexual’s post-night-out YouTube binge.Kylie’s 30 greatest singles – ranked!Read morePerforming aspecial mashupof Can’t Get You Out of My Head and New Order’s Blue Monday by then white-hot DJ and producer Erol Alkan, whose Trash club night was London’s hottest ticket, Kylie arrives on stage lying down on a giant CD – her name emblazoned on it in neon pink – seemingly holding on for dear life while wearing a Dolce & Gabbana minidress and knee-high silver boots. As the giant CD is ejected out of the player and lifts up so the crowd can see her for the first time, you’ll believe you can hear God. The performance was a perfect balancing act: audacious, spectacular, camp, sexy and silly in all the right ways.“I feel like I’m on a wave and I actually know how to stand on the board at this point,” Kylie said as Can’t Get You Out of My Head and her imperial era kicked in. “I don’t know where it’s taking me, but everything feels really good.”Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylieby Michael Craggis published on 24 September by Faber.Explore more on these topicsKylie MinoguePop and rockextractsShareReuse this content

title: Who better to defend Reform’s latest millions than Honest Bob Jenrick?  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The man who once helped Richard ‘Dirty’ Desmond save a load of tax was wheeled out to face Laura Kuenssberg
Author: John Crace
Headline: The man who once helped Richard ‘Dirty’ Desmond save a load of tax was wheeled out to face Laura Kuenssberg
Content: ‘Everything is totally above board,’ Jenrick told Kuenssberg. ‘In fact it is a huge vote of confidence in Reform.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Everything is totally above board,’ Jenrick told Kuenssberg. ‘In fact it is a huge vote of confidence in Reform.’Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/ReutersThe politics sketchReform UKWho better to defend Reform’s latest millions than Honest Bob Jenrick?John CraceThe man who once helped Richard ‘Dirty’ Desmond save a load of tax was wheeled out to face Laura KuenssbergSun 13 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareYou wait years for one party donation of £36m and thentwo come along at once. Reform can hardly believe its luck. All hail the crypto billionaires. Tacky pale turquoise suits all round. And Nigel Farage won’t have to worry about spending any of his own money – if you can call the £5m freebie his own money – on his security. Nor do those champagne and oyster lunches to discuss loose change donations of £500k from people living overseas pay for themselves. From now on Reform won’t need to bother getting out of bed for anything less than eight figures.Fair to say that if it had been Labour or the Tories trousering £72m from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo then Reform would be on full outrage rampage. How the political system was rigged against it and how the two main parties are hotwired cash machines. In bed with the super-rich. But since the money is heading towards its own bank account, everyone in the party is totally chilled. This is just the way life ought to be. Who wouldn’t want a country where two billionaires can attempt to buy the democratic process?So it was a joy to find that Reform had sent out Robert Jenrick to gloat about its unexpected cash windfall on the Laura Kuenssberg show. Who better to speak about the party’s incorruptibility than the man, who as a junior minister in the Tory government, unlawfully overruled the government’s own planning inspector and just happened to save the Tory donor cum pornographer, Richard “Dirty” Desmond, the best part of £45m in tax. And what did the Tories get in return? A gift of about £12k. You’d have hoped the lesson Honest Bob had learned from that was not to sell his soul – if he has one – so cheaply.“Everything was totally above board,” he insisted. Though forgive us all for asking the question. Reform is currently the subject of at least two – or is it three? it’s so easy to lose count – police investigations into alleged financial wrongdoing, and the party has acquired a reputation for being at the sleazier end of British politics. A place where Dicky Tice shuffles money from Posh George into and out of his accounts and Nige is so blase he can’t even be bothered to listen when two potential donors talk at length on how they are planning to break the law. Remarkable stuff. Nige can even not listen while maintaining a conversation.Laura did suggest that Reform mighthave to give some of the money backif the government were to retrospectively implement the findings of the Rycroft review into party funding. But Honest Bob wasn’t having any of it. There was no way he would be handing back a penny. Finders keepers. Possession nine-tenths of the law. You’d be amazed how Reform can make money disappear when it feels like it. Though, of course, everything would be done in a totally legitimate way.What we all had to understand was that this was a huge vote of confidence in Reform. Far from being an indication that the party’s funding had become exponentially more murky, this was proof that it was being totally transparent. Think of it this way. When he had been a Conservative MP, Honest Bob had been more than happy for his party to shower peerages on donors. Some only had to hand over less than £100k to end up in the Lords. But Delo and Harborne weren’t asking for anything like that. All they wanted was for the laws around crypto currencies to be relaxed a little. Where was the conflict of interest in that?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDonations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskierRead moreBen and Christopher were just regular guys who just happened to be billionaires. And yes, it was unfortunate that Ben had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation – somehow the fact he had been pardoned by Donald Trump made him sound doubly guilty – but this had just been an oversight. He was a very busy man and it had been the sort of mistake anyone could make.“They are both just patriots,” Honest Bob continued. So patriotic that Delo had spent much of the last few years based in Hong Kong while Harborne lived in Thailand. We should try to feel their pain. They were both just run-of-the-mill billionaires who happened to have been priced out of Mayfair. Rather than indulge in the politics of envy, we should applaud them for their philanthropy. Two guys just trying to make a difference. Making Britain better.Now and again, Honest Bob found himself getting a little confused. For example, when he came to think about it, Delo and Harborne giving £72m from their crypto empires was much the same as tens of thousands of ordinary workers donating to Labour through their union subscriptions. Because what Ben and Chris wanted most was for the income tax threshold to be raised to £15k. That £500 they would get back could make the difference between them remaining tax exiles and returning to this country.The money would be spent on the professionalisation of Reform. When all welfare payments – those that were left – would be paid in crypto. When Reform would rise above the ashes of sleaze. When all bus sites and billboards would be covered with adverts for Reform. When all TV stations promoted Reform without question. It wasn’t enough to have GB News doing that for nothing. There would be no rest until the BBC had also been captured. Make no mistake. This £72m was only the start.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchParty fundingnewsShareReuse this content

title: A joyful harvest: the young Welsh farmers growing food for Birmingham | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: A charity in Powys provides the land while growers do the hard work, producing bumper crops for city children
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: A charity in Powys provides the land while growers do the hard work, producing bumper crops for city children
Content: Tilly Gomersall harvesting dill on her farm in Powys.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTilly Gomersall harvesting dill on her farm in Powys.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianFood & drink industryA joyful harvest: the young Welsh farmers growing food for BirminghamA charity in Powys provides the land while growers do the hard work, producing bumper crops for city childrenJoanna Partridgein PowysSun 13 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKilos and kilos of courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes and salad leaves are ripe and ready for picking on a small Welsh farm in the rural county of Powys.The haul being harvested by Tilly Gomersall is not just impressive aftera difficult growing seasonhit by a record string of heatwaves and drought across all of Wales and most of England, but all the more remarkable given that 18 months ago the site was uncultivated pasture.“Until now, I’ve just been turning the earth with my own power,” Gomersall says. “We’ve got a two-wheel tractor, but you do have to heft that around with your body quite a lot and we’re cultivating from pasture, so it’s really hard work.”The site at Wern farm, near Newtown, is part of a scheme to encourage young growers to supply fresh produce to nearby towns and cities and boost domestic production in the face of increasingrisks to national food supplies.The 15-hectare (36-acre) site is divided into three plots, each with a holiday chalet where the growers live, as well as shared facilities including a barn and diesel generator, to cover any power not provided by the farm’s solar panels.Gomersall’s farm,Cân y Pridd(Welsh for Song of the Soil), totals 4.9 hectares but she is now only growing on half a hectare, including in polytunnels, where she says she is “producing very big volumes for the scale”.View image in fullscreenDuncan Fisher, of Our Food Trust, which works to increase levels of homegrown produce.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianShe and her two neighbours are already providing fresh fruit and vegetables for the local community, through a veg box subscription service and at markets. In late July, they also started supplying fresh produce toBirminghamcity council, where it is distributed to holiday clubs, giving disadvantaged children a taste of homegrown veg for perhaps the first time.The Wern farm project was launched by Our Food Trust, a charity which is working to increase levels of homegrown produce and aims to tackle Britain’sfood insecurity.The UK depends on imports for about 40% of its food and has one of thelowest food self-sufficiencyratios among large western European countries,leaving it exposed to supply shocksprompted by the climate crisis, or other risks including geopolitical tensions and cyber-attacks.Just 0.2% of land inWalesis used for horticulture, according to the charity, giving huge scope for expansion. “We have to produce a lot more food for the regional and local market and for our cities,” says Duncan Fisher, joint chief executive at the charity.One way to do this is to remove barriers for young people who want to get into growing, Fisher says, but who often find themselves priced out of renting or buying land and a suitable home. “There are lots of well-trained and skilful growers who can’t find land to grow food on,” he says. “The price of land here is set by the market, by people who are not going to farm it.”The charity has given Gomersall the chance to turn a dream into reality and start a farm just 10 miles from where she grew up, while her neighbour, Lydia Dibben, says she was “quite blown away by the opportunity”.View image in fullscreenLydia Dibben and Charlie James on their plot in Powys, which they have namedTir a nNant(Land and Stream).Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian“It was amazing to be offered seven acres, which is a big amount for small-scale vegetable production, with a house with affordable rent and shared infrastructure,” says Dibben, 28. She and her partner Charlie James have named their plotTir aNant(Land and Stream).OurFoodworked with the landowner, Powys county council, on the project, securing a 95-year lease for the plot and changes to the county’s planning guidance for rural enterprise dwellings, to enable growers to have a home on the land they work.The council leader, Jake Berriman, says “there was a perception that planning was a barrier and we wanted to remove that barrier”. He says local worries about extreme weather had also encouraged the authority to get involved. “We are starting to see genuine concern,” he says. “We have gone from flood to drought to fire.”The charity also negotiated the contract for the farmers to supply Birmingham, which has two aims: to give the growers a guaranteed buyer for some produce as they find their feet, while ensuring nutritious and sustainably produced fruit and vegetables reach deprived areas.The farmers have 35 customers for their veg box subscription service, along with selling to a local wholesaler and at regional markets. While they stress the importance of growing for their community, they do not believe that doing so would currently sustain their businesses.View image in fullscreenJake Berriman, leader of Powys county council.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The Guardian“Because of the cost of living crisis, there’s a limited amount of people who can afford to buy the veg we produce, and we are growing a hell of lot more than we can sell locally,” says Dibben, adding it was “really amazing being able to sell a hundred kilos of courgettes a week” to Birmingham.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGomersall reels off a list of the produce the farmers have supplied to the city in the course of a few short weeks, including a “couple of bathtubs” of salad leaves, 28kg of spring onions and 18kg of French beans.The gently rolling hills above Wern farm feel a world away from the urban sprawl of Britain’s second-largest city, although it is just 70 miles away on the other side of the Shropshire hills.The UK, and its largest cities in particular, have become toodependent on international supply chainsand imported food sold by large retailers, according to food experts such as Tim Lang, a professor emeritus of food policy at City St George’s, University of London.This challenge is recognised by Birmingham council and its food system team, led by Sarah Newton.“Birmingham is an urban area surrounded by urban areas,” she says. “If you’re going to feed 1.2 million people, supply chains are the absolute crux of the matter, and we need to strengthen them.”Produce grown at Wern farm is sent to the city’s holiday activities and food programme, part of a national scheme for children from low-income families. About 1,000 children who attended these summer holiday clubs received boxes filled with vegetables from Powys, which they could eat fresh or cook as part of activities.Newton adds: “You’ve got children who have not had exposure to different vegetables. There are huge barriers to trying new foods if you’ve never had the opportunity to be exposed to it, it takes 10 to 15 tastes to develop the liking for food.”View image in fullscreenLydia Dibben at work on her farm in Powys, which she runs with her partner, Charlie James.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianThe Powys scheme is deliberately small-scale, she says, with one van of produce travelling from Wales to Birmingham each week. The goal is to prove that a direct relationship between food growers and a city of diners can work.“It’s connecting the entire supply chain on a small scale, looking at all the barriers and the facilitators on the way,” says Newton. “If we had a coordinated, national approach that we should be eating target foods, you could line up supply and demand nationally and then you’d get a meaningful shift in economies of scale.”This kind of national approach to overhauling food systems is already under way in other countries: the French government introduced itsprojetsalimentairesterritoriaux(territorial food projects) in 2014, which work to connect local production with public health priorities.Back at Wern farm, the growers are planning how to expand their cultivated area as they further develop the site.Gomersall says: “What’s so joyful about the Birmingham project is … we really enjoy harvesting knowing that kids are going to be eating it and enjoying the flavours of real food.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryFarmingWalesFruitVegetablesFoodClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Plan your parking, don’t rush at night and never panic – 15 expert tips to become a better driver  | Life and style | The Guardian
description: No matter how long you’ve had your licence, there’s always scope to improve your skills behind the wheel. Driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motorist
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: No matter how long you’ve had your licence, there’s always scope to improve your skills behind the wheel. Driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motorist
Content: Composite: Guardian design; Catherine Falls Commercial;Noel Hendrickson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design; Catherine Falls Commercial;Noel Hendrickson/Getty ImagesThe expertsLife and stylePlan your parking, don’t rush at night and never panic – 15 expert tips to become a better driverNo matter how long you’ve had your licence, there’s always scope to improve your skills behind the wheel. Driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motoristSarah PhillipsSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether you have just passed your test or been behind the wheel for decades, driving skills can always be sharpened up. From dealing with road rage to traffic jams, tight parking spaces to hire cars, driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motorist in the most challenging scenarios.If you are running lateGyokhan Zlatev, of theDerin Driving School, says there is one major problem that many drivers are guilty of: “They are always in a rush. They refuse to leave home two minutes earlier to go somewhere in time.” This can make you more likely to drive in a risky way, he says.But leaving more time is easier said than done given the world we live in, says Kev Field, ofConfident Driversin Leighton Buzzard. “We want to be there before we’ve actually got there,” says Field, “and people are in our way, or we’re running late for work.” Field says he spends a lot of time helping learner drivers to overcome this mentality. He asks them to imagine they’re in the office: “Would you run and risk running into your boss?” It’s best to walk, and drive, calmly.If you are delayedField says that most people crave predictability, which causes stress when there are changes to our route, such as road closures, roadworks or bad traffic. The key to being a good driver, he says, is being able to react and adapt our driving when faced with such challenges.View image in fullscreenDon’t get too close to the driver in front if you’re stuck in traffic.Photograph: Steve Atkins Photography/AlamyIf you are running late and stuck in bad traffic, use hands-free to call and let someone know you are stuck to alleviate the worry of being late, says Field. Ensure you are familiar with the rules around hands-free usage, he continues, asprosecution is still possible if it distracts from driving– if in doubt and if possible, pull over to call. Don’t be tempted to text someone when in a queue, as this is against the law in the UK.“In traffic, a lot of experienced drivers get really close,” saysVenus Ubah, a driving instructor in Manchester. “You are supposed to give a safe amount of space for the driver in front – a car’s length away.” Other reckless driving that she regularly spots includes drivers running red lights or not signalling to change lanes.If you are the victim of road rageView image in fullscreen‘People’s behaviour changes when they get into a metal box …’Photograph: ozgurcankaya/Getty ImagesAs hard as it is, do not engage, says Zlatev. When someone becomes aggressive, “don’t look at them, don’t make eye contact, or try to prove a point. Just let them go, and create distance – it is much safer for you.” We all make mistakes, says Zlatev, “even Formula One drivers”.“People’s behaviour changes when they get into a metal box and they feel they have the right to wave their hands, shout, and act in a manner that is aggressive or bullying,” says Field. To counter this, stay calm. “Then think about what options you have. If the driver can overtake you, give them some space.”Never feel you have to break the speed limit because the driver behind you is in a hurry and tailgating, says Field. “Most people have probably heard of the two-second rule – leave a two-second gap to the car in front of you. If the car behind you is really close, leave a three- or four-second gap, just because we don’t want to go into the back of someone else.”If you are anxious about driving“Know that you are in control of your car,” says Field, “and don’t let other people control what you do. Don’t feel that you have to keep up with others who are more experienced.”“When I first started driving, I used to panic a lot – like if I stalled before moving off and I got beeped or sworn at,” says Ubah. How can others cope with this? “Don’t look at them, because that can start to bring up an emotional reaction. Look ahead and take your time.”If you are driving abroadView image in fullscreenBefore you travel, do some research on the road rules abroad.Photograph: Matthew Richardson/Alamy“Don’t assume everywhere is like the UK,” says Ubah. “I do some research while in the holiday booking process. I look up the road rules, the side they drive on, speed limits, what the signs look like.”It is essential to check for any differences in countries you are new to driving in. “In America, if you’re turning right at a set of traffic lights, you can [usually] turn on a red light,” as long as it is clear, says Field – although this has been banned in some places.Zlatev recently drove from the UK to Turkey and back, which he says he found fine, except for the fact that “satnav doesn’t work well in some countries, Belgium, for example”. He says that in Germany some junctions are tough, and he saw a lot of British people clinging to the slow lane on speed-limitless autobahns.If you hire a carMake sure you know how everything works before you set off, says Field. “It’s a bit like when you get a new car: you wouldn’t just jump in it and drive out of the showroom.”“Adjust your seat and mirrors,” says Zlatev. Check that the lights and wipers are working: “If there’s any noise on the brakes, tell them immediately.”“When I hire a car,” says Ubah, “I’ll take a video from the office to the car, so they know it’s the first time I’ve come across it. Then I’ll do a 360 around the car, checking all the doors, tyres, windows, the boot – videoing everything.” Always make sure you are fully insured, in case of any prangs.With hire cars, you don’t actually have to buy insurance through the rental company, points out Denise Rawson, an instructor from Bury in Greater Manchester. “You can goindependently online. Or if you just want everything in one place and you feel safer with that, that’s absolutely fine. Just make sure [the car] is covered for everything.”If you are lostIf you take a wrong turn, “don’t panic, just carry on; don’t do a sudden brake”, advises Zlatev. “Just take the next junction.” That’s the safest opportunity to correct your route, he says.“It is much safer to carry on on the wrong road than to drive dangerously to the right one,” says Ubah. Getting lost “is a distraction, isn’t it?” says Field. “And the distraction is we’re going to look at the satnav rather than actually look outside.”Pull over to re-route, he says; don’t be tempted to try this while you are driving. “Satnav is designed to help you,” says Field. “Sometimes we just need to allow the technology a little bit of time as well, and it will re-route us and get us back on track to where we need to go.”Be prepared for some good old-fashioned sign or map reading if your satnav loses signal or runs out of battery, he says. It can’t always be relied on.If you are driving in a city you don’t knowView image in fullscreenTurn on the audio on satnav when driving in an unfamiliar city.Photograph: Colin Underhill/AlamyField used to be a lorry driver and had to travel through central London, which he describes as “an interesting one”. What tips does he have on city centre driving?“There’s probably going to be more traffic. People tend to drive quicker, especially if they know the area, even though the speed limit is lower. So be aware of how other people might drive differently to what we’re used to.” Also look out for pedestrians, cyclists, scooters and motorbikes, he says.Zlatev recommends turning the audio on satnav, so you can listen to instructions rather than look at them, and fully focus on what is going on around you.If you are parking under pressureIn a city you don’t know, it is best to leave your car in a car park, says Zlatev: “Pay for it, and make your life easier.”Rawson advises planning several parking options before you set off and even checking what spaces look like on Google Images.Take your time when getting into a tight space and try not to feel self-conscious, says Zlatev. Other drivers “can watch and learn something from you. You don’t need to stress.”“Make sure the space is actually big enough for your car,” says Field. And don’t forget to keep watching out for changes in what is going on around you, be it cars or pedestrians.There is no shame in driving off if you can’t get into a space. “I’m a driving instructor and I’ve done it,” says Ubah. “There is no prize for getting into the teeniest, tiniest parking space.”If you struggle to parallel parkView image in fullscreenPractise parallel parking.Photograph: Colin Underhill/Alamy“If you’re going to parallel park, make sure you’ve practised before you actually go and do it in a busy place,” says Field. “Don’t overcomplicate it. Make sure that you know where the kerb is, and you are far enough back so that when you start to turn, you don’t hit the car that you’re trying to parallel park behind. It is as simple as that.”Rawson has a different approach: “We get lined up with the car and then we do a full lock of the steering wheel to the left. Let the car roll out so we’re facing a 2 o’clock angle if we started at 12. And then we reverse in a straight line, so we straighten the wheel back towards the kerb, and as the kerb lines up with your back door handle, we’ll do a full lock to the right, and then it’ll tuck in nicely.”In all Zlatev’s vehicles, he uses blind spot mirrors, which can be handy when reverse parking. These are small circle mirrors that you put on the wing mirrors to improve visibility of what is alongside the vehicle. “When all my clients pass their test, I give them the gift of a pair of blind spot mirrors,” says Zlatev.If you are driving a manual for the first time in a whileIn the UK, you have to pass in a manual to have a full licence, explains Ubah, and this can impact on your insurance and jobs you can apply for. Many of us learned in a manual but have moved over to automatic. How can you revert if needed?“Before you start to move,” says Field, familiarise yourself with the clutch pedal, because the brake pedal tends to be bigger in an automatic. Practise changing gears and going into reverse, so you know where they are before you move. “There’s different ways of changing gears,” says Field. “Some people do it by speed. Some listen [to the engine]. Some do it by the rev counter.”If you stall, “first of all breathe”, says Ubah. “Give yourself some time. Put the clutch back down, and find that biting point again.”If you are driving at nightView image in fullscreenMake sure you use your lights properly at night.Photograph: Tim Graham/Alamy“Don’t let the road being quiet make you think that you can drive faster,” says Ubah. “I see that a lot when I do my evening lessons.”“You need to make sure that you’re fit to drive,” says Zlatev; tiredness is amajor cause of accidents. “Use your lights properly, and avoid looking directly into the headlights of oncoming vehicles, because you can be dazzled easily.” Be more generous with the gap you leave between vehicles ahead. “Take your time: no rush, no risk.”If you encounter bad weatherView image in fullscreenGo through large puddles very slowly.Photograph: LeManna/Getty Images/iStockphotoIf you are already driving and it starts pouring, “slow down, increase the distance between you and the vehicle in front, and avoid sudden braking”, says Zlatev. “If you see a big puddle in front of you and you don’t know the area, try to avoid that puddle or go through it very slowly, because you don’t know how deep it is and you can damage your car.”Make sure you keep your windscreen clear, says Ubah: “We need to be able to see our next five seconds – minimum. In the rain, if it is a road that is 60mph, it doesn’t mean you have to drive at60mph – the speed limit is a limit, not a target. If you can’t see properly, reduce your speed.”In ice, “just remember that you’re going to need to be delicate with everything”, says Rawson. “Even steering is a slight turn – and do everything a lot slower.”If you are worried about running out of chargeor fuel“I haven’t got an electric car,” says Field, “so I don’t have that fear of the charge running out. But it is exactly the same with fuel – it’s just that there are more fuelling places than charging ones. But it’s getting better. So it is just about thinking before you set off: ‘How much fuel have I got?’ or, ‘How much charge have I got?’ And then being aware that you can find out where your nearest points are using the satnav. But also, the night before, just make sure that you’ve got enough to get to where you’re going.”If you have an accidentView image in fullscreenTake a photo of any damage.Photograph: Daisy-Daisy/Alamy“Exchange details, and take a photo,” says Zlatev. “If you have any dashcam record, keep it safe. If you’re able to drive the car safely, you can. But if not, call the breakdown cover.”Afterwards, “remind yourself that having an accident doesn’t make you a bad driver”, says Ubah. “You’ve got to have empathy for yourself. If you need to take a break from the road for a bit, that’s completely fine. Don’t judge yourself for it, and just know that the road is there whenever you want to drive again.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe expertsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve lost everything – my child, my house, my money’: how Israel’s war on Gaza has changed men | Mental health | The Guardian
description: The impact of the conflict on Palestinian men is a largely undiscussed topic. Four civilians talk about their lives and relationships
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The impact of the conflict on Palestinian men is a largely undiscussed topic. Four civilians talk about their lives and relationships
Content: Ahmed says there is a ‘strange intimacy’ as his family spends so much time together.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAhmed says there is a ‘strange intimacy’ as his family spends so much time together.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianMen and warMental health‘I’ve lost everything – my child, my house, my money’: how Israel’s war on Gaza has changed menThe impact of the conflict on Palestinian men is a largely undiscussed topic. Four civilians talk about their lives and relationshipsSupported byAbout this contentSun 13 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAhmed: ‘The lack of privacy has created an emotional silence’Before the war, Ahmed, 39, had a busy life. He was pursuing a PhD in factchecking and had three jobs: as a radio presenter, editor of a local factchecking website and researcher at an academic centre. He says he felt “happy” to be able to provide for his family while being intellectually stimulated.But the war “blew our lives apart completely”, Ahmed says. Where previously he would spend hours lost in research, now he spends hours standing in line to fill water jugs or use the bathroom.He says war changed his sense of self and that he no longer “feels the pillar of his family”, adding: “As a man, I derived my appreciation for myself from my accomplishments in my work and my studies.”View image in fullscreenAhmed says he tries to reassure his children but wonders what new hardships the war will bring.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianAhmed had been living alongside his parents and siblings in the same building, each of his siblings with their family in a separate flat. In May 2024, they were all forced to evacuate their homes and have lived in tents ever since. He has found the lack of privacy in his new life hard and says it has created “emotional silence” between couples.“Before, the home was a private kingdom, a place to decompress at the end of the day, to speak freely. Now life is communal and there’s no privacy. A man can’t express his emotions to his wife as he used to. Everyone can hear; they can’t discuss and work through issues as they used to.”As a husband and father, he says he feels a responsibility to be a source of reassurance for his family. “I have children who don’t know what walls are, what a bed is, what stairs are.” He says he tries to make them feel that “everything will be OK”, but privately wonders what new hardships the war will bring and often lapses into silence. “That is the price of manhood in the catastrophe of this war.”Nidal: ‘I can’t stand anyone, even myself’Back in 2023, Nidal, 40, says he ran a small business out of a storage room in his block of flats inGazaCity, selling mobile phones and home appliances on credit. He used to spend his days going from door to door collecting payments. “It wasn’t just work. I got to know people and had lots of friends and acquaintances. My life was good. We had everything we needed,” he says.View image in fullscreenNidal says he feels less calm and more angry now. He spends most of his time by his tent, not speaking to anyone.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianBoth Nidal and his extended family, who lived in the same block, were soon displaced after an Israeli missile strike that killed his sister-in-law. In a further tragedy, his daughter Malek was killed after a second airstrike on a school where they were staying.Nidal and the remaining members of his family eventually returned to the rubble of their home and erected a tent. The collapsed roof of the block of flats offers them some shade and shelter from the rain. But Nidal says he feels no hope of rebuilding his life properly again and spends most of his days by the tent, rarely speaking to anyone. “The war took away everything – my child, my house, my money.”He says he feels a different person now, less calm and more angry. He feels embarrassed to ask his clients for money they owe him, given the loss everyone has suffered, and is sad most of the time.View image in fullscreenNidal says he has been rendered helpless in his ability to provide for his family.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The Guardian“I can’t stand anyone and can’t even stand myself. I don’t even want to call myself an unemployed man – I am a man rendered helpless. Not helpless physically, but helpless in my ability to provide for my family. I secure for them the bare minimum that keeps them alive.“May God spare every man from this: the breaking of a father before the eyes of his children.”Hussein: ‘I was very, very, very ashamed at first’Before the war, Hussein, 24, had his own flat, was a technology student at university and ran workshops on AI. His life had a daily routine to it and he was thinking about finding a partner and getting married. Early on in the conflict, however, his home was bombed, injuring his father and leaving his sister-in-law in hospital for six months.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHussein wanted to work in digital forensics and cybersecurity, but the war has changed everything for him.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianHussein says he “started from zero … there was no food, no work, nothing”. To survive, he turned to whatever work he could find, beginning by charging and repairing phones before moving on to buying and selling them and providing technical support. He is proud that he managed to adapt and make money so soon after losing his family’s home, he says.“I was very, very, very ashamed of myself at first. The war changed everything, even my future.”View image in fullscreenHussein has had to start again from nothing after his home was bombed.Photograph: Abd Abo Riash/The GuardianHe cannot imagine bringing a future wife into the tent where he now lives, “it’s not logical”, and says he must at least provide a home with privacy and running water. But he still hopes to marry and have children. “It [the war] has affected me and all young people. We have to repopulate this land and rebuild it. It’s us, the young people, who will fix it, restore it, make it even more beautiful than it was before.”Hamza: ‘When a person feels extinction, they are drawn to reproduce’Hamza, 22, was a second-year medical student when the war began, spending most of his time at his desk at home in Jabaliya in the north of Gaza. But he soon found himself volunteering as an emergency frontline doctor after refusing to follow Israeli evacuation orders to move south.View image in fullscreenHamza, pictured in the cloister of Milan University, says the war helped him realise the importance of family and friends.Photograph: Marta Clinco/The GuardianThere were countless patients with head injuries and only three neurosurgeons in the north. Working gave him purpose, he says. “It was an impossible mission for a student like me to work at the hospital and do the work I did. I consider myself a hero, to be honest.”Hamza says war has changed his perspective on family and friends. He does not let his studying isolate him any more. “You always have to sacrifice something for something. The war changed all of that … and that is something I am grateful for.”He says he has been drawn closer to his family. “We love each other more, respect each other more. We slept on the same mattress, sometimes in a space of two square metres. We were hungry together, we almost died together. We weren’t like this before the war. We became very tight-knit.”View image in fullscreenHamza’s parents remain in Gaza.Photograph: Marta Clinco/The GuardianBefore the war, Hamza says he had put off thinking about marriage to focus on a plan to study neurosurgery overseas and be able to provide his future wife with a good life, a nice home and a car. But war and the death of family members has changed that, he says, and he now plans to start a family sooner.“In war, when a person feels extinction, they are drawn to reproduce. God has made us this way. We have lost so much; there’s a feeling that we want to compensate.”Explore more on these topicsMental healthMen and warGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineFamilyPost-traumatic stress disorderHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rules | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: PM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UK
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: PM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UK
Content: Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenChristopher Harborne, Nigel Farage and Ben Delo.Photograph: LPN/Getty Images/The Ben Delo FoundationReform UKTrade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rulesPM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UKJessica ElgotDeputy political editorSun 13 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law.Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors.Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors –Christopher Harborneand Ben Delo –gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue.The communities secretary,Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK.How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?Read moreThe two donors who gave Reform £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand. Reform said both donations were within the rules.Senior government sources indicated the government was prepared to look again at the issue of domestic donations once it receives advice from a newly commissioned taskforce and from the Electoral Commission.One No 10 source said they did not want to delay the elections bill – which gives votes to 16-year-olds and puts new curbs on foreign donors – but said the bill was “not the right vehicle but this is not the end of the story”.SeveralLabourMPs said they had been assured by ministers that further legislation could still come before the general election. Trade unions are also understood to be wavering on the issue and a possible donations cap is expected to be part of discussions at the TUC congress next week, where Rayner and Burnham will speak.Unions have been central to the decision not to impose a domestic donations cap after several, especially GMB, argued it would be a slippery slope towards future rightwing governments curbing union donations.On Sunday the Unite trade union said it was in favour of a cap – and the largest trade union, Unison, said it would fight attempts by billionaires to influence politics.“For individual donors there must be a cap,” said Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary. “I think at some point it gets beyond what people think as normal.”Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary, said: “As his support dwindles in this country, Farage is turning to crypto billionaires in an attempt to undermine our democracy. The trade union movement will oppose him every step of the way.”Stella Creasy, the Labour MP whose amendment on donations caps attracted support in the Commons, is liaising with peers about how they can raise the issue when the bill returns to the House of Lords this week.The Labour peer Michael Wills said: “The government has already committed to urgently reviewing the questions of caps on donations. Now the bill is in the Lords, it offers an unmissable opportunity to say when that review will complete its work, and what its remit will be.”View image in fullscreenStella Creasy’s amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations.Photograph: Milo Chandler/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Creasy said the Reform donations had “concentrated people’s minds about what is now happening in our politics and what it will do to the voices of working people if it’s not stopped – we have the chance with the Lords to amend this bill with a cap”.Her amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. It was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe former shadow chancellor John McDonnell said it was time for the government to move faster and for unions to get onboard. “It’s clear now to the trade unions meeting in congress this week that action is needed to protect our democracy and there’s a growing expectation the government will respond with urgency,” he said.Two influential big party donors also called for a cap on Sunday. The billionaire businessman and Phones 4U founder, John Caudwell, who previously donated to the Conservative party in 2019, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House: “There should be a definite change in law. We should not have very wealthy people making undue influence.”Dale Vince, the Ecotricity founder who has given donations to the Labour party, said it was “urgent” the government dealt with donations rules. “Ridiculous sums of money don’t level the playing field – they distort it.“Our current system of funding is anti-democratic – those with big money have more say than the simple vote we all have. A cap on donations would be a step in the right direction – the end game should be publicly funded politics.”View image in fullscreenThe TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak: ‘We are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics.’Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAThe TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, suggested he was sympathetic to further action. Speaking before the opening of the TUC congress, he said: “No one wants the UK to become a country for hire in the way Reform is clearly a party for hire. Without a doubt, we are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics. But we’ll have to do that in a way that doesn’t cut across workers having their voice heard politically.”Donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskierRead moreReform has said it is confident that its two donors will not be caught in a retrospective cap on donations from Britons living abroad. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill.As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingLabourChristopher HarborneAndy BurnhamTrade unionsAngela RaynernewsShareReuse this content

title: Train carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near border
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Ukrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near border
Content: Firefighters spray water at a burning train carriage hit by a drone strike in Ukraine near the border with Poland.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters spray water at a burning train carriage hit by a drone strike in Ukraine near the border with Poland.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersUkraineTrain carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials sayUkrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near borderAmy HawkinsandCharlotte Higginsin KyivSun 13 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways.Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described the attack as “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”.Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.The strikes prompted air-raid warnings inPoland, which shares a border with western Ukraine.Ukrainian and Polish authorities said a lorry less than 1km from the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between the two countries was also hit.Katerina Sergatskova, the director of Daily Humanity, an organisation that provides training to people working in high-risk environments, was travelling on aWarsaw-bound train and witnessed the attack.She said passengers were told to evacuate at about 9am as the train approached the Polish border having already been told to disembark for two hours in the middle of the night. “At this point, the mood was different, we were asked to move very fast,” she said. “Then I heard the first drone.“Seeing and hearing Shahed [drones] just a few hundred metres from the border is a very unpleasant experience.”No casualties were reported on the train.View image in fullscreenThe wrecked passenger train hit by a Russian strike.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersA British economist who preferred not to be named, travelling on a night train from Kyiv towards Chelm in Poland, also witnessed the attack. “We spent 10 hours at the border and were evacuated three times. On the third evacuation a missile came over and totalled a locomotive in front of our train.”Railway officials instructed the “grimly focused” passengers to hide in bushes by a lake, said the economist, calling the Ukrainian response “timely and disciplined”.
