They “gave us good warning of the evacuation and had a plan, which everyone followed”.Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon TisdallRead more“The conductor said when we boarded that there was a high risk that we would be evacuated during the journey. The lady and her eight-year-old son who were in my compartment said they had been travelling back and forth every month to Kyiv from Warsaw since 2022 and they had never been evacuated, or the train attacked, while travelling the route. This is clearly an escalation by Putin and the Russians.”Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries, as well as Johnson, the former British prime minister, and the former CIA chief Petraeus, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” the rail company said.Johnson wrote on X: “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways.”Three people were killed in the eastern Donetsk region, and a 71-year-old woman was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region.Sybiha said the Russian strikes were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders”.“This is Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he wrote on X.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.View image in fullscreenDonald Tusk chairs a special meeting in Warsaw on Sunday after the drone strikes near the border with Ukraine.Photograph: Piotr Nowak/EPAPoland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who visited Kyiv this week, said on X after Sunday morning’s attack: “Putin is escalating.”The Polish interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said: “We treat these events with the utmost seriousness. The situation is being monitored continuously. Russia is the enemy of the free world.”Russia claimed it struck “railway infrastructure” in western Ukraine used to “transport military cargo” from Europe.“Strikes have continued on railway infrastructure in the western regions of Ukraine, which are used to transport military cargo from European countries,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement.Ukraine and Russia have increased attacks oncritical infrastructurein each other’s countries as long-range drones and missiles take the war away from the frontlines.The US president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday that Zelenskyy should “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing shortages.“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said, adding that shortages were caused by the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the US war in the Middle East.In Lithuania, authorities briefly closed the airport in Vilnius, the capital, after a perceived drone sighting. Nato scrambled at least one fighter jet in response to the alert, which turned out to be a flock of birds. The airport reopened within 40 minutes, according to Lithuanian authorities.Explore more on these topicsUkrainePolandRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hospitality industry urges Andy Burnham to lay out VAT cut plans | Hospitality industry | The Guardian
description: More than 800 businesses ask PM to make good on pledge, or risk more closures and job losses
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: More than 800 businesses ask PM to make good on pledge, or risk more closures and job losses
Content: Soon after taking office, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PAView image in fullscreenSoon after taking office, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues.Photograph: Richard Pohle/The Times/PAHospitality industryHospitality industry urges Andy Burnham to lay out VAT cut plansMore than 800 businesses ask PM to make good on pledge, or risk more closures and job lossesJulia KolleweSun 13 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of UK hospitality businesses, backed by celebrity chefs including Angela Hartnett and Heston Blumenthal, have askedAndy Burnhamto lay out plans to lower VAT for the sector, urging him to make good on his previous pledge.More than 800 businesses have written an open letter to the prime minister as part of the #VATsTheProblem campaign, to warn that without a “fairer tax burden for hospitality”, there will be more closures and job losses, and fewer opportunities for young people.The signatories include pubs, bars and brewers such as Fuller’s, Greene King, Mitchell’s & Butlers and Wetherspoons, along with restaurant groups including Franco Manca, Pizza Express and Wagamama, hotel chains such as Best Western Hotels and Marriott international, along with the leisure groups Center Parcs and Parkdean Resorts. However, most of the signatories are small and medium-sized businesses, including independent, single-site pubs and hotels.Among the celebrity chefs who signed the letter are Andi Oliver, Clare Smyth, Jason Atherton, Nathan Outlaw, Paul Ainsworth and Tom Kerridge.In February, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, publicly said he would argue fora hospitality VAT rate in line with Europebecause of the social value businesses bring to towns. More than 370,000 people have signed the#VATsTheProblempetition calling for a 10% rate of VAT for hospitality, bringing the UK in line with the European average.The campaign comes after the prime minister’s announcement tocut business rates by 20% for pubs, clubs and live music venuesin his first week in office as part of a £100m aid package – but Burnham immediately faced calls to go further.The letter said: “It’s time for a fairer tax burden for hospitality. Without action, closures will only continue to accelerate, jobs will continue to be lost and opportunities for young people reduced.“A lower rate of VAT for hospitality can turn closures into openings, lost jobs into new jobs, and boarded up high streets into thriving centres of community.”Kerridge added:“The reality is that 20% VAT is holding hospitality back. Hospitality is different from many other businesses because so much of what we spend our money on is our teams. You can reclaim VAT on a product, but you can’t reclaim VAT on a person. That makes a 20% rate particularly tough for a sector where labour is one of our biggest costs.“And this is all happening at a time when businesses are already dealing with rising wages, energy bills, food costs and business rates. We’re seeing the consequences, with businesses closing their doors every single week.”The letter came as the government said it would work closely with publicans to give more options for pub tenants who want greater freedom in running their pubs, so they get fairer lease agreements and a better price on beer, following a review into the 2016 pubs code. Other changes are being considered, including to allow pub companies and tenants to agree to a longer-term relationship.There is an option for tenants to go “free of tie” from their pub company and instead pay market rent and buy products freely from other companies. The review found that between April 2022 and March 2025, fewer than 400 tenants applied for a free of tie agreement, saying they felt deterred by the cost and complexity.Explore more on these topicsHospitality industryAndy BurnhamFood & drink industryPubsTax and spendingRestaurantsTravel & leisurenewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Rare show of unity from rival developers after safety warnings from Anthropic boss and AI researchers
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Rare show of unity from rival developers after safety warnings from Anthropic boss and AI researchers
Content: Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules after cases of AI agents going rogue and researchers quitting over safety concerns.Photograph: Dragon Claws/AlamyView image in fullscreenGrowing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules after cases of AI agents going rogue and researchers quitting over safety concerns.Photograph: Dragon Claws/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI developmentRare show of unity from rival developers after safety warnings from Anthropic boss and AI researchersAnalysis: critics perplexed and suspicious of call for a slowdownThe Guardian view: humanity cannot outsource its survivalRobert BoothandJulia KolleweSun 13 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Altman and Elon Musk have backed acall from the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei,to “slow the pace” of AI development after he warned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.In a rare show of unity, the rival technology leaders threw their weight behind the appeal from the founder and chief executive of the artificial intelligence companyAnthropic, which came after a series of warnings from AI researchers last week. Amodei also called for safety coordination with China.But the US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”.“We’re leading China in AI,” he said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.Amodei laid out his thoughts on “why the AI industry should slow down”,in an essaywith a three-part plan for doing so, starting with giving independent monitors constant access to developers’ research processes. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless” and he feared that after hundreds of OpenAI agents hacked into the Hugging Face website this summer, a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet”. This wasdisputed by some AI expertsas not particularly plausible and to be treated with scepticism.Musk, the founder of Tesla and SpaceX, responded to Amodei’s slowdown plan with a series of posts on X: “Dario is right.”He said: “I’ve been sounding the alarm on AI for a long time,” and referred to a 2014 post where he said: “We need to be super careful with AI. Potentially more dangerous than nukes.”Amodei’s call comes as Anthropic prepares to float on the US stock market, in what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time. It is expected to start marketing its planned $2tn-plus (£1.5tn) IPO soon.View image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Elon Musk, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini,julien de Rosa,mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesSam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, responded to Amodei’s comments on Saturday. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” he said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”He also said OpenAI would not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns overartificial intelligence.“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altmantold Fortune. Asked why he, Amodei, Musk, and the chief executives of Meta and Google did not sit down and “get on the same page” about a collective slowdown, he said: “I think that will happen.”OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Sam Altman saysRead moreDemis Hassabis, a co-founder and chair of Google Deep Mind, also said: “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.”But some safety experts questioned whether Amodei’s plan went far enough. David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”Amodei’s plan seeks a waiver from the US government to allow the frontier AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But David Sacks, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology, said: “Stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission … Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyber-attack.”Meanwhile, King Charles is preparing to meet leading figures from the most prominent AI companies on Thursday to ask them how the technology can be developed under the theme “AI for good”. One session is set to be called “prudence at the frontier”, which is expected to explore the possibility for clear red lines on the uses of AI to create bioweapons and launch cyber-attacks on critical systems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThose expected to attend the event overseen by the Ditchley Foundation, which has drawn up a draft charter for AI leaders, include: senior executives atOpenAIand Anthropic; the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang; Hassabis; Niccolo de Masi, the chair and chief executive of IonQ,; and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope on issues of AI and technology ethicsThe OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlincalledAmodei’s essay “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.Amodei said his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps, saying Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​arecalling for new rulesto govern AI systems after cases of AI agentsgoing rogueto hack external systems and AI ​safety researchersquittingtheir companies over concerns about the technology’s risks.Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. At the weekend the New York Times reported that Barack Obama on Thursday privately urged the Democrats to prioritise AI oversight in their agenda, telling party leaders on Thursday: “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous.”The former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, who advises Anthropic, wrote on Sunday: “We have had a wake-up call to take AI safety more seriously, to work out how to set limits on research. If governments don’t heed this, the risk of a serious accident will become unacceptably high.”On Wednesday, a former Anthropic employee had warned thatAI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in aseries of poststhat he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.Asked to comment on his former employee’s view, Amodei said: “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him … I think there’s some chance that things go wrong but it’s not all that high.”“I am not a doomer about this,” he told CNN. “I think this technology can be built safely.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingOpenAIAnthropicSam AltmanElon MuskTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes counted | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Race too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc win
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Race too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc win
Content: The Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, arrives at the party's election night watch party.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, arrives at the party's election night watch party.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPASwedenSwedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes countedRace too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc winSweden general election – live updatesMiranda BryantNordic correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority.Earlier in the night, exit polls suggested that the country was on course for a brand new left-leaning government. But as the votes were counted, it was apparent it could take days for the outcome to become clear.With 80% of votes counted, there was just one seat between the left and right blocs. The left-leaning opposition parties, led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, had 175 and the rightwing parties, led by the Moderates prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, had 174.At 10:30pm local time, broadcaster SVT predicted there were only 20,000 votes between the blocs.The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday.Kristersson, the incumbent prime minister, said the voters had had their say, but “we still don’t have a final result.”“Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question, and we will do everything we can to ensure that this government will be the very best for our country,” Kristersson told supporters.The Social Democrats remain Sweden’s biggest party, but look to have had their worst result in decades. Speaking just before midnight local time, Andersson addressed supporters to say that every vote must be counted.“We will have to wait for the final election results. But my message is clear: we Social Democrats will always be ready to take responsibility for the result. It seems like it will be very even,” she said.“But right now we are leading. If it stands, then Sweden will have a new government. But we have to wait for the final result, so let me end where I began, in democracy, the finest thing we have.”It was also a bad night for the far-right Sweden Democrats, who are hoping to enter government for the first time. They slipped from the country’s second biggest party to third.The deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, of the Christian Democrats, told her supporters that Sweden would be going “to bed with uncertainty” and may have to wait until Wednesday for a result. But she remained adamant that the ruling right-leaning coalition should remain in government.“This is a very clear message for the only unified government alternative in this election campaign,” she said in an upbeat speech. “This will be a real nail-biter, this could be uncertain all the way until Wednesday.”It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Pollssuggested an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). Enthusiasm among voters appeared to be high. A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting and there were reports of long queues at some polling stations.Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.2:51‘I hope for a decent period in politics’: views of voters as Sweden goes to the polls – videoThe right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden | Martin GelinRead moreSD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it hasshifted much of the Swedish establishment to the rightand had a strong influence on policies, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader why she was so angry during a TV debate.View image in fullscreenThe Sweden Democrats leader, Jimmie Åkesson, at a polling station in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, on Saturday.Photograph: Claudio Bresciani/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesAnother leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.0:31Abba’s Benny Andersson remixes ‘Mamma Mia’ hit at Social Democrat election day rally – videoKristersson, had put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused the Social Democrat leader of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.After voting in the town of Strängnäs, west of the capital, Kristersson said “momentum is on our side”. Despite dropping in the latest polls, he said the role of his party was to be “team leaders … uniting for the best of the country”.Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count  | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns
Content: ‘I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact,’ said McNeill.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact,’ said McNeill.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianForeign policy‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid countKirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concernsSupported byAbout this contentHeather StewartEconomics editorSun 13 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending.McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”.But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges.“I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said.Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday.She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño.“It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UNhas warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding.The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending.Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK supportto some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts.At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development.View image in fullscreenMcNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, has served as the minister of state for international development since July.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian“As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said.“I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’”Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources.She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”.“The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added.“That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.”A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries.“Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?”McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party.Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board.“The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourAidManifestos 2024Humanitarian responseDebt reliefnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police release images of six men sought after violent disorder in Portsmouth | Portsmouth | The Guardian
description: Hampshire and Isle of Wight force says it wants to speak to men in connection with anti-migrant unrest that left seven officers injured
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Hampshire and Isle of Wight force says it wants to speak to men in connection with anti-migrant unrest that left seven officers injured
Content: CCTV images issued by police of six men they would like to speak to after scenes of violent disorder at Eastney Marina.Photograph: Hampshire Constabulary/PAView image in fullscreenCCTV images issued by police of six men they would like to speak to after scenes of violent disorder at Eastney Marina.Photograph: Hampshire Constabulary/PAPortsmouthPolice release images of six men sought after violent disorder in PortsmouthHampshire and Isle of Wight force says it wants to speak to men in connection with anti-migrant unrest that left seven officers injuredNadia KhomamiSun 13 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice have released images of six men they would like to speak to after violent disorder inPortsmouthlast week that left seven officers injured.About200 people gathered at Eastney Marinaon Sunday night after a small boat carrying asylum seekers arrived on the south coast having crossed the Channel. The activists dispersed the following day in the early hours.Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said seven police officers were injured and treated at the scene, while vehicles belonging to the Coastguard and Border Force were damaged.The force said it reviewed “hundreds of hours’ worth” of footage from the disorder and released images of six men it believes “can assist our investigation”.The first person charged in connection with the demonstration in the city appeared in court on Saturday morning.Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove, Portsmouth, appeared at the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable.A 16-year-old boy from Waterlooville was also arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in connection with last Sunday’s events. He has been released on bail until 12 December.Anti-immigration activists returned to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday afternoon, where they faced counter-protests from anti-racism groups.Tony Rowlinson, assistant chief constable, said the scenes at Eastney Marina had gone beyond peaceful protest. “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest,” he said. “Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder.”Rowlinson said officers had worked to protect people in the area and warned that police would pursue those responsible after reviewing footage.“The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences,” he said.He added that none of the seven injured officers had been seriously hurt, but said they “did not deserve to be assaulted” while policing the demonstration.Police also said they were investigating online threats and abuse directed at officers and staff from partner agencies after the disorder.The force has appealed to anyone who recognises the six men to contact police on 101 or report information online, quoting reference 44260435943.Rowlinson said: “If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution.”Explore more on these topicsPortsmouthProtestRefugeesImmigration and asylumFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restoration | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration
Content: Items dating back to the 1800s have been found under the floorboards and in the very fabric of Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenItems dating back to the 1800s have been found under the floorboards and in the very fabric of Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAMonarchyHidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restorationWhist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restorationCaroline DaviesSun 13 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the UK monarchy’s HQ.Misplaced belongings, found beneath the floorboards, in other areas of the royal residence and preserved within the fabric of the building, include a ticket to a whist drive run by the royal household’s social club from nearly 80 years ago.View image in fullscreenA packet of Silk Cut cigarettesPhotograph: Aaron Chown/PABlank Littlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957, a pair of battered black hobnail boots and an empty Silk Cut cigarette packet were among the everyday objects unearthed, as well as an almost 140-year-old fragment of the West End theatre listings from the Standard newspaper in 1889.View image in fullscreenLittlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe discoveries were made during the decade-long £370m reservicing of the palace which has included rewiring electrics, upgrading plumbing and heating and overhauling its infrastructure to prevent long-term damage.View image in fullscreenAbout 1.2 miles of Vulcanised Indian Rubber cabling was discovered and removed as a priority.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAElectrical wire covered with Vulcanised Indian Rubber (VIR) cabling, which posed the risk of fire to the building, were also located. The cabling, which becomes brittle with age, was removed as a priority when the project, which is due to be completed next year, began in 2017. About 1.2 miles (2km) of the rubber cabling has been replaced so far.View image in fullscreenThe ticket to the whist drive organised by the staff social club, dated 14 April 1949, was embedded in a lump of rock.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe small whist drive ticket, priced at 6d, a sixpence, and dated 14 April 1949 – during the reign of the king’s grandfather, George VI – was found embedded in a lump of building rock.The pass to the staff social club gathering in the palace reads “Royal Household Social Club – Buckingham Palace: A Whist Drive to be held on” followed by the faded, stamped date “14 APR 1949”.At that time,Queen Elizabeth IIwas still Princess Elizabeth and had been married to Prince Philip for less than 18 months and their eldest son, Charles, was only five months old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPages from the Daily Express in 1966 detailing the prison housing the Great Train Robbers.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAPages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailed the maximum security prison housing the Great Train Robbers, picturing the inside of Durham prison and reporting that “the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings”.View image in fullscreenInstructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenA bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAInstructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception informed them that the queen and other members of the royal family would move round the ballroom in a “clockwise direction”.Aides were to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the glittering white tie and tiaras annual gathering, according to the manually typed sheet, which also said that smoking was banned in the certain state rooms and the reception kept to a strict timetable.Other findings included a section of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dating from around the mid-1800s, an aged Pewter tankard, a bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyQueen Elizabeth IIKing Charles IIILondonHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations? | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Harborne and Delo’s cash could buy a massive head start in an election, but spending big has possible pitfalls
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Harborne and Delo’s cash could buy a massive head start in an election, but spending big has possible pitfalls
Content: The money could give Reform UK a lot of power for on-the-ground campaigning and social media.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe money could give Reform UK a lot of power for on-the-ground campaigning and social media.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianReform UKAnalysisHow could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorHarborne and Delo’s cash could buy a massive head start in an election, but spending big has possible pitfallsSun 13 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareNigel Farage once said he could spend his £5m gift from Christopher Harborne on Ferraris if he wanted to, given its unconditional nature.With thenew donations to his partyfrom Harborne and his fellow crypto billionaire Ben Delo of £72m over the past weekend alone, Farage’s party now has nearly enough cash to buy a Reform UK branded Ferrari for a party organiser in each of Britain’s 632 constituencies (though that would certainly be a waste and a bit of a tax headache).But what the cash can buy first and foremost for Reform is manpower. Already the party is seeking to recruit more than 60 local organisers in key areas of the country.Though the donation is certainly enough to staff every constituency in England, Scotland and Wales with organisers, that would also be a massive waste of resources in seatsReform UKis never likely to win. Instead, experienced regional staff can build impeccable targeting data for the seats Reform UK needs to win a majority.Reform has already invested heavily in improving its canvassing tools and its ReformPro software – but it is boots on the ground that ensure the data being fed into those tools is as accurate as it can be. That requires door-to-door canvassing to identify switching voters and non-voters who might be persuaded to turn out.For most parties, those kinds of local resources are only really deployed far closer to an election. Beginning that level of organising and data collection this far out could give Reform UK a massive head start at the next election, though other parties have very valuable legacy data from previous elections of which Reform has much less available.Local parties could also print and send a many more direct mail drops, which are uncapped outside of the election period, with voters receiving “local newspapers” which are in fact Reform UK campaigning mailouts.As well as on the ground, the cash also gives Reform UK massive potential power in the air war, on social media in particular with paid ads that can be micro-targeted locally and professionally produced and filmed. It can spend large amounts of money buying social media advertising completely legally and without limit, including on YouTube and Facebook.Again, there will be little competition in this space as many parties will not use their resources on this so early in the electoral cycle. Already Reform has professionally built broadcast studios, and splashes the cash liberally on major policy announcements at aircraft hangars, and stadiums for rallies.Reform UK’s £72m donations may be caught by new bill, Rayner suggestsRead moreTheo Bertram, the director of the Social Market Foundation thinktank, who was previously a Labour adviser and vice-president at TikTok,said in a post on Xthat he believed Reform would also wish to invest the money in getting in serious policy expertise and preparation for government.Parties often rely on goodwill from expert supporters to help prepare for government or draft their manifesto. But Reform UK could recruit some of the best legal and constitutional experts to help it find ways of implementing some of its most radical and controversial policies, including mass deportations and evicting non-UK citizens from social housing. Bertram estimates that getting the best and most expensive consultants on the issues would cost the party about £25m.Candidate vetting has also been a nightmare for Reform and cash could be used to considerably sharpen the process. There would be a vast war chest for legal challenges – Reform UK has often threatened or begun judicial reviews of government policies – which keep the party in the headlines.There is one way that Reform UK may come a cropper if it spends the money like water over the coming months. Should Andy Burnham call a snap general election before next autumn, election spending rules are retrospective for the previous years.That means the spending cap, roughly £34m across Great Britain, applies for the previous 12 months, leaving the party in a bit of a trap if it has already outspent that amount outside the six-week election campaign. Might that be one reason to tempt Burnham into an early poll?Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Researchers hope powerful new microscope will reveal ‘root cause’ of incurable bowel disease | Health | The Guardian
description: No run-of-the-mill tech, ‘Curie’ operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional microscopy and could spur discoveries leading to new treatment
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: No run-of-the-mill tech, ‘Curie’ operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional microscopy and could spur discoveries leading to new treatment
Content: Dr Karina Pombo-Garcia peers into a new microscope that could unlock new knowledge about bowel conditions like Crohn’s.Photograph: Adam Gasson/Rosalind Franklin InstituteView image in fullscreenDr Karina Pombo-Garcia peers into a new microscope that could unlock new knowledge about bowel conditions like Crohn’s.Photograph: Adam Gasson/Rosalind Franklin InstituteHealthResearchers hope powerful new microscope will reveal ‘root cause’ of incurable bowel diseaseNo run-of-the-mill tech, ‘Curie’ operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional microscopy and could spur discoveries leading to new treatmentNicola DavisScience correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of young people living with debilitating and incurable bowel conditions worldwide isgrowing, but researchers now hope a one-of-a-kind microscope will help them understand such diseases and find new treatments.According to the British Society of Gastroenterology,more than half a million peoplein the UK are living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis the two main forms.While such conditions can develop at any age,expertssay they are most often diagnosed between the ages of 15 and 40,blighting livesat a crucial time for education, work and relationships.Now a new piece of kit could bring fresh hope to those affected by IBD.“What this microscope technology and what the science we do in the lab can bring is really to understand the mechanism [of IBD] better,” said Dr Karina Pombo-Garcia, a group leader at the Rosalind Franklin Institute at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus, Oxfordshire, where the microscope is housed.“With IBD, and with other many diseases that we collaborate with other groups to study, there [are] some treatments, but maybe those treatments still are not maybe the best or the most targeted that we can do because we … fundamentally don’t understand the disease fully.”View image in fullscreenDr Pombo-Garcia and Dimitrios Ioannidis, a PhD student, with the new kit, which allows them to see details down to just 20nm in size.Photograph: Adam Gasson/Rosalind Franklin InstituteWith its black casing, grey hoses and a plethora of wires, the microscope is remarkably unobtrusive.Yet this is no run-of-the-mill bit of tech: the microscope operates at 10 times the resolution of conventional light microscopy, allowing researchers to see the details down to just 20nm in size.chartHow stimulated emission depletion works.To do so, the microscope, which researchers have nicknamed “Curie”, uses a two-laser technique known as stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy that scooped its inventors theNobel prize in physics in 2014.In this setup, features of interest within cells are labelled with fluorescent tags – these absorb energy from the first laser beam and then emit light, or fluorescence.A second, doughnut-shaped laser beam overlaps with the area illuminated by the first. Crucially, this second beam “switches off” fluorescence within its outer ring, meaning fluorescence is only detected from the centre of the doughnut – a very small region.“This allows the microscope to distinguish structures that are much closer together than would be possible using a conventional fluorescence microscope, producing images with exceptionally high resolution,” said Pombo-Garcia.The microscope also has additional features, making it the only one of its kind in the UK. These, Pombo-Garcia notes, include deformable mirrors that can correct for optical distortions caused by the sample.“This allows researchers to obtain clear images from deeper within relatively thick tissues and mini-organs,” she said. “It also has a temperature-controlled stage, enabling living cells and mini-organs to be studied under conditions close to normal body temperature.”View image in fullscreenPhD student Dimitrios Ioannidis is using the microscope to understand how cells that line our internal organs create protective barriers.Photograph: Adam Gasson/Rosalind Franklin InstituteBowel disease breakthrough as researchers make ‘holy grail’ discoveryRead moreDimitrios Ioannidis, a PhD student, is using the microscope to understand how cells that line our internal organs, including the intestines, come together and create protective barriers.“For this to happen, we have specific protein complexes, which we hypothesise might change over time. So using this piece of equipment, we are able to visualise these complexes beyond what [we can see with a] conventional microscope,” he said, adding that he was looking at how the structure of these protein complexes changes from foetal development to adulthood. “If the structure changes, so does the function,” he said.Ioannidis noted that by understanding what healthy tissue should look like, and then comparing and understanding the differences seen in people with disease, there was the potential to shed light on what had gone wrong.“And then if you work and dig a little bit deeper, you can potentially find the root cause of some of the diseases that are affecting individuals,” he said, noting that this included IBD.The microscope was unveiled by science minister Chris McDonald, alongside the announcement of £67m of funding for the Rosalind Franklin Institute over the next five years from April 2027, and a further £90m over the same period for the Henry Royce Institute, which focuses on materials research. In both cases, the funding has come from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council via the core budget of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) set in the 2025 spending review.The announcement comes at a difficult time for UK science facilities. Earlier this year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), also part of UKRI, revealed it needs to make £162m in savings by 2030 as a result of factors such as soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates.World-leading UK science facilities at risk amid £162m funding crisisRead moreThe situation has put some national facilities at risk of closure, with the Diamond Light Source, Central Laser Facility and ISIS Neutron and Muon Source – all of which sit on the same campus as the Rosalind Franklin Institute – jointly facing a 15% drop in funding, leading to concerns from the scientific community.However, McDonald maintained such facilities still receive a very high level of funding, and stressed not every project or initiative backed by the STFC will be funded in perpetuity.“I’m not particularly happy about the characterisation of cuts because that’s not the case at the high-level budget,” he said. “But it is right that STFC live within their means and prioritise their own budget,” he said.Explore more on these topicsHealthPhysicsNobel prizesResearch fundingPeople in sciencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world. Our mission is clear | US politics | The Guardian
description: An unholy alliance is working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. It’s becoming clear how we stop them
Author: Naomi Klein
Headline: An unholy alliance is working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. It’s becoming clear how we stop them
Content: Illustration: Sophy Hollington/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Sophy Hollington/The GuardianThe featured essayUS politicsThe end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world. Our mission is clearAn unholy alliance is working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. It’s becoming clear how we stop themNaomi Klein and Astra Taylor: the future according to end times fascism – videoNaomi KleinandAstra TaylorSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTShareWhen Jeff Bezos announced his plan for an opulent Venetian wedding in early 2025, many locals found the idea offensive, even obscene. A growing number of residents were struggling to find secure and affordable housing in a city overrun by tourists and Airbnb, and the billionaire was planning to, in effect, rent out the municipality for three days, forking over an estimated $50m forfestivitiesthat would clog central canals and block well-trafficked streets. Worse, Amazon’s carbon emissions were soaring, thanks to artificial intelligence and the datacentre build out – and that’s personal in Venice, where the streets already flood dozens of times a year.Marta Sottoriva, a 35-year-old high school teacher, told us that she first heard about the wedding plans just when Bezos’s rocket company, Blue Origin, was grabbing headlines. Bezos had sent a “crew” of female influencers and celebrities, including his fiancee, Lauren Sánchez, and the pop singer Katy Perry, to the suborbital edge of space in a seemingly pointless publicity stunt. “The idea that you are so rich and powerful that you can use space as a 10-minute trip,” Sottoriva recalled, only intensified the “feeling that our city was being taken away from us in such an arrogant way”. Federica Toninello, another young activist, agreed, telling us that it felt as if both space and Venice were being “colonized”.Colonizing spaceis exactly what Bezos hopes to do. Blue Origin, Bezos claims in his well-rehearsed sales pitch, will secure humanity’s survival by allowing a trillion people to one day spread across the solar system. The unbearable horror he imagines himself saving our species from? The threat of what he calls a “civilization of stasis”, otherwise known as having to contend with real ecological limits and devising a way to share the planet’s finite resources. To avoid this reckoning, Bezos imagines a future in which “Earth will be zoned residential and light industrial” and set aside as a sort of preserve out of reach for most of its native inhabitants. The vast majority of humans will pursue the nebulous benefit of “exponential growth” in the forbidding void of space, trapped on Blue Origin spacecrafts. It would seem that Bezos believes the prospect of humanity living sustainably and peaceably on our precious, singular home is a nightmarish possibility unworthy of his consideration.Predictably, it turned out that most Venetians would rather continue living in magnificent Venice. Unlike Bezos, they don’t fret about hypothetical civilizational stagnation; they worry about economic stagnation as a result of government divestment, a lack of jobs and opportunity, and being forced out of the city and country they love. Young Italians often have little choice but to emigrate to find work; over the last decade, more than 1 million citizens have moved, a third of them between the ages of 25 and 34.To date, the precarity and anger many Italians feel has mostly benefited the neofascist right. But those same forces also drew people to the anti-Bezos cause, helping to coalesce a budding, self-consciously antifascist movement.The rise of end times fascism | Naomi Klein and Astra TaylorRead moreThe spirited, disruptive “No Space for Bezos” campaign tapped into wells of outrage against billionaires, climate breakdown and militarism – and it also gave the organizers a megaphone to broadcast ideas for different, less lethal ways we could choose to live together. Activists printed posters and stickers showing Bezos’s head on a rocket blasting into space. They made a dummy of Bezos clutching fistfuls of fake money while clinging to a giant buoyant Amazon package, then set it free to float down the canals. They unfurled banners from Venice’s iconic buildings and bridges and across its piazzas: “Tax the rich to give back to the planet.” And they chanted that the money for the wedding would be better spent rebuilding Gaza. For days, they caused gleeful chaos and relentlessly poked fun at the groom and his star-studded guest list, which included his billionaire bunker neighbors Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and a gaggle of Kardashians.Not long before the wedding, officials announced that theevent was being movedto a less central location due to the protests. Even Bezos’s two yachts, Koru and Abeona, were denied permission to dock locally. Organizers declared victory and celebrated. The international press devoured the visual-rich showdown. And the online right didn’t know who to root for: the Davos elites spraying one another with foam on a superyacht, or the leftist riffraff making agitprop?Like Donald Trump’senormous ballroom, Bezos’s extravagant wedding epitomized the obscenities of our networked gilded age. For the Amazon founder, it wasn’t enough to be part of one of Europe’s most beautiful cities – he needed to consume it and swallow it whole. A year later he would do the same with New York City’s Met Gala, sparking similar outrage and grassrootscreativity.The Venice protests, which dwelled on Bezos’s dreams of outer space at the expense of Earth, pointed to something fundamental about the age ofend times fascism– a concept at the center of ournew book, referring to an unholy alliance working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. Today’s battle lines are not simply between people who struggle to survive under increasingly degraded and costly conditions and an oligarch class thinking of ever more ludicrous ways to waste their wealth. They are more cosmological than that.On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground, and who therefore are committed to staying right here, in the complexity of our earthbound reality, with one another. We know we need to do what is necessary to make “here” – this planet and all of its ecologies and communities – and safer for the multitude of beings who rely upon them, fully aware this is our one and only home.On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet, whether those plans take the form of heavenly ascension, earthly bunkers and fortressed nations, or fantasies of colonizing space andmerging with machines. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth (or even pulling back from pouring fuel on the fires), end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.View image in fullscreenAn absence of aweBezos’s fixation on space gets at something else that is key to understanding end times fascism and its fixation on bunkering and abandoning our shared world: the apparent inability of the people driving this project to marvel at, or even notice, the wonders that surround them.That was glaringly apparent in 2021, when Bezos sent another crew to space. This time William Shatner, best known as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, was on board (to fulfill one of Bezos’s boyhood fantasies, of course). “Space. The final frontier,” Shatner had said at the start of each episode. But as the now 90-year-old actor watched our blue-and-green planet recede from the window, he was suddenly flooded with terror. “The contrast between the vicious coldness of space and the warm nurturing of Earth below filled me with overwhelming sadness,” he laterrecalled, explaining that he had gained a much deeper appreciation for our planet’s sublime and fragile gifts.“Every day, we are confronted with the knowledge of further destruction of Earth at our hands: the extinction of animal species, of flora and fauna … things that took five billion years to evolve, and suddenly we will never see them again because of the interference of mankind,” Shatner wrote. He took the trip expecting to be awestruck by the universe and instead he longed for home the minute he left: “I discovered that the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here, with all of us.”Perhaps Shatner’s insight about our precious imperiled planet resonates with the Amazon founder, but the billionaire’s plans for space colonization and his company’s large expansion of carbon-spewing data centers both suggest otherwise. And among tech oligarchs, Bezos is all too typical. Peter Thiel, for one, oncerevealedthat his three best ideas for achieving true freedom are “cyberspace”, “outerspace” and “seasteading” (the idea of building new countries on floating oil rigs). In other words, this man, whose enormous wealth affords him access to the most spectacular settings our planet has to offer, actually believes these three cold, dead places are superior to the Earth we have, verdant and alive.Our tech overlords are planning for conscious AI to conquer the cosmos. What could go wrong? | Eduardo PorterRead moreSomething similar seems amiss with Elon Musk, a man who seems to look up at the wonders of the night sky and see only opportunities to fill that inky unknown with his own space junk. The venerable novelist Joyce Carol Oates highlighted these apparent limits in the fall of 2025 when she roasted him ruthlessly on his own platform, X. “So curious,” shewrote, “that such a wealthy man never posts anything that indicates that he enjoys or is even aware of what virtually everyone appreciates – scenes from nature, pet dog or cat, praise for a movie, music, a book (but doubt that he reads); pride in a friend’s or relative’s accomplishment; condolences for someone who has died; pleasure in sports, acclaim for a favorite team; references to history. In fact he seems totally uneducated, uncultured. The poorest persons on Twitter [X] may have access to more beauty & meaning in life than the ‘most wealthy person in the world.’”The observation clearly got under the tech baron’s notoriously thin skin: he called her “a lazy liar” and began posting approvingly about various movies to prove Oates wrong. Yet in Musk’s euphoria on the dayhis aerospace company, SpaceX,went public, he made no attempt to hide his boredom with our blue planet and its challenges: “We want to solve [problems] here on Earth and we should solve them. But there also have to be things that get you excited about the future, that make you glad to wake up in the morning because you can’t wait to see what happens next.” It would seem that only abandoning Earth provides that thrill.Most people have the capacity for awe, to gasp at the jeweled beauty of a songbird or the otherworldliness of a whale’s exhalation or the intricate latticework of an ancient holy site. Children have the capacity for pure awe; so do 90-year-old actors in suborbital space. To experience awe is to dissolve into the swirl of the universe, to feel small in the best way. This sense of interconnection is also why we grieve when we witness strangers suffering, and feel the great sorrow of extinction. The fact that this capacity seems to be missing from the men who hold our collective fate in their hands is a personal loss for them – and an existential crisis for the rest of us.One dangerous part of the tech oligarchs’ world-abandoning project is that the tools they are building are designed to remake us in their own broken image. Popular platforms and apps train us to share Silicon Valley’s dream of discarnate freedom, perpetually nudging us to forsake real places and in-person connection in favor of simulations – and to view Earth, our bodies and our relationships as prisons to hack and flee. Altman, for one, has made it clear that he sees “certain advantages to being a machine”, and he has repeatedly insisted that his own children will never be smarter than AI, as though intelligence can be reduced to no more than computation. Like similar services, ChatGPT is trained to hijack our empathic response systems so we, too, will elevate machines and imbue them with more significance than they deserve.The inability to appreciate this planet and its marvelous cast of characters helps explain why they are so prepared to sacrifice it. Indeed, the tech right’s willingness to eliminate our life-sustaining labor andreplacehuman relationships with synthetic ones cannot be separated from their indifference to what little remains of the planet’s fast-vanishing wildlife and plant diversity. They don’t seem to know how to love this place, to savor the pleasure of other people’s company, or to marvel at the mysteries presented by other species.In short, we are up against an ideology that has given up not only on the premise and promise of liberal democracy but on the livability of our shared world – on its beauty, on its people, on our children, on other species. There is something treasonous in this. Treasonous not to an abstraction like a flag or a nation, for we are not nationalists. But treasonous to the unspoken pact made with the web of life that sustains us.They are traitors to creation, to the wonders of here.View image in fullscreenTheantithesis offascismThere is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism. Whether it’s Venetians taking on Jeff Bezos orAlbanians telling Jared and Ivanka Trumpthat their country is not for sale or a small town in Kentucky organizing against a sprawling datacentre, every front in this fight takes on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City – and his approach to governance since his election – embody many of them. Start from love of place, then conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives, embrace common goals across difference, get outside and gather offline and in person, take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul.Mamdani has pounded away at his core policies to make the city more affordable, and has made good on many of those promises in his pursuit, for example, to lower rent and expand universal childcare. But he has also done something more sublime, dwelling on the boisterous, charming corners of the city that are the reason so many people choose to endure the pressures pushing them to leave.As Mamdani’s star was rising, fascists and neofascists across the country and around the world did what they do. They sorted and separated, ranked and expelled. They sowed confusion and division by claiming Mamdani wasn’t a real American, and blamed the left for every social problem and grievance. They held up multicultural New York as a supposedly terrifying example of what happens when the“great replacement”succeeds. JD Vance spoke out in defense of people’s right to not want to live next to people from “a totally different culture”, and Stephen Miller railed on X: “NYC is the clearest warning yet of what happens to a society when it fails to control migration.”As the fascists drew their rigid lines – in versus out, protected versus disposable, “heritage” versus. invader – the campaign to elect Mamdani threw a year-long party that celebrated one of the most racially and ethnically diverse places ever known, five boroughs shaped by wave after wave of new immigrants who have made their homes on Lenape lands. With its every action, the campaign asserted that shared identity can be forged not just by ancestry but by a commitment to a shared home, and to a shared set of values about how to live together in that home.New York is a city of people carrying countless hyphenations and keeping myriad cultural practices alive. But as Mamdani put it: “No matter what you eat, what language you speak, how you pray, or where you come from, the words that most define us are the two we all share: New Yorkers.”So Mamdani explained the complexities of ranked-choice voting in the Democratic primary using a line of mango lassis as props. He canvassed for votes at queer clubs, shouted out Haitian revolutionary history at the massive Bayo concert, shared his favorite bagel order, and broke fast during Ramadan over biryani in the Bronx. Once in office, he also turned the now legendary Knicks playoff run and the 2026 World Cup into a summer-long party few will forget. In these ways and others, Mamdani re-enchanted a city that had faced relentless vilification from Washington as dangerous, dirty and dysfunctional.It was a perfect encapsulation of “hereness” – an idea developed by theJewish Labour Bund, a Yiddish socialist group that was founded in the 19th century and grounded in fierce commitment to place and community not based on bloodlines.Molly Crabapple, a proud New Yorker and artist who recently published a bestselling history of the Bund, made the connection in a piece published in the Guardian. “Like New York itself, Mamdani’s campaign was multicultural, multiracial, polyglottal,”she wrote. “When Andrew Cuomo tried to bait him as un-American, he released ads in Spanish and Bangla, Hindi and Arabic. He ran a campaign devoted to class-first politics that sought to speak to everyone in their own idiom, while never once apologizing for who he was.Amid all this celebration of difference, Mamdani’s campaign also emphasized the kinds of daily experiences and anxieties that are common and unifying for nearly all New Yorkers, lingering in the ordinary places that are too often overlooked or reviled. Mamdani rubbed shoulders with commuters on packed subway cars, paid homage to the glories of the Staten Island Ferry, and visited countless bodegas, approaching the strangers he met with nonjudgmental curiosity and a smile so wide it became a punchline on Saturday Night Live.But the campaign was not only antifascist – in the myriad ways that it celebrated the unruliness that makes New York lovable, it was also theantithesisof fascism. More than a rejection of hate, it was an invitation to kindness, to a world in which we avert our eyes from no one. That meant lifting up and honoring the very people fascists are most eager to eject and discard: the working-class, immigrant workforce that keeps the city functioning. The campaign shined a spotlight on delivery workers getting ripped off by platforms such as DoorDash, on Amazon warehouse workers fighting to have their unions recognized, and on taxi drivers in line at LaGuardia, one part of a nocturnal workforce that makes it possible for New York to boast of being the city that never sleeps.Faced with the prospect of a fairer city funded by marginally higher taxes, some prophesied a billionaire exodus. Hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman threatened to leave along with other high earners and Fox forecast a “Mamdani Migration”. Luxury real estate agents reported being bombarded with calls from clients wanting to sell their penthouses and move to Palm Beach.The threats of defection only underscored the mutually reinforcing nature of the two core themes of Mamdani’s campaign – the joyous love of here, even if here is kind of a wreck, and the concrete plans for repair and improvement. Because the more devoted you are to a place, the easier it is to put in the resources and energy required to improve it. It’s a politics based not on wanting to escape this earthly realm, whether our cities or our animate bodies, but on a deep desire to stay, and to protect all that is irreplaceable, human and alive.This is the very same spirit that we’ve seen motivating people to protect their air and water from sprawling datacenters and to defend their immigrant neighbors from ICE. While reporting on the weeks-long uprising in Minneapolis, the journalist Adam Serwer memorably described the guiding ideology of the resistance as “neighborism”, or the “commitment to protecting the people around you, no matter who they are or where they came from”. It was an openhearted, welcoming ethic that united huge numbers of ordinary people to do something deceptively simple: protect the most vulnerable members of their community from what looked very much like an invading army. That meant everything from braving bullets, to cooking dinner to opening up spare rooms to families who were no longer safe at home.In these and countless other ways, Minnesotans rose up to insist that their neighbors were already where they belonged, whether they were, as Serwer put it, born in Minneapolis or Mogadishu.The human networks that neighbors are building, block by block, group chat by group chat, are about more than refusal. In our time of serial shocks and intersecting crises, they are also the basis for a different kind of survivalism. But while the various strains of fascists build bunkers for the few, ours are survival networks grounded in the principle that every one of us, without exception, deserves to live and thrive. They are also bound by a belief that keeping one another safe when the inevitable shocks arrive is a sacred duty. Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.View image in fullscreenSome worlds must endThose stories cannot be about returning to something called “normal”, to what passed for calm before Brexit and Trump and Silicon Valley’s authoritarian turn. Those were the years during which too many problems were allowed to compound and fester: fascism is always a warped response to real crises. And end times fascism is a response to real planetary-scale crises, including ever-concentrating levels of carbon in the atmosphere and wealth in the hands of the super-rich. The responses it proposes – mass sacrifices of humans and non-humans alike – are monstrous and must be purged from our midst.To achieve this, we will have to figure out how to address the underlying crises contemporary fascism feeds off of. Because boundariesarebeing crossed. Limitsarebeing exceeded. Wallsarebeing hit. Fascists want us to believe that what is hitting the wall is the human story: it’s over, so make sure you are among the chosen who transcend to the next world. Pray to your God for salvation. Implant the chip, merge with the machines. Militarize and purify your bunkered nation. Arm yourself to the hilt and hide behind your fortune. Don’t worry about the humans, the animals, the trees, the rivers and reefs that won’t make it.But they are wrong. It’s not the human story that is hitting the wall. Rather, it is the story we have been trapped inside of. The one about how greed must be the engine of civilization. About how growth can go on for ever. About how there are always more efficiencies to be found, more workers to be rationalized, more resources to be sacrificed, more people, places and planets to colonize. These myths are hitting the wall of reality and much will have to change as a result.AI companies will fail. We can salvage something from the wreckage | Cory DoctorowRead moreThe logics that must be abandoned should be clear by now. Unlimited violence. Unconstrained exploitation. Insatiable wealth. Unchecked dominance. Those are the drives that make coexistence impossible. Looking forward, two paths beckon. We can abandon and betray this world, or we can break with capitalism and build new economic and political systems that honor life and prioritize care and repair.Thankfully we are not starting from scratch. Our movement ancestors have left us maps to earthly Zions where everyone is welcome, to inclusive futures where peace and safety are core principles. Not the post-human future desired by end times fascists, but a post-capitalist and pro- (all of) life one. Deeply democratic, socialist, feminist, multiracial, multispecies, internationalist, generous, courageous and animate. Embodied and sensory, proudly earthbound.And that, fundamentally, is the prospect that terrifies end times fascists more than anything else. It’s why Thiel denounces anyone attempting to regulate fossil fuels and AI as the antichrist; and why Trump and Vance smear nonviolent Minnesotans defending their neighbors as “domestic terrorists”. What keeps these men up at night is … us. It’s the possibility that a popular and vigorous movement will rise up and defend this planet and the many life-forms who call it home.We didn’t choose to be born into a fight quite so fateful, but we have reached a choice point. We can either follow end times fascists into oblivion, or we can commit to building the unruly, boundary-crossing movement they so deeply fear. One that wrests away their weapons, holds them accountable for their crimes, and defends the paradise of here.This essay was adapted from the bookEnd Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, out15 September via Farrar, Straus and GirouxNaomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British ColumbiaAstra Taylor is a writer, organizer and documentary maker and a co-founder of the Debt CollectiveIllustrations by Sophy Hollington

title: Apocalypse review – the stupidity of these people will make you scream yourself hoarse | Television | The Guardian
description: This ‘radical social experiment’, in which 14 strangers have to see if they could survive the end times, will make you fear for the future of both TV and humanity
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This ‘radical social experiment’, in which 14 strangers have to see if they could survive the end times, will make you fear for the future of both TV and humanity
