Content: Kiera and Steven on toilet disposal duty.Photograph: channel 4View image in fullscreenKiera and Steven on toilet disposal duty.Photograph: channel 4TV reviewTelevisionReviewApocalypse review – the stupidity of these people will make you scream yourself hoarseThis ‘radical social experiment’, in which 14 strangers have to see if they could survive the end times, will make you fear for the future of both TV and humanityLucy ManganSun 13 Sep 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave always assumed that my main use in the event of an apocalypse would be as protein. Ideally, I’d have a few weeks of peace first, eating whatever was in my now defunct fridge and reading a few last books, before tough, athletic, practically skilled survivors found me and chopped me up for parts. I’ve always been aware that I am built for mod cons, not dystopia.But the new Channel 4 reality show – sorry, “radical social experiment” (give it UP, Channel 4, you’re racing as fast to the bottom as every other broadcaster) – Apocalypse has made me rethink my chances. All I need to do, I now realise, is find an Australian cattle farmer and I’m golden.To explain: 14 people are split into rival camps (East and West). Two teams of seven comprising two or three TV archetypes apiece – each team unaware of the other’s existence – have been plonked in a 1,000-acre abandoned town deep in rural Indiana that is now used only by the US military for urban warfare practice. There they must survive for 28 days and eight episodes using only what they can scavenge or create from what they find. According to the surrounding publicity, the participants received three days’ training for how to do so before they were turned loose. This is not mentioned in the programme itself. Probably because no one would believe it.For the first hour the teams do almost nothing but stand, sit or lie around, unless you count choosing the two biggest, draughtiest buildings available in which to make their base camps. Can they rebuild society from scratch, asks the voiceover. To which the short and honest answer from the available evidence is – no, mate.At least 13 of them seem to be pretty useless. Two of the women in the West team are immediately at each other’s throats, alternately scoffing and raging about “setting boundaries” and being “disrespected” instead of “gathering firewood” or “finding tins”. The next day, a pair of Westerners find the town’s massive supermarket. But it’s boarded up. Oh well. They go back to base, where the emergent leader – Welsh sheep farmer Ioan – suggests they tidy up the place rather than go back to the big building that likely contains plentiful supplies of food and other vital items and see if they can break in. For absolutely unfathomable reasons, the famished team complies.In the East, content creator Steven is insisting that nobody so much as scratches their arse without a collective decision to do so. Psychologist Kiera (“I’m a bit of a princess. I own it”) lets Steven go to the toilet before her to do a poo, which is among the top three stupidest things you can do even with modern plumbing – and these guys have a bucket. “We’re fucked on quite a few fronts,” says theatre director Bertie, not inaccurately. Bertie cries a lot, which is heart-rending but not an awful lot of use.View image in fullscreenCan Celia save the day?Photograph: Channel 4The only thing thatisa bit of use involves Scott, the aforementioned Australian cattle farmer. When Steven insists that their first move should be foraging in the forest, Scott calls him “as much use as tits on a bull” and heads off to raid buildings, taking Bertie – who is enjoying a brief dry-eyed period – with him. They find the supermarket, break in and return with food while the foragers are still peering at berries and trying to decide which ones look most like a McDonald’s. Scott institutes immediate rationing of the food (“I want rice!” “No”) until they all decide – I don’t know … that the Spam tins are like the magic porridge pot in the fairytale? That the emptied supermarket will be refilled by producers overnight? – and demolish most of it. They leave just enough for the Westerners to swing by the next day and steal it, because the two people left to guard it do not guard it.The stupidity that dominates the opening episodes is deeply boring. You can only scream for so long before you give up, especially as you know they are not in any true danger of starving to death. Things get more interesting by the third episode (only three were available for review) as a group’s engineer starts cobbling helpful machines together from the junkyard, someone finds a hunting rifle and Nigerian-born politician Celia turns out to be God’s forthright gift to television (“Men think with their dicks. Women think with their brains. So do not ever think men are making the best decisions.”)But, fundamentally, the venality and impenetrable individualism that mean no one is willing to concede to an expert, prioritise sensibly or follow orders, and which thus hamper every endeavour, is depressing. I fear for the future – of programming mostly but, sure, humanity too.Apocalypse is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Not glamorous, but common: how to manage dandruff at home and when to get help | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Experts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can help
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: Experts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can help
Content: Dandruff is the mildest form of a condition called seborrheic dermatitis. At its worst, this condition leads to patches of red skin covered in tiny, greasy scales.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDandruff is the mildest form of a condition called seborrheic dermatitis. At its worst, this condition leads to patches of red skin covered in tiny, greasy scales.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyNot glamorous, but common: how to manage dandruff at home and when to get helpExperts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can helpKeren LandmanSun 13 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou spy a scatter of white flakes on your collar. Or you’ve got an itch that won’t quit, no matter how much you wash your hair. Dandruff isn’t glamorous, but it’s common: abouthalfthe world’s population has it.An itchy, flaking scalp is rarely dangerous, but it can be annoying. Here’s what you need to know about what might be causing your flakes, what you can do about it, and when it’s time to get help.What causes dandruff?Dandruff is the mildest form of a condition called seborrheic dermatitis, a type of skin inflammation that usually affects the head, face or trunk. At its worst, this condition leads to patches of red skin covered in tiny, greasy scales. However, most people with dandruff have just minor scaliness and no redness, affecting only the scalp.Experts still don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, and it’s likely there are various contributing factors. A yeast called Malassezia is a leading suspect, says James Pathoulas, an assistant professor of dermatology at the University of Minnesota medical school who specializes in hair and scalp disorders. Malassezia usually lives harmlessly on the scalp, but overgrowth has beenlinkedwith scalp inflammation.It’s better to think about seborrheic dermatitis as a system in dysfunction rather than one organism causing trouble, according to Natasha Mesinkovska, an associate professor of dermatology at the University of California, Irvine. Scalp health comes down to a “trifecta” of factors, she says: the scalp’s microorganisms, its ability to keep those organisms out of deeper skin layers, and the skin’s immune response to them.Who gets dandruff?It’s not clear why some people get dandruff and others don’t. Genetics may play a role – at least11 gene variantshave been linked to the condition – as can hot, humid weather or a supercharged workout routine.Hormones that drive oil production can also ramp symptoms up or down, beginning around puberty and changing during pregnancy or menopause.What should I do about it?If you’re seeing occasional light scale on your scalp with no significant redness or itch, over-the-counter dandruff shampoo can help. Zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide and ketoconazole are the three most common active ingredients. They’re allequally goodat lowering Malasseziapopulations, tamping down inflammation, and stopping the flakes.Pathoulas recommends massaging the shampoo into your scalp, not just your hair, and leaving it on for a few minutes before rinsing. Use it three times a week; either your regular conditioner or a dandruff-specific product is fine. If you want to wash your hair on in-between days, your regular shampoo and conditioner are fine.Ketoconazole and selenium sulfide can dry out hair and cause breakage, especially for dry, highly textured or coily hair, Pathoulas says. If that occurs, or you already rely on hair oils or leave-in conditioner, look for a gentler,sulfate-free zinc pyrithione formulationmade for textured hair.Go fragrance-free where you can, says Pathoulas. Fragrance is a common cause of scalp contact allergy, and it doesn’t have to be syntheticto cause a reaction: natural botanical fragrances can also wreak havoc.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOnce symptoms clear, most people can taper dandruff shampoo use to once a week. If a shampoo that’s worked for months suddenly stops being effective, the yeast may have grown resistant to it, Pathoulas says. Switching to a different active ingredient for a while, then back again, can restore control.When do I need to see a doctor?If your scalp clears up with a medicated shampoo but flaking resumes within days of stopping, that’s a signal the underlying problem needs more attention, says Mesinkovska.Thick, red, sharply defined plaques with silvery-white scale point toward psoriasis rather than dandruff, especially if you also have them on the elbows and knees. If the redness or scaly skin shows up elsewhere on your body, it could indicate an allergic reaction, depending on its location and your exposures, says Mesinkovska. Dandruff shampoo won’t have any effect on scalp flakes resulting from either of these conditions.Hair loss or a burning or stinging sensation accompanying flakes is never normal, says Pathoulas. If you have these symptoms, a clinician should evaluate you forscarring alopecia.If an evaluation shows that you just have ordinary dandruff but it isn’t responding to the basics, there are prescription options. The experts suggest ciclopirox shampoo, an antifungal with some antibacterial activity built in, and prescription-strength ketoconazole.Roflumilastis a newer option that you apply to your dry scalp as a foam.Some researchers are trying to understand if manipulating the scalp’s bacterial populations might help – that is, adding good germs to outcompete any bad ones that might be causing problems. But that research is still in itsearlystages, so for now, experts aren’t recommending approaches like applying yoghurt or kombucha.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorHair careWomen's hairMen's hairfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stitching our warped reality together: a cartoonist and art critic take different approaches to the Bayeux tapestry | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: One Guardian contributor was tasked with creating a modern-day version of the medieval masterpiece, the other with reviewing the original. Both their visions proved terrifyingly pertinent. Here’s how they both tackled it
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: One Guardian contributor was tasked with creating a modern-day version of the medieval masterpiece, the other with reviewing the original. Both their visions proved terrifyingly pertinent. Here’s how they both tackled it
Content: Details from our updated version of the Bayeux tapestryInside the GuardianBayeux tapestryStitching our warped reality together: a cartoonist and art critic take different approaches to the Bayeux tapestryOne Guardian contributor was tasked with creating a modern-day version of the medieval masterpiece, the other with reviewing the original. Both their visions proved terrifyingly pertinent. Here’s how they both tackled itGautam MalkaniSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOur journalists often draw connections between seemingly disparate issues or events to give people a fuller grasp of how things interrelate. But not every story can convey the scope and complexity of today’s algorithmically warped reality.One of the Guardian’s regular cartoonists has managed this feat by drawing inspiration from a medieval embroidery made almost 1,000 years ago.Edith Pritchettwas asked by her editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine to draw a modern-day version of the Bayeux tapestry, the 11th-century artwork that has been capturing imaginations this month as it goes on public display in the UK for the first time since its creation. Her updated version was included as a pullout poster in the print edition of the Guardian last weekend and also published as a specialscrollable digital feature.The trollers v the scrollers: Edith Pritchett’s Bayeux tapestry for the modern ageRead moreWhereas the originalBayeux tapestrytells the story of the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England in 1066, Edith’s take on it depicts today’s battles with online trolls, social media addiction, the manosphere, AI agents and a natural world ravaged by fossil fuels. But her version is more than just a topical reimagining: it gives the viewer a genuine feel for how the different components of today’s dystopia amplify each other.“I decided on the main topics such as techno-feudalism, the climate crisis, the super-rich, Elon Musk, the online swirling vortex of hatred,” says Edith, “then I tried to work out how to piece it together into a kind of flowing narrative.”Unlike Edith, the Guardian art critic Jonathan Jones tried to avoid thinking about the Bayeux tapestry in contemporary terms when he encountered the actual artwork at the British Museum for hisreview of the landmark exhibition. “I’m always against grafting contemporary issues on to [historic] works of art,” he says. “Yet when I saw it, my genuine visceral response was to see some of those parallels. There is real horror in it – the horror of war – and it really did strike me very freshly.”View image in fullscreenA detail of the Bayeux tapestry depicting the scene of King Harold’s deathPhotograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersWhile the Bayeux tapestry might be made of frail linen, it’s hard to overstate its weight as a treasured artwork, historical document and, more latterly, an instrument ofFranco-British diplomatic goodwill. Edith was understandably unnerved by the prospect of trying to update it: “I depressed myself by looking at the tapestry online and thinking about how beautiful and amazing it is. I thought, ‘Oh no, I’m going to do this cheap rip-off of it’.”But she also felt inspired by the challenge. “I knew I was going to be wading into the big questions of today’s age,” she says. “I had an initial jumble of ideas and then picked out things that could be represented in an immediate visual language.” For instance, AI agents are depicted as retro-looking robots. However, she had to ditch some aspects of today’s tech-dominated world. “I would have loved to have included something about datacentres, but how do you draw a datacentre in a way that’s visually engaging? It would have looked rubbish.”The prominent role of tech titans proved prescient: last week, the Guardian revealed that the tech billionaire Peter Thiel had beengranted a private viewingof the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum ahead of the British and French heads of state.View image in fullscreenBritish prime minister Andy Burnham, French  president Emmanuel Macron and Britain’s King Charles attend a preview event for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition at the British MuseumPhotograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesGiven the tapestry’s political significance and history, how did Jonathan avoid approaching it with preconceptions? “I have a fairly visual mind and when I go to an exhibition I avoid reading captions and text as much as possible. I don’t read catalogues until years afterwards,” he explains. “If you focus on the visual experience, what you see is fresh and raw – you’re not seeing it through other people’s words. One of the problems I have as a critic is that, for perfectly good reasons, curators want to talk to you in a show, and I have to politely ask them to leave me alone. It needs to be about what’s directly in front of my eyes. That physical, visceral experience in a direct, unmediated way so that you just open yourself to the images.”View image in fullscreenA detail from Edith’s modern take on the Bayeaux TapestryIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianThe original artwork stretches to 68.3 metres long. Jonathan describes the experience of viewing it as almost cinematic. But as well as being swept along, his eyes were drawn to the intricate borders above and below the main narrative. These famously feature images of animals and symbolic portents that either mirror the story’s actions and emotions or provide a kind of ambiguous commentary. “So this felt like a whole multifaceted world that aspires to take in the whole of creation,” says Jonathan.In today’s speak, you could say the borders reveal the vibes. Re-creating them gave Edith further scope to show how some of today’s dystopian tendencies work in tandem. “For instance, I drew an incel narrative along the bottom border,” she says, pointing to images of red and blue pills beneath a scene about the manosphere. Other details include a bitcoin symbol beneath a superyacht; wall-mounted mirrors that literally reflect the social media-induced misery of teenagers; dead animals above an oil rig, while other animals succumb to phone addiction and grapple with four-legged AI robots.Edith refrained from illustrating some of the more horrifying consequences of today’s dynamics, such as droughts, wildfires and armed conflict, because she didn’t want to be reductive. “As an illustrator, you want to have a visual shorthand for things you’re trying to represent, but you also want to give them dignity. So there are certain things that, if you try to draw them, you would skip all nuance.”Despite the horrors depicted in the original tapestry, Jonathan was surprised by the levity of some of the panels. “The surreal and comedy aspects were surprising. It felt more contemporary than I thought it would be. It was more raw and shocking as well as funnier.”View image in fullscreenVisitors view the Bayeux tapestry on display at the British MuseumPhotograph: Toby Melville/ReutersDid the tapestry also seem contemporary in terms of its format and the ways in which people consume narrative content today? “You could say its time has come because we’re more visual,” he agrees. “We don’t read as much, and here’s this raw masterpiece of visual storytelling.”That said, building a digital version of Edith’s illustration presented unique challenges for our design team. “How do you show readers details in wide images when we’re all looking at these little vertical screens without chopping them up or pinching and zooming?” explains Tara Herman, the Guardian’s executive editor for design. The team’s solution was an interactive format that combines the act of scrolling vertically with the experience of viewing things unfold horizontally – almost as if you’re swiping instead of scrolling. “Our interactive format is an attempt to emulate the experience of being in a gallery where you’re taking your turn looking at a picture and pausing to take in different details.”This article is taken from the Guardian’s weekly email for supporters, sent on Tuesdays. title: Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can | John Harris | The Guardian
description: While fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online, ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge them, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: While fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online, ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge them, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianOpinionLiteracyWarning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still canJohn HarrisWhile fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online,  ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge themSun 13 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTShareImagine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organisedshows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth(and, on Wednesday, outside the Londonoffices of the Daily Mail, demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skipthrough 260 videos in under 35 minutes. And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for aworrying statistic from YouGov last week. Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.Those figures probably highlight one of the most worrying aspects of the times we live in: the decline of reading. Millions of us know what that phenomenon feels like: trying desperately to keep your attention glued to a book or news article with the nagging certainty that you will be tempted back to the more ephemeral attractions offered by your phone. But a background in the pre-digital world helps people not just follow national and global events, but clarify and contextualise them. In this case, at the risk of sounding hopelessly pompous, the fear many of us felt as we watched what happened in both ports was surely full of the perspectives gleaned from years of soaking up books and newspapers – and the sense that history often either repeats itself, or rhymes.Black-clad – let’s be honest: uniformed – menwho want to“reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British”, while claiming to be protecting women and girls: the whole spectacle was pitched halfway between Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts – and, therefore, Hitler and the Nazis – and the Ku Klux Klan, with the seemingly ubiquitous balaclavas lacing everything with a flavour of the Troubles. But if you receive most of your information in the form of a distracting and seemingly infinite jumble of random moving images, what would you know about most of that?All this crossed my mind thanks to anexcellent new bookmarking what may well be a transformative moment for societies all over the world. The New Dark Ages is the work of the Times columnist James Marriott, and subtitled The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society. Presumably to accommodate itself to the changes it describes, it is short: 208 pages. But it is also full of insight and urgency.In the 20 years since the UK’s National Literacy Trust began looking at children’s and young people’s reading, there has been a36% fall in the numberwho say they enjoy reading in their spare time, to its lowest level on record. In 2024, the Guardian reporteda survey by the Reading Agency charity, which found that 35% of adults said they were now “lapsed readers”, meaning that they used to regularly read for pleasure, but “rarely or never” did any more.View image in fullscreenBlack-clad men in balaclavas outside the offices of the Daily Mail in London, 9 September 2026.Photograph: Denise Laura Baker/Getty ImagesThe Atlantic magazine recently ran an articlebaldly headlined The End of Reading Is Here, whose author, Rose Horowitch, made plenty of sobering claims. “The literate era will prove to be a brief interlude between the oral and digital ages,” she wrote – and drew on no end of evidence and anecdotes. A program director at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, for instance, ran focus groups asking high-school students about recreational reading. The conclusion: “most thought of it as an alien practice”. When Marriott first wrote about this, he says, “some professors reported that it was not that the young men and women in their classes were unwilling to read, but that they seemed almost unable to”.In Britain, more than 320 newspapersclosed down between 2009 and 2019, a statistic the book follows with a stark suggestion: “It is increasingly possible to get through life without any exposure to the news at all.” In the wake of the 2016 Brexit referendum, I met people who said they had simply stopped paying attention to current affairs because they were so maddening: now, I wonder if what was really powering this switch-off was technology. The resulting ignorance – a strong word, but it feels justified – is firewalled by phone screens: it feels as if the only stuff that can break through has to be angry, paranoid and visually shocking.And because of the decline of reading, the people who purvey all the nonsense and poison can be increasingly confident that fewer and fewer people will come across anything halfway critical or analytical. In that sense, the screen age is exemplified by – oh yes – Donald Trump, who,according to an economic adviserin his first term, “won’t read anything – not one-page memos, not the brief policy papers, nothing”. His style of speechmaking is equally non-literate: as Marriott writes, “he doesn’t supply evidence for his ideas. Rather than organising his information analytically via clauses and subclauses in the manner of literate communication, he merely piles up assertions”.Hisproposed election bribe of $5,000is one surreal example, but there are plenty of others. I recently watched anonline video of Sean Duffy, the former Fox Business host who is now Trump’s secretary of transportation. He was rejoicing in the administration’s quest to do away with start-stop ignition buttons in cars – mainly, I sensed, because of some weird quasi-Freudian attachment to the phallic(ish) shape of traditional keys. Written down in an attempt at coherent argument, his case would have looked ridiculous. But folksily barked out as Duffy’s “pet peeve”, I could imagine it being warmly greeted by exactly the people it was aimed at. The same, of course, applies to any number of much more malignant Trumpian positions and passions: climate denial, brazen racism towards Somali-Americans, unapologetic Islamophobia and the idea that the US is about to be overrun by criminals and the occupants of other countries’ prisons and mental institutions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mass literacy is a recent phenomenon,” Marriott writes. “So is mass democracy. We simply don’t know whether one can survive without the other.” Meanwhile, on millions of screens, fascist faux-militias, populists funded by crypto tycoons,and other merchants of loathing and absurdity blur into acrobatic skateboarders, arguments on the tube and dogs that do tricks. That strips them of context and thereby normalises their rise – and inch by inch, we move towards a future with echoes of the past that too many people will have failed to understand. And this time, there will be no books to burn, because we will have stopped reading them.John Harris is a Guardian columnistThis article was amended on 13 September 2026. An earlier version misspelled Oswald Mosley’s surname.Explore more on these topicsLiteracyOpinionSocial mediaThe far rightTikTokcommentShareReuse this content

title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A rescue worker puts out a fire in a building destroyed after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Alex Babenko/APView image in fullscreenA rescue worker puts out a fire in a building destroyed after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Alex Babenko/APOpinionUkrainePutin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step inSimon TisdallThe Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their handsSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareUkraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life.Wave after waveof terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroyingsupermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia willagain try to blow upUkraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year,was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t.Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys,Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022,then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to producePatriot missile interceptorsand paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’snauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About60% oppose ceding Donbas landto Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians alsowant it to stop. And like Moscow,Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly adeal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump meet at the Elmendorf-Richardson military facility in Alaska, 15 August 2025.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APEfforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has nowextended to the Red Sea(Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modernforever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but towin a Nobel peace prize(plus lucrative Russian energy deals).Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas.Trump’s “board of peace”and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fearfighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led towar crime atrocitiessuch as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedlykilled more than 100 schoolgirlsin February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightlyrestricted international journalists’ accessto Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost ofsuccessful Iranian strikes on US basesin the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWestern democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly,urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Ketchup on a Sunday roast? This is the worst thing gen Z has ever done | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Swapping roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for kimchi and avocado – how can they live with themselves?
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Swapping roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for kimchi and avocado – how can they live with themselves?
Content: Sacrilegious … survey shows a rise in a monstrous use of ketchup.Photograph: Liudmila Chernetska/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSacrilegious … survey shows a rise in a monstrous use of ketchup.Photograph: Liudmila Chernetska/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleKetchup on a Sunday roast? This is the worst thing gen Z has ever donePolly HudsonSwapping roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for kimchi and avocado – how can they live with themselves?Sun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTShareTrigger warning: the following contains a description of the most heinous abomination known to humankind. Ready? A diabolical 39% of gen Z add ketchup to their Sunday roast. This is as sacrilegious as it is unappetising. But what makes it even more appalling is that these monsters aren’t even ashamed. Instead of lurking in the shadows, hiding their Heinz, they’re happily admitting to their culinary crime in anew survey.And their misdemeanours do not end there. In news that is particularly distressing on the eve of glorious roast season, it turns out they’re also exchanging roast potatoes and yorkshire puddings for hot sauce, kimchi and – sounds like a punchline, but isn’t – literally avocado.Sorry, buthow dare they? You do not mess with perfection, which is what a roast is – that’s why so many of us choose it for our imaginary death row last meal. It’s comforting, delicious, a ritual and a treat. Peak food. Never mind the audacity of tweaking it at all – the tweaks themselves add insult to injury. The roast potato is the star of the plate, for goodness sake! Substituting it is like taking Meryl Streep out of a movie, and replacing her with … well, an avocado.Gen Z are also determined to cut off their noses to spite their faces, with a horrifying 14% of them eschewing gravy. This is clearly a travesty. Leaving your roast dry is not allowing it to achieve its full potential, cheating it of fulfilling its destiny. How can they live with themselves?The danger of this knowledge is that some people will do just about anything to look younger. That means there may now be individuals asking for ketchup, and no gravy thanks, simply to try to seem cool, down with the kids. They deserve all they get, which will be a ruined roast – a fate worse than no roast at all. Perhaps afterwards they can then settle down with a good film – something like The Avocado Wears Prada.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘An error of judgement’: Pro Ref admits mistake in awarding Haaland’s derby winner | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Pro Ref has admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have counted after the VAR ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Pro Ref has admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have counted after the VAR ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup
Content: Enzo Fernández dives at the ball from an offside position as Lisandro Martínez appeals, before Erling Haaland turns in Manchester City’s winner.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández dives at the ball from an offside position as Lisandro Martínez appeals, before Erling Haaland turns in Manchester City’s winner.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesManchester United‘An error of judgement’: Pro Ref admits mistake in awarding Haaland’s derby winnerOfficiating body announces it will review the incidentUnhappy Carrick says error was ‘as obvious as it gets’Jamie Jacksonat Old TraffordSun 13 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePro Ref admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have been allowed after the video assistant referee ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the build-up. The elite officiating body will review the decision and has contactedManchester United.Manchester City recover from Foden red card as Haaland wins derby at UnitedRead moreHaaland’s 60th minute goal forManchester Cityat Old Trafford was initially ruled offside before the VAR’s intervention. It came after Josko Gvardiol’s cross hit Patrick Dorgu’s boot, passed Fernández and the United defender Lisandro Martínez, and was finished by the City No 9. VAR decided Fernández was not interfering despite Martínez marking the midfielder.A Pro Ref statement said: “Following the incident in the 60th minute of Sunday’s Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Manchester City at Old Trafford, we can provide clarification regarding Erling Haaland’s awarded goal.“The on-field decision was offside against Haaland – that was checked by VAR and he was found to be in an onside position.“In the same attack, it was established that Fernández did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective, however, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review.“Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place.”After the match but before the Pro Ref statement, an unhappyMichael Carrickexpressed concern over Haaland’s winner.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“At the time I hadn’t totally seen it. But the explanation I got was he wasn’t interfering with play, so I just don’t get it,” the United manager said. “I can’t understand how they’re trying to help referees and putting so many layers behind them with so many people, screens, and so many whatever offices to try and come up with the right decisions.“If that’s how the rules are interpreted, that you’re not interfering with play because you’ve thrown yourself at the ball six yards from goal and pretty much nearly touched it, which then Lisandro has to react from – it’s worrying if that’s really how the game’s seen by those who are officiating it.”Carrick was asked if an apology from Pro Ref would be welcome. “Yeah, that’d be great, that. Yeah, I can’t wait for that one,” he said. “I don’t really know how you go and get another explanation on that one. I think we all understand what that rule means [regarding interfering with play], and it’s pretty obvious. It’s as obvious as it gets.”Enzo Maresca, though, was adamant that Fernández was not interfering. “Yeah – and the fourth official said Erling is onside,” the City manager said.The 199th Manchester derby’s other controversial decision was Phil Foden’s 23rd-minute red card. The forward kicked Bruno Fernandes in the stomach, but only after United’s captain had kicked him. Maresca backed Michael Oliver’s red card but suggested the referee should also have sent off Fernandes.“Phil Foden red card is a red card, but I also think it is red card from Bruno,” City’s manager said. “Reviewing the action, it is a clear red card for Phil because it is a reaction but you can also see Bruno’s [action].”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick looks on from the touchline during the Manchester derby.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCity now have 12 points, second only to Arsenal on goal difference, while United have only four points and are 13th. “We will get there, I’m convinced of that,” Carrick said.“We haven’t got as many points as we wanted and we should have. We’ve got to accept that and take that. It doesn’t change us moving forward and our hopes for the season and what we can achieve as a team. We’ve made really good strides over a period of time and we will continue to do that.”Carrick was asked about the pre-game protest against the club’s move to eradicate ticket touts that some believe to be draconian. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.Carrick said: “The details in terms of all what goes behind it, I’m not always in line to get to the bottom of it, but I definitely appreciate the supporters.“If they do feel [unhappy] in certain ways then, of course, we want to try everything to make them happy. That’s part of performances on the pitch and off the pitch. That’s obvious. They’re a huge part of this football club. They’re everything for this football club.”Inside the stadium The Red Army hung a banner over the tunnel that said, “The Way You Treat Us Is A Disgrace.” All usual banners were removed from the Stretford End.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickEnzo MarescaManchester CityErling HaalandRefereesVideo assistant referees (VARs)newsShareReuse this content

title: Alexander Zverev claims first US Open after four-set battle with Ben Shelton | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Alexander Zverev, the No 1 seed, beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2, the American’s hopes dashed in his first grand slam final
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Alexander Zverev, the No 1 seed, beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2, the American’s hopes dashed in his first grand slam final
Content: Alexander Zverev celebrates with the US Open trophy after beating Ben Shelton.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenAlexander Zverev celebrates with the US Open trophy after beating Ben Shelton.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026Alexander Zverev claims first US Open after four-set battle with Ben SheltonNo 1 seed wins 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2American’s hopes dashed in tense finalTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsSun 13 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a passing moment at the end of a rugged third set, hope sprung anew for Ben Shelton. He had been outserved and outplayed for nearly three hours, but at 6-5 in the third set, one game from defeat, the American finally broke through. He burst into the return game finally pounding his forehand freely and he willed himself into an unexpected fourth set.After he had finished pumping his fist, cupping his ear to the crowd and admirably trying to initiate a drastic momentum shift, the next sequence was most revealing. Shelton opened the fourth set with a shaky game, immediately losing his serve at the start of the set. He worked hard until the end, but he was beaten by Zverev, the top seed, who closed out a 6-3, 7-6 (2), 5-7, 6-2 victory to lift his second grand slam title of the year.Elena Rybakina joins elite with US Open title but questions remain over coach | Tumaini CarayolRead moreHaving started his season desperately searching for his first major title, Zverev has become just the fourth man in the open era, after Jimmy Connors, Guillermo Vilas and Jannik Sinner to win his first two grand slam titlesin the same campaign.He ended Shelton’s hopes of becoming the first Black American man since Arthur Ashe in 1968 and the first American man since Andy Roddick in 2003 to win the US Open.Perhaps the most relevant detail in this rivalry is the head to head. Zverev now leads Shelton 6-0, a comfortable match-up for the German who served far better than Shelton, remained far steadier from the baseline and, as usual, nullified the effects of the left-hander’s forehand with the quality of his elite two-handed backhand.In a match between two of the biggest servers, the first job for both players was to take care of his service. A visibly tense Shelton served terribly during the decisive moments of the first set, double-faulting on break point in the first game of the match. Shelton then double-faulted on set point to hand over a second break. He was no match for Zverev from the baseline, and his forehand was far too erratic. Zverev, meanwhile, served extremely well throughout the match, landing 69% of first serves and winning 85% of first-serve points.Shelton managed to build rhythm behind his service games in set two, putting Zverev under some pressure by forcing a tie-break, but the German handled the most important moment of the match well. He snatched the first mini-break with an excellent forehand passing-shot winner off a timid approach from Shelton, then he ended a similarly tense exchange with a vicious down-the-line forehand to take the second mini-break. Two big unreturned serves later, Zverev led 5-0 in the tie-break and the set was all but over.Although Shelton worked hard to force a fourth set, it did not take long for Zverev to close out a victory that appeared inevitable from the first game.View image in fullscreenBen Shelton was left face down after one gruelling rally.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAThis match was a fitting ending to a dreary grand slam season on the ATP tour that has been dictated by the injuries and physical issues suffered by Carlos Alcaraz, who returned from a long injury layoff at this tournament, and Jannik Sinner. Their challenges presented so many players at the top of the sport with golden opportunities to step up and compete for major titles, but so few of them over the past five months even managed to put themselves in real contention. Zverev has been rewarded for his consistency and ability to continue to put himself in positive positions deep in the majors. Each victory has clearly strengthened him mentally.For plenty of tennis fans and viewers around the world, however, no amount of on-court success can erase the discomfort that comes with seeing Zverev succeed. He has been accused by two of his former girlfriends, Olya Sharypova and Brenda Patea, of physical abuse. In June 2024, during his run to the French Open final, Zverev settled an assault case against him in Germanyfor allegedly pushing and strangling Patea, his ex-girlfriend and the mother of their daughter. The case was declared no verdict, with a court spokesperson stating: “The truth remains open.” Zverev denied those charges and he has denied all allegations against him.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFastPasses, Mega Honey Deuces and $55 chopped cheese: welcome to the US Open in 2041 | Bryan Armen GrahamRead moreAt the Australian Open last year, Zverev was heckled by a fan before his trophy ceremony speech, with the fan declaring: “Australia believes Olya and Brenda.” Zverev’s three grand slam finals this year have progressed without issue and he remains a popular player at major tournaments.For Shelton, who began his North American hard court swing attempting to recover from a painful first round loss at Wimbledon, the greatest summer of his career included a second Masters 1000 title at the Canadian Open, a first grand slam final and a new career high ranking of No 4.His success is testament to his continued improvement and at 23 years old there is much more to come. However, some of those deficiencies, particularly his ground game and return of serve, can still be exposed by the elite, as it was during his lonely Sunday afternoon inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own making | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Refereeing is now an impossible job owing to the culture of micro-analysis the Arsenal manager has helped to create
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Refereeing is now an impossible job owing to the culture of micro-analysis the Arsenal manager has helped to create
Content: Mikel Arteta took issue with Sunderland’s penalty award in Arsenal’s win on Saturday.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta took issue with Sunderland’s penalty award in Arsenal’s win on Saturday.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APPremier LeagueAnalysisArteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own makingBarney RonayRefereeing is now an impossible job owing to the culture of micro-analysis the Arsenal manager has helped to createSun 13 Sep 2026 16.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareA gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. Nobody really knows who said this first. But it could easily be a line from the Elite Football Manager’s Guide to Press Conferences (Premier League edition). Because nothing happens by accident in these spaces.Every word spoken in front of the board covered in adverts is metered and planned. A manager is never angry, or concerned, or even charming unintentionally. The gameisthe game, but so are all the other bits spilling out either side of it.‘An error of judgement’: Pro Ref admits mistake in awarding Haaland’s derby winnerRead moreIt was hard not to think about this while listening to Mikel Arteta talk about thepenalty awarded to Sunderlandat the Stadium of Light for a perceived act of grappling on Dan Ballard by Ezri Konsa. This is said with genuine professional respect. As everyone who has ever done a podcast knows – and this is, let’s be clear, everyone – there are lost Amazonian tribes discussing Girls season three in their own dark corner of Spotify – there are moments when you just have to flip the switch, up the energy and turn on full clip‑this‑bit‑up‑please‑Dave sincerity mode.Arteta did this beautifully in the moment, appearing genuinely struck by what he was saying, radiating wounded integrity, like a disappointed junior headmaster appealing for the return of the school minibus keys.Let’s be clear though. Arteta is not “very worried” about all this. He’s not “sad” or indeed, as he later emphasised for good measure, “really sad”. He’s not concerned solely with “protecting the game”, speaking here for all of us, just a fan of football.Come off it. This is a manager we know to be obsessed with the most marginal of gains, to micro-plan the micro-details. As is all elite sport now. There has been talk of rowing coaches installing fibreglass toilet seats at their training hubs having calculated the average athlete spends 20 minutes in there and this is all key glute management time. Arteta loves this stuff. There’s no way Ben White isn’t sat fiddling with his phone at the training ground on a gold-standard Easy‑Cup Mega-Soft Evacu-Throne.So it is with his public statements. This will have all been gamed and contingency‑planned in advance. And for hard, rational, tactical reasons, because this is how the game is played and run now. So what does it mean?View image in fullscreenEzri Konsa is penalised for a contentious foul on Dan Ballard in the box.Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThere are three things we know for sure. First, Arteta was right. This was a bad refereeing decision. Most obviously it was factually wrong. Ballard very skilfully pulled Konsa down on top of him, while simultaneously feigning shock that such a thing could happen.It was doubly bad because the referee’s response was pre-planned, flagged by the early-season chat about refereeing in a more interventionist fashion. Go into any situation with a voice in your head, a vaguely worded mission to fulfil: this will skew your judgment.The second thing is that referees are not biased. They’re just not very good. Two things have happened to them. First, the barrage of information to be absorbed in real time during a game is now utterly mind-boggling.Most referees are not from a high-pressure data-processing background. These are not military pilots or traders on a currency floor. Less than a quarter have an academic degree. The task is beyond them. This is not a slur or an insult. It’s a simple description of what is happening, as supported by the evidence.This is doubly annoying because referees have become fundamentally confused about their role.Refereesare not ringmasters, or curators of the spectacle. They don’t get to decide what our sport should look like. Pro Ref is a private company with nolocus standito rule on the aesthetics of football. A referee should exist at the very edge of the spectacle. You’re not a local government planning officer with a mandate to decide which double-glazed French doors are or aren’t in character with the neighbourhood. Stop getting football not just wrong, butwrong.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta has a word with the fourth official, Elliot Bell, at Sunderland.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersBut Arteta was also ready for this. Arsenal’s coaches will have known this would happen at some point. That press conference response was already in the chamber. Arteta may even have practised his sad-not-angry face, his key lines.And this would be the correct thing to do. None of this is breaking the rules, just as Arsenal are not a dirty team or a bunch of cheats. They play the game that is being presented to us, a sport that is being made to operate at the edge of its own ludicrously micro‑analysed rules on small issues of physical contact.Arteta’s Arsenal have been masterful at finding advantages in this. Defenders are very good at playing with the ball at their feet now. Defenders are not selected for their ability to resist physical challenges. It is logical to exploit this, just as it is logical to seek to protect your ability to do so by speaking in public about how the rules are applied. This is why Arteta is good, and why he wins.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is also true that this has created a strange environment. The tone of the wider Arsenal fanbase is another element here. There is no one type of football fan. All human life is here. But the fact remains, the loudest voices in the online Arsenal hive mind, even the atmosphere in the stadium is unique in its absolute conviction of victimhood, of conspiracy, of a galvanising sense of adversity.There is no other ground where every single refereeing decision, even the who-knows 50-50s, is so violently and eloquently disputed. There are supporters who seem to spend most of the game up on their feet in a state of performative, weaponised indignation, whose entire interaction with the spectacle is an attitude of aggrieved injustice.This makes sense, too. It speaks directly to the game we have created. Aggrieved middle-aged rule pedantry. This is the new cauldron of hate.View image in fullscreenSet-piece grappling was a theme once more in Arsenal’s win at Sunderland.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APIs it based in reality? Not perhaps on the outline numbers. Arsenal have been awarded more fouls than any other team this season. Only six teams last season had more fouls awarded against them, and the same the year before. They had the fewest yellow cards last season. They haven’t had a single red since they had six of them in 2024‑25.Still, certain key incidents continue to grate and fester. There was the incorrectly denied penalty claim for Bruno Guimarãesat Aston Villa. The balls-up with VAR lines against Brentford in 2023, which, if it really was deliberate conspiracy-cheating, was the worst, most public attempt at deliberate conspiracy-cheating ever conceived.There is discontent at the way some rules seem to be applied more severely to Arsenal, the silly little stuff like delaying or fiddling about with restarts. But then again, if you make the game about that, if you plan to play on the margins, and successfully so, more stuff might happen in that place while you’re doing it.Arteta has also played the role of arms-length rage conjurer expertly, has gone from rarely commenting on referees to heartfelt and carefully targeted critic. TheSunderlandpenalty award was a first opportunity to unload on the refereeing backlash to Arsenal’s tactics, to launch his pre-prepared defence; and to point out something demonstrably true. Referees have lost control of this, because the game has got beyond them.In many ways this was a perfect storm for Arteta. Not just a decision that didn’t matter, because the penalty was saved. But a decision that was clearly incorrect too, a chance to get your lobbying in while very obviously in the right.There will be more of this as the season plays out, as Arsenal work to preserve the advantages they have made for themselves in close quarters, tactical attack and defence. Factor in that masterful turn at a press conferencej’accuse, and Saturday was a significant win in more ways than one.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueMikel ArtetaArsenalSunderlandRefereesanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘No stopping him’: Hamilton admits defeat as Antonelli charges towards F1 world title | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton has conceded his Formula One world title hopes are over after he retired and Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton has conceded his Formula One world title hopes are over after he retired and Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix
Content: Lewis Hamilton had to retire on lap six in Madrid after a brake problem.Photograph: Eleanor Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton had to retire on lap six in Madrid after a brake problem.Photograph: Eleanor Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockFormula One 2026‘No stopping him’: Hamilton admits defeat as Antonelli charges towards F1 world titleRetirement in Madrid leaves Hamilton 101 points backAntonelli leads way by 81 points after Spanish GP winGiles Richardsat the MadringSun 13 Sep 2026 15.17 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLewis Hamilton has conceded his Formula One world title hopes are over as he praised the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, saying there was no stopping the Italian afterhis victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.Hamilton, in third place in the championship, had to retire from the race at the Madring with a brake problem on lap six. After Antonelli’s victory it leaves the seven-time world champion 101 points behind the 20-year-old Italian, who took over his seat at Mercedes when Hamilton joinedFerrari.Kimi Antonelli holds off Max Verstappen during Madring debut to win F1 Spanish GPRead more“There’s no stopping him and Mercedes this year,” Hamilton said. “They’ve done a phenomenal job and they deserve it.”George Russell, Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate, is in second place 81 points behind with nine meetings remaining, a chasm. But Hamilton, whowon his first race for Ferrariat Barcelona this season, insisted he felt there was still more to come from the team, even if Antonelli could not be caught.“I think we have a good [car]. We’ve had a pretty decent car, a good car this weekend and we will continue to try and improve it and we have better results coming in the future.”Antonelli’s win came after Lando Norris was unlucky with the timing of a virtual safety car, called just after the McLaren driver had passed the pit entry. Antonelli, behind Norris on track, was able to dive into the pits under the VSC and subsequently Norris lost track position. He was unable to make it back with overtaking all but impossible at the circuit and finished third.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The defending world champion felt it was unfair and it was time the rules around pit stops under the VSC were reconsidered. “It just hurts because there was nothing more I could do as a driver.I got pole, I led the race, and to lose it for nothing in my control is not how a race should be won,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There are things that can be changed to make it more simple, and more fair. We could be covered for at least one lap and that allows us all the opportunity to do a pit-stop, or the pit entry could be blocked. This needs to be part of a wider discussion, and as a group of drivers, I think it is something we would all want.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonKimi AntonelliFerrariFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Josh Kerr bags $150,000 for 1500m victory at Ultimate Championship | Athletics | The Guardian
description: The Scot won with ease ahead of Yared Nuguse and Cameron Myers, while Charlotte Henrich’s final leg earned Britain silver in the 4x400m mixed relay
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Scot won with ease ahead of Yared Nuguse and Cameron Myers, while Charlotte Henrich’s final leg earned Britain silver in the 4x400m mixed relay
Content: Josh Kerr produced a substantial lead over the rest of the field to win the men’s 1500m.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPAView image in fullscreenJosh Kerr produced a substantial lead over the rest of the field to win the men’s 1500m.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/EPAAthleticsJosh Kerr bags $150,000 for 1500m victory at Ultimate ChampionshipScot wins with ease ahead of Nuguse and MyersHenrich’s final leg earns Britain silver in mixed relaySean Inglein BudapestSun 13 Sep 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThroughout Josh Kerr’s perfect season, he has made the sublime look routine. So when the bell rang for the final lap of the men’s Ultimate 1500m final, with the Scot in third and closing on the leader, Yared Nuguse, the next 53 seconds felt preordained.So it proved. First Kerr sauntered past Robert Farken into second. Then with 250m remaining, he scootered past Nuguse. The 20‑year‑old Australian star Cam Myers chased valiantly but Kerr smoothly nursed a three-metre lead to the finish.‘Just making a joke’: Usain Bolt retracts claim stairs got him out of breathRead moreAs Kerr crossed the line in 3min 29.35sec, with Myers 0.33 back, he cupped his hand to his ear. The sound he was hearing? The adoration of the crowd, and the kerching of the $150,000 (£111,000) first prize. “To be honest, I didn’t feel amazing in the warmup,” Kerr said. “But these are the things you have to overcome.”Asked about Myers, who won the Diamond League final last week, Kerr replied: “He’s an awesome athlete but I was able to peek over the screen. I pressed again at 120m, and then the gap didn’t change, and I knew that at that point I had it.”The only shame was that Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who won a brilliant 5,000m victory on Friday, decided to skip what would have been a mouthwatering clash. But Kerr was generous to his great rival afterwards, describing Ingebrigtsen’s victory as “very impressive” and praising his decision to rest up to protect the longevity of his career.Kerr will now take a holiday having ended his season having shattered the world mile record and walked away with three major prizes: world indoor championship gold over 3,000m, Commonwealth Games gold over the mile, and now the Ultimate Championship trophy. But the 28-year-old continues to have big plans for the future – including an attempt on the world 1500m record next year. “I want to roll this into 2027 and 2028,” he said.“These are the peak years, and we’re really starting to get some offensive going. But I’m a human being, and I understand the highs of the sport are sometimes followed by a lot of real lows. I had that in 2025. I’m not taking it for granted.”View image in fullscreenCharlotte Henrich (centre) gained three places to earn Britain silver and $10,000 each for herself and her teammates.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAElsewhere the American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden had plenty of jaws crashing to the floor in the 200m. Against the Olympic champion Gabby Thomas, Jefferson-Wooden ran 21:47 – the fourth fastest time in history. It was 0.13sec off Florence Griffith Joyner’s world record, despite a -0.6m/s headwind.Thomas was second in an impressive 21.77, while Britain’s Amy Hunt was fourth in a season’s best 22.10 in what was her 47th race of the year.“My coach has given us eight weeks off,” Hunt said. “I’m not an early-morning person and so I’m looking forward to being on the beach, spending time with my family, and try to pack it with fun stuff – art galleries, museums, and the cinema.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier, the new 400m hurdles world record-holder, Alison Dos Santos, again proved he was top dog in his event by running the third fastest time in history, 45.98, against the world champion, Rai Benjamin, and the former world champion Karsten Warholm. “What we are doing is so important and so impressive that people sometimes take it for granted,” Benjamin said, which seemed an entirely fair comment given the trio now hold the 38 best times in history.In the men’s javelin, Rumesh Pathirage capped a brilliant breakthrough season by throwing 91.09m to take first prize – and said later that cricket had helped him to become the best in the world. “I inputted almost all my technique from cricket into the javelin throw because there are some similarities,” he said.In the men’s 800m, Marco Arop’s brave frontrunning tactics came just short of sealing victory as he was overtaken by the Algerian Djamel Sedjati, who won in 1:41.91.There were two other spectacular performances on the night. In the high jump, the Italian Gianmarco Tamberi jumped a world-leading 2.37m to take first, while in the men’s 200m Kenny Bednarek ran a world lead 19.52 sec to comfortably beat the Olympic champion, Letsile Tebogo, who ran 19.76 in second.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe win Solheim Cup against USA to give captain Anna Nordqvist last laugh | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: The captain Anna Nordqvist led Europe to a 15-13 victory in the Solheim Cup a month after retiring from competitive golf
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: The captain Anna Nordqvist led Europe to a 15-13 victory in the Solheim Cup a month after retiring from competitive golf
Content: Anna Nordqvist lifts the Solheim Cup at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenAnna Nordqvist lifts the Solheim Cup at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APSolheim CupEurope win Solheim Cup against USA to give captain Anna Nordqvist last laughEurope beat USA 15-13 after 7-5 win in singles matchesLottie Woad seals victory with putt against Auston KimEwan Murrayat Bernardus GolfSun 13 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEyebrows were raised when Anna Nordqvist somewhat abruptly announced her retirement from competitive golf last month at the age of just 39. Heads were turned when Nordqvist keptSolheim Cupfaith with the pairing of Charley Hull and Lottie Woad despite a miserable points return in the Netherlands. Nordqvist sounded unsure about elements of the Solheim Cup’s captains’ agreement before a ball was whacked in anger. The last laugh belongs to the Swede herself, who can sail off into the sunset having added a triumphant Solheim Cup captaincy to a career that had already returned three major wins.What a rousing afternoon this soon became for women’s golf in Europe. The understated Nordqvist was on the podium once more.Solheim Cup golf 2026: final day – Europe seal glory after dominant singles victory over USARead moreThe wait for a USA win on foreign soil, stretching back to 2015, goes on. Europe are due huge praise for their singles performance here, which had felt unlikely from a four-session ­position of an 8-8 tie. Nordqvist and her players, including four rookies, were underdogs. On day three, there was seldom any doubt they would upset the odds. The record books will show 15-13 as the margin of victory when, in essence, there was more between the teams on Sunday.“I think there has just been so many emotions bottled up,” ­Nordqvist said. “It’s just been such a long road. It’s been a lot of hard work. It’s been really hard retiring weeks ago, then doing this and doing them both at the same time.“I’ve been living my dream. I’m forever grateful for everything that’s happened. It doesn’t feel like I worked a day in my life. Having my family support from very far away, living in the US on my own, but to have them here at every single ­Solheim Cup, and now to share it with my nieces and nephews, seeing my brothers cry, my sister-in-law, it’s just always been a family affair for me.”In fact, it feels inadequate that ­Nordqvist wants to step away from it all.The defining moment belonged to Woad. Her tap-in to secure a 2up win against Auston Kim meant Europe reached 14 points. Carlota Ciganda was 3up on Jennifer Kupcho with the same number of holes to play, ­meaning the 14½ Europe needed to reclaim the trophy was inevitable. Ciganda made sure she won, which completed the formality of taking Europe to 15 points. “I am very happy to do this for Anna,” Ciganda said.View image in fullscreenLottie Woad drinks in the celebrations after sealing victory in her match against Auston Kim.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesThere was also an element of revenge for Ciganda, who was undone by two moments of brilliance by Kupchoin Saturday’s fourball session. On Saturday evening Ciganda received a message of encouragement from José María Olazábal, her Spanish compatriot and a Ryder Cup icon.Europe flew out of the traps. Hull played like a golfer with a point to prove in seeing off Megan Khang 3&2 in the opening match. Hull justified her captain’s constant faith by winning the opening hole and staying ahead from that juncture. “It was a no-brainer to put Charley first,” Nordqvist said.“We saw the stats yesterday, ­Charley and Lottie were actually in the top‑four players that made the most birdies for the week. They just played really tough matches. People don’t understand how good all these ­players are and how good the golf has been all day in the last three days.“Lottie has been playing so good this week and not really getting anything off of it. But holing the winning putt, I don’t think that’s ever going to be hard to remember for her.” Hull was being force-fed champagne by her captain as victory sunk in.Esther Henseleit rampaged to 4up on Alison Lee after seven and still that after 11. What happened next is the finest comeback in Solheim Cup history. Lee won on the final green.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCarlota Ciganda brings up Europe’s 15th point on the 16th green against Jennifer Kupcho.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APThe problem for Angela Stanford and her USA team was the lack of progress to back up Lee’s sensational work. Sweden’s Linn Grant comfortably dispatched Angel Yin. Nanna Koerstz Madsen saw off Allisen Corpuz. Nastasia Nadaud, who excelled on her Solheim debut, defeated Andrea Lee for yet another European point. Julia López Ramírez supplied further blue.Leona Maguire surprisingly lost, 2&1 against Lauren Coughlin, but Woad’s moment had arrived anyway by that point. The USA achieved another win with Lindy ­Duncan’s 3&1 success against Maja Stark. Céline ­Boutier and Rose Zhang in game 12 were in the unenviable position of playing out a match with the ­destination of the cup already clear. Zhang took the honours on the last green with a European party well under way.“I felt like we did a lot of things right,” Stanford said. “The ­Europeans played great today and that’s the way it goes. Their backs were against the wall, they had absolutely nothing to lose and they came out and played well. I try not to have regrets, I believed in all 12 players.”Stanford’s subsequent comments made it sound unlikely she will have the chance for redemption at Valhalla in 2028.
