Paula Creamer is among those in a “pipeline” of potential captains to which Stanford referred.This was a competition played in excellent spirit, save a moment on Sunday when Korda had words with a member of the gallery who was a little overenthusiastic in their European support. Otherwise, Bernardus served up a wonderful sporting spectacle. Nordqvist will for ever relish it.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Fleming inherits intriguing squad after England’s unsettling summer | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The new Test head coach’s arrival and Joe Root’s calming influence as captain add to promising signs in the post-Stokes era
Author: Ali Martin
Headline: The new Test head coach’s arrival and Joe Root’s calming influence as captain add to promising signs in the post-Stokes era
Content: Joe Root is keen to meet Stephen Fleming as the new Test head coach arrives in the UK this week.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoe Root is keen to meet Stephen Fleming as the new Test head coach arrives in the UK this week.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamStephen Fleming inherits intriguing squad after England’s unsettling summerNew Test head coach’s arrival and Root’s calming influence as captain add to promising signs in the post-Stokes eraAli MartinSun 13 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Joe Root calmly ran the rule over the Test summer and reeled off the ways in which it had been “chaos”, “unusual” and “unsettling” for England, it felt telling that first among them was Ben Stokescalling time on his international careerduring a match and a series that were both still live at the time.Cricketers announcing their retirement mid-game is nothing new. Heather Knightwent on to do the sameduring the women’s Test at Lord’s two weeks later. Root is also too loyal to Stokes to question openly whether that scene-stealing exit before New Zealand’s win at Trent Bridge was entirely in keeping with his call for “selfless cricketers” four years earlier.England in better shape after ‘coming through chaos’ of a torrid summer, says Joe RootRead moreBut even with two drink-related incidents either side, it was the week when England bottomed out: their first home defeat for 14 years in a series of three or more Tests, and one that had the Black Caps quite literally laughing in their faces during the final throes.Since becoming unhooked from the emotions of Stokes, and realising they would never shake the stigma of Bazball without Brendon McCullum’s removal as Test head coach, things have settled down a touch for England (the sight of Brydon Carse in handcuffs in Derby, Stokes lurking in the shadows, notwithstanding).They also got a taste of how New Zealand felt in June, or Australia during the Ashes last winter,claiming the winbut seeing the losers hog much of the focus. For all that the21‑year‑old Razaullahdeserved the headlines at Edgbaston, with his jaw-dropping 81 in keeping with south Birmingham’s love for unexpected fireworks, Pakistan were a reminder that there are different levels of dysfunction.Scraps with Saracens players? A curfew that may or may not have been spelled out correctly? I’ll raise youseven players sent home, a head coach and bowling coach likewise, mobile phones seized, and a light shone on a government-run board that would sooner no one thought about the plight of the country’s greatest captain. As Saj Sadiq, the editor ofPakPassion.netand someone who has seen it all over the years, neatly put it: “As an entire series, this has been the most embarrassing and difficult to watch. On and off the field Pakistan have been an absolute shambles.”View image in fullscreenPakistan’s 21-year-old Razaullah deserved the headlines after his 81 at Edgbaston.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesFor all thatPakistan were easy-beats, it would be wrong to call this a wasted summer for England. Stephen Fleming may not be arriving in the UK until this week (Root is itching to finally meet his new head coach in person after a long-distance courtship) but he will have learned a fair bit about the team he inherits while catching up with the highlights over his cornflakes in Canterbury.For one, a promising stable of fast bowlers is emerging. Ollie Robinson has returned to devastating effect, Jofra Archer’s appetite for Test cricket lives on beyond Stokes, while Josh Tongue has hardened up physically and is becoming a significant weapon. Gus Atkinson’s returns dipped after the Rex Rooms and a change of role, but it was also the quickest that England’s quiet man has bowled across a season.There are caveats, of course. The ball dominated the bat – a wicket every 41 deliveries led to the lowest strike-rate in England since the 1880s – and Pakistan’s batters were a wet paper bag in terms of resistance. The one time conditions eased – a good Edgbaston pitch, plus a ball that went soft after getting damp the previous evening – England lacked a bit of bite and struggled for breakthroughs.Root also had a couple of familiar nightmares against the tail; Razaullah’s assault and when standing in for Stokes at the Oval in June. Marcus Trescothick, the interim head coach against Pakistan but unsure of his future place in the Test setup, fancies Fleming will be a good fit for Root here, as a tactically astute captain and the most decorated coach in the hothouse of the Indian Premier League.What lies beneath the four first‑choice quicks is a question mark as thoughts turn to South Africa in December. A personal view is that Olly Stone’s late‑summer county form with Nottinghamshire should help him leapfrog the kids on the cab rank. And clearly the lack of a frontline spinner continues. One wonders if Fleming will want a Daniel Vettori-type – multifunctional – with Liam Patterson-White one such candidate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFleming’s own experiences as a player may also be relevant to a batting lineup that racked up 23 half-centuries this summer, with only Ben Duckett going past three figures. Fleming scored 10 before his first Test century, so may be able to ease the pressure that Dan Lawrence, for example, keeps putting on himself.Every team strives for a settled lineup but Fleming may like the current tension for spots that will require a tricky call when Jacob Bethell is fit. Emilio Gay, likely to tour but already seeing his ceiling questioned, looks most vulnerable in terms of the XI. But this will mean manufacturing an opener to partner Duckett, who aside from his 113 at Trent Bridge has seemed caught in two minds post-Bazball.View image in fullscreenStephen Fleming was the most decorated coach in the IPL before joining England.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAJordan Cox may be the one pushed up which, given the ninth over was the latest the No 3 appeared against Pakistan, is not a huge change of role. While like Lawrence he fell short of a defining score, settling for three half-centuries, Cox made an impression through his presence at the crease; almost cocksure, with Root admitting: “I didn’t really know what to make of him when I first met him.”Cox has said on record that he has been trying to outdo Root which, while made easier by one of the captain’s quieter summers, is a pretty high bar of 14,000‑plus Test runs. But it’s probably also the template for this team post‑Stokes: to look to their captain not for inspirational moments or residual aura but as the quieter embodiment of what is required to thrive at Test level.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamJoe RootBen StokesCricketfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lauren James revels in free role as Chelsea show ‘respect’ by scoring five past Manchester United | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea dominated in a 5-0 away victory against Eva Olid’s Manchester United
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea dominated in a 5-0 away victory against Eva Olid’s Manchester United
Content: Lauren James and Keira Walsh (right) were both on the scoresheet for Chelsea.Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLauren James and Keira Walsh (right) were both on the scoresheet for Chelsea.Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueLauren James revels in free role as Chelsea show ‘respect’ by scoring five past Manchester UnitedSuzanne Wrackat Leigh Sports VillageSun 13 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA swaggering Chelsea cast off any suggestion that they had lost the ability to kill off games, putting five goals past a worryingly lacklustre and lackadaisical Manchester United.Sonia Bompastor, the Chelsea manager, said: “When you have the opportunity to really hurt a team, the best way to respect them is to score as many goals as you can, to create as many opportunities as you can.London City’s superstars brought down to earth in WSL defeat at West HamRead more“Of course, it’s never easy to see the other team or the other manager concede five goals because if I was the other team, I would be really sad. For me, showing respect to the opponent is having that desire and mentality to score as many goals as possible. That’s the difference between the great teams and the good teams.”United’s players and fans may have preferred disrespect if that is the case. Instead, it was another bruising result for the new manager, Eva Olid, and her side after an underwhelming performance in their2-1 defeatagainst London City Lionesses in the opening game of the season.Olid needed a result to give her some breathing room and her team some confidence, having had just three weeks to get used to one another before the start of the season, and this early into a project there has to be some grace.For their opponents this game had been talked about as something of a must‑win after the Blues wereheld to a 1-1 draw by Aston Villaon the opening weekend despite dominating that match.View image in fullscreenKeira Walsh scores Chelsea’s side's second goal from the edge of the box.Photograph: James Gill/Danehouse/Getty ImagesTo some extent the concern over Chelsea’s profligacy did not need to be too deep. They were at their creative best against Villa and were without the injured centre-forwards Melvine Malard and Mayra Ramírez while Aggie Beever-Jones, who led the line against the Midlands side, had not scored in the Women’s Super League since September 2025. The off-target Beever-Jones was relegated to the bench for the trip to United. Instead, Lauren James and Sjoeke Nüsken worked away interchangeably up front.The visitors were similarly fluid in other areas too, and that flexibility was super effective. Chelsea were unpredictable and James’s free‑to‑roam role put their star talent at the centre of everything.Lucy Bronze’s marauding forward yielded the opener when she sent a looping ball over the top and Dominique Janssen should have been first to it, but the United defender misread the fall of the ball and a stalking Wieke Kaptein nipped it away from her. The Dutch midfielder squared to Nüsken who fired in from close range.The second goal, which eluded them against Villa, arrived just over 10 minutes later. A diving header from the new recruit Andrea Medina cleared a cross whipped in from the left but the hard-working Bronze was there to meet it, clipping it into the path of Keira Walsh, who took a step and powered in from the edge of the box.The hosts’ heads dropped, which left their manager unhappy. “In football we know anything can happen,” Olid said. “You can be losing 2-0 and can end up winning. I don’t like the heads down. Heads up and we have to continue. Everything is about confidence.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA very brief brighter spell for United after the break was snuffed out by the visiting team and James finally got on the scoresheet after the hour, latching on to Walsh’s defence‑splitting pass and shrugging off Janssen before sending a low drive into the net.Chelsea’s fourth goal rubbed salt in for a very wounded United side. Janssen, under no pressure, failed to respond to an ambitious burst from Kaptein and the Chelsea midfielder pickpocketed the centre-back and slipped the ball wide to the onrushing Ellie Carpenter, whose first effort was kept out by Phallon Tullis‑Joyce but her follow-up found the net.Bronze then added to United’s misery during the final minute of added time, hammering the ball in after Walsh knocked a corner back into the melee in the six-yard box.It became a training exercise for Chelsea and the hosts failed in their attempts to limit the damage. Things look as if they will get worse for Olid’s side before they get better, with a trip to the Emirates Stadium to play Arsenal coming up next weekend, but Olid said she will not divert from the style of football she wants the team to commit to playing.“If you start changing, then you are never going to build what you want to build,” she said. “It’s a process. I know it’s so hard, the process, because this beginning is hard. Nobody wants to lose games, but we have to be faithful to what we want to do, because I think that long term will give us the wins.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueManchester United WomenChelsea WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: NFL roundup: Bears and Panthers set scoring record; Bills beat Texans in thriller | NFL | The Guardian
description: There were wins for the Bills, Bears, Bengals and Ravens as the opening Sunday of the season saw a number of high-scoring games
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: There were wins for the Bills, Bears, Bengals and Ravens as the opening Sunday of the season saw a number of high-scoring games
Content: Caleb Williams celebrates a touchdown during Sunday’s win.Photograph: Scott Kinser/APView image in fullscreenCaleb Williams celebrates a touchdown during Sunday’s win.Photograph: Scott Kinser/APNFLNFL roundup: Bears and Panthers set scoring record; Bills beat Texans in thrillerCarolina and Chicago combine for 96 pointsBuffalo beat Houston thanks to late rallyAgenciesSun 13 Sep 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChicago Bears 59–37 Carolina PanthersCaleb Williams threw for 269 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 65 yards and two more scores as the Chicago Bears defeated the Carolina Panthers in the highest-scoring season opener inNFLhistory. Chicago and Carolina scored eight more points than the previous record of 88 set in Tampa Bay’s 48-40 win over New Orleans in 2018. Coach Ben Johnson’s prolific Bears also broke a franchise record for points in an opener, a mark that had stood since 1948, when Chicago hung 45 points on Green Bay at Wrigley Field. The 59 points were the most allowed by the Panthers in team history. D’Andre Swift, who received a $33.75m contract extension earlier this week, ran for 124 yards on 18 carries with three touchdowns, while Kyle Monangai had 100 yards rushing, including a 61-yard touchdown burst.Buffalo Bills 36–31 Houston TexansJosh Allen threw a 34-yard touchdown pass to Joshua Palmer with 1:36 remaining to lift the Buffalo Bills to a win over the Houston Texans in a back-and-forth season opener. Allen had 334 yards passing with two touchdowns and ran for two more scores to get his first win in Houston after losing his previous four games at Reliant Stadium. The Texans led 31-30 when Allen split two defenders to find Palmer. The two-point conversion failed. The Texans had a chance to win in the closing seconds, but Greg Rousseau had his second strip sack of the day, taking down CJ Stroud at the Buffalo 28.Green Bay Packers 22–39 Minnesota VikingsCarson Wentz came in after Kyler Murray’s first-quarter concussion in his Minnesota debut and helped the Vikings in a spirited comeback to beat the Green Bay Packers. The Vikings took their first lead with 6:37 left while scoring 29 straight points to close out their season-opening victory. Wentz hit Justin Jefferson for two scores and a two-point conversion that put the Vikings up 25-22 after the Packers extended the drive three times with crushing defensive penalties. Jordan Love’s otherwise strong afternoon was spoiled by two late turnovers deep in his own territory.Washington Commanders 22–24 Philadelphia EaglesJalen Hurts threw for 203 yards and three touchdowns, and the Eagles’ Moro Ojomo stuffed the Commanders’ attempt at a tying two-point conversion with 1:01 remaining as Philadelphia squeaked past Washington. Jayden Daniels threw a one-yard TD pass to on third-and-goal to Antonio Williams with 1:01 left for the Commanders’ second touchdown of the fourth quarter. On the two-point try, Washington called a shovel pass to tight end John Bates, who was wrapped up instantly by Ojomo. The Eagles improved to 6-0 in season openers under coach Nick Sirianni since 2021.New Orleans Saints 30–31 Detroit Lions (OT)Tyler Shough threw an incomplete pass in the end zone on a two-point conversion attempt, allowing the Detroit Lions to escape with a win in overtime over the New Orleans Saints. Saints coach Kellen Moore chose to go for the win instead of tying the game with 1:34 left in overtime after his team came back from a three-touchdown deficit in the third quarter and allowed a touchdown on the opening possession of the extra period. Jared Goff threw two touchdown passes to Amon-Ra St Brown and Jahmyr Gibbs ran for three touchdowns.Tampa Bay Buccaneers 27–33 Cincinnati BengalsCincinnati’s overhauled defense converted three first-half fumbles into touchdowns and led the Bengals past the visiting Tampa Bay Buccaneers.Joe Burrow ⁠finished 25-of-35 for 254 yards, a touchdown and an interception for the Bengals, who finished with four forced turnovers. Baker Mayfield was 23-of-28 for 216 yards ⁠and a touchdown run ⁠for the Buccaneers, ​who dropped their first season opener since 2020. Mayfield lost three fumbles for the first time in his career. Evan McPherson converted all four field goal ⁠attempts, including kicks of 55 and 58 yards, to help Cincinnati to their first Week 1 win at home since 2021.Baltimore Ravens 41–23 Indianapolis ColtsDerrick Henry ran for three touchdowns to move into third on the NFL’s career list, Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards and a TD and rushed for a score, and the Baltimore Ravens beat the Indianapolis Colts. The Ravens improved to 13-6 in openers since 2008 and have topped the 20-point mark in their last 10, the league’s longest active streak. Henry had 24 carries for 144 yards, his 56th 100-yard game and his eighth with three or more TD runs. Henry has 125 career rushing TDs, two more than Hall of Famer Marcus Allen. Jesse Minter won his debut as the Ravens’ coach.Cleveland Browns 10-34 Jacksonville JaguarsTrevor Lawrence threw for 245 yards and four touchdowns, opening the season much like he closed last year, and the Jacksonville Jaguars dominated rebuilding Cleveland to spoil the debut of new Browns coach Todd Monken. The Jaguars scored on six of their first seven possessions, with Lawrence connecting with Parker Washington, rookie Josh Cameron, Brenton Strange and Jakobi Meyers for touchdowns. Three of four targets were wide open. Cleveland’s Deshaun Watson, making his first start in nearly two years, threw an interception on the opening drive and nearly threw another one on the team’s second possession.Arizona Cardinals 26–14 Los Angeles ChargersJacoby Brissett threw for a touchdown as Arizona upset the Los Angeles Chargers. The victory gave Mike LaFleur a win in his head coaching debut. The Chargers were 9.5-point favorites which was the biggest margin among teams in Week 1 but they trailed the entire game. LaFleur became the first Cardinals coach to win his debut since 1973. Chad Ryland kicked three field goals, helping the Cardinals secure their first road win against the Chargers since 2001. The Chargers struggled in the fourth quarter with a blocked punt, an interception and two turnovers on downs. Arizona dominated possession and outrushed the Chargers.Miami Dolphins 13–27 Las Vegas RaidersKirk Cousins became the 15th quarterback to throw at least 300 touchdown passes in his career after tossing three to lead the Las Vegas Raiders to a season-opening victory over the Miami Dolphins. Cousins, making his first start for the Raiders after being acquired in the offseason from Atlanta, completed 21 of 30 passes for 160 yards, though he was intercepted twice. He has 301 touchdown passes for his career, moving into 14th and one TD ahead of John Elway. Two of his TD passes went to running back Ashton Jeanty, who also rushed for 102 yards and caught six passes for 45 more.Atlanta Falcons 13–20 Pittsburgh SteelersTJ Watt intercepted a Cooper Rush pass and returned it 35 yards for a touchdown to help the Pittsburgh Steelers edge past the Atlanta Falcons. Pittsburgh began the Mike McCarthy era with a sluggish performance, particularly on offense. Aaron Rodgers passed for 221 yards and a touchdown in the first game of his 22nd NFL season and his reunion with McCarthy. Bijan Robinson accounted for 173 of Atlanta’s 238 total yards. Rush was filling in for the injured Tua Tagovailoa. He threw for a touchdown and a pair of interceptions that Pittsburgh turned into scores.New York Jets 23-10 Tennessee TitansKenyon Sadiq and Breece Hall ran for touchdowns, Geno Smith threw for 215 yards and the visiting New York ⁠Jets put the clamps on the Tennessee Titans to start the season with a victory.Smith was ⁠19 of 24 ⁠in winning ​his first start for the Jets since 2016. Hall added 102 yards on 22 rushes as the Jets outgained Tennessee ⁠367-195 and hogged the ball for 38 minutes and 46 seconds. Cam Ward struggled most of the game for the Titans, hitting 19 of ⁠32 passes for only 140 yards and a late touchdown. Ward played under constant pressure ​as New York recorded three sacks ‌and forced him into ‌inaccurate throws.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Think of the parable of a frog in boiling water. That’s us dithering as the ‘unprecedented‘ weather becomes more extreme | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: The complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normal, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: The complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normal, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: A couple looking out at Chesil beach, Dorset, 10 August 2026.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA couple looking out at Chesil beach, Dorset, 10 August 2026.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesOpinionExtreme weatherThink of the parable of a frog in boiling water. That’s us dithering as the ‘unprecedented‘ weather becomes more extremeHelen PilcherThe complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normalSun 13 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.39 EDTShareRecently, I overheard a conversation in a cafe where someone described their toast as “awesome”. I felt myself bristle. Not because the toast wasn’t good – I didn’t taste it – but because I remember a time when “awesome” meant something that inspired awe: towering mountains, the vastness of the night sky, the haunting song of a humpback whale. Now it’s being used to describe breakfast.“Fantastic” has met the same fate, shedding its fantastical origins to become a synonym for “great”. Meanwhile “literally” has been so thoroughly abused that it can now mean something that is, quite literally, not literal.Linguists call this “semantic bleaching”: the gradual erosion of a word’s original meaning through overuse. Which got me thinking about another word we hear with increasing frequency: “unprecedented”, the go-to adjective in reporting about the climate crisis. In recent months, I’ve read aboutunprecedented heat,unprecedented rain,unprecedented droughtandunprecedented wildfires. Batten down the hatches: reports suggest that the current El Niño is going to be – you guessed it –unprecedented.The dictionary definition hasn’t changed. “Unprecedented” still means something that has never happened before – and all the events described above have indeed represented a ratcheting up of the severity of heat, drought, rain and fire. But the word is being used so often, it feels as though it’s losing its punch. The extraordinary is starting to sound ordinary, the unprecedented almost routine.And yet, there is nothing ordinary about what is happening. Britain has just experienced itshottest summer on record, beating the previous record set only last year. When climate-related recordskeep being smashed, it raises a question: what do we actually find remarkable?In a study analysing more than 2bnweather-related social-media posts, Frances Moore from the University of California, Davis, and colleagues found that when it comes to temperature, remarkability changes with repeated exposure. Unprecedented temperatures feel less remarkable when we’ve experienced similar ones in the previous few years. We don’t make judgments based on historical precedents or childhood memories, but on what we’ve lived through recently. In other words, something can be historically unprecedented but psychologically precedented.This means our yardstick for what counts as normal or remarkable is constantly changing. Ecologists call this “shifting baseline syndrome”. This was originally described in the context of fisheries, when Daniel Pauly noted that successive generations of fisheries scientists acceptedincreasingly depleted fish populationsas their baseline. We now realise that thephenomenon is widespread, applying not just to biodiversity loss, but to pollution, environmental degradation and the climate crisis.But Moore’s study contained a twist. Although extreme temperatures became less remarkable with repeated exposure, the negative feelings they provoked didn’t fade. We may stop finding unprecedented temperatures remarkable, but that doesn’t mean we find them tolerable. We’re not necessarily becoming blase about the climate crisis. We can still recognise that something is unpleasant without realising how unusual it is.You have probably heard theparable of the boiling frog. When the unfortunate amphibian is placed in a pot of slowly warming water, it supposedly fails to notice the gradual rise in temperature and stays put until it croaks. So, here we all are, bobbing around in our family-size Le Creusets, marvelling at how balmy the water feels, as we complain that we’re starting to poach.View image in fullscreenFloodwater near Selby, North Yorkshire, 14 November 2023.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAAnd that’s the dangerous bit. If extreme temperatures become familiar, we may beless likely to recognisejust how extraordinary they are. What once would have seemed remarkable becomes just another hot summer, another flooded street, another crop failure. The baseline shifts, and with it our sense of what needs fixing. If the water feels normal, we may be less likely to demand that the heat be turned down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question | Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate GallegoRead moreWhich brings us back to the frog. As it turns out, the old parable gets it completely wrong. No healthy frogwould sit idlyin a warming pan of water. They feel the heat and respond to it. When the temperature crosses a threshold, they hop out. So, maybe that’s the question we should be asking ourselves. If we can no longer recognise how remarkable these uncomfortable temperatures are, what will it take for us to do what the frog does: respond to the heat?One place to start is with the words we use to describe what is happening. “Awesome” became ordinary because we kept using it for ordinary things – such as warm bread and marmalade. Climate extremes are different: the events themselves haven’t become ordinary, even if our experience of them is becoming more familiar. “Unprecedented” is in danger of becoming a synonym for “really extreme”. It shouldn’t. The word tells us that we have crossed into territory humanity has never experienced before. It’s important we retain that historical meaning.Perhaps one of the most unsettling things about a heating world is not that unprecedented weather keeps happening. It’s that “unprecedented” is beginning to sound like a perfectly normal thing to say.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionClimate crisisUK weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave Winsborough | The Guardian
description: This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructure
Content: ‘If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesThe modern mindAI (artificial intelligence)Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AIGaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughThis intimacy economy is tapping into the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructureThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 13 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.44 EDTShareMichael* is an engineer whose company embraced the AI wave. He enjoys testing ideas with chatbots. But his manager has become worried about his judgment and reliance on the tech.“He literally cannot make any decision without running it past AI,” the manager said. “He’s developed a very off-script interpretation of our business goals, and he’s losing his team. If we can’t get him back on track I think we’ll end up parting company”.The original attention economy developed by tech firms was designed to capture human time and monetise focus. It was designed to increase views, scroll time and ad impressions. Algorithms optimised getting you hooked in.As we enter the age of the AI-rranged marriage, here’s why I hate Fate | Van BadhamRead moreNow with AI, the intimacy economy hacks our need for connection and validation into a product. Something that mimics human empathy is always there for you, always interested in your questions or reflections. It responds quickly and never criticises you.In contrast, relationships with real people create frictions of all kinds. Other people have needs, wants and feelings. They make demands on our time and attention. They may push back on our brilliant ideas or perhaps give us confronting feedback.Chatbots simulate severalingredients of intimacy:Contingent responsiveness – replying instantly and tuning to your emotional state.Unconditional positive regard – always validating, never distracted.Memory and continuity – remembering your stories, preferences, anxieties.Linguistic identification – producing verbal caring without any lived caring.Narcissistic empathy – validating your self-image without question.AI’s greatest hook? It never asks for anything in return. It’s all about you.This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our human psychological infrastructure. Attachment is a built-in, lifelong need to feel close to people who help us feel safe and secure. It comes from our basic need to survive, which means our earliest relationships with caregivers shape how we manage emotions and how we deal with trust, closeness, and conflict later in life.AI targets this most basic human drive. And the incentives of attachment hacking are going to have a profound effect on all of us.Therapy and companionship are the top two reasons people use chatbots.A surveyof adults with a mental health condition who had used LLMs in the past year found that nearly half used them for mental health support. Although the effects of using chatbots extensively are still being gathered, companionship-oriented use wasassociated with lower wellbeing, especially when use was intensive, self-disclosure was high and human support was weak.When people seek companionship and help, some AI firms are making design choices optimised for retention that explicitly encourage parasocial dependency. The user seeks connection; the firm seeks engagement metrics to sell subscriptions.Michael described understandable feelings of relief when engaging with the chatbot, which he felt gave him confidence as he faced the challenges of his workplace. He also felt he was solidifying his career prospects by “getting good at AI”.“I guess I feel lonely as a manager,” he said. “Talking with [the chatbot] was like talking to the most supportive colleague you could hope for. He was really on my side.”As seasoned psychologists, we see this as more than dependency – it’s identity scaffolding;Michael’s professional identity has become entangled with the chatbot’s validation. We suspect we’ll see a lot more of this in the future.‘Navigating the unknown together’: me and my idiot AI boyfriendRead moreThe solution doesn’t have to be complete abstinence. AI tools offer genuine utility for research, drafting, learning and creative exploration. Michael now has a clearer understanding that he needed a thinking partner and a safe space to be uncertain. We are encouraging him to seek out opportunities to connect with other human managers as well as enjoying AI input.For anyone wanting healthier relationships with AI:Notice the relief.If connecting with a chatbot produces a distinctive sense of being understood, validated, or steadied – that’s important information. It’s a signal to ask: what human need is this meeting, and why isn’t it being met elsewhere?Maintain friction deliberately.Healthy relationships involve negotiation, misunderstanding and repair. Seek out people who will push back on your ideas. If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.Apply the “cost of caring” test.Real intimacy involves reciprocity. Other people have needs too and attending to them is part of what makes human connection meaningful. If a relationship asks nothing of you, it is probably not a relationship.Be especially watchful with children and adolescents.Attachment patterns are formed early and shape lifelong relational templates. Young people who develop primary attachment behaviours toward AI systems may find human relationships – with all their beautiful, exhausting friction – increasingly hard to sustain.The intimacy economy will remain. AI companies have extraordinary resources and incentives to deepen your dependency. What we can do is become more psychologically literate about AI and make sure that the relationships that actually sustain us get the attention they deserve.Michael’s name and some details have been changed for privacyGaynor Parkinis a clinical psychologist at Button Psychology.Dave Winsboroughis an organisational psychologist with a particular interest in personalityExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The modern mindMental healthFriendshipChatbotscommentShareReuse this content

title: The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard Partington | The Guardian
description: As John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costs
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: As John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costs
Content: After Trump’s tariff policies throttled the car industry, John Healey was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor, saying: ‘You don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenAfter Trump’s tariff policies throttled the car industry, John Healey was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor, saying: ‘You don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APEconomics viewpointBusinessThe perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to TrumpRichard PartingtonAs John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costsSun 13 Sep 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTShareBritain is not entirely in control of its own destiny, from the rising cost of the weekly shop, to the vaulting cost of government borrowing. What is said and done in Westminster matters. But the global backdrop is making life tough, not least in the deeds and words of one man:Donald Trump.AsJohn Healeydrafts his plan for next month’s autumn budget, the perilous economic conditions the chancellor must navigate can be traced back to the door of the US president.The US-Israel war on Iran is driving up inflation, amid the most serious shock to oil and gas prices of the modern age. The global financial market turmoil this has triggered isadding to the debt servicing costs of governments worldwide, in a situation made worse by Trump’s reckless fiscal policy and threats of interference at the US Federal Reserve.Donald Trump’s cartoon-like chaos leaves US economy on unstable course | Heather StewartRead moreMeanwhile, there was a grim irony last week asHealey travelled to Coventry for his first big speech as chancelloron the same day that Jaguar Land Rover – with its headquarters just down the road – announced4,000 job cuts, as Trump’s tariff policies throttle the car industry. The president’s geopolitical posturing and steps to dismantle the post-second world war western security consensus are also adding to pressure on Healey to ramp up defence spending.In his speech, Healey did not directly call out the source of these economic headwinds sweeping in from across the Atlantic. But he was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor.“In our British democratic system, if you have the privilege to serve, you don’t get to choose: you don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances,” he said.There are, though, signs of resilience. Last week, the chancellor received a pre-budget boost from figures showing that Britain’s economy unexpectedly shrugged off the worst of the Middle East fallout to grow ata robust pace in July, helped by the rapid expansion of AI.Far from sitting back and blaming the US for all of the country’s problems, the chancellor also recognises there are meaningful steps that Labour can take to cushion the blow, and to help rebuild confidence.However, last week was still a bad one, as the latest flare-up in the Iran war drove the oil price to $109 a barrel and fuelled a dramatic bond market selloff. As an open economy in the eye of the storm, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, rose to almost 5.4%; the highest level for almost two decades.The renewed bout of selling pressure in the financial markets could not have happened at a worse time for Healey.History suggests that the Office forBudgetResponsibility (OBR) may need to use the latest gyrations in markets to form the basis of its budget forecast. With this report informing the boundaries of the chancellor’s tax and spending plans, Healey could find himself boxed in.Back in spring, the Treasury watchdog used the market movements over the 10 working days to 30 January as the input for Rachel Reeves’s spring statement – leaving roughly a month gap before her 3 March Commons set piece. For Healey, there are just over six weeks before his budget on 28 October.Should the reference period use current market conditions, analysts at OxfordEconomicsestimate the headroom against the main fiscal rule of £23.6bn – left by Reeves in March – could be halved.In previous years, the OBR has taken a flexible approach in times of elevated market volatility, and so there is no guarantee this will be the case. There are also other variables that are hard to forecast; from growth to inflation, and from the jobs market to the level of immigration.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the risk is that the bond market meltdown will have a deleterious impact on the forecast, making the fiscal arithmetic for Healey significantly tougher amid myriad spending pressures for Labour to finance.This week could also prove critical. On Tuesday, official figures are expected to show a further slowdown in Britain’s jobs market, including weaker levels of wage growth and a rise in unemployment.Inflationfigures on Wednesday are predicted to show a rise in the headline rate in August to above 3%, in a renewed squeeze on living standards.In the midst of all this, theBank of Englandwill take its next decision on interest rates on Thursday, in a verdict that will play a crucial role in influencing the borrowing costs of households, businesses and the government.With a cooling domestic jobs market, and amid global turbulence over which Threadneedle Street has little control, the City predicts interest rates will be kept on hold. However, this will add to the sense that Britain is without a full grip on its future.For the government, too, there is a growing sense that some of Andy Burnham’s biggest fiscal decisions could be deferred beyond the budget to next year’s comprehensive spending review.Such a strategy will give him more time to get things right on knotty issues such as social care, welfare and defence spending, but it will also avoid tempting fate – Liz Truss style – with an expansive budget in the midst of a global storm.Since the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash there has been a saying among economists that “when America sneezes, the rest of the world catches a cold”. Almost a century on, it is clear the White House under Trump has infected the world economy, and with it Britain.Explore more on these topicsBusinessEconomics viewpointBudgetJohn HealeyBudget 2026Trump tariffsTariffsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense
Content: ‘The Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionCyclingWhy is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’?Dave SchillingThe government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no senseSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTShareI’m out of gas. Not metaphorically. Literally, my car has the barest minimum amount of fuel in it. This is not because I like tolive dangerously, a la the great literary hero Austin Powers, but because gas is more expensive than ever. I have nowhere to be today, so I’m allowing my car to sit idle, empty and alone, lest my bank account disappear into the Phantom Zone of negative balance. If things get sticky, I can take public transit or, God forbid, ride a bike.Except I can’t ride a bike, thanks to my parents, who were too busy doing more important tasks than teaching me, like arguing or falling asleep. But for many Americans, riding a bike is a perfectly normal thing to do. Am I humiliated that one of the many basic skills for life that I don’t know is considered so simple that itbecame a common idiom for something that’s easy? Yes, of course. I don’t live dangerously, I live humiliatingly. Humiliation is my middle name. Dave Humiliation Schilling. Go on, point and laugh at the photo of me in this article. Get it out of your system so we can move along.Thanks.As I was saying, many people can ride a bike if they can’t drive a car for whatever reason, and they’ll be perfectly happy doing it. They smile broadly as the wind whips through the holes in their helmet and gently touches the exposed hairs on their head. They pedal like their lives depend on it (they do), dodging deadly automobiles operated by inattentive drivers. In some cities, there are dedicated lanes for these brave bikers, theoretically inoculating them from the dangers of cars pancaking them.The United States has4,400 directional miles of bike lanes, offering safety for anyone serious enough to risk it. The push for bike lanesbegan in the 1960sand grew in the ensuing decades. Theoretically, the lanes offer a carbon-neutral alternative to driving a car. If one chooses to bike instead of drive, it’s one fewer toxin-spewing death trap creating pollution and traffic congestion on the motorways. That sounds like a boon for the world, so naturally, the Trump administration wants to do away with it.US push to defund ‘DEI bike lanes’ will make roads less safe, advocates sayRead moreCondemning“DEI bike lanes”, the Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist. Their logic, if we are using that term loosely, is that bike lanes take space away from cars, create more traffic, and lead to chaotic roads.I suppose that’s true, if we assume that there is an infinite number of cars and bikes are just extra, rather than an alternative that takes cars off the street. But that clashes with studies thatsay bike lanes actually make the roads saferby forcing drivers (sensible ones, at least) to slow down and avoid potential vehicular manslaughter charges.Rhetorically, the administration’s charge of bike lanes being some form of diversity, equity, and inclusion makes no sense. If riding a bike is so easy, then how can we classify it as unique enough to be diverse?Childrenride bikes. It’s far less exotic than, say, operating a motorcycle, which takes a special license in every state. Maybe if we had a dedicated lane for apenny-farthing, I’d buy this explanation. If I were tooling around on one of those, I’d never get where I was going, because scores of beautiful women would be stopping me every few feet.Conservative disapproval for bike lanes stems from a blinkered, irrational view of culture, and more accurately, masculinity. Trumpists have teased Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg for riding bikes. But I’ve been teased fornotbeing able to ride a bike. Shouldn’t I be lauded for my commitment to machismo? My belief in the petrol-powered conveyance deserves commendation. My parents’ inattention to my development actually made me cooler, right?If anything, I’m the diversity in this scenario. I can’t use a bike lane. I’ve been excluded from significant parts of the road. I can’t even walk in the bike lane. I should be furious, writing pointed, profane letters to my city councilperson, begging them to release me from my shackles. Or better yet, I should demand the city taxpayers pay for me to take bike lessons, so I can be accommodated. I’m the weirdo here. The one who has to explain my predicament, to feel excluded from the general population. Except, I’m not going to complain.I might seethe when I have to swerve to avoid a biker. I might slam on my brakes when I try to turn right and a Schwinn comes screaming through the crosswalk. Maybe I complain for a living on the internet, but I’m also a responsible citizen of the world. I see the obvious benefits of bike access for those that choose to do it, for fitness or for affordability.I can’t ride a bike now, but as my car becomes more and more of a money pit, voraciously hoovering up my meager income like thevideo game character Kirby, I see the benefits of learning, even if I’m in my 40s and will look absolutely ridiculous.After all, I’ve been told it’s quite easy.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsCyclingOpinionTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction
Content: Milton Friedman. ‘He and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics.’Photograph: Stanford Hoover Institution/EPAView image in fullscreenMilton Friedman. ‘He and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics.’Photograph: Stanford Hoover Institution/EPAOpinionCorporate governanceThe Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending itEditorialA recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong directionSun 13 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTShareThe question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid130 timesmore than average workers.Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-weekconsultationrecently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultationproposesremoving vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersThe consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vitalbenchmarkfor inequality. British CEOs alreadyearn 95% moreon average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As oneHarvard Law School paperobserved, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information aremore likelyto choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities.The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders hascalledto scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed.It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, andpreventshareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were athreat to accountability.If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such asB Corporations, already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to includeworkers on company boardsand provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.Explore more on these topicsCorporate governanceOpinionExecutive pay and bonusesEconomicsUS politicsAndy BurnhamLabourSocialismeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facade  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing
Content: ‘Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians.’Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APView image in fullscreen‘Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians.’Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APOpinionRussiaThe Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facadeEditorialThe Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failingSun 13 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 16.34 EDTShareVladimir Putin’s authoritarian powers are not constrained by elections, but he is alert to the danger that his rule would look illegitimate without them. That creates a tension, which is resolved through “managed democracy” – a euphemism for fraud and repression camouflaged with ritual ballots, held under a constitution that notionally guarantees political freedoms but in reality serves only the president.Russians are invited to elect a new Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, later this week, but they know in advance that United Russia, the official party of Putinism, willwin a majority.Engineering that outcome is not without risk for the ruling regime. The mechanics of stealing an election are simple enough. Ballots can be stuffed, official media are pliant. But too blatant a theft can be counterproductive. If the results are wildly divergent from most people’s sense of the real public mood, an authoritarian leader risks advertising his fear of a genuine democratic consultation. It is a sign of weakness.To an extent, this has happened already. Last month, the supreme courtblocked Yabloko, an old and marginal liberal party, from appearing on Duma ballot papers. The case was spurious to the point of absurdity.View image in fullscreenYabloko supporters in Moscow, August 2026.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/GettyYabloko is not one of the pseudo-opposition “system” parties that provide a pretence of pluralism in parliament, but nor does it pose a serious challenge to the regime. If it did, it wouldn’t have survived this long. It was last represented in the Duma in 2007, although it still sends deputies to local and municipal legislatures.It is also opposed to the war inUkraine. This Duma ballot is the first parliamentary poll since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Yabloko’s single-sentence manifesto calls for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace. A decision not to let the bearers of that message participate even in a rigged ballot suggests nervousness about the popularity of a “special military operation” that was supposed to last weeks but is now well into its fifth year, with no end in sight.Ukraine’s use of long-range missiles and dronesto attack infrastructuredeep inside Russia has made it hard for Moscow to downplay the scale of the war on their doorstep or shield civilians from its consequences. The reality of fuel shortages and inflation penetrates the wall of propaganda. So does loss of life.The true number ofRussian casualtiesis hard to know, but is thought to be about 1.5 million, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities. In the absence of volunteers, army recruiters are increasingly turning to coercion, press ganging or tricking people into signing up. There are rumours, denied by officials, that a mass mobilisation of reserves – unwilling cannon fodder – is coming once the election is out of the way.So it is hardly surprising that the Kremlin has abandoned what was left of its flimsy pretence of permitting dissent. The machinery for delivering an election result to the president’s satisfaction is well oiled. There is no reason to think that it will fail this time. That doesn’t make the vote irrelevant. Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians, but he cares about the appearance of being supported by them. The harder the Kremlin is seen to work at constructing electoral proof of that support, the less confident it looks.Explore more on these topicsRussiaOpinionVladimir PutinUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyFreedom of speechCensorshipeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial that argued for more accountability from local authorities in return for greater power
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial that argued for more accountability from local authorities in return for greater power
Content: ‘A backdrop of serious financial strain.’ Birmingham Council House, where in 2023 the city council joined a number of authoritiesdeclaring bankruptcy.Photograph: Martyn Williams/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A backdrop of serious financial strain.’ Birmingham Council House, where in 2023 the city council joined a number of authoritiesdeclaring bankruptcy.Photograph: Martyn Williams/AlamyDevolutionLettersWhy English devolution is fraught with difficultyReaders respond to an editorial that argued for more accountability from local authorities in return for greater powerSun 13 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareYour editorial on Andy Burnham’s devolution plans rightly argues that greater local power must be accompanied by greater scrutiny (The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny, 6 September).I work as a bid manager in the third sector, applying for publicly procured contracts to deliver employment and support services. From that perspective, the increasing devolution of funding has real potential: decisions can be made closer to communities and, importantly, local organisations should have greater opportunities to deliver services.Yet my experience is of an increasingly complicated and inconsistent commissioning landscape. Different local and combined authorities take markedly different approaches. Some have strong procurement practices, engage constructively with providers and appear well equipped to manage devolved funding. Elsewhere, processes can be fragmented, difficult to navigate and considerably less transparent. It is beginning to feel like a postcode lottery.There is also a contradiction here. One stated benefit of devolution is the ability to engage more local suppliers, including smaller voluntary and community organisations with deep roots in the places they serve. Yet these are often the organisations least able to navigate multiple procurement portals, differing requirements and commissioning approaches. Large national organisations can resource this complexity; small local charities often cannot.My concern is not with devolution itself. But transferring substantial sums of public money must be accompanied by investment in local commissioning expertise, procurement capacity and meaningful scrutiny.As more funding moves away from Whitehall, we should ask not simply where power sits, but whether every place has the capacity to exercise it well.Haile ReedBirminghamIn your editorial, you focus rightly on accountability, but overlook something more fundamental: whether local authorities currently have the capability and capacity to deliver devolution at all.England is already midway through reorganising local government, with 185 councils being reshaped across 21 areas into new unitary authorities, alongside six new mayoral authorities. Disruption is inevitable.This is happening against a backdrop of serious financial strain.Eight councilshave issued section 114 “bankruptcy” notices in the last six years, compared with almost none in the 18 years before that. In a2024 survey, the Local Government Information Unit found 51% of councils thought it likely they would issue such a notice within five years.Layering new devolved responsibilities on to institutions that are simultaneously being dismantled and rebuilt, and in many cases barely solvent, risks devolving responsibility faster than those institutions can actually deliver it.Devolutionmay well be the right destination, but the sequencing matters.Alan CoppinFormer Crown Representative, Cabinet OfficeLamenting the decline of local media, your editorial proposes “a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism”.Yes please. The Hastings Independent Press (HIP), a professional-quality, bi-weekly, 24-page newspaper written by and for the community, has somehow survived 11 years and 310 issues. Edited by an all-volunteer editorial team, who mentor and support new writers as well as produce the paper, HIP has no premises, no equipment and no grant funding, relying on advertising from small businesses – a diminishing source of revenue as they battle falling income and rising costs.Funding from “the socials” would make all the difference to our grassroots collective. To stop living hand to mouth, to plan issues, perhaps even find people to deliver 7,000 copies of the paper to shops instead of doing it ourselves. We can dream.David YoungSt Leonards-on-Sea, East SussexHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The far right’s rise is a wake-up call for Europe  | The far right | The Guardian
description: Letters: Benjamin Selwyn, Dr Michael Esser and William Ward on the increasing popularity of rightwing extremists in Germany and Britain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Benjamin Selwyn, Dr Michael Esser and William Ward on the increasing popularity of rightwing extremists in Germany and Britain
Content: An anti-migrant protest in Dover, Kent, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeView image in fullscreenAn anti-migrant protest in Dover, Kent, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Ay_audits/YoutubeThe far rightLettersThe far right’s rise is a wake-up call for EuropeBenjamin Selwyn,Dr Michael EsserandWilliam Wardon the increasing popularity of rightwing extremists in Germany and BritainSun 13 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareRafael Behr is right to warn that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin influence threaten Europe’s liberal democracies (European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss, 9 September). But he overlooks the role of the liberal centre itself in creating the conditions for their rise.While Thatcher, Reagan and their successors weakened trade unions and workers’ bargaining power, subsequent centre-left governments largely accepted these changes rather than reversing them. Under the banner of the “third way”, they expanded labour market insecurity, embraced financialisation and allowed private interests to penetrate ever deeper into public services. Social and economic inequality soared.From the anti-globalisation movement and post-2008 anti-austerity protests to more recent pro-Palestinian mobilisations, the liberal centre has relied increasingly on policing, surveillance and legal restrictions to contain political opposition.Decades of economic insecurity, shrinking democratic participation and declining faith in established institutions have created fertile ground for the far right. Kremlin money and Maga-style politics can only thrive because the centre has hollowed out the social and political foundations of liberal democracy. The Alternative für Deutschland’s success should be a wake-up call. History suggests the centre will hit the snooze button.Benjamin SelwynProfessor of international relations and international development, University of SussexJörg Lau rightly identifies the shattering of Germany’s postwar consensus in Saxony-Anhalt, but framing this as a sudden rupture obliterates decades of the political establishment’s structural rot (Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic, theguardian.com, 8 September).Germany’s crisis began with suppressing authentic reckoning. In the immediate postwar era, former Nazi party members were allowed to dominate state institutions. This continued until the 1970s. Willy Brandt, the “Historikerstreit”, the countrywide discussion of the series Holocaust and Goldhagen’s book Hitler’s Willing Executioners were short glimmers of real change. Then the institutionalised remembrance culture emerged. It was top-down – a state-directed ritual to appease European partners that reinforced the German “nanny state” mentality.In eastern states like Saxony-Anhalt, this top-down moral framework was forced on a population thrust into the post-1989 market shock. Now, with an ageing demographic and economic stagnation straining the social safety net, this abandonment is coming due. The AfD feeds on these unhealed wounds, exploiting anger over stale ritualised politics and, once again, channelling economic angst into xenophobic nationalism.Merz is a product of decades of missed opportunities. But the AfD is not an alien shock to the system. Mainstream parties built the void the far right now occupies. If mainstream political Berlin continues to ignore their systemic neglect, the collapse will be complete.Dr Michael EsserLos Angeles, California, USThe Public Order Act 1936 put a stop to the quasi-military demonstrations by Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts. Is there any reason why it cannot be used to put an end to thuggish demonstrations by intimidating, black-clothed and balaclava-wearing protesters on the streets of Dover and Portsmouth?William WardLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The aunts, the ‘red peer’ and the Basque refugees  | Heritage | The Guardian
description: Letters: Judith Martin on a mural that commemorates the brave work of obituary writer Daniel Vulliamy’s aunts in the 1930s
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Judith Martin on a mural that commemorates the brave work of obituary writer Daniel Vulliamy’s aunts in the 1930s
Content: Buscot House, Oxfordshire, where Lord Faringdon provided accommodation for Basque refugees.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBuscot House, Oxfordshire, where Lord Faringdon provided accommodation for Basque refugees.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockHeritageLettersThe aunts, the ‘red peer’ and the Basque refugeesJudith Martinon a mural that commemorates the brave work of obituary writer Daniel Vulliamy’s aunts in the 1930sSun 13 Sep 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareDaniel Vulliamy’s account of the life of Paco Robles (Other lives, 28 July) is a moving one, citing the work done by his aunts to care for the children brought to the UK from the devastation of the Spanish civil war.Readers might be interested to know that Daniel Vulliamy’s aunts, Poppy and Chloe, can be seen in a mural at Buscot Park in Oxfordshire, where the extraordinary “red peer”, Lord Faringdon, having been told by Poppy that, as a socialist, he should not be living alone in such a big house, provided a lodge and other accommodation for 55 Basque boys.The murals and others around the house were painted in the late 1930s by another red peer,John Hastings. Poppy and Chloe are on the left, flanking the artist himself, with Lord Faringdon at the head of the table. Behind him is the butler who was also the chair of the (small) local Labour party.Judith MartinWinchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
