title: A painful truth about post-Brexit immigration | Home Office | The Guardian
description: Letter: While the media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting similar cruelty, says Vera-Lynn Watson
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: While the media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting similar cruelty, says Vera-Lynn Watson
Content: ‘Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”.’Photograph: AlamyHome OfficeLettersA painful truth about post-Brexit immigrationWhile the media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting similar cruelty, saysVera-Lynn WatsonSun 13 Sep 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTShareYour report (Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene, 3 September) highlights a painful truth about post-Brexit immigration: families are being treated as administrative burdens rather than human beings. However, this harsh treatment cuts both ways.I am a 71-year-old German-American citizen, married to my British husband for 38 years. We have only ever been apart for work. We bought property in the UK in 2023 so my husband could retire there. After retiring from my job in Germany, I applied for a UK family visa on 1 April 2026, expecting to settle down with him and my two adult sons within six weeks. The lawyer was rather optimistic.Five months later, and over £7,000 on costs, I am still waiting. My application remains “under consideration”. I have hired a lawyer, involved an MP, filed official complaints, and paid for priority services, yet theHome Officeremains an impenetrable wall.While British media rightly highlights the harsh treatment of UK citizens abroad, the UK Home Office is quietly inflicting the exact same cruelty on older spouses from allied nations. At 71, my husband and I are losing precious time together to bureaucratic inertia. If we expect European countries to show humanity to British citizens, the UK must show the same decency to the families of its own people.Vera-Lynn WatsonBirkenfeld, GermanyExplore more on these topicsHome OfficeImmigration and asylumBrexitEuropean UnionEuropelettersShareReuse this content

title: Leaders at Celtic summit to affirm right to seek independence from UK | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Call for ‘constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland’ likely to challenge Burnham’s devolution agenda
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Call for ‘constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland’ likely to challenge Burnham’s devolution agenda
Content: From left to right, the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney, the Sinn Féin vice -president, Michelle O’Neill, and the Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth.Composite: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty/Brian Lawless/Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenFrom left to right, the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney, the Sinn Féin vice -president, Michelle O’Neill, and the Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth.Composite: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty/Brian Lawless/Jonathan Brady/PADevolutionLeaders at Celtic summit to affirm right to seek independence from UKCall for constitutional change in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales likely to challenge Burnham’s devolution agendaBethan McKernanandPatrick GreenfieldSun 13 Sep 2026 12.41 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first ministers of Wales, Scotland andNorthern Irelandare to affirm their countries’ right to seek independence from the UK at a summit that is likely to challenge Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda.The Plaid Cymru leader,Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney, and the Sinn Féin vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding at a landmark conference in Cardiff on Monday that will call on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”.The three are meeting in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments, alongside the Sinn Féin president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald. They will also discuss Europe, international cooperation, the economy and energy issues.Plaid Cymru’s victoryin May’s Senedd elections ushered in a new era for the Celtic independence movements, with separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time.Burnham must understand Wales is ‘not a region in England’, says first ministerRead moreBurnham has made much of his support for regional devolution of power and resources in England since becoming prime minister in July, but his approach to the devolved administrations in Belfast, Cardiff and Edinburgh isless clear.He wrote to Swinney last week to reiterate that a repeat of 2014’sScottish independencereferendum remains “off limits” after apparently misspeaking during prime minister’s questions.Donald Trump also weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK during a weekend visit to Ireland, telling reporters at a press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, that he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and the unionist power-sharing members of the Northern Ireland executive.Asked about the diplomatic backlash, Trump said on Sunday: “I love my comments.” Shortly after reiterating his stance on Irish unity, the US president said he would save his opinion on Scottish independence for another day.Ap Iorwerthtold the Guardian this weekthat he has been encouraged by warm initial discussions with Burnham – astark contrastto his interactions with Keir Starmer – but that he was wary about the new prime minister being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers.A Plaid Cymru source called Monday’s summit an opportunity for “a new partnership between our nations”.“Following the historic Senedd election inWalesand the changing political landscape across these islands, there is a strong case for practical political cooperation on areas including energy, the economy and our relationship with Europe, as well as on the wider political and constitutional questions facing our nations and on the right to self-determination,” they said.Catastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolution | Phillip InmanRead more“Our parties have much to gain from working together, as partners and as equals, where we share common interests and where cooperation can improve the lives of the people we represent.”Speaking before his visit to Cardiff, Swinney said: “We are at a pivotal moment of constitutional change, and our parties share the common belief that our interests will never be served by Westminster, and that the people of our respective nations must have a meaningful say over their future.“This discussion comes the week after the prime minister accepted that a referendum should take place when there is majority support for independence inScotland. That acknowledgment that the people of Scotland can and should determine their own constitutional future is long overdue.”Latestpollingsuggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum, while data suggest it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland.Explore more on these topicsDevolutionScotlandWalesNorthern IrelandScottish independenceAndy BurnhamJohn SwinneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland woman falls to her death at Bali cliff popular with tourists  | Bali | The Guardian
description: Twenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Twenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police say
Content: The Australian tourist woman was found stuck on the side of the Kelingking beach cliff in Bali on Saturday morning, police said.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Australian tourist woman was found stuck on the side of the Kelingking beach cliff in Bali on Saturday morning, police said.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesBaliQueensland woman falls to her death at Bali cliff popular with touristsTwenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police sayAustralian Associated PressSun 13 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of an Australian woman in a cliff fall at a popularBalitourist destination has been described as “incredibly sad”.Police say the 29-year-old Queenslander was found stuck on the side of Kelingking beach cliff on Saturday morning, local time. Emergency services rushed to the scene but she fell further before they could reach her.“The victim is estimated to have fallen around 9am,” said Nusa Penida’s alert unit coordinator, Cakra Negara.“At the time, she was seeking an independent path toward the edge of the cliff before slipping and falling into the ravine,” he said.“When found, the victim had sustained several fractures; we secured her onto a stretcher to facilitate the evacuation process.”Kelingking beach is one of the most popular destinations forBalitourists, offering panoramic views from the 180-metre-high coastal cliff.Nusa Penida police said the woman was visiting the area on a holiday.View image in fullscreenBali’s police shared imagery of rescue efforts at Kelingking beach in Bali after a woman fell off a cliffA Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson confirmed that the government was providing consular assistance to the woman’s family.“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time,” they said. “The family have requested privacy at this difficult time.”Queensland’s premier, David Crisafulli, described the death as “tremendously sad”.Bali and the not-so-great glass elevator: construction on Kelingking beach prompts outrage from localsRead more“To have a life taken away in a heartbeat like that … it’s just incredibly, incredibly sad,” he told reporters on Sunday. “I just express my sympathies to her family and those loved ones with her and back at home.“I think all of Queensland collectively looks at that and just feels ... just a huge degree of sorrow.”Swimming at Kelingking beach, sometimes referred to as T-Rex Bay, is banned year-round due to dangerous currents.The trek down to the beach can take two hours on atreacherouspath.The site gained international notoriety last year after a developer began construction ona giant, 182-metre tall glass elevatorthat was meant to increase tourism to the area and ease the hike down.The project came at the expense of the untouched view and prompted swift outrage from local lawmakers and tourists alike.Bali’s governor said in November he had ordered the company behind it to demolish the structure within six months. But a protracted legal fight continues and a metal skeleton remains attached to the cliff face.Explore more on these topicsBaliQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Director who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting given senior council housing role | Housing | The Guardian
description: Fire survivors and bereaved urge Barnet Group to ‘reconsider’ appointment of Laura Johnson, who pushed for cheaper contractor
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Fire survivors and bereaved urge Barnet Group to ‘reconsider’ appointment of Laura Johnson, who pushed for cheaper contractor
Content: Grenfell Tower, in west London, and a memorial to the 72 people who died in the fire in June 2017.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenGrenfell Tower, in west London, and a memorial to the 72 people who died in the fire in June 2017.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAHousingDirector who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting given senior council housing roleFire survivors and bereaved urge Barnet Group to ‘reconsider’ appointment of Laura Johnson, who pushed for cheaper contractorJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrenfell survivors and bereaved relatives have criticised the “outrageous decision” to hire a director who oversaw cost-cutting at Grenfell Tower in a £150,000-a-year senior council housing role.Laura Johnson, the director of housing at the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea (RBKC) at the time of the 2017 Grenfell fire, has been appointed the permanent director of development and property at the Barnet Group, which manages the borough’s 13,000 council homes.The Grenfell inquiry found that, in her previous role, Johnsonpushed for a new contractor to carry out the tower’s renovation workson a lower budget, which ultimately meant metal cladding was swapped for combustible plastic-filled panels to save money.It also found she slowed down the installation of self-closing mechanisms on fire doors in the tower for “financial and practical reasons”, despite warnings from theLondonfire brigade that their absence compromised fire escape routes.Ed Daffarn, who escaped from the 16th floor of the tower after repeatedly warning about serious fire risks at Grenfell, said: “It is an absolutely outrageous decision.“The fact that we, as bereaved survivors, haven’t received any justice nine years after the fire, and yet the people that were involved in senior decision-making are able to carry on working in the social housing sector, have responsibility for health and safety, and receive massive salaries – it feels so disrespectful.“If I was a resident in a Barnet council home, I’d be absolutely petrified.”View image in fullscreenGrenfell survivor Ed Daffarn.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianJohnson had been working in her role at the Barnet Group on an interim basis before she was appointed permanently in August with a salary of £157,078.A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said she was the “strongest candidate” in a competitive field.“We were aware of the Grenfell inquiry findings and considered them carefully during the recruitment process,” they said. “We also took into account Ms Johnson’s professional experience, subsequent performance, references, qualifications and overall suitability for the role.“Following a robust and publicly advertised recruitment process, we concluded that she was the strongest candidate and legally eligible to hold the position.”Grenfell United, the group representing the bereaved and survivors, has urged Barnet Group – which is owned by Barnet council – to reconsider its decision to hire Johnson, saying it showed “a staggering disregard for the inquiry’s findings”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“She should not be in a position of power,” Daffarn said. “No one named in the Grenfell inquiry should be while we are still awaiting the outcome of the police investigation.”The Metropolitan police said it wasseeking charges against 57 individuals and 20 companiesin relation to the fire, with the Crown Prosecution Service saying it expected to make decisions on charges by June 2027, the 10th anniversary of the disaster.“Although the police have not publicly identified those individuals, it is extraordinary that Barnet council would make this appointment permanent before the criminal justice process arising from Grenfell has concluded,” Grenfell United said.A spokesperson for the Barnet Group said: “Barnet Homes and Barnet council will not discuss matters relating to members of staff which took place during previous employment.“Our thoughts remain with the survivors and family and friends of all those affected by the tragicGrenfell Tower fire. The safety and wellbeing of our residents is our top priority.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsHousingGrenfell Tower fireGrenfell Tower inquirySocial housingLondonEnglandCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midterms | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Plan to give US adults $5,000 has been greeted with incredulity across the political spectrum as well as outrage
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Plan to give US adults $5,000 has been greeted with incredulity across the political spectrum as well as outrage
Content: Donald Trump visits Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland, on Sunday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump visits Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland, on Sunday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPATrump administrationTrump reiterates $5,000 ‘dividend’ pledge if Republicans win midtermsPlan to give US adults $5,000 has been greeted with incredulity across the political spectrum as well as outrageGuardian staffSun 13 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpon Sunday doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if his Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after November’s midterm elections.The plan has been greeted with expressions of incredulity across the US political spectrum as well as outraged accusations of seeking tobribe voters. The plan – which would cost more than a trillion dollars – also comes amid huge concern over the US national debt, whichtopped $40tn for the first timein August.“I don’t ‌know but ‌it’s easy if the ‌Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we’re taking in ‌so much money,” Trump told reporters in Ireland where he is on a visit to a golf course.Trump had been asked if ​Congress would need to approve the $5,000 pledge and continued: “TheDemocratscan’t make that pledge ⁠because it would all go to ​hell ​right away, ​we’d go into a ​depression … ‌I made ​that pledge, ​I always keep my pledge.”Taxes wouldn’t fund $5,000 Trump ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms, says commerce secretaryRead moreThe US has roughly 240 million adult citizens, suggesting a cost of $1.2tn. The federal government spent about $7tn in fiscal year 2025, with about $2tn taken on as debt.When the plan was first touted by Trump last week at a rally in Texas, Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget wrote on X: “The result would be a huge spike in the deficit, and almost certainly in the inflation rate.”Democratic political leaders also reacted with a mix of outrage, disbelief and condemnation to the remarkable suggestion, which comes at a time when Trump is struggling with low poll numbers and a disastrous conflict in Iran, which is having an impact on the health of the US economy.“After making you sicker and poorer with his war,Donald Trumpnow wants to buy your vote with $5,000 in taxpayer-funded blood money,” said California governor, Gavin Newsom. “The most corrupt man ever to occupy the Oval Office.”But some Republicans have backed the idea.“I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election,” said US senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, in a social media post on X.Any such payment would need ‌to be approved by Congress and on Sunday Mike Johnson, the House speaker and a Louisiana Republican, told CNN: “Of course, the devil’s in the ‌details. We have to figure all that out.”But Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talkshows in the US dismissed the idea. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, told ABC’s This Week that the plan isnot a “serious proposal”.Reuters and the Associated Press contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026US domestic policyRepublicansDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sour times: pickled onions enjoy revival as Britons think outside the jar | Food | The Guardian
description: With sales up 12%, pickles are moving beyond traditional role as a side to become an ingredient in their own right
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: With sales up 12%, pickles are moving beyond traditional role as a side to become an ingredient in their own right
Content: Pickled and fermented foods are enjoying a surge in popularity, with their role in gut health particularly appealing.Photograph: MehmetO/AlamyView image in fullscreenPickled and fermented foods are enjoying a surge in popularity, with their role in gut health particularly appealing.Photograph: MehmetO/AlamyFoodSour times: pickled onions enjoy revival as Britons think outside the jarWith sales up 12%, pickles are moving beyond traditional role as a side to become an ingredient in their own rightSarah MarshConsumer affairs correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe humble pickled onion, long associated with classic pub culture, the ploughman’s lunch and cold festive buffets, is enjoying a revival as Britain’s appetite for pickles grows.About 8.5m UK households bought pickled onions over the past year, according to the consumer data firm Worldpanel by Numerator, with particularly strong momentum in recent months.In the 12 weeks to early August, the value of pickled onion sales rose 12% year on year, compared with 4% growth across total grocery. While higher prices have contributed to the increase, demand is strengthening, with about 300,000 more households buying them and more than 550,000 additional shopping trips made to buy them.Pickles are more broadly moving beyond their traditional role as a side or accompaniment to become a flavour and ingredient in their own right.Michelin-star chefs are even using them in their dishes, and this weekend marks the launch of London’s first major festival dedicated to pickling and fermentation: the Big Brine.James Goodyear, the head chef at the Michelin-starred restaurant Gordon Ramsay High, said: “There’s a resurgence happening around pickling and preserving right now. Palates have evolved, so diners are naturally craving that sharp, mouthwatering punch of acidity and crunch to cut through richer dishes. Between social media demystifying the craft and a growing curiosity around gut health and natural fermentation, people are far more eager to explore beyond the basic supermarket jar.”He said guests cared about “sustainability”, and having “jars quietly working away on the shelves” was a “smarter way of running a restaurant”. He added: “It lets us celebrate every single part of an ingredient and completely rethink surplus.”Molly Scanlan, 39, from London is attending the Big Brine this weekend with her son and has noticed newer pickle brands in the supermarket. She “even noticed in a meal deal” recently the option of a “plastic sachet of snacking cornichons”.View image in fullscreenPickling enables restaurants to ‘celebrate every single part of an ingredient’.Photograph: olgakr/Getty Images/iStockphotoOcado data shows the pickles, gherkins and olives category is up 30% year on year, while fresh pickled and fermented products have grown 16%. Some individual products have had even more dramatic increases, including raw organic fresh ginger and lemon sauerkraut, up 393%, Opies cocktail gherkins, up 305%, Baxters sliced beetroot, up 246%, and Epicure spicy crinkle-cut pickles, up 242%.Scanlan has been a fan of pickled foods from a young age. She says her son loves pickles, too, and he also likes kimchi.Gherkins are Scanlan’s longstanding favourite, but she says there is a growing interest in a much wider range of fermented foods, with products such as kimchi and sauerkraut becoming more widely available. Part of the appeal, she says, is that “you can pickle anything”.Matt Harris, the founder of Pickle Project, a London-based food brand that makes small-batch, handcrafted pickles using an ultrasonic brining process, said the brand had been created to bring “energy and fun” to what he described as an old-fashioned category. “Despite pickles having ‘a moment’, what’s available on supermarket shelves is very traditional,” he said.Harris has introduced flavours such as deli dill pickle chips, while also experimenting with ultrasound technology to extract flavours from herbs and spices during the brining process. The brand has launched with Ocado and Whole Foods Market, and Harris said it had experienced “huge growth” over the past nine months.Kat Goldin, a co-founder of the pickle brand Goat Rodeo Goods, said: “Over the last year, we’ve seen around 11-times growth in sales, which has been massive for us.” She added: “That also fits intothis wider ‘lipstick effect’ culturewe’re seeing. People might be cutting back on their grocery spending, but they still want to add a little bit of luxury or something special to everyday meals. A nice condiment or pickle can make a simple sandwich or salad feel more exciting without being a huge purchase.”The pickle boom is also spawning entirely new formats, such as the UK’s first pickle sparkling water. Within its first week at Planet Organic, Yew sparkling water became the retailer’s bestselling soft drink, outselling even bottled water, while the brand says retailers have reported customers specifically asking for the pickle flavour.Explore more on these topicsFoodRetail industryBritish food and drinkPickling, fermenting and preservingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticides | Pesticides | The Guardian
description: When pesticide proved no match for the insect, desperate Phyllis Nvuda tried a new way to save her infested orchard
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When pesticide proved no match for the insect, desperate Phyllis Nvuda tried a new way to save her infested orchard
Content: Pesticide use in Kenya has risen steadily over the last few decades, with imports more than doubling between 2015-19Photograph: Imago/AlamyView image in fullscreenPesticide use in Kenya has risen steadily over the last few decades, with imports more than doubling between 2015-19Photograph: Imago/AlamyThe alternativesPesticides‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticidesWhen pesticide proved no match for the insect, desperate Phyllis Nvuda tried a new way to save her infested orchardMilliam MurigiSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor two decades, Phyllis Nduva, 72, has grown mangoes and citrus in Wote, a town in Kenya’s eastern Makueni County. In the beginning, she only had to worry about ordinary fruit flies. She handled them simply, buying chemical pesticides and spraying her trees whenever they appeared.But then, in 2014,the false codling mothturned up on her farm. The small brown creature had been causing havoc in South Africa for years, and in 2007 it was spotted in Kenya.Research into how to deal with the moth was continuing, but no one Nduva knew had information about how to stop it from spreading across her 8-hectare (20-acre) orchard.“We tried looking for answers, but we couldn’t get [any],” she said. “So we continued using readily available pesticides, but they were not effective.”Driven by desperation, she sprayed her trees frequently but in 2016 lost more than 60% of her harvest to the pest. That was when she began to investigate the alternatives and became interested in integrated pest management (IPM), where farmers reduce their pesticide use and instead combine approaches including traps, natural predators, field sanitation and selective pesticide use.IPM was developed in response to steadily increasing pesticide use and becameinternationally recognisedin the 1960s and 1970s after concerns grew about pesticide resistance, environmental pollution, health risks to farmers and consumers and destruction of beneficial insects such as bees and natural predators.A review by theBritish government in 2020found that IPM could be effective at reducing pesticide use while controlling pests and diseases. It was complex, but it reduced costs for farmers and was beneficial for biodiversity.Willing to try anything, Nduva started small by placing fruit fly traps around her farm. It helped, but her orchard was already heavily infested. To fight back properly, she deployed a full arsenal of IPM techniques, including nocturnal solar traps and augmentorium bags, used to break pest breeding cycles by collecting the infected fruits and sealing them away so the pests die off, reducing future infestation.“The shift from chemical pesticides to IPM was not just an agricultural decision; it was a moral one,” Nduva said. “I realised that what I was doing was harming the environment, exposing my family and consumers to chemicals and contributing to climate change.“Before, we would just leave the damaged fruits on the farm. This caused the pests to continue multiplying. Now we are controlling pests in a way that protects both the crop and the environment.”Pesticide use in Kenyahas risen steadilyover the past few decades: pesticideimportssurged from 6,400 tonnes in 2015 to more than 15,600 tonnes in 2019, with farmers nowspendingan estimated $70m (£52m) annually.A2026 studyin the Journal of Environmental Management found that climate breakdown was increasing pest pressure on crops, driving up pesticide use among smallholders.Roughly 63% of these areclassifiedas highly hazardous and 44% contain active ingredients banned in the EU. The ecological toll is severe: a2025 studydetected 56 different pesticides in water systems around Kenya’s Lake Naivasha, while a Nature Sustainabilitystudy in 2024linked rising pyrethroid and neonicotinoid use to widespread declines in the wild bee population.The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization said it reflected aglobal trend. In an analytical brief on pesticide use and trade, it said: “Total pesticides use in agriculture in 2024 was 3.92m tonnes of active ingredients, a 5% increase from 2023, an 18% increase in a decade and more than a doubling since 1990.”But Nduva and other IPM adopters have experienced ecological and economic recovery. Nduva’s harvest losses have dropped to under 20% and pollinators have returned to her farm, boosting fruit quality. Without the mandatory chemical withdrawal periods, she can harvest and sell her fruit the moment a buyer is ready.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHer organic approach commands a premium. A kilogram of her fruit fetches 400 shillings (£2.30) in the market, while pesticide-treated fruits sell for 50 shillings. Today most of her harvest is bought by off-takers for export.“This gives us more flexibility, improves marketability and ensures that our fruits are safe and healthy for consumers,” she said.Other horticulture farmers in east African countries, particularly in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania, have beenturning to IPMas export markets tighten their rules on pesticide residues. The method issupported by the governmentin China and is being adopted by farmers in Brazil and India.In Kenya, Nduva trains other farmers: 600 in Makueni County alone have adopted IPM, although according to Josephine Makumbi, the Wote/Nziu ward agricultural officer, its use across the area remains uneven. About three in every 10 farmers in her ward have adopted IPM practices.Cost remains a barrier. An augmentorium bag, for instance, costs about 6,000 shillings, while fruit fly traps are approximately 350 shillings, and IPM requires at least four an acre. For many smallholders such upfront investments are difficult to afford, but the county is now giving out some of the tools for free.Kelvin Musyoki, 29,a plant doctor trained by theCentre for Agriculture and Bioscience International, the shift towards low-chemical farming is not only helping to fight pests naturally but is also addressing a growing concern: food safety.“It’s not every time you see a pest that you spray,” Musyoki said. “There are biological ways, there are cultural practices. Spraying should be the last option.”This article is published in collaboration withEgabExplore more on these topicsPesticidesThe alternativesFarmingFood safetyKenyaAfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: George Osborne calls for UK to rejoin EU customs union and boost trade | Economic growth (GDP) | The Guardian
description: Ex-Tory chancellor says economy has ‘fallen off a cliff’ since Brexit but rejoining union could be ‘quite simple’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ex-Tory chancellor says economy has ‘fallen off a cliff’ since Brexit but rejoining union could be ‘quite simple’
Content: ‘Brexit has been a mess,’  the ex-chancellor George Osborne said. ‘Britain has basically gone off a cliff. It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be.’Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Brexit has been a mess,’  the ex-chancellor George Osborne said. ‘Britain has basically gone off a cliff. It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be.’Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAEconomic growth (GDP)George Osborne calls for UK to rejoin EU customs union and boost tradeEx-Tory chancellor says economy has ‘fallen off a cliff’ since Brexit but rejoining union could be ‘quite simple’Press AssociationSun 13 Sep 2026 06.48 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former chancellor George Osborne said Britain’s economy had “fallen off a cliff” since Brexit and that rejoining the European Union’s customs union would be the fastest route to recovery.Osborne, who was sacked as chancellor by Theresa May after being part of David Cameron’s cabinet at the time of the referendum, said it was important to rebuild links with the EU.“Brexit has been a mess,” he toldthe Independent. “Britain has basically gone off a cliff. It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be.”Acknowledging that rejoining the EU would be difficult a decade on from the Brexit referendum, Osborne said closer ties withEuropecould boost the economy.“I would rejoin the customs union,” he said. “It’s a quite simple thing to do. That was never part of theBrexitdebate. No one knew we were leaving it and it has had a devastating impact on trade.“The reason we weren’t supposed to be in the customs union – according to the Brexiteers – was these great trade deals we were going to strike with America. That all looks pretty fanciful now.“People now realise you can’t look at Britain’s growth problem without beginning to think: ‘How can we revive trade with the continent, how can we get investment?’“If I was Andy Burnham, I don’t see why you wouldn’t rejoin the customs union. It’s a pretty straightforward decision because unlike (rejoining) the single market it does not require you to accept the free movement of people – which is a pretty complicated issue to sell to people in Britain at the moment.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis article was amended on 13 September 2025. An earlier version saidGeorge Osborneresigned as chancellor, when in fact he was sacked by Theresa May.Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)International tradeBrexitGeorge OsborneEuropean UnionEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Mohamed Al Fayed abuse compensation claims could reach £150m, says law firm | Harrods | The Guardian
description: Combined value of 275 women’s claims is far greater than amount Harrods has set aside for payouts
Author: David Batty
Headline: Combined value of 275 women’s claims is far greater than amount Harrods has set aside for payouts
Content: Harrods said it was ‘committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered’.Photograph: Mina Kim/ReutersView image in fullscreenHarrods said it was ‘committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered’.Photograph: Mina Kim/ReutersHarrodsMohamed Al Fayed abuse compensation claims could reach £150m, says law firmCombined value of 275 women’s claims is far greater than amount Harrods has set aside for payoutsDavid BattySun 13 Sep 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCompensation claims by 275 survivors of alleged sexual abuse by the former owner of HarrodsMohamed Al Fayedcould reach between £100m and £150m, according to a law firm representing the women.The combined value of their claims, calculated byKP Law(KPL), which represents more than half of known survivors, is around two to three times greater than the amount the luxury department store has set aside for all abuse payouts.This suggests thatHarrodsand the late billionaire’s estate together could face a combined compensation bill of more than £200m.Harrods’ latestannual report, published in August, showed it had paid out only £4.1m from the £57m it set aside for compensation in 2025, excluding legal and administration costs. The accounts also showed that the retailer reduced the amount set aside by £1.1m, leaving a compensation pot worth £51.8m in January 2026.View image in fullscreenMohamed Al Fayed.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersLucy Traynor, a senior associate at KPL, said Harrods’own compensation scheme, whichstopped accepting claims on 31 March, was “not fit for purpose” and underestimated the impact of the alleged abuse on survivors’ lives and careers.She added: “The evidence available to us indicates that the average value of the claims being pursued is likely to be hundreds of thousand pounds higher than the apparent average payment under the Harrods scheme. We’re seeing figures in the millions for [a client’s] loss of earnings and future loss of earnings.”Harrods said it had made settlements with 113 women through its redress scheme to date. The store did not clarify how many settlements were covered by the £4.1m paid out last year, but noted thatmore than 50 were made by mid-February this year.Traynor said this suggested that the average payout to survivors under the redress scheme would be approximately £82,000. “As Harrods say that payments were made to more than 50 survivors, the actual average would be lower still,” she added.This estimate is also significantly lower than the maximum payout of £385,000 under the Harrods scheme, which includes general damages of up to £200,000 and a work impact payment of up to £150,000, as well as payments for treatment costs and “wrongful”medical tests for sexually transmitted diseases.A Harrods spokesperson said the store did not “provide ongoing commentary on settlement values”,but that it was “committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered”.More than 400 allegations including rape, sexual assault, sexual exploitation and human trafficking have been made against Fayed, who died three years ago.One of KPL’s clients, Carrie Lazell, from Norfolk, said her nascent career as a designer ended after she was groomed and sexually assaulted by the former Harrods boss.Lazell, who worked as a designer at the luxury store in her early 20s, said: “I lost a career, and I’ve gone through a whole load of very unpleasant, unnecessary trauma with a man I did not want to engage sexually with at all. I was really enjoying work [at Harrods]. I think I was set to become a successful designer.”View image in fullscreenCarrie Lazell.Photograph: SuppliedBut she said her performance suffered as a result of the alleged abuse. Lazell added: “I couldn’t say it’s because every day the chairman of Harrods is abusing me. And I was threatened that I should never tell anybody because bad things would happen to me or my family.”KPL said it had begun issuing settlement formal offers against Harrods and the estate.The law firm said its negotiations with Harrods and the estate halted earlier this summer. Traynor said this delay was due to the department store’s action to replace the executors of estate – believed to be Fayed’s close relatives. But Harrods denied this had any bearing on survivors accessing compensation.Sarah Savogi.Photograph: SuppliedSarah Savogi, another KPL client, who says she was sexually assaulted by Fayed in a restaurant, said only once her claim was settled could she fully lead her life.“I have severe PTSD and relapses of what happened and sometimes I wake up in the night, I think I can’t breathe, I have awful nightmares about Al Fayed,” she said.“Sometimes I’ll see a man and he looks like him and it will all come back to me again. There’s only so much that a therapist and counselling session can do, and I feel like I’ve reached the end of everything they can do to help me.”Holly Johnson and Heidi Givens, KPL clients and sisters from Texas, said the delay to reaching a settlement was aggravating their distress.The twins, who say they were sexually abused by Fayed when they worked at Harrods and Fayed’s Park Lane offices, said they felt unable to move on in their lives.Givens said: “I don’t think that the estate or Harrods understand what it feels like for all of us to just keep going. Right now it’s like an open wound that can’t heal.”Harrods said it “continues to work at a pace dictated by survivors and their legal representatives towards redress through the route of their choice. However, the timely progression of claims was only possible where the information required is made available, in line with established legal principles.”It added that any suggestion to survivors that Harrods was preventing access to compensation was a misrepresentation, and harmful to survivors’ trust in the process.The survivors also criticised Harrods for closing its redress scheme before recent significant developments in the police investigation, which suggested the scandal was greater and more complex than previously thought.This includes several women being recognised as trafficking victims, the Met police interviewing seven suspects under caution, including one who was a Harrods employee until 2025, and a file being sent to the Crown Prosecution Service for charge advice about a man in his 80s over indecent assaults on two women.In response Harrods said: “Harrods has reiterated that the scheme is one route to redress and compensation open to survivors. We support all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continue to work closely with the Met police on its investigation.”View image in fullscreenShanta Sundarason.Photograph: c/o KP LawShanta Sundarason, another of KPL’s clients, said: “I don’t even know if [Harrods] really cared to truly understand the scale of the abuse. I think what they were trying to do was to pay off as many women as they possibly could as quickly as possible.”In a statement, Harrods said it was “committed to ensuring all eligible survivors receive compensation for the appalling abuse they suffered”.It added: “More than 260 survivors have engaged with the Harrods redress scheme, with 113 claims settled to date. Any suggestion to survivors by their legal representatives that Harrods is preventing survivors from accessing compensation is a misrepresentation of the facts, and harmful to survivors’ trust in this process.“Harrods continues to work at a pace dictated by survivors and their legal representatives towards redress through the route of their choice.”The statement added that Harrods believed the appointment of new executors to the Fayed estate was for the benefit of all survivors“We have continued concerns over the solvency of the estate and its ability to pay all survivors in a timely and appropriate manner,” it stated.The estate was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsHarrodsMohamed Al FayedLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Female asylum seekers report being sexually assaulted by British men | Violence against women and girls | The Guardian
description: Women say they are wary of pursuing criminal prosecution of rapes, for fear of having their asylum claims refused
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Women say they are wary of pursuing criminal prosecution of rapes, for fear of having their asylum claims refused
Content: A woman who had just arrived in the UK from Iran and had been placed in a hotel near Heathrow by the Home Office said she was raped by a security guard at the hotel.Photograph: MBI/AlamyView image in fullscreenA woman who had just arrived in the UK from Iran and had been placed in a hotel near Heathrow by the Home Office said she was raped by a security guard at the hotel.Photograph: MBI/AlamyViolence against women and girlsFemale asylum seekers report being sexually assaulted by British menWomen say they are wary of pursuing criminal prosecution of rapes, for fear of having their asylum claims refusedDiane TaylorSun 13 Sep 2026 05.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFemale asylum seekers are reporting rapes and sexual assaults by British men but many say they are too fearful to pursue criminal prosecutions.Their voices are rarely heard but some have spoken to the Guardian at a time when the far right is intensifying tropes about endemic rape of English women and girls by “fighting age” male asylum seekers.The rallying cry by far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, to motivate his black balaclava-clad followers last weekend when theyprotestedabout the arrival of asylum seekers in Dover and Portsmouth, focused almost exclusively on unsubstantiated claims of widespread rape perpetrated by asylum seekers.While there have been a handful of convictions of asylum seekers for serious sexual offences, which have attracted widespread media coverage, there is no comprehensive published data about crimes committed by asylum seekers.One woman, who spent two years in an asylum hotel after fleeing religious persecution and domestic violence, said she was repeatedly verbally and physically harassed by a staff member at the hotel she was accommodated in. This included unwanted touching and holding on to her hands when handing over documents. After a while he started visiting her room regularly, asking her out for drinks and on dates. He took her number from the hotel database and started texting her repeatedly from his personal phone asking for sex. At that point she reported him to hotel staff and was moved to another hotel.“It was awful,” she said. “He told me he wanted to have sex with me.”In another case, a woman who had just arrived in the UK from Iran and had been placed in a hotel near Heathrow by theHome Office, said she was raped by a security guard at her hotel.“It was very terrifying. I didn’t know what to do. I reported the attack to the hotel staff and I was asked if I wanted to make a statement to the police. I did not know if the police here would be like the police in Iran, so I was too scared to do anything.“I was also worried that if I reported the rape it would make it more likely that my asylum claim would be refused.”She was moved to another hotel soon after reporting the rape and does not know what happened to the perpetrator.In a third case, a lesbian asylum seeker from Uganda whose asylum claim was based on fear of imprisonment or death in her home country if her sexual orientation was discovered, was unable to find a legal aid lawyer to represent her.“I managed to find a private immigration lawyer but I had no money to pay him, so he forced me to have sex with him as a form of payment even though he knew what my asylum case was,” she said. “I felt there was nothing I could do to prevent this.”All three women were later granted refugee status. It is likely that incidents of sexual assault and rape of asylum seekers are under-reported to Home Office accommodation contractors.A home affairs select committeeinquiryinto asylum accommodation heard evidence about inadequate safeguarding in asylum accommodation. The British Red Cross told the inquiry that this lack of safeguarding had placed “extraordinary strain” on their frontline refugee support teams. They provided examples including a staff member at a hotel trying to use a key card to get into a woman’s room late one night when she was taking a bath. They referred to a “pervasive culture of sexual harassment” in one hotel, including instances of sexual assault.A spokesperson from Women for Refugee Women, which supports women in the asylum system, said: “The weaponisation of violence against women and girls by far-right groups does nothing to make women safer. It distorts the reality of abuse, creates barriers to support and justice for survivors, and allows perpetrators to hide behind racist stereotypes instead of being held accountable.“Using violence against women and girls to demonise people seeking safety here is a dangerous distraction. This violence is a systemic problem, not one confined to any nationality or immigration status, and it must urgently be treated as one.”Ciara Bergman, chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales said: “We remain seriously concerned about a lack of appropriate safeguards in place to protect women seeking asylum in the UK from sexual violence, abuse and exploitation.“This cohort of women and girls are particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse and exploitation. Many have limited or no information about their rights at all, let alone meaningful avenues through which to enforce them.“Our government has committed to halving violence against women and girls in a decade; it is vital that this includes those seeking asylum and living within the asylum complex.”Home Office sources said there is published guidance about issues of this kind in Home Office accommodation known as the statement of requirements for asylum accommodation and support. The guidance states: “This would typically include assessing any immediate risk to the alleged victim and others, considering what support services may be required, and determining whether any protective measures are necessary.”Explore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsImmigration and asylumRape and sexual assaultSexual harassmentRefugeesHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesco alerts police as supermarket becomes latest victim of scam ‘endorsement’ ads | Scams | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Supermarket joins line of firms and sports stars including Bellingham and Haaland to have their image hijacked via ads
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Exclusive: Supermarket joins line of firms and sports stars including Bellingham and Haaland to have their image hijacked via ads
Content: The fake ‘Tesco casino’ ad on Facebook which even had its own page on the platform until the Guardian sent questions to the social media site’s owner, Meta.Photograph: ScreenshotView image in fullscreenThe fake ‘Tesco casino’ ad on Facebook which even had its own page on the platform until the Guardian sent questions to the social media site’s owner, Meta.Photograph: ScreenshotScamsTesco alerts police as supermarket becomes latest victim of scam ‘endorsement’ adsExclusive: Supermarket joins line of firms and sports stars including Bellingham and Haaland to have their image hijacked via adsRob DaviesSun 13 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTesco has alerted City of London police after it became the latest in a string of companies and sports stars, including Barclays bank andLewis Hamilton, to have its image hijacked in a “scam” by unlicensed casinos advertising via Facebook and Instagram.The supermarket chain is among several household-name businesses to have been targeted in an apparent effort by casinos that cannot legally operate in Britain to capitalise on their brand recognition.Their branding has featured in ads and websites, promoted via the US social media companyMeta, that gave the false impression that the businesses had launched their own casinos.Sports stars including Lewis Hamilton andTyson Furyhave also had their faces used without consent, while one offshore casino used a lookalike of the footballer Erling Haaland wearing a Norway shirt.View image in fullscreenSports stars such as Jude Bellingham have had their images hijacked by unlicensed casinos to promote their businesses.Photograph: Manu Fernández/APEngland’s Jude Bellingham and the Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes havealso previously had their images used without consentby rogue gambling firms.Both the Gambling Commission and theAdvertisingStandards Authority are aware of the problem, but appear to have had little success in preventing the spread of the ads.A fake “Tesco casino” was advertised onFacebookand even had its own page on the platform until the Guardian sent questions to the social media site’s owner, Meta.The ads were linked to a website, which is still accessible in the UK, that claims to be “the officialTescocasino”.The site boasts that its slot machine games are “laid out as clearly as the aisles at a Tesco Extra” and claims that its casino is “built on the trust of Tesco, a FTSE 100 company with 107 years of UK trading history since 1919”.However, it does not have a licence to provide gambling services in Great Britain, a legal requirement to operate.Tesco declined to comment but the supermarket chain referred its concerns to the National Cyber Security Centre and Report Fraud service, run by City of London police. A spokesperson for City of London police said it had received the complaint but had not yet referred it to a police force for investigation “at this time”.Barclays’ branding has been co-opted in promotional material that features the face of Lewis Hamilton.In one Facebook advert for “Barclays Slots”, now taken down, an apparently AI-generated woman had her trousers pulled down to expose her buttocks. She then turned round to reveal that she was playing a Barclays casino game on her phone.Barclays said it “does not endorse or have any involvement” with the material, and took appropriate action to protect customers from misleading use of its intellectual property.Other ads that featured on Facebook andInstagrampromoted fake casinos including Monzo slots, using the online bank’s imagery.Monzo said this was an “AI-enabled scam where criminals take advantage of our much-loved brand to trick people”, and urged its customers to be alert to such material.Meta said it had taken down the ads after the Guardian’s inquiries. But the company is understood to believe that advertisers – not its platforms – are responsible for complying with local regulations.The boxer Tyson Fury responded to the appearance of an online casino bearing his name by filming a video for his Instagram followers, disavowing any involvement.He said he had turned down “millions” offered by gambling companies in the past, and would never promote the industry. There is no suggestion the fake Tyson Fury casino was advertised on Meta platforms.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne cryptocurrency casino called Rainbet, which claims to be licensed by the Indian ocean island of Anjouan, uses an apparent lookalike of Manchester City and Norway striker Erling Haaland acting as a casino croupier, wearing a Norway top.The site is not available to users in the UK, but was advertised via Meta.Legitimate gambling companies, including Coral and Gala Bingo, have also fallen victim to the apparent deliberate impersonation by unlicensed casinos.Bejay Patel, the managing director of UK and Ireland at Entain, which owns both brands, said any casino masquerading as a licensed operator was “exploiting British consumers and legitimate businesses alike and paying no taxes, while some of the world’s largest technology platforms continue to profit from hosting their adverts”.He added: “Ofcom needs to take a harder line on the companies facilitating this activity.”TheGamblingCommission has previously criticised Meta’s failure to act on unlicensed casinos, as the regulator struggles to keep a lid on a surge in rogue casinos.The commission said: “Illegal activity linked to gambling is a threat we take seriously, and using a trusted brand’s identity to funnel people towards unlicensed casino products is a particularly cynical version of it.”It said it would act to take down unlicensed websites that target UK consumers and would be better able to do so from autumn, when it will get more powers as a result of the crime and policing bill.The unauthorised use of intellectual property is outside the commission’s remit. The regulator said it was working with the ASA.Several of the sites analysed by the Guardian claim to be licensed in Curacao, a Caribbean former Dutch colony that is known as a haven for online gambling companies that do not have a licence in big economies such as the UK or US.That means that any which offer their services to British customers are doing so illegally.The Tyson Fury-branded casino and Tesco casino appear to be targeting UK consumers, but link to a contact page did not work. In the case of the Tyson Fury casino, it led to a page that simply contained the text: “Silence is golden.”The Guardian has approached representatives of Haaland and Hamilton for comment.Explore more on these topicsScamsTescoBarclaysGamblingConsumer affairsSupermarketsFacebooknewsShareReuse this content

title: Missing US hiker, 70, found injured on remote island after week-long search | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Craig Berg was hypothermic but alert when located on Isle Royale by Michigan police and officials during solo hike
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Craig Berg was hypothermic but alert when located on Isle Royale by Michigan police and officials during solo hike
Content: Isle Royale, Michigan, a national park in the middle of Lake Superior.Photograph: Per Breiehagen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsle Royale, Michigan, a national park in the middle of Lake Superior.Photograph: Per Breiehagen/Getty ImagesMichiganMissing US hiker, 70, found injured on remote island after week-long searchCraig Berg was hypothermic but alert when located on Isle Royale by Michigan police and officials during solo hikeKeely AougaSun 13 Sep 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 70-year-old hiker who had been missing for a week on aMichiganisland was rescued on Saturday, according to the US Coast Guard.Craig Berg was located on Isle Royale with the help of backpackers, Michigan state police troopers and local officials. Even though Berg was found injured and hypothermic, he is “alive and alert”, according to a statement posted to the Isle Royale national park’s Facebookpage.After Berg was located, a MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from US Coast Guard Air Station Traverse City hoisted Berg from the island and transported him to Marquette regional airport in Gwinn,Michigan, 140 miles (230km) away.The Isle Royale national park’s statement reported that Berg had been missing since 5 September.Berg was on what was planned as a nine-day solo backpacking hike on the large Lake Superior island. He was supposed to take a ferry back to Michigan’s Upper Peninsula on 5 September, but family members said that he did not arrive home.According toLocal 4, a Detroit station, Berg’s family reported him missing when the hiker did not return as planned. Search and rescue missions began on 6 September.Crews first focused on Rock Harbor, where Berg planned to end his hike, then expanded to other areas – including the Greenstone Ridge trail, where a trail camera captured Berg on 30 August, the report added.In an interview withTV6, Berg’s son, Evan, said that he is happy and relieved that his father has been located.“He was in rough shape, but he’s okay,” Evan said. “He’s able to speak. He asked for food and water. We’re just so grateful, and we couldn’t be more happy and relieved, and we appreciate all the support we’ve had on social media, and we are just so grateful.”The National Park Service thanks the employees and partners who helped during the search.​Isle Royale is a remote national park with no roads or wheeled vehicles allowed. Ground search teams navigating the island’s 200 sq miles of solid land must move strictly by foot through dense boreal forest and rocky ridges.Berg’s rescue brings a successful conclusion to an intensive, week-long multi-agency operation across the remote, roadless island.Explore more on these topicsMichigannewsShareReuse this content

title: The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many more | Ecuador | The Guardian
description: Thirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globally
Author: Stephen Moss
Headline: Thirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globally
Content: A male Ecuadorian hillstar, a hummingbird native to the Andes, sitting on a chuquiragua, an Andean wildflower, in the Chakana nature reserve in Ecuador.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaView image in fullscreenA male Ecuadorian hillstar, a hummingbird native to the Andes, sitting on a chuquiragua, an Andean wildflower, in the Chakana nature reserve in Ecuador.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaThe age of extinctionEcuadorThe bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many moreThirty years after a US ornithologist first sighted a jocotoco antpitta, the foundation he set up to restore biodiversity is a model for conservation globallyThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentStephen MossSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTShareI have to confess that I rarely enjoy birding in montane cloud forests. The birds that live in these mountainous, cool and humid habitats are masters of disguise, usually passing themselves off as a leaf or other form of foliage. But if I want to see antpittas – elusive, ground-dwelling birds that rarely show themselves – then I have no choice.So, on a cool, cloudy morning my guide, Juan Carlos Crespo, Fredy Ramón Castillo, a local ranger, and I are standing on a steep, muddy path close to Tapichalaca Lodge, 2,500 metres above sea level in the eastern Andes, waiting for the jocotoco antpitta to emerge from the undergrowth.Fortunately, antpittas have a soft spot for food, especially the large, juicy earthworms Castillo has placed on a low branch nearby. He calls the bird, with increasingly loud and urgent shouts of “venga,venga!” (“come on, come on!”). The minutes tick by, until I begin to wonder if this is a lost cause.Then, out of nowhere, a plump, thrush-sized bird with a chestnut back, grey front, black crown and white face-patch materialises just a few feet away. It proceeds to gulp down the earthworms as if it has not eaten for days.View image in fullscreenA jocotoco antpitta in the Tapichalaca reserve.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaI have seen a lot of different birds, but never one that so changed the course of bird conservation. In November 1997, a group led by the influential US ornithologist Robert Ridgely was exploring this area of southernEcuadorto see what they could find.As they ascended a forest trail at dawn, they heard the sound of a bird in the far distance. As Ridgely recalled many years later, “It had this crazy call, sounding like an owl; but we had no idea what it was, and to be honest I never thought we would find out.”Ridgely walked ahead of the group, and heard the sound much closer than before. He recorded the call and played it back to the mystery creature, which came crashing through the dense bamboo, right out into the open.“I knew right away that this was something really special, which no one apart from the local people had ever seen – an entirely new species to science.” It was, in fact, one of the greatest ornithological breakthroughs of the late 20th century: while new species are sometimes discovered, they are rarely so large, noisy and so obviously different from other members of their family.Talking to local farmers, Ridgely discovered that they were familiar with the bird, which they had named “jocotoco” to represent its loud, barking call. Two years later, the species was officially described, and named the jocotoco antpitta; the scientific name,Grallaria ridgelyi, commemorating its proud discoverer.Ridgely soon realised that if the bird was to be saved from extinction its forest home needed to be urgently protected. He and a group of like-minded friends created an organisation dedicated to saving the bird and its habitat, raising funds from donors in the US and Europe to buy and restore the land. In 1998 the Jocotoco Foundation was born.Today, the foundation protects and manages 19 reserves throughout Ecuador, covering about 50,000 hectares (193 sq miles), and manages a further 82,000 hectares of privately and communally owned land. Together, these sites are home to more than 1,350 species of birds – that’s 80% of all those found in Ecuador, and an astonishing one in eight of all bird species on the planet, as well as many other plant and animal species. The foundation also works closely with nearby communities, employing local people as park rangers – many of whom grew up on the land they now protect – and through jobs in wildlife tourism.View image in fullscreenThe wet cloud forest landscape of the Tapichalaca reserve.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaView image in fullscreenAn umbrellabird in the Buenaventura reserve.Photograph: Leovigildo CabreraView image in fullscreenA violet-bellied hummingbird in the Buenaventura reserve.Photograph: Alex WilesView image in fullscreenA male masked trogon on the nest at the Buenaventura reserve.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaThe model for the foundation’s reserves is simple and very effective. First, it restores habitat by planting a variety of native trees and other plants, or in some places simply allows the vegetation to regenerate on its own. Park guards, all of whom come from local communities, protect the reserves against illegal incursions such as cattle grazing, logging and poaching, aided by new technology including camera traps and audio recorders.They also use these to monitor the fortunes of key species, while providing nest boxes to encourage them to breed, making up for the loss of natural tree cavities while the old-growth forests are being restored.A recent studyat Canandé, in the Chocó region of north-west Ecuador, revealed that even after deforestation, nature can recover very rapidly. The study showed that in just three decades – a single human generation – of being managed for biodiversity, formerly cleared lands have recovered 90% of the biomass – the weight of all animals – and 90% of the number of species found in nearby mature forests. While the new mix of species is not fully the same as in a mature forest, 75% of the original species present in an old-growth forest have returned.View image in fullscreenNurturing young plants for a reforestation project on Buenaventura reserve.Photograph: James MuchmoreMike Parr, the president of the American Bird Conservancy, has no doubt about the importance of this work. “Beyond safeguarding Ecuador’s rarest birds, migrating species and incredible overall biodiversity, Jocotoco’s strategic integration of ecotourism, public awareness, community engagement and scientific research are world class. They have done an amazing job covering the previously unprotected endangered species of Ecuador.”During recent visits to Ecuador I have visited 10 of the foundation’s reserves, including those in the Chocó region north-west of Quito and Copalinga in the Amazon foothills, along with the Los Petreles reserve on San Cristóbal Island in the Galápagos, a refuge for a critically endangered seabird, the Galápagos petrel.On a visit to Buenaventura reserve, a restored cattle ranch in the western foothills of the Andes, we went in search of an even rarer bird: the El Oro parakeet. This charismatic parrot was only discovered as recently as 1980, and has a tiny home range, with fewer than 1,000 individuals.Another early start took us to an open area of grassland and scattered trees where the birds are known to gather. Moments later, we heard a raucous call, and there they were: several flocks totalling about 20 of these emerald-green birds, the males with a distinctive red forehead.View image in fullscreenA rare El Oro parakeet on the Buenaventura reserve in the western foothills of the Andes.Photograph: James MuchmoreView image in fullscreenPurple-coloured meriania growing in the Tapichalaca reserve – Ecuador is home to more than 30 species of meriania, which comes in a variety of vibrant colours.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaView image in fullscreenAn Andean condor soars high above the Chakana reserve.Photograph: Afuera ProduccionesView image in fullscreenAn Andean bear stalks the Chakana nature reserve.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de RuedaBut even this memorable moment was eclipsed by my visit to the Chakana nature reserve, more than 4,000 metres above sea level in the páramo grasslands of the high Andes – yet just an hour south-east of Quito. On an unexpectedly fine and sunny day, against a stunning backdrop of the snow-capped Cotopaxi volcano, we enjoyed closeup views of the Ecuadorian hillstar, a specialist high-altitude hummingbird, along with nine Andean condors soaring right around us, before they rose high into the clear blue sky.Numbers of the Andean condor, the world’s largest flying bird by a combination of weight and wingspan, have fallen rapidly in recent years, due mainly to deliberate poisoning. But here, these mighty raptors are now returning to their ancestral home.Dr Martin Schaefer, chief executive of Jocotoco, believes that even in these dark times there is room for optimism. “The power to restore what we have lost is in our hands.”Ian J Davidson,Americasregional director for BirdLife International, agrees. “By creating a network of protected habitat ‘arks’, Jocotoco has given these remarkable species a genuine chance not only to endure, but to recover and expand beyond their remaining strongholds.View image in fullscreenA striking yellow-throated toucan at the Buenaventura reserve.Photograph: Javier Aznar González de Rueda“Their work stands as a global conservation success story, an inspiring example of what determination, science and long-term stewardship can achieve for nature.”At a time when President Trump has withdrawn US government funding for conservation projects around the world, the Jocotoco Foundation is a classic model of how scientists and local people can work together to save endangered birds and the precious places where they live.Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

title: Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor | Spain | The Guardian
description: Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas
Author: Timothy Pratt
Headline: Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas
Content: Fergie Chambers at home in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFergie Chambers at home in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesSpainPressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donorKey government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for HamasTimothy PrattSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case.Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence.The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest.They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid.FBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrestRead moreIt is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.Chambers’ defense has submitted its brief to the government ahead of a meeting by Spain’scouncil of ministersexpected to take place on 22 September. The council can decide whether or not to allow the US extradition request to proceed, based in part on an evaluation of supporting materials the Trump administration supplied to the government on 26 August.Under Spanish law, at this “administrative” stage, the 22-member council has the power to deny the request, before it reaches a “judicial” stage.The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group Hamas. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators gather at Puerta del Sol in Madrid during a rally demanding the release of the US activist Fergie Chambers and opposing his extradition to the US on 5 September 2026Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockChambers’ team say he has been supporting humanitarian aid and other projects. The 41–year-old self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s additional charges of “international money laundering” don’t hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. Chambers’ donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries for several years – including theSameer Project,in Gaza.“It would set an alarming precedent in all of Europe if Spain allowed the Trump administration to criminalize offering vital humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people and defending their rights,” saidBaltasar Garzón, the acclaimed human rights lawyer and a member of Chambers’ legal team.“That’s what Fergie has financed: humanitarian aid and support for people in a situation of great need,” said Garzón. “That’s not terrorism, according to Spanish and European legal standards.”Meanwhile, Schnabel has met with members of Sumar and Podemos – progressive political movements vital to the coalition government of the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – and has written a one-page letter to Sánchez asking him to make “the only morally acceptable decision”, that of denying extradition. Sánchez forms part of the council of ministers.Schnabel has not escaped scrutiny since her partner was detained on 10 July in Ibiza. On a recent trip to New York, the FBI pulled her aside at JFK airport and confiscated her phone, she said.Support for Chambers in the lead-up to the 20 September meeting has come from Ione Bellara, leader of Podemos, who opened the party’s quarterly meeting lastSaturdaywith a statement opposing the extradition request, saying that Chambers was “on the right side of history” with his financial support of Palestinians in Gaza.Similarly, Sumar, the leftwing coalition that governs jointly with Sánchez’s Socialist party, filed a statement in Spain’s congress earlier this week urging the government to deny the petition, “given that the goal of the extradition request … is to criminalize, persecute or punish [Chambers] due to his political opinions, his public activity or his participation in political movements – in this case, in support of the Palestinian people”.Irene Montero, member of Podemos and Spanish representative to the European parliament, told the Guardian that “Our laws don’t contemplate the actions he is accused of … [and] we can’t become a subject of the United States.”Activists have held rallies in recent days in at least six cities across Spain in support of Chambers, with plans for more.Other shows of support from farther afield have included a petition delivered to the Spanish government signed by actors, academics, activists and others, including Richard Gere, Greta Thunberg and Angela Davis. In Tunisia, supporters of the Club Africain football team displayed banners and T-shirts at a recent match that read, “Free Fergie”. In Portugal, atFesta do Avante, one of that country’s largest cultural festivals, fans held up a banner saying: “Free Fergie – supporting Palestine isn’t a crime.”Schnabel told the Guardianlast monththat the $7.5m went to support Club Africain. Hamed Mbarek, one of the club’s supporters and an organizer of fans at last Saturday’s match, said Club Africain was “pro-Palestine” and that Chambers and the club had “synchronicity”.Chambers’ money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time.His views and donations have been extensivelyprofiledin US media.
