title: AI will transform capitalism – but how? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like
Author: Paul Mason
Headline: Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks like
Content: Illustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Elia Barbieri/The GuardianThe big ideaAI (artificial intelligence)AI will transform capitalism – but how?Technology is going to drastically reshape the economy, and it’s within our power to decide what that looks likePaul MasonSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea that autonomous, thinking machines may one day destroy property, hierarchy and inequality is as old as western political thought. In Aristotle’s Politics, the philosopher cites a fantasy from the Iliad, in which machines begin to act independently of human direction, concluding: “If every tool could perform its own work when ordered, or by seeing what to do in advance … if thus shuttles wove and quills played harps of themselves, master-craftsmen would have no need of assistants and masters no need of slaves.”The dream that automation could inaugurate a classless society is also present in the writings of Karl Marx. In 1858 he imagined the replacement of intellectual property with “socialised knowledge”, which would merge into a “general intellect”, blowing the foundations of capitalism sky high.Today this prospect has begun to haunt Silicon Valley. In July, Dean Ball, head of strategic futures at OpenAI, claimed China’s advocacy of open-source models of artificial intelligence might bring about “full AI communism”.For China, Ball complained, “AI is a public good which will ultimately be provided by the state as a kind of ‘digital public infrastructure’.” This, he concluded, “strikes me as a dystopian hellscape”.Though I relish Ball’s discomfort, I doubt the rise of rival Chinese models – Kimi, Qwen and Deepseek – heralds the end of capitalism. Rather, it is an attempt to counter one strategy for global domination with another.The US AI strategy – which is to hoard computing power, giving users access only via the internet – is designed to force the rest of us to use American software, cloud computing services and regulations. The Chinese counterplay is to make the AI open source, allowing users to run versions locally on their own servers and to firewall their data from being exploited by a Chinese AI provider.Beijing gambles that if AI does indeed become a “general purpose technology”, the People’s Republic of China can win the battle for supremacy in the technologies built on top of it, such as brain-machine interfaces, bioengineering and what it calls the “low altitude economy” (the realm of delivery drones, and so on).double quotation markIt’s not just the jobs of workers that come under threat, but those of capitalistsWho wins this contest will determine the trajectory of information technology for the rest of the century. But what if there was a third way? What if, instead of a contest between two flavours of hierarchical and unequal info-capitalism, we decided to shape artificial intelligence towards the ends Marx and Aristotle imagined?Large language models (LLMs) already exhibit the features of what Marx described as the “general intellect”: they are designed to embody and learn from every item of human knowledge ever produced. Frontier models are already surpassing the output of some trained and experienced knowledge workers.And while we are all aware that this has begun to eliminate tasks and even entire job functions, few of us have understood what it is likely to do to capitalism.For now, of course, the monopoly positions carved out by the AI companies are making shareholders and the workforce very rich. But the job-destroying quality of AI makes it different from every previous technological revolution. Few can say with confidence that the jobs destroyed will be replaced by new kinds of activity – as vaudeville theatres were replaced by Hollywood, for example.And it’s not just the jobs of workers that come under threat, but those of capitalists. If a machine can replace a junior solicitor, or a web designer, it can also replace the entrepreneur, the innovator and the forex dealer. The economist Philippe Aghion said that AI might not only automate entrepreneurial skill but destroy the link between innovation and profit: for who would patent a discovery if the filed blueprint could be immediately emulated and bettered by a machine? So we face a choice: delay and obstruct AI adoption in the name of social justice, or embrace it in a radically altered form. I prefer the latter.Marx described the advance of industry in the 19th century as moving humans “to the side” of the production process, turning them into machine supervisors rather than machine operatives. Artificial intelligence does this for brain work, and to very high standards, less than five years into the deployment of LLMs. The impacts will be profound – because capitalism without human workers, innovators and entrepreneurs won’t function like capitalism.So the rational question is not how Britain builds a sovereign AI to rival those of China and America. It is: how does humanity shape AI towards the fulfilment of human need?There are some obvious starting points: break the link between work and wages, through the provision of universal basic services and incomes; promote co-operative and non-profit business models; and use AI to do what Soviet-style planning could never do – replace the market as the rational allocation mechanism. But that still leaves the question of whatkindof artificial intelligence we need to design.American AI looks like it does – brash, exploitative, secretive and mercantilist – because it is designed to replicate a specific social reality. Likewise, the Chinese models, for all their openness, are built to further the project of global hegemony.It is not out of the question for those who want a green, social-democratic, co-operative or even anarchist future to devote resources in the here and now to diverting the path of technological development towards these goals.If we are prepared to trail six months behind Claude or Kimi, we can simply use them to design an un-ownable AI model with humanism and universal values built in.And if China’s open-sourced models are eating into the market share of the Silicon Valley giants, why couldn’t ours – since ours would be free and theirs reliant on the $20-a month subscriptions from millions of people?A green and social-democratic AI model would look very different even to the self-proclaimed ethical models offered by US vendors. It would aim to economise on energy and computing power; it might be weighted towards altruism, not competition and individualism. Its starting point might be the community, not the individual.So while I don’t think AI automatically creates a classless society, it does stand a chance of creating a huge, generalised crisis of the existing model, in which those prepared to imagine the future, not cling to the past, have a chance to shape it.Paul Mason is a broadcaster and author of Reds: A Global History of Communism (Apollo).Further readingAtlas of AIby Kate Crawford (Yale, £12.99)Fully Automated Luxury Communismby Aaron Bastani (Verso, £9.99)AI Superpowers: China, Silicon Valley, and the New World Order by Kai-Fu Lee (Harper Business, £12.99)Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The big ideaComputingEconomicsPolitics booksTechnology booksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with fun | Movies | The Guardian
description: There’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventure
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: There’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventure
Content: A love story of sorts … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Rediat AbaynehView image in fullscreenA love story of sorts … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Rediat AbaynehMoviesReviewShaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with funThere’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventurePeter BradshawSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer is over and Halloween is on the way … not for a fair bit, of course, but if all the UK’s Halloween merch and continuing pop culture content is up to the standard of this film, then no one is going to be complaining. This is the third in Aardman’s thoroughly enjoyable and cleverly written Shaun the Sheep stop-motion franchise of what are effectively silent movies, with a few intelligible words. It is the story of gutsy and heroic sheep involved in amazing adventures in the sleepy village of Mossy Bottom, starring characters who first appeared in theWallace and Gromit short film A Close Shave.‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movieRead moreThis one is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found inAardmanfilms. We get nods to The Archers, The Wombles and The Simpsons; there’s a wacky chase worthy of What’s Up, Doc?; a homage to the notorious waxing scene from Judd Apatow’s The 40-Year-Old Virgin; and even what appears to be a brief visual walk-on for George Bernard Shaw as Bigfoot. As ever with Shaun the Sheep and Aardman Animations generally, the standard of writing is extremely high and the script here, from Mark Burton and Giles Pilbrow, sparkles with good-natured fun. One high-street hairdressing salon in the wool-producing district where it’s set is called Barber Black Sheep – and if no real-life shop has stolen this joke yet, they ought to.A klutzy, balding sheep farmer (voiced by John Sparkes), on whose premises Shaun and the gang are to be found, is poignantly in love with a visiting vet (voiced by Nina Sosanya); he longs to invite her to a local country music hoedown, but is shy and moreover ashamed of being follicularly challenged. As for the sheep themselves, they are secretly cultivating a pumpkin patch to harvest a bunch of scary jack-o-lanterns for their forthcoming Halloween frolics. The clumsy big-booted farmer ruins them all, and the resourceful sheep turn to the dark magic of technology and sinister GM techniques (as discovered in a children’s science book) to grow supersized new pumpkins from a rescued seed. But some of their occult new miracle growth-boost liquid finds its way into the farmer’s baldness-cure bottle.The pitchfork-wielding villagers of Mossy Bottom are hilariously stunned at the terrifying appearance of a rampaging, hairy beast who has been spotted in the outlying fields and woodlands at the very moment that the farmer himself has mysteriously disappeared. Has the beast somehow kidnapped or eaten the farmer? It is a nightmarish mystery that will need every ounce of Shaun and his pals’ courage and ingenuity to sort out, not to mention that of the vet, who uses a hi-tech DNA machine to examine the genetic provenance of a piece of the beast’s fur she has managed to snip off.It is a love story of sorts, perhaps a little like that of Beauty and the Beast, but about two people who for most the story’s running time don’t know that they are going to be in love. As for the sheep, their faces convey amazingly distinct expressions and moods with just a few deft movements. It’s sharp, smart, funny and precise; there is nothing woolly about it.Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is out on 17 September in Australia, and on 18 September in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFamily filmsShaun the Sheep MovieAardmanComedy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Babies review – Anna Kendrick and Seth Rogen embrace childlessness in breezy comedy | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: To be a parent or not to be a parent is the question propelling this often insightful yet largely run-of-the-mill riff on a Judd Apatow movie
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: To be a parent or not to be a parent is the question propelling this often insightful yet largely run-of-the-mill riff on a Judd Apatow movie
Content: Writer-director Lauren Miller Rogen recruited her husband, Seth, and Anna Kendrick to play Aaron and Annie, a Los Angeles couple.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenWriter-director Lauren Miller Rogen recruited her husband, Seth, and Anna Kendrick to play Aaron and Annie, a Los Angeles couple.Photograph: Toronto film festivalFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewBabies review – Anna Kendrick and Seth Rogen embrace childlessness in breezy comedyToronto film festival:To be a parent or not to be a parent is the question propelling this often insightful yet largely run-of-the-mill riff on a Judd Apatow movieBenjamin Leein TorontoSun 13 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 18.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a question still casually and routinely asked to couples everywhere regardless of familiarity, one that many fear and some feel actively offended by: are you guys gonna have kids?Despite living in an age where we’re supposedly more accepting of people who make choices that don’t conform to whatever dusty old standards our parents and their parents had to live by, there’s still an odd regressive judgment attached to those who dare to say no or even maybe. There’s the sad tilt of the head and maybe a “but you’d make such great parents” on top, as if either would make a difference to one of life’s biggest decisions. It’s a question that writer-director Lauren Miller Rogenknows all too welland as the wife ofSeth Rogen, it’s one that has an answer that immediately becomes aheadline.Trash Mountain review – Caleb Hearon’s coming home indie is a funny if familiar journeyRead moreShe has used this frustration to fuel Babies, a mostly likable if a little run-of-the-mill comedy about a couple faced with similarly intrusive questioning. She has recruited her husband and paired him withAnna Kendrick, the pair playing the Los Angeles couple of Aaron and Annie. We meet them at a pool party with friends that, as of recent years, has turned into more of a kids’ party. Annie’s voiceover, a rather lazy and inconsistently used device that the film could do without, informs us that she is almost constantly weighing up the pros and cons, laid out as we see her moon after a cute kid before expressing repulsion at them another having a tantrum. It’s creating a gap with Aaron’s friends (who don’t have as much time as he has to delve into the Bosch universe, one of the script’s funnier jokes), but more so with Annie’s friends Becky and Eliza, played byIssa RaeandKate Berlant, whose lives are constricting, offering less space for her. The decision is both helped and hindered by Aaron’s easygoing nature, a loving husband but one who doesn’t seem to care either way, allowing her to make the choice.When Eliza leaves her husband (Dan Stevens) she invites herself, with daughter Eve (a child Annie actually likes), to stay with Annie and Aaron until they can find a better solution. “Having a kid in the house will push us in a direction,” Annie tells Aaron – although it’s one of many occasions when we can feel Miller Rogentelling us too, as if she doesn’t trust her ability to just show us (too many conversations in the film feel like they have been had for the first time, as if the characters didn’t exist before someone yelled “action”). The couple are then forced, by the film, to see whether having a child around the house will push them closer to or further away the the idea of parenthood.As Annie and Aaron wrestle with whether or not to parent, Miller Rogen also wrestles what kind of film she wants to be making. There’s an amiable shagginess to certain scenes (it was described as a “hangout” movie in its premiere introduction), but at other times, one can feel a strain to keep the film within a familiar, formulaic, audience-pleasing structure with so many characters and subplots that it almost feels like an extended sitcom pilot. (Her last film as director, 2018’s unremarkable Kristen Bell comedyLike Father, felt very much like one.) There’s also David Strathairn as Annie’s father dealing with his wife’s dementia, Ed Helms as a sleazy investor to a gallery that Annie and Becky want to open, and brief cameos from Sharon Stone and Ashley Park. There are obvious echoes ofJudd Apatow, with Rogen helping to amplify, but his finest films balanced so much and so well that one didn’t picture him plotting everything out with quite so much flashcards-on-a-corkboard precision.Closing Night review – fiery women face off in Almodóvar-lite melodramaRead moreThe bigger laughs don’t always land (a failed date between Stone and Strathairn is a missed opportunity, while there are many unsuccessful poop jokes) but some of the smaller, more richly observed moments do, as Annie grapples with the shifting world around her and how your long-term friends changing their priorities shouldn’t affect your own. There is a scene at a baby shower when she finally reaches her limit with the smug cliches that come from the “you wouldn’t understand” type of mother that many non-parents will find incredibly satisfying to watch. It’s refreshing to see a film that isn’t afraid to comfort those who are often made tofeel otheredsimply fornot wanting childrenwithout feeling like an attack on those who do.Kendrick delivers all of this with the passion of someone who haspublicly saidshe also doesn’t want to have kids, and it’s one of her better comic modes, spiky but likable with it. Rogen is doing Rogen – but that’s rarely a bad thing – while Berlant, who can be extremely funny when taking on a specific comedy character, is a little lost in the film’s more dramatic moments. As Miller Rogen starts tying everything up, some scenes lacking in more detailed insight are somewhat saved by a final monologue, delivered as a response to the film’s eternal question. It’s clearly one that’s been extensively thought through by an understandably exhausted Miller Rogen – and it’s an intelligent, even-handed and genuinely rather moving way to end her film, a bumpy ride that truly sticks the landing. I pray no one asks her that question ever again.Babies is premiering at theToronto film festivaland will be released in 2027Explore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalAnna KendrickSeth RogenSharon StoneIssa RaeComedy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I Play Rocky review – crowd-pleasing Stallone biopic is heavy on fan service, light on real emotion | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: There’s a knockout central performance from Anthony Ippolito in this otherwise rather lightweight making-of comedy drama
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: There’s a knockout central performance from Anthony Ippolito in this otherwise rather lightweight making-of comedy drama
Content: Anthony Ippolito in I Play Rocky.Photograph: Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios/APView image in fullscreenAnthony Ippolito in I Play Rocky.Photograph: Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios/APFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewI Play Rocky review – crowd-pleasing Stallone biopic is heavy on fan service, light on real emotionToronto film festival:There’s a knockout central performance from Anthony Ippolito in this otherwise rather lightweight making-of comedy dramaRadheyan Simonpillaiin TorontoSun 13 Sep 2026 12.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe first see Anthony Ippolito sauntering into a harsh spotlight in I Play Rocky’s opening frames. He’s squirrelling around an audition space, physicalizing the battle between his nerves and the stubborn self-confidence that gets him into those rooms, knowing casting agents typically count him out. He collects his wits, puts his chest out to perform as “Thug #2”, and bellows out the lines, in that deep slow growl as though he’s speaking while chewing through a New York striploin. We don’t find out if his character got the “Thug #2” gig, but in those opening moments, Ippolito nails his part asSylvester Stallone.Trash Mountain review – Caleb Hearon’s coming home indie is a funny if familiar journeyRead moreIppolito is a casting coup for I PlayRocky, Peter Farrelly’s lightweight comedy about the making of Rocky, which leans hard on easy nostalgia for the 50-year-old Oscar-winning crowd-pleaser. His looks, physicality and performance are so on point and uncanny that I never broke away from seeing Stallone, not even when he’s recreating scenes so firmly lodged in mine and pop culture’s memory. The movie’s title says more than it lets on, because Ippolito doesn’t just play Sylvester Stallone playing Rocky Balboa. His performance, perhaps intentionally, blurs the line between Stallone and Rocky. When Ippolito’s Stallone is flirting with his soon to be wife Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb, soulful) or sitting in an office sparring with producers Irwin Winkler (PJ Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell), trying to convince them he’s worthy of a shot, I saw Rocky.The difficulty when separating the two is part-and-parcel with the material. I Play Rocky can at times feel like finding a trap door into remaking Rocky, because Stallone poured so much of himself into the character. Both are muscular, soft-hearted men who work in the gutter but strive for greatness, whether it’s in the ring or in front of the camera.How Stallone got in front of that camera begins with Stallone, the struggling actor, walking into a bar. There’s a fight on TV, Chuck Wepner versus Muhammed Ali. The bartender figures Ali is going to drop the schmuck in three rounds. Wepner ends up lasting nearly all 15, getting the entire bar to cheer on their feet and root for him as opposed to Ali. That’s how Rocky was born.This is a fitting subject for Farrelly, the director of 2018’s Green Book, a reverse Driving Miss Daisy, in which the boisterous Italian bouncer Tony Vallelonga (Viggo Mortensen) is hired as a chauffeur to concert pianist Don Shirley (Mahershala Ali). Like Stallone, Farrelly made an Oscar winner about a white man whose story was deemed worthy of a movie because of his proximity to a great Black man.You could also feel the director’s genuine affinity for these characters, whose fish out of water scenarios can be traced all the way back to Dumb and Dumber, one of the many delightfully crude comedies Farrelly made alongside his brother and co-director Bob. Farrelly’s left turn to making a crowd-pleasing dramedy courting Oscars in Green Book was received as an unexpected level up, as if he had entered a more “refined” class of prestige storytellers. Green Book’s Tony Vallelonga and Stallone are exactly Farrelly’s brand of heroes, working class louts on the surface who no one expects to be as perceptive and wise as they actually are, muscling their way into the wings of high society concert halls or meeting rooms with Hollywood execs.I Play Rocky has a field day with those Hollywood meetings. Farrelly and screenwriter Peter Gamble scrub out Stallone’s agents from the narrative so that they could instead stage riotous scenes with the actor in the room. Stallone gives a dumbfounded but resolute stare as producers incrementally raise the price for his script, up to $400,000, if only the writer would give up his dream of playing the lead role in favour of Clint Eastwood or Ryan O’Neal.Farrelly wrings the most wicked laughs from standoffs like these throughout I Play Rocky, where he can lean into the skillset that made hits like There’s Something About Mary all-timers. If comedy was boxing, he’s an ace at cooking up scenarios that hit with a jab, cross, hook, occasionally landing an upper caught that got the Toronto premiere audience to their feet.But after that initial test of wills, I Play Rocky largely settles into fan service mode, moving through the production of Rocky, recreating the most memorable scenes with a viewfinder remove. When Rocky sprints up those steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Arts, we’re not just rooting for him but also the Steadicam making that historic shot possible.Scenes that can feel perfunctory are often saved by the rotating supporting cast. Stephan James warms things up with his lovely jive talking impression of the late Carl Weathers. Jay Duplass is a riot as director John Avildsen, who insists they’re not making a boxing movie, but a character study in the ring. PJ Byrne is the scene stealer as Winkler. He’s hilariously caught between immovable figures like Stallone and the fictional, cynical studio boss played by Tracy Letts, spiralling out because the former doesn’t know the first thing about making a movie while the latter is on his ass because no one understands the movie they’re trying to make.It’s all very amusing but I Play Rocky rarely has pathos in its corner. Save for some truly touching moments involving Stallone’s struggle to care for his dog Butkus, it’s often as emotionally vacant as Stallone’s stare. So many of the psychological stakes and insights are written shorthand, soundbites about traumas and insecurities are calculatingly delivered by Matt Dillon’s Stallone Sr and a wonderful Robb as Stallone’s first wife Sasha Czack. The latter drops the most insightful line about the actor’s desperate need to be seen, which Farrelly and writer Gamble refuse to mine for more.Instead, they just lightly unpack the big emotional swings in the 1976 original, hoping their prime source does all the heavy lifting.Rocky packed a punch. I Play Rocky appreciates that and settles for some good tickles.I Play Rocky is premiering at theToronto film festivaland opens in cinemas on 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewRockyDrama filmsSylvester StalloneToronto film festivalBoxingFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Closing Night review – fiery women face off in Almodóvar-lite melodrama | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts and Dianne Wiest are all impressive in actor-turned-director Cody Fern’s debut but they’re left stranded
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts and Dianne Wiest are all impressive in actor-turned-director Cody Fern’s debut but they’re left stranded
Content: Sarah Paulson in Closing Night.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenSarah Paulson in Closing Night.Photograph: Toronto film festivalFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewClosing Night review – fiery women face off in Almodóvar-lite melodramaToronto film festival:Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts and Dianne Wiest are all impressive in actor-turned-director Cody Fern’s debut but they’re left strandedBenjamin Leein TorontoSun 13 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are three relatively substantive roles for female actors over the age of 50 in actor-turned-film-maker Cody Fern’s talky drama Closing Night. It’s a sadly impressive feat even at a time when the industry has slowly become more aware that women don’t get sent to a farm upstate after their 40th birthday.Everybody Wants to F*ck Me review – Taron Egerton is hounded in sharp-toothed dating nightmareRead moreInstead they usually get sent to work with Ryan Murphy on television and his shadow looms over Australian actor Cody Fern’s debut as writer-director. Fern worked with him on three seasons of American Horror Story and one of American Crime Story and while there are many legitimate criticisms to be levelled at Murphy and his specific brand of sensationalist television (reaching a new low with last year’s criminally awful legal drama All’s Fair), he has continued to provide sustained work for many women who had otherwise been put out to pasture by the industry. For Closing Night, Fern has recruited Sarah Paulson, whoonce saidshe owes Murphy “everything” after super-sizing her career, Naomi Watts, who has now starred in four Murphy shows, and Dianne Wiest, who despite winning two Oscars hasadmittedshe has struggled to financially sustain herself with the amount of work she has been offered.It’s a considerable pleasure to see them power afilm premiering at Toronto, the kind of sell that might have been more common back in the 40s or 50s when women’s pictures were being routinely produced by studios. But while the women all bring their A-game, the film isn’t even close to their level, like inviting three Olympian sprinters to run laps around a gravel pit.On paper at least, it offers the potential for fireworks. Paulson is Sandra Vale, an acclaimed actor about to kick off a Broadway run as the lead of Mother Courage. She has invited her estranged sister April (Watts), mother Diane (Wiest) and nephew Theo (Euphoria’s Toby Wallace) to watch with Theo’s secretly pregnant girlfriend Lucy (Odessa A’zion) tagging along. But Diane can’t leave the salon back in Michigan and April is already unravelling, arriving at Theo’s apartment in a state, suggesting they do anything but see the sister she still hasn’t forgiven for sleeping with her boyfriend three decades ago. Theo convinces her to go and once at the theatre, Dutch courage convinces her to stay but mid-performance, after a shaky rehearsal, Sandra forgets her lines and collapses. At the hospital the sisters reunite and while April remains in town, Sandra receives a devastating diagnosis.There’s the initial promise of something grittier, closer to John Cassavetes’s similarly titled Opening Night, also about an actor going through a crisis surrounding a Broadway premiere, but Fern’s psychological insights are far too limited and his plotting far too creaky. One then hopes for something campier or juicier, especially given Fern’s Murphy tutelage, but there’s not enough acid to his dialogue, co-written by former child actor Devon Bostick, or bite to the ensuing confrontations which all play out closer to something from a daytime soap. It ultimately becomes something closer to a Pedro Almodóvar melodrama but without the meaningful life experience threaded through which downgrades it to something Xavier Dolan might have made back in the day, the film perhaps best described as what his remake of The Room Next Door might look like without his terrible needle drops. Like that film, it progresses into a more morose drama about dealing with illness, death and how to plan the end of a life.I Play Rocky review – crowd-pleasing Stallone biopic is heavy on fan service, light on real emotionRead moreGiven the ingredients, it’s tempting to wonder what someone like Murphy could have done with the same material. He might be a hit-and-miss provocateur but he does know a thing or two about capturing an audience’s attention and while Fern might have inherited his respect of older female actors who might not be respected enough elsewhere but he’s learned little else. Paulson, who recentlyrevealedshe has rarely been offered major film roles even after her award-winning run as Marcia Clark, clearly relishes such a grand opportunity and even if it affords here more screentime than real emotion to play with, she does an excellent job at strenuously raising the bar for Fern’s writing to try and meet her. It’s also a great mode for Watts, an actor who works extensively yet can’t always find the way back to her sweet spot. Even at this festival, she’s miscast as a secret Nazi home-maker inThe Housewife, another middling Canadian drama. As a spiraling Michigan mum, she’s a surprisingly comfortable fit and in her moments of tear-strewn, red-faced mania, she recalls one of her finest roles back in 21 Grams. But again it’s all down to her performance with very little interesting character work on paper. She’s painted in the broadest of midwest brushes and even Fern’s attempts to add idiosyncratic detail, like her random urge to steal small things, feel cribbed from the most obvious of playbooks.Fern just doesn’t seem to know the right balance between camp theatrics and serious, of-this-world drama. As fantastically fun as Wiest might be as a cruel, fur coat-wearing alcoholic salon owner, she’s less real person and more “wouldn’t it be fun if?” future Halloween costume. If the slightly juiceless conflict-heavy family drama doesn’t cut as deep as we like, there’s at least a frantic energy to these scenes (A’zion once again is an actor who excels under that sort of pressure). But when the film leans fully into glum end-of-life territory, Fern can’t conjure the tears that such a monumentally sad story like this desperately deserves, as if the dolls we had seen him play dress-up with suddenly came to life. Closing Night is heavy-lifted by three incredible women but dragged back down to Earth by the man who brought them together.Closing Night is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalFestivalsNaomi WattsDrama filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mahler Academy Orchestra/Steinaecker review – trailblazing performance that pushes work to the limits | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: Penultimate Prom showcases antique brass and woodwind and humongous tubular bells in a magical mystery tour through an alien musical landscape
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Penultimate Prom showcases antique brass and woodwind and humongous tubular bells in a magical mystery tour through an alien musical landscape
Content: An ability to shock an audience to its core … Philipp von Steinaecker conducting Mahler’s Ninth with the Mahler Academy Orchestra.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCView image in fullscreenAn ability to shock an audience to its core … Philipp von Steinaecker conducting Mahler’s Ninth with the Mahler Academy Orchestra.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCProms 2026ReviewMahler Academy Orchestra/Steinaecker review – trailblazing performance that pushes work to the limitsRoyal Albert Hall, LondonPenultimate Prom showcases antique brass and woodwind and humongous tubular bells in a magical mystery tour through an alien musical landscapeClive PagetSun 13 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOther conductors and orchestras have taken a historically informed view of Mahler – Roger Norrington was among the first, and more recently Les Siècles – but the logical conclusion drawn by the Mahler Academy Orchestra at this penultimate Prom still had the power to shock an audience to its core. Their intention was to perform on – and push to the limits – the instruments the composer would have known, replicating period technique to explore what musicians of the day would have considered beautiful and what might have been thought vulgar (bearing in mind Mahler himself was frequently accused of questionable taste).Forget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewardsRead moreIt’s the brainchild of conductor Philipp von Steinaecker who scoured auction rooms and attics seeking out antique Viennese brass and woodwind, French harps, Turkish cymbals (smaller than you might think) and the humongous tubular bells Mahler demanded but rarely got. Gut strings and minimal vibrato were expected, but the extremes of portamento and rubato deployed in this radical performance of the Ninth Symphony stretched an ear-opening interpretation almost to breaking point. The result, even for seasoned original instrument fans, was a magical mystery tour through an alien musical landscape.The orchestral layout adopted was similarly original, with basses up high behind the brass, strings divided either side of the conductor and harps and horns on the audience’s right instead of the usual left. It took a while for the ear to adjust. The first movement felt a touch self-conscious, with scooping portamenti and spotlighted instrumental solos that seemed to cry out “listen to the kind of noises I can make”. The playing nevertheless was superlative, with magnificently secure horns, bright, needling trumpets, woody flutes and the spiciest of oboes, all of them poking their heads through cotton candy clouds of gut strings.View image in fullscreenSteinaecker and the Mahler Academy Orchestra.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBCThe clodhopping Ländler, which often comes over a trifle tipsy, was practically paralytic here, its dramatic transitions sinking into a final drunken stupor. The Rondo-Burleske snorted and snarled, the orchestral motor firmly in overdrive. The elegiac finale was breathtaking as Steinaecker steered the silken Academy strings towards a pin-drop conclusion. It set the seal on a trailblazing performance that will surely be talked about for years to come.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Last Night of the Proms review – musical chaos ensues in near four-hour finale | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky Spence
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky Spence
Content: On top of his brief … tenor Nicky Spence (centre) with conductor Sakari Oramo (right) on stage with the BBC Symphony Orchestra for the Last Night of the Proms.Photograph: Jennifer Hawthorn /BBCView image in fullscreenOn top of his brief … tenor Nicky Spence (centre) with conductor Sakari Oramo (right) on stage with the BBC Symphony Orchestra for the Last Night of the Proms.Photograph: Jennifer Hawthorn /BBCProms 2026ReviewLast Night of the Proms review – musical chaos ensues in near four-hour finaleRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky SpenceAlexandra CoghlanSun 13 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Richard Strauss’s Ariadne auf Naxos, a wealthy man commissions an evening’s entertainment: a lofty new opera and a comic burlesque. But when time constraints force them to be performed simultaneously, surreal musical chaos ensues. One can only assume that the BBC was taking notes.The Last Night of the Proms is the finale to eight weeks of concerts, and the BBC’s annual identity crisis. Is this the celebratory end to a season of serious music or a standalone party, whose first half is something to be endured before the real fun begins? It’s both, of course. And that’s where the trouble starts.Playing With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworldsRead moreConsider the running time of nearly four hours. That’s longer than Rheingold, pushing into Tristan und Isolde territory: a bloated classical variety performance where all shall have prizes (this year even, perhaps to her heavenly surprise, Dolly Parton) and no music shall be left behind – not even Samuel Barber’s inscrutable, gruffly virtuosic 1962 Piano Concerto. Try waving your flag to that.But try the audience did. There’s a place in musical hell for the person who let off a howling rocket balloon just as the soaring central theme of Holst’s Jupiter began, and again in the ravishing cello solo of Tom Bowling, but you can hardly blame the steady trickle of walkouts during piano megastar Yuja Wang’s stylish, near-superhuman account of the Barber, nor the restless, pre-emptive burst of applause at the not-end of Smetana’s Vltava.View image in fullscreenConductor Sakari Oramo and pianist Yuja Wang.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBC/PAThe conductor, Sakari Oramo, the evening’s ever-genial MC, offered us an alternative definition of AI during his traditional speech: Artistic Integrity. When the night got it right it sang off the stage: in the sardonic dances of Alexander Tsfasman’s Soviet-era Jazz Suite (Wang back as a dazzling blur of a soloist, with a little help from Richard Hosford’s outrageous solo clarinet), in the lightly worn choral excellence of the BBC Singers delivering the world premiere of Anne Dudley’s Iris of Life, and roaring and blazing from tenor Nicky Spence.Has any Last Night soloist better understood the assignment? Whether giving us heartfelt heroism in the Prince’s aria from Rusalka or Broadway pizzazz in Guys and Dolls’ Sit Down, You’re Rocking the Boat (complete with hip flask and New York accent) or a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it tour through his native Scotland’s music that smuggled in the Proclaimers and Yes Sir, I Can Boogie alongside folk songs and an athletic dance-routine, Spence was absolutely himself, absolutely in his element. Sometimes authenticity sounds like a symphony orchestra, sometimes it comes dressed in a Magic Mike­-style pair of breakaway tartan trousers.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October and onBBC iPlayeruntil August 2027.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I grew my hair and dropped out of society after hearing Black Sabbath’: J Mascis’s honest playlist | Dinosaur Jr | The Guardian
description: The Dinosaur Jr axe man stole from his mum to buy a Beach Boys record and squeaks to Tom Petty – but which punk banger made him cry?
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The Dinosaur Jr axe man stole from his mum to buy a Beach Boys record and squeaks to Tom Petty – but which punk banger made him cry?
Content: In a field of his own … J Mascis.Photograph: Jeffrey FowlerView image in fullscreenIn a field of his own … J Mascis.Photograph: Jeffrey FowlerHonest playlistDinosaur Jr‘I grew my hair and dropped out of society after hearing Black Sabbath’: J Mascis’s honest playlistThe Dinosaur Jr axe man stole from his mum to buy a Beach Boys record and squeaks to Tom Petty – but which punk banger made him cry?As told toPriya ElanSun 13 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the first song you fell in love with?Monster Mash by Bobby “Boris” Pickett. Monsters appealed to me as a kid. I found it funny, not spooky. Since I had a kid, Halloween has become the biggest holiday of the year.What was the first single you bought?I bought Darlin’ by the Beach Boys with the money I would steal from my mom. I always liked the Beach Boys. I remember they were quite unhip for a while: I played them at a gig around 1989 before we came on and people hated it. Now they’ve become more hip again.What’s the song you do at karaoke?Here Comes My Girl by Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers. It’s a little high for me but I can usually squeak it out. My wife liked that the first time I did it, so I guess since she likes it I tend to keep doing it.What’s the best song to play at a party?I’ve DJ’d with my wife a couple of times recently, and What’s She Done to Your Mind by Rain Parade seems to be a big hit. When I DJ I do seven-inches only, which is good for limiting things.The best song to have sex to?Sugar Hiccup by the Cocteau Twins.What’s the song you inexplicably know every lyric to?Straight Outta Compton by NWA was so awesome when it came out, I listened to it so much. It just stuck in my brain. I saw the movie they made about them but I’ve already forgotten much of it. I don’t remember if I liked it or not.What’s the song that changed your life?The Thrill of It All by Black Sabbath was really my anthem of dropping out of society. I heard it when I was 11 or 12 and I grew my hair and dropped out of the popular crowd after that.What’s the song that gets you up in the morning?Fight Back by Discharge. It’s a peppy number to get you going.What’s the song that makes you cry?I remember somebody telling me that when she sawJohn Prineonce she cried. I told her that I cried when [US hardcore punk band]  Negative Approach played Can’t Tell No One and she was somehow horrified. But I’d seen them when I was a kid and then seeing them back together really touched something in me.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine.
