It just seems like the perfect funeral song. Just so sad.Dinosaur Jr’s albumThere Nearisout now.Explore more on these topicsDinosaur JrHonest playlistPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Spiritbox review – Canadian metal ranges from gothic and guttural to Auto-Tune pop | Music | The Guardian
description: Singer Courtney LaPlante’s delivery typifies the tension between hard and soft in a confident show that could do with more grit
Author: Claire Biddles
Headline: Singer Courtney LaPlante’s delivery typifies the tension between hard and soft in a confident show that could do with more grit
Content: Compelling … Spiritbox’s Courtney LaPlante.Photograph: Alana Ann LopezView image in fullscreenCompelling … Spiritbox’s Courtney LaPlante.Photograph: Alana Ann LopezMusicReviewSpiritbox review – Canadian metal ranges from gothic and guttural to Auto-Tune popSEC, GlasgowSinger Courtney LaPlante’s delivery typifies the tension between hard and soft in a confident show that could do with more gritClaire BiddlesSun 13 Sep 2026 08.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt tonight’s Spiritbox show, vocalist Courtney LaPlante addresses the anxiety and isolation of the Canadian band’s origins: “We grew up on Vancouver Island, far away from our dreams.” Now touring Europe in support of their acclaimed 2025 albumTsunami Sea, Spiritbox show no trace of these early struggles, delivering a confident, polished performance of anthemic metal.This UK tour follows a US run opening for nu-metal icons Evanescence, with whom they share a fascination with the musical tension between hard and soft – and in LaPlante, a compelling gothic frontperson. They share a flexible approach to genre with much contemporary metalcore, deftly incorporating elements of drum’n’bass, R&B and industrial music. Circle With Me has Running Up That Hill-esque drums and reverb-laden guitar. The EDM-inflected Crystal Roses doesn’t completely gel, but LaPlante’s Auto-Tuned vocals add an interesting new texture to the mix.View image in fullscreenExtreme polish … Spiritbox.Photograph: Alana Ann LopezFlanked by bassist Josh Gilbert and guitarist Mike Stringer, LaPlante is the anchor of the band’s dynamism, known for both her guttural metal scream (exceptional during Cellar Door) and the purity of her clean vocals. If you ever wondered what a metal band fronted by Ariana Grande would sound like, it’s The Void, all smoky R&B vocals and propulsive guitars. For Keep Sweet (dedicated to “the girls, the gays and the theys”, of which there are many present) she switches between both modes with impressive control, like another nu-metal icon: Chester Bennington of Linkin Park. She also has great stage presence, striding in PVC trousers, trailing straps and ribbons.Despite this, it’s sometimes difficult to feel involved in the show. The drapes framing the stage box the band in and disrupt sightlines. Drummer Zev Rose– also a hugely dynamic player, especially when using electronic percussion – is cut off from his bandmates on a high drum riser. The extreme polish of the music can veer into flatness, and it feels incongruous that such heavy music has little room for grit or unpredictability.“It’s time to wash away all the baggage from the past” LaPlante declares before closing the set with new single Mourning. Now that Spiritbox have definitively shed their demons, introducing some disruption into their supremely confident approach could take them even further.Spiritbox are touring the UKuntil 19 September.Explore more on these topicsMusicMetalScotlandreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Children review – Meera Syal and co go nuclear in poignant drama | Stage | The Guardian
description: A catastrophic explosion forces retired nuclear engineers Syal and Declan Conlon to confront their past after a visit by Kerry Fox in this revival of Lucy Kirkwood’s debut
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: A catastrophic explosion forces retired nuclear engineers Syal and Declan Conlon to confront their past after a visit by Kerry Fox in this revival of Lucy Kirkwood’s debut
Content: Complex characters … Kerry Fox, Meera Syal and Declan Conlon in The Children.Photograph: Helen MaybanksView image in fullscreenComplex characters … Kerry Fox, Meera Syal and Declan Conlon in The Children.Photograph: Helen MaybanksStageReviewThe Children review – Meera Syal and co go nuclear in poignant dramaLyric Hammersmith, LondonA catastrophic explosion forces retired nuclear engineers Syal and Declan Conlon to confront their past after a visit by Kerry Fox in this revival of Lucy Kirkwood’s debutMiriam GillinsonSun 13 Sep 2026 06.28 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years on fromits powerful debut, Lucy Kirkwood’s clever and funny play feels just as potent – if not more so. There’s so much to admire and enjoy here: Kirkwood’s skilful and layered writing; Rachel O’Riordan’s precise and thoughtful direction; Gary McCann’s striking design and, above all, a trio of richly nuanced performances from three brilliant older actors: Meera Syal, Declan Conlon and Kerry Fox. For all the ideas about the legacy we leave behind for our children, I found myself reflecting on how much we still overlook our elders, and what a terrible failing and waste that is.O’Riordan’s softly rumbling production unfolds sometime in the near future (although that supposed future feels horribly close these days). There has been a catastrophic explosion at a nuclear power plant. Exclusion zones have been established and lives redrawn. Husband and wife, Robin and Hazel (who are both nuclear engineers), have retired to a nearby crumbling cottage. When old friend and fellow engineer, Rose, turns up unannounced – determined to lure them back to work at the power plant – all three are forced to confront painful mistakes from their past and think deeply about their futures.View image in fullscreenEmotions that turn in a flash … Conlon and Syal in The Children.Photograph: Helen MaybanksThe three characters are fascinating, complex and intriguingly volatile. Syal’s Hazel starts off as warm and funny: a determinedly healthy retiree wedded to yoghurt and yoga. But Syal’s performance has depth and bite and her character gradually emerges as a deeply perceptive woman with a steely centre. Conlon’s Robin has a boyish energy about him, which initially feels lighthearted but gradually turns terribly sad. Fox’s Rose is strong and resourceful, yet still capable of trembling with desires unspent. The emotions of all three – and the temperature of the scenes – turn in a flash. Sexy one second. Dangerous the next. Loving and tender. Seething with resentment and regret.McCann’s impressive set frames the fading cottage with huge metallic circles, which arch over the stage and occasionally glow ominously. There’s the suggestion of an underground bunker but it also lends the production a scientific feel, as we’re peering at these characters through a microscope. Here is humanity in all its messy glory. Here is everything, for better and worse, we stand to lose. So what are we going to do about it?AtLyric Hammersmith, London, until 3 October.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreMeera SyalLucy KirkwoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Céline Dion review – singer’s first live show in years marks a triumphant, emotional return | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description:
Plenitude Arena, Paris
Dion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndrome
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: Plenitude Arena, ParisDion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndrome
Content: Celine Dion walks on stage at the Plenitude Arena, Paris on Saturday night. The show was her first full-length concert in six years.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenCeline Dion walks on stage at the Plenitude Arena, Paris on Saturday night. The show was her first full-length concert in six years.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersCéline DionReviewCéline Dion review – singer’s first live show in years marks a triumphant, emotional returnPlenitude Arena, ParisDion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndromeAlim KherajSat 12 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022, when Céline Dion shared that she had been diagnosed with a rare incurable neurological disorder calledstiff person syndrome (SPS),there was no guarantee that the 58-year-old would ever tour again. Her condition, which resulted in muscle spasms so strong thatit left her with broken ribs, had made it impossible to perform, and in a 2024 documentary,I Am: Céline Dion, fans saw how the disease had constricted her once seemingly infallible voice. Through it all, though, Dion was resolute that she would one day return to the stage. “If I can’t run, I’ll walk. If I can’t walk, I’ll crawl,” she said in the film. “But I won’t stop.”‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackRead moreThankfully at the opening night of her sold out five-week residency in Paris, her first full-length concerts in six years, no crawling is needed:Céline Dionis back. She glides on to the stage in a black dress, an enormous diamond necklace clasped around her throat, and launches into On ne change pas. There are tears almost immediately: she struggles through the second verse, her voice cracking as she begins to cry. By the time the strum of Destin has kicked in, though, that emotion is replaced with sheer elation. “I made a promise to be back on stage. Singing for you. Singing for me,” she says. “Singing for life.”View image in fullscreenDion performs during her first concert of a series at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, west of Paris on 12 September.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesThat she does. There is no cure for SPS, but the work Dion has put into managing her condition so she can perform again is astounding. Still, clearly some necessary allowances have been made. Some songs such as Because You Loved Me, The Power of Love and My Heart Will Go On have all been transposed down. It’s understandable given the effect her condition has had on her voice, although, in the case of Because You Loved Me and It’s All Coming Back To Me Now, it does somewhat dampen their melodramatic potency.That is not to say that Dion’s voice is weakened: when she needs to, as she does on the driving Tout l’or des hommes, she can still belt out a note. There’s also some welcome texture to her vocal, too: recently released ballad Dansons sees her embracing her lower register, while Courage, recorded following the death of her late husband René Angélil, is genuinely affecting as Dion allows her voice to get fragile and raspy.For some, Dion’s success – she has sold more than 200m records and is the third most successful female artist of all time – is inexplicable: to them, her music is the apotheosis of saccharin and anodyne adult contemporary. But for the 30,000-plus in the crowd tonight, that contempt is decidedly absent. After all, you don’t attend a Céline Dion show expecting anything avant garde. You’re there to hear Beauty and the Beast, an unexpected highlight.View image in fullscreenDion wipes away tears.Photograph: Samir Hussein/WireImageStill, Dion does have some surprises up her sleeve: the run of J’irai où tu iras, Ne bouge pas and Dans un autre monde provides some rollicking respite from the balladry, Dion strutting up and down the stage while doing vocal acrobatics or fake boxing with backing singer. This is followed by an outlandishly camp disco section, complete with covers of Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (oddly enough, Moroder’s sequenced synths really are a great match), Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) and a chandelier that quickly morphs into a glitter ball. As Dion shimmies about, separating the covers with a souped-up electronic take on That’s The Way It Is, a sly smile reveals that she, too, knows how ridiculous it all is.Most astonishing, though, is a rendition of Ebben? Ne andrò lontana from Alfredo Catalani’s opera La Wally: wearing a pink feathered coat and standing a protruding rock that has just emerged from below the stage, Dion pays homage to Maria Callas as fake snow falls from the ceiling on to the audience below. It is brilliant and ludicrous and purists will loathe it. Nevertheless, the kookiness all feels very Céline.Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!Read moreThe biggest response from the crowd, many of whom have likely been outpractising at one of the many mass karaoke eventscelebrating Dion’s music throughout Paris this week, arrives during Pour que tu m’aimes encore. The singing is so loud it almost drowns Dion out. It is All By Myself, however, that seems like the most significant for Dion. As the piano solo and slide guitar gives way, she glances upwards before unleashing herself on that final chorus. When she realises she hit the big notes, it’s relief – then triumph – that spreads across her face. Given where she has come from, and her performance on stage tonight, it’s a feeling that is clearly well deserved.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionFranceEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Burning Man at 40: the once anarchic desert festival faces a midlife crisis | Burning Man festival | The Guardian
description: The subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-rich
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: The subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-rich
Content: The Burning Man festival on 31 September 2006. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year are growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger ‘burners’.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyView image in fullscreenThe Burning Man festival on 31 September 2006. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year are growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger ‘burners’.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyBurning Man festivalBurning Man at 40: the once anarchic desert festival faces a midlife crisisThe subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-richLois BeckettSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurning Man, the infamous arts festival in the Nevada desert, turned 40 this year, and it’s showing some distinct signs of middle age.It’s not just the tech billionaires who show up to party, thechartered flightsstraight to the desert or theHBO documentaryaboutbehind-the-scenes power struggles. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year to create a tent city in the wilderness appear to be growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger “burners”, as festival participants are called.People in their 20s used to make up nearly a third of the participants in this utopian experiment, in which volunteers build a new version of Black Rock City in the desert each year, party nonstop for a week and then burn much of the art they have created, including a massive effigy of the “Man.”Since the festival paused for two years during the pandemic, the number of attenders in their 20s has dropped sharply, falling to only 10% in 2025, according to estimates from theBlack Rock City census, an annual participant survey that has been conducted in different forms since 2002. Meanwhile, the share of attenders in their 40 and 50s grew to nearly 42% last year. While data for 2026 is not yet available, the “preliminary 2026 census data suggest a slightly younger age profile than in 2025”, the organization said.View image in fullscreenBurners revel at the Burning Man festival in the Black Rock desert in Nevada on 30 August 2008.Photograph: Frederic Larson /San Francisco Chronicle via GettyBurners are used to adapting to new circumstances, and they have weathered plenty of scorn and skepticism from what they call the “default world”. But a permanent shift in the event’s demographics could have big implications for what’s possible on the ground.As Burning Man’s spiritual seekers age, can the festival remain an evolving experiment in radical communal living? Or is it doomed to become just another tech networking conference for the wealthy – one where almost everyone is high and a surprising number of people are naked?Deaths in the desertThe number of deaths connected with the festivalticked upwards to three this year, all of them men over 50. Two of the men, one in his mid-50s and the other 51, died after receiving medical treatment. A third man, aged 60, was found dead in the trailer he shared with his significant other.Local authorities said there were no signs of foul play in any of the deaths, and that more information about the causes of death would be released in about six to eight weeks, after they conducted the required autopsies and toxicology tests.“It is premature to attribute these deaths to the age of Burning Man’s participant population,” a spokesperson for the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “The deaths resulted from separate incidents, the individual causes have not been released, and age alone does not establish cause.“We encourage and ask people to focus on the contributions of the individuals lost and avoid speculation out of respect for the participants and their families.”In many ways, it’s impressive that a chaotic event that draws upwards of 70,000 people annually has only typically seen about one death per year, particularly given the festival’s notoriety for drugs,cage-fighting in the Thunderdome, live flame performances and improvised vehicles careering across the dark desert – not to mention theOrgy Dome.Thephysical conditionscan be punishing. Since 1990, Burning Man has been held on Nevada’s Black Rock playa, a gorgeous, barren stretch of dusty land that was once a prehistoric lake. There is no vegetation, no running water – virtually no signs of life. The playa is prone to sudden, ferocious dust storms: participants are encouraged to carry dust masks and goggles. Heavy rains cause flooding and turn the ground to mud.View image in fullscreenAbout 4,500 people gathered in the Black Rock desert of northern Nevada for the Burning Man festival in 1995.Photograph: Tomas Ovalle/Tri-Valley Times via GettyThe social conditions can be even more dire: endless substance use, no sleep, house music pounding across the desert nearly 24 hours a day – and, if you didn’t prepare enough, intermittent access to food. The portable toilets throughout the tent city have sometimes been decorated with PSAs urging festivalgoers to “Piss clear, cowgirl!” warning them that dark-colored urine means they’re starting to become severely dehydrated.Repeat burners tend to scoff at breathless media coverage of the festival’s weather and other disasters – like in 2023, when heavy rain and floodsforced Diplo to hitchhikeandleft tens of thousands stranded, but many participants said they were well-prepared and simply partied on.“In 2023, they were like, ‘There are diseases, they’re eating people,’” a person identified only as “Bone” toldSFGate on another muddy day this year. “Meanwhile, I’m like dancing with beautiful European women and having the best time of my life.”The inhospitable natural conditions are, after all, part of Burning Man’s design. In some ways, the 200-sq-mile desert playa functions as a kind of massive sauna, where the extreme desert heat helps participants enter a more relaxed and communal state. Festival participants rely on each other to meet their basic needs, from food, to shelter, to extremely brief and improvised showers. Buying or selling anything during the festival is forbidden, which means the 70,000-person tent city operates as a gift economy, with different groups of campers offering up different free activities, food or drink.This can make Burning Man feel like a dream: it’s possible to float across the desert from campground to campground, filling a reusable mug with endless free beers and cocktails, and occasionally catching a ride on an improvised “art car”, which might be shaped like a dragon or feature a giant playground slide. Massive handmade temples, statues and monuments loom out of the dust; by the end of the week, most of them will be set ablaze.View image in fullscreenA huge dust storm forces burners to take cover in tents or vehicles in Black Rock City on 30 August 2007.Photograph: Michael Macor/San Francisco Chronicle via GettyFor the times when that dream turns abruptly into a nightmare, Burning Man’s organizers have emphasized free community care. Volunteers provide first aid and quiet places where people having a bad trip on drugs can recover. The festival has its own free emergency room, Rampart, which is equipped with “X-ray machines, a pharmacy with over 100 medications, blood products, ventilators, chest tubes, arterial lines, [and] IV pumps”,SFGate reported. It treated nearly 1,500 patients last year.One of the men who died this year at Burning Man had been found on one of the festival’s streets and was given CPR, and then brought to the hospital, the Pershing county sheriff’s office said in a statement.“Black Rock City is a temporary, rural city of approximately 60,000 people, supported by a substantial medical and emergency-response system operating around the clock,” the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “Participants experience medical emergencies for many of the same reasons people do in any city.”A once-edgy celebration past its prime?Over its four decades, the festival has been nothing but resilient, but many early participants feel a middle-aged sense of disillusionment over what Burning Man has become.It’s not just the age of the crowd. Once a dadaist experiment, an attempt to create a “temporary autonomous-zone” in the desert, Burning Man is now a marker of class status for tech bros and “creative professionals” around the globe, a kind of west coast Wimbledon for the weird.“Early Burning Man wasn’t a ready-made escape you could buy your way into. It was an anarchistic collaboration of equals, conjured into being by a few hundred people of goodwill, far from anyone’s control,” John Law, one of the Burning Man’s co-founders,wrote in the SF Standardthis August.View image in fullscreenFestivalgoers at Burning Man on 3 September 1999.Photograph: Hector Mata/AFP via Getty ImagesToday, he wrote, it’s become an “immersive spectacle built for the consumption of western elites and the middle-class creatives who service them”.To be fair, to the art punks who built it in the first place, Burning Man hasn’t been cool for decades. Law hasn’t been back to the desert since his last burn 30 years ago.You could argue that Burning Man has been over since 1996, when it made the cover of Wired magazine, or since 2001, when Eric Schmidt wasfamously selectedas Google’s new CEO after a vetting trip to Burning Man with Sergey Brin and Larry Page.Even though today’s Burning Man still relies on a “gift economy” once participants arrive, getting there is very far from cheap. The growing number of elder burners is hardly surprising, given the increasing cost of a Burning Man experience, with entry tickets alone costing between$550 and $3,000 this year, not including the costs of food, shelter, creative outfits, vehicle rental and entry fee, and the multiple stages of travel needed to reach the remote Nevada desert.View image in fullscreenThe Serpent Mother by the Flaming Lotus Girls of San Francisco at the conclusion of Burning Man in 2006.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyAnd that’s just for an ordinary camp-in-a-tent Burn, not what Law describes as the much-derided “plug-and-play” Burning Man experiences, which might involve a chartered flight directly to the playa, air-conditioned accommodation, specially prepared costumes and a private chef.Three-quarters of Burning Man participants last year said they had a household income of more than $100,000 a year, and nearly 30% said their household income was more than $300,000, according to thecensus estimates.Though one of the principles of the festival is “radical inclusion”, the event continues to attract an overwhelmingly white crowd: in many years, estimates have put it at over 80% white. This year, the figure was 75%.Explore more on these topicsBurning Man festivalThe super-richSilicon ValleySan FranciscoCaliforniaNevadaFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He would have been the center of everything’: the art exhibition imagining if Emmett Till lived | Photography | The Guardian
description: Dedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in America
Author: Briana Ellis-Gibbs
Headline: Dedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in America
Content: Emmett Till, a black 14-year-old Chicago boy, who was brutally murdered in Mississippi in 1955 after whistling at a white woman.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenEmmett Till, a black 14-year-old Chicago boy, who was brutally murdered in Mississippi in 1955 after whistling at a white woman.Photograph: APPhotography‘He would have been the center of everything’: the art exhibition imagining if Emmett Till livedDedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in AmericaBriana Ellis-GibbsSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareSeventy-one years after the brutal murder of Emmett Till, the way that the US as a country honors his memory is still being contested. Markers commemorating his life have beenshot at, stolen and become the site of white supremacist group recruiting events. A new exhibit opening in Chicago asks the country to memorialize his life not only by remembering his death, but by asking America to consider the question: What if Emmett Till Lived?Open now and running until December, the exhibitionIf Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Groundat the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago is an imagined photo library depicting the life Till never got to live. Through the images on display, co-curators of the show, Sarah Elizabeth Lewis, a Harvard professor and founder of the Vision & Justice initiative, and Reverend Wheeler Parker Jr, Emmett Till’s cousin, best friend and last surviving witness to his kidnapping, ask the nation to consider who gets to be remembered on American soil and how the country chooses to see its history.“When I see the exhibition on the walls, it brings to mind the question I’ve always asked myself: “What would he have been?” And knowing him, he would have been the center of everything going on,” Parker Jr said. “He wouldn’t let life pass him by without getting involved. So, you think about what it would have been like. Then I look at the other side, at the laws that were passed and the things that were created because of his death. You’re appreciative and you thank God for that, but he’s still not here. So you have a lot of mixed emotions about him and death.”View image in fullscreenDr Sarah Lewis and Reverend Parker Jr outside the Mississippi barn where Emmett Till was murdered, July 2026.Photograph: Lance Omar ThurmanIn the months leading up to the exhibit’s opening, the state of Illinois officially designated 25 July, Till’s birthday, as Emmett Till Day. Last month, the barn where Emmett Till was murdered was bought by Patrick Weems’s Emmett Till Interpretive Center, with plans to make the space a site of remembrance. And this week, the church where Emmett Till’s funeral was heldunveileda re-creation of the historic neon sign in honor of Till, signaling the exhibition’s opening.“Every American needs to do their part to honor Emmett Till,” Lewis says. “I would not have understood the urgency, though, unless I went toMississippi. When you see the resistance to honoring Emmett Till’s life 70 years later, you start to realize that there’s more to be done. I realized that I not only needed to do my part, but needed to extend the space of the exhibition to constitute a new arena for reimagining society, and that’s what birthed this exhibition.”In the summer of 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black boy fromChicago, was visiting relatives in Mississippi with his cousin, Reverend Parker. While standing outside Bryant’s Grocery & Meat Market, he whistled at a shopkeeper, a white woman. Four days later, the woman’s husband and half-brother kidnapped him and took him to a barn where they tortured, mutilated and killed him. At trial, the woman’s relatives were acquitted but later confessed to the murder in Look magazine.Lewis argues that it is important to remember Till despite efforts to erase his name from American memory. “My hope is that when you reckon with these roadblocks to equity in American democracy and the resistance to honoring Till, you really begin to grasp why bravery is required, why courage is required and why something more than the work of politics and law is required,” she says. “What’s needed is a transformation of how we see each other.”Seventy-one years ago, Mamie Till-Mobley, Till’s mother, set out to change how the nation saw her son and, in turn, how Americans saw each other. On 4 September 1955, she held an open casket funeral at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, for nearly 100,000 attenders.View image in fullscreenMamie Till Mobley weeps at her son’s funeral on 6 September 1955, in Chicago. The mother of Emmett Till insisted that her son’s body be displayed in an open casket, forcing the country to see the brutality directed at Black people in the South at the time.Photograph: AP“We have averted our eyes far too long, turning away from the ugly reality facing us as a nation,” Mamie Till-Mobley is quoted as saying in thebookIf Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Ground, which accompanies the exhibition.Till-Mobley hired photographer David Jackson to photograph Till’s brutalized body at his funeral for Jet magazine. “I wanted the world to see what they did to my baby,” she said in September 1955.“Till-Mobley was prophetic in her understanding that witnessing would be critical for grasping the crucible of American democracy,” Lewis says. With the new show, Lewis and Parker Jr aimed to create “a creative monument” for the nation to see the hopes and possibilities of the life Till did not get to live.The photographers featured are wide-ranging, from Henri Cartier-Bresson, Carrie Mae Weems, Teju Cole and Gordon Parks to relatives of Till, like his cousin, Lance Omar Thurman. Lewis notes that she wanted to include photographs from an extensive range of image makers.View image in fullscreenReverend Wheeler Parker Jr chose this image, Hopscotch, 1952, to show the innocence of children.Photograph: Walter Rosenblum/Extended loan of the Baum Family Collection, Nina and Lisa Rosenblum“I approached the show with the democratic ethos,” she says. “I went into the collection, looking for works, regardless of the name of the artist and their stature. I went looking for works that contained a message and an episode in Emmett Till’s life. And it meant that everyone could be part of the story.”One of the most striking images Lewis chose is the photograph on the book’s cover, taken by Stephen Marc. The photograph is a black-and-white image of a man looking up at a young boy he has thrown into the air, next to a body of water. For Lewis, the image “represents both hope and possibility”.“I think of Marc’s aunt, Dr Carla Hayden, the former librarian of Congress, as a symbol of the power of the archive,” he says. “These images let us recreate the archive we don’t often see, the possibility for lives cut short. Marc’s photograph, with its paradox of possibility and life cut short, became the metaphor for the exhibition. It became a way to see both Till and the Till in all of us as we live.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, from Changing Chicago, 1988. Gelatin silver print.Photograph: Stephen Marc/Gift of Jack A Jaffe, Focus/Infinity FundFor the exhibition, Lewis and Parker Jr asked many notable people, including Dr Chelsea Clinton, Ava DuVernay, Dr Henry Louis Gates Jr, congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, Hank Willis Thomas and others, to select images and write their own reflections on Till’s life.Thomas chose a striking image taken by Dawoud Bey of Barack Obama sitting in a chair, his gaze piercing the camera. In the photograph, the former US president’s facial expression looks present, as if the only thing in the world at that moment is him and the camera. As Thomas notes, the image shows the possibilities that could have come to fruition in Till’s life if he had the opportunity to grow old.“Emmett Till was denied the chance to grow into a man, to be honored, to age into possibility,” Thomas writes in the book If Emmett Till Lived. “This photograph allows us to sit with one version of what history fought to make possible: a Black man looking directly at a camera and into us, with the full force of his humanity intact.”The images in the show are memorials to the life taken from Till. As Lewis writes in If Emmett Till Lived, “sometimes a photograph can be a monument. Sometimes, a photograph has to be a monument when all attempts at making a monument, for decades, have been and are still denied.”View image in fullscreenBarack Obama, 2006Photograph: Dawoud Bey/Columbia College Chicago commissionThe “exhibition is going to help a lot of people”, Parker Jr says. “It helps the cause. As I heard Mamie said, ‘I hope you didn’t die in vain.’”Though the exhibit focuses on honoring the life of Till, Lewis argues that the show also pays tribute to the lives taken from numerous young Black people. “There are many Emmett Tills today,” he says. “Till is a proxy for understanding aNolan Wells. A proxy for understandingBreonna Taylor.”“One of the ways this question of what we do in the face of the visibility of this tragedy is to ask, is witnessing enough? Is witnessing injustice enough to transform the moral imagination? People are seeing the video of George Floyd. Is it enough to let people see? We might have to require people to see, entice them to see and make the invitation to see the truth of American society irresistible.”View image in fullscreenRailroad Yards, South Chicago, 1966. The train route Emmett Till would have taken if he made it home alive.Photograph: David Plowden/Extended loan of the Baum Family Collection.If Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Groundis at the Museum of Contemporary Photography, Chicago, until 19 December

title: Elkie Brooks looks back: ‘Before I went on stage I used to drink Guinness and a few shots of brandy’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter on her rock’n’roll past, playing second fiddle to the Beatles, and the key to being an energetic performer in your 80s
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The singer-songwriter on her rock’n’roll past, playing second fiddle to the Beatles, and the key to being an energetic performer in your 80s
Content: FlashbackFamilyElkie Brooks looks back: ‘Before I went on stage I used to drink Guinness and a few shots of brandy’The singer-songwriter on her rock’n’roll past, playing second fiddle to the Beatles, and the key to being an energetic performer in your 80sHarriet GibsoneSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElkie Brooks in white jumpsuit, standing outside the Royal Albert Hall in London in 1977 and 2026Elkie Brooks in 1977 and 2026. Later photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian. Hair and makeup: Céline Nonon at Arlington Artists. Archive photograph: courtesy of Elkie BrooksBorn Elaine Bookbinder in Salford in 1945, Elkie Brooks is a rock, blues and jazz singer known as the British Queen of Blues. She spent much of the 1960s on the cabaret circuit, during which time she supported the Beatles. She joined Dada in 1970, before forming Vinegar Joe withRobert Palmerin 1971. She went solo after their split, breaking through with Pearl’s a Singer and Sunshine After the Rain, scoring 13 UK Top 75 singles. A celebration of six decades in music, The Long Farewell Tour, is now on the road.This is me in a white jumpsuit outside the Royal Albert Hall in London.I have very few memories of the gig, but I know I would have felt daunted as it’s such a large venue. To overcome the nerves, I’d have tried to focus on the music and remembered, “It’s just another gig.”Vinegar Joe had folded three years before. We’d had a fantastic time and it broke my heart when we disbanded as I had thought that it would last for ever. But Robert Palmer decided he was going to embark on a solo career and the rest of the band said, “Oh, well, that’s it then.” It was pretty hard going for me – the only real fallow part of my life. I had a couple of months of not doing very much. Then I got asked to join a band in the southern states of the US called Wet Willie, and after that I started my own solo project. Pearl’s a Singer was released in 1977 and we went out on tour, finishing the year with this Albert Hall show. As the end of Vinegar Joe had been emotional for me, and it had taken many years to get a group of people together who all got on and were brilliant musicians, this day, that gig, would have been quite a moment.Ever since I can remember, I have been singing, often in the bath,to my mummy. When I was seven I would get invited to sing Mr Sandman with the band that would play at weddings and barmitzvahs. As I got older, I adored Johnnie Ray and Ella Fitzgerald, then Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, Dakota Staton, Esther Phillips and Aretha Franklin. The cantor at the local synagogue used to give me singing lessons, all in Hebrew and Yiddish. He was the one who taught me the correct way to project my voice.double quotation markI still train now, which is one of the reasons why I managed to get into this jumpsuit 50 years laterEven as a child I had a low voice. When I auditioned for the primary school choir, I sang All Things Bright and Beautiful. The headteacher, who used to play the piano and lead the choir, said to me, “Bookbinder – you sound like a blinking boy.” Was I embarrassed? Not really. Deep down I’ve always had a reasonable amount of confidence in the fact that I have a natural singing voice. Not the greatest singing voice in the world, but few people practise as much as I do. She let me into the choir, anyway.My first show was at the Laurent Club on Cheetham Hill Road in Manchester, when I was just 13. I went up with a jazz trio and afterwards the owner of the club said, “Would you like to do a few little songs here every night this week?” A few years later I saw in the Jewish Telegraph thatDon Arden, Sharon Osbourne’s father, was holding auditions at the Palace theatre in Manchester one Saturday morning. I went along and sang a Cliff Richard B-side. Don thought I was wonderful and put me on the show that night. When he drove me in his car to another gig, he said, “You can’t be called Bookbinder any more.” Don had Jewish heritage and was obviously concerned that people wouldn’t like me if I had a Jewish name, as there was a lot of antisemitism around. At the next gig, he introduced me as “Elaine Mansfield”, which I hated. I managed to get rid of the name years later: a friend told me that my name in Yiddish was Elkie, so I took that and shortened Bookbinder to Brooks.For most of my career I have been in a male-dominated industry,but it was never uncomfortable – I was tomboyish and brought up around blokes, as I’ve got two big brothers. The most trying experience of being outnumbered was at the Beatles’ Christmas show in 1964. I was not only the only woman on the entire bill, but in all the production as well. About 200 men, and me. It was bad because nobody took any notice of me, which made me feel dismissed. The fans were all getting ice-creams and walking around the theatre when I played, but when the Beatles came on, the girls all screamed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIain Stirling looks back: ‘I was worried about doing the Love Island voiceover, but it opened doors I thought would close’Read moreThe demise of Vinegar Joe was a hard moment creatively, but personally, too, because my first husband had left me shortly before. It wasn’t an easy time and I struggled to think sensibly. I managed to pull through – I always do, because I focus on the music. Where does my strength come from? My mum. She told me she was going to have an abortion when she was pregnant with me, as she didn’t want any more children – she already had two sons and had a few serious health issues. The doctor, a lovely man, said, “It’s going to be a girl. I know you want a girl. Don’t have an abortion. You’ll be fine.” So she had me.Being on the road in the 1970s was often rock’n’roll – before I went on stage, I used to drink Guinness and a few shots of brandy. These days I like everything in moderation; I haven’t had a drink before going on stage since my eldest son, Jay, was a baby, nearly 50 years ago. Having had so many hangovers in my youth, I now only like a little taste on special occasions. I don’t want to ruin a workout the next day. I’ve always tried to eat well, too. When I was with Wet Willie, they’d always stop off at hamburger places, but if I ate them I’d get pimples on my back, so I realised, “This is not for me.” I haven’t eaten a cheeseburger since 1974. Instead I adore hummus, and fruit and nuts.I am very active, too. In 1995, I achieved my black belt in karate. I still train now, which is one of the reasons why I managed to get into this jumpsuit 50 years later. I fell through a stage when I was with Vinegar Joe at the Marquee Club in London, and it wasn’t until many years later, when I had an X-ray, that doctors told me I had a fractured hip. Last year I had a hip operation and, blinking heck, I have felt fantastic ever since. I did six backdrops this morning.Aged81, this is the best time of my life for many reasons.There were moments when I was young where people were a bit dominating in areas of my work – telling me how I should look or what I should sing – and various people, who shall remain nameless, have tried to knock my self-esteem throughout my career. I never lost it entirely, and always had a strong sense of who I was.Not only do I feel great, but for the first time in years I’ve actually got a band I like – we all chat to each other, and performing live is a wonderful feeling. I’m thoroughly enjoying myself – and plan to keep doing so.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackPhotographyBluesPop and rockJazzfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dining across the divide: ‘The young have so much idealism – but for him everything was determined by getting the Conservatives elected’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A Tory twentysomething and a lifelong leftwinger agreed on the need for more housing stock, but did they concur on welfare and net zero?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: A Tory twentysomething and a lifelong leftwinger agreed on the need for more housing stock, but did they concur on welfare and net zero?
Content: Oliver (left) and Adrian. All photographs: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOliver (left) and Adrian. All photographs: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianDining across the divideLife and styleDining across the divide: ‘The young have so much idealism – but for him everything was determined by getting the Conservatives elected’A Tory twentysomething and a lifelong leftwinger agreed on the need for more housing stock, but did they concur on welfare and net zero?Want to meet someone from across the divide? Clickhereto find out howZoe WilliamsSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOliver, 22, LondonView image in fullscreenOccupationJournalist for ConservativeHomeVoting recordConservativeAmuse boucheOliver goes to a different park every Sunday to feed the ducks, and he posts where he’s going on Instagram. Others, usually his friends, join him, then they go for a pintAdrian, 63, West WycombeView image in fullscreenOccupationRetired. Used to work in PRVoting recordLabour or Green. In any general election under first-past-the-post, would vote LabourAmuse boucheAdrian went coffee-picking in Nicaragua when he was 25 to show solidarity with the Sandinistas. He came away with an understanding of what was going on, and full of hope, which has since been cruelly quashedFor startersAdrianHe was really a nice young guy, a lot younger than I expected.OliverHe came in wearing shorts. I felt overdressed in chinos. But he was a really friendly guy. We shared a burrata watermelon chaat. Some coconut tofu. Hoisin duck pancakes.AdrianIt was all vegetarian, so it was mock duck. But I don’t know if he knew that.View image in fullscreenThe big beefAdrianAs far as Oliver is concerned, it’s too easy and too attractive to claim benefits. I think the welfare budget has to be determined by the need that’s there. We shouldn’t do anything that stigmatises or penalises people who need support.OliverIf the welfare bill keeps going up, no amount of tax is going to be enough. He said, obviously there’s people that need it. And I said, yeah of course, but particularly with young people, it’s been open to exploitation. The number of graduate claimants has gone up massively since Covid. We need to make it easier for businesses to employ people. Current legislation, employer national insurance rises, are making it harder.AdrianYou have all this idealism when you’re young, and I couldn’t quite work out what that was for Oliver. He seemed very politically minded, but in a very strategic, pragmatic way. Everything was determined by what might get the Conservative party elected. Without really any ideas or even an ideology, to be honest.OliverI’m a Tory. I believe in fiscal conservatism. The culture war, I don’t really care about that. I think people should be able to live freely.View image in fullscreenSharing plateAdrianWe agreed we needed more housing stock. He thought we needed less regulation, whereas I thought there was a sticking point in terms of developers land-banking and choosing not to build houses, and wanting to build them in inappropriate areas, so you get out-of-town developments where people have to drive everywhere.OliverI said we needed to relax the planning system. I mentioned a specific niche recommendation: every window needs to be cleanable by 95% of elderly ladies. He said we need more regulation, the free market has failed. He thinks all new housing developments should have an inbuilt windfarm or energy source. I said that’s going to make it even harder to build houses. He thinks we need to be thinking of the future. I said we’ve got a shortage now – we should worry about the rest later.View image in fullscreenFor aftersAdrianThere’s a clear case for accelerating change, cleaner energy, more electric vehicles, more heat pumps, a working home insulation programme. He challenged that in terms of who would pay for it, whether that would be passed on to consumers and whether people could afford that. My point was that you make polluters pay, to disincentivise pollution.Dining across the divide: ‘He says he feels pride about being English, but I don’t’Read moreOliverWe’re both in favour of moving towards an economy that’s more supportive of net zero. We agree that there are job opportunities there. At the end of the day, net zero is an arbitrary target. There’s no real meaning in it. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t deny that climate change exists. She just wants to rethink how to tackle it in a practical way, rather than pursuing a policy blindly, without thinking about the possible consequences on jobs and the economy.View image in fullscreenTakeawaysAdrianHe’s clearly got the ambition, but maybe he will find a different way to channel it. I don’t know. It was a really nice evening and he’s a nice young man.OliverHe was this really nice guy. By the end of the meal we agreed on quite a lot – we just want politics to be better and the country to be less divided. It was really wholesome.View image in fullscreenAdditional reporting: Kitty DrakeAdrian and Oliver ate atTangrain London W1Want to meet someone from across the divide?Find out how to take partExplore more on these topicsLife and styleDining across the divideSocial trendsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From the perfect jeans to wedgie-free knickers: fashion experts’ guide to the best women’s basics | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Want to know the essentials fashion insiders swear by? Whether it’s great T-shirts or forever trainers, Guardian writers and stylists reveal the pieces they rate
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Want to know the essentials fashion insiders swear by? Whether it’s great T-shirts or forever trainers, Guardian writers and stylists reveal the pieces they rate
Content: The best basics are the pieces that work hardest in your wardrobe.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe best basics are the pieces that work hardest in your wardrobe.Composite: Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFashionFrom the perfect jeans to wedgie-free knickers: fashion experts’ guide to the best women’s basicsWant to know the essentials fashion insiders swear by? Whether it’s great T-shirts or forever trainers, Guardian writers and stylists reveal the pieces they rateJess Cartner-Morley’s September style essentialsEllie Violet BramleySun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether it’s a great pair of pants or the perfect T-shirt, nailing the basics can make or break your wardrobe. “They have to work harder than anything else,” says British Vogue style editor Funmi Fetto.I askedFetto and other stylists and style writers, along with members of the Guardian fashion desk – who all spend more time than most thinking about this stuff – for their most-loved basics. And don’t worry, most of them won’t break the bank.The best wardrobe essentialsKnickersMost people I spoke to namecheckedMarks & Spencerfor underwear.You’d also struggle to find a softer pair thanStripe & Stare’s Tencel pants. The UK brand claims they’re wedgie-free (in my experience, they are), plus they’re available in cuts to fit all tastes. My favourite is the high-rise. Acting fashion editor Chloe Mac Donnell is also a recent convert: “They’re a better fit around the bum,” she says, “and sit better under trousers.”Lucinda Chambers, stylist, founder of online lifestyle platform Collagerie and former Vogue fashion director, recommends pants from the French company Baserange,which does a great line of simple, no-frills knickers. They’re made from bamboo lyocell in Portugal and don’t come cheap, but they’re high quality.For a pair of pants with a bit of extra coverage and support, I recommend thehigh-waisted Beyond Nine ones, which have a waiting list for several sizes for good reason – not cheap, but they last.View image in fullscreenStripe & Stare Tencel high-rise knickers£18 at Stripe & StareSocksView image in fullscreenA good sock should be soft, comfortable and stay put without constricting.Photograph: Peter Cade/GettyAgain, M&S came out on top. Stylist Bay Garnett goes to the men’s department, where she has found her perfect socks that sit higher up the leg: “Multipack. Cotton. Mid-calf”. But she also has an altogether holier recommendation:these amazing socksfrom Gammarelli, which has been in the business of dressing popes since 1798. You have to fill out a form to get them, but you can’t expect to get the pope’s socks without a bit of effort.Cheaper but less hallowed isArketand its multicoloured sock wall. “The quality is really nice,” says Chambers. She likes that they’re “Prada length, which is just on the shin”. Meanwhile, Fetto appreciates socks made byFalke, which is known for its high-quality designs.On the Guardian fashion desk, senior style writer Lauren Cochrane lovesNikefor sports socks andMujifor thicker, woolly winter ones. For their fit, Mac Donnell likes Uniqlo’sJW Anderson socksbecause “they don’t cut off circulation at the ankle”. Although those pairs are out of stock,other Uniqlo stylesoffer a similarly soft fit around the ankle, without digging in or leaving marks. I am yet to find a softer, more comfortable pair of socks thanthese from the Danish company Dilling.View image in fullscreenM&S cotton-rich socks, seven pairs£10 at M&SView image in fullscreenMuji women’s wool-blend room socks£14.95 at MujiCotton T-shirtsCosis Fetto’s go-to because, she says, they hang really well and aren’t too tight. Guardian writer Morwenna Ferrier, who usually buys everything except undies and socks secondhand, favoursCos’s V-neckT-shirts, while Mac Donnell says a crew neck “is a good height for when you want it to peek out from under a jumper”.The quality “is really good”, adds Chambers.Garnett opts for the more expensive but high-qualitySunspel, “because the cotton’s really nice”, and if Chambers is after something more fitted, less boxy, she recommendsthe luxury T-shirts of James Perse. “Sometimes, with things like that, I think they’re worth the investment,” she says.I recently took the plunge and replaced all my moth-eaten, grubby old T-shirts with a bulk buy fromLA-based Everybody.World. I can’t recommend the quality or the colours highly enough, and that’s not to mention that they’re biodegradable and made from cotton waste by a fair-wage workforce.View image in fullscreenCos clean-cut T-shirt£30 at CosA white shirtGarnett, a thrifting pioneer, has a lot of love for the men’s rail in charity shops when she’s on the hunt for a good white shirt. But Ferrier has found something she, the Duchess of Sussex and, apparently, Akshata Murty agree on: the shirts of London-based brand With Nothing Underneath. Founded by a former Vogue stylist, the brand makes good-quality shirts in different cuts and silhouettes – the Oxford one I own is pleasingly crisp and clearly made to last. I also recently scored a shirt fromminimalist-leaning womenswear brand Frankie Shopon Vinted – the poplin is lovely, and the secondhand price feels like a steal.View image in fullscreenWith Nothing Underneath The BoyfriendOxford shirt£100 at With Nothing UnderneathA simple jumperView image in fullscreenCashmere works best as a basic when the fit is right.Photograph: Elena Noviello/GettyGarnett says the older she gets, the more she likes classics, like the sweaters from N.Peal: “The cashmere is really good,” she says. Mac Donnell rates the cashmere atRise & Falland has a lot of love forCos’s “not too fitted” cashmere jumpers.Fetto isn’t a jumpers person but ratesAPC’s designs, which aren’t too heavy: “[They’re] fitted but not super tight.”Chambers will spend more on a good polo neck; on a bad hair day, you can tuck your hair in and forget about it, she says.She rates Soft Goat, although at £400+ for a jumper, it’s definitely an investment: “I’m wearing them every day, so you want them to last and not bobble and do horrible things that you’re constantly getting your cashmere shaver out [for].”View image in fullscreenCos cashmere crew-neck jumperskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£169 at CosJeansView image in fullscreenThe perfect jeans are all about shape – and finding a fit you’ll keep coming back to.Photograph: Grace Cary/GettyCochrane, “like the rest of the fashion industry”, is forever in thrall to a perfect pair of vintage Levi’s 501s. “But in the meantime,” she says, “I buy the JW Anderson straight-leg Uniqlo ones. They’re a good price, good denim and have an approximation of the fit I want.” Ferrier agrees: “The first new thing I’ve bought in years. They have a great shape and a low waist,” she says, “but they can lose their shape.” So make peace with them doing their thing and enjoy them on wash day. Sadly, though, they are out of stock for now –watch this space. Butthese from M&Sare a decent alternative. Ferrier also has a soft spot for “Levi’s Superlow in blackand CK [Calvin Klein] low-rise baggy (90s from Vinted)”.For Chambers, if she’s after “a pair of really plain [jeans in] fabulous denim”, she’ll opt for a pair fromLos Angeles-based Citizens of Humanity. “I just love their shape,” she says. Fetto is loyal to the jeans of Raey, which is out of business but being relaunched this year. In the meantime, they’re still available on secondhand sites,such as Vinted.A few members of the fashion desk are impressed bythis pair from Reformation. Mac Donnell bought them three years ago, and they’re still a favourite. They’re pricey, but “they’ve kept their shape and haven’t faded”, she says.View image in fullscreenM&S mid-rise straight-leg ankle-length jeans£26 at M&SA basic trainer-y shoeView image in fullscreenA classic trainer earns its place by being easy to wear with almost anything.Photograph: Edward Berthelot/Getty“Converse forever,” says Ferrier. Chambers also wears the brand’s high-tops pretty much every day, in black but also bright red, “which go with everything”. Cochrane is all about theConverse One Star.Fetto has about seven pairs ofGrace Wales Bonner’s shoes for Adidas, which she wears on rotation, and considers them the perfect basic shoes.For more of a blank slate, I love thearch support of a Superga, and, for something with more style chops that is still versatile and incredibly comfy, the Nike Air Rift. Butgiven historical ethical concerns, maybe find yours on Vinted, where they are abundant.View image in fullscreenConverse One Star Pro£39.99 at ConverseView image in fullscreenSuperga 2750 Cotu classic£35 at Superga£52 at M&SA useful bagGarnett is a fan of a classicLL Bean tote bag, as well as a straw bag in summer, which she’ll usually pick up wherever she goes on holiday (our own Jess Cartner-Morley swears bySézane’sstraw baskets).Chambers is “a total tote toter” and a big fan ofRadley’s large striped tote– the perfect size and her favourite colour combination: tobacco and black. “It’s really hard-wearing, you can fling it around, curl it into the back of the car, it’s brilliant.” It’s out of stock, but London brand Osprey has achocolate suede totethat is a good match.I find a bag stashed into the bag you actually want to wear is a smart idea for any overflow when you buy bananas on the way home. That might bea little Bagguor, if you’re worried about your back, a totallypackable-down Ticket to the Moon rucksackmade from waste nylon.View image in fullscreenLL Bean boat and tote open-top bag£37 at Free PeopleView image in fullscreenBaggu pleated bag£30 at Junior EditionOther basicsFor Ferrier, it’s “some smart black balloon trousers WITH A CREASE. You can get into any do/event/meeting/A-list gathering if they have a crease”.These, from Maje, are “not cheap, but they’re well made and look like Dior”, she says.Garnett rarely goes without a belt – she thinks she caught the habit from time spent with Anita Pallenberg. She tends to find them secondhand, championingEtsyas a good place to look.Garnett is also a sucker for a good blazer – her collection is the result of many incredible charity shop finds. “I find it hard not to buy them,” she says. If you’re on the hunt, the first thing to look at is size: “If it’s too big, it looks shit,” she says. “Then look for the print, then how big the lapels are. I like a strong lapel.” But there’s also a bit of intuition involved, she says: “As soon as you put it on, you know, immediately.”Mac Donnell sees PJs as a basic.“H&M cotton muslin pyjamasare really comfortable,” she says, “and feel and look very fancy.”View image in fullscreenMajeballoon suit trousers£279 at MajeFor more, readJess Cartner-Morley’s September style essentialsEllie Violet Bramley is a writer who has been delving into style and what it means for nearly a decade – mostly for the Guardian’s fashion deskExplore more on these topicsFashionThe FilterLingerieWomen's shirtsTights and socksWomen's topsJeansWomen's shoesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make chocolate mousse – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: The little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classic
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: The little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classic
Content: Felicity Cloake’s chocolate mousse.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s chocolate mousse.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make chocolate mousse – recipeThe little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classicFelicity CloakeSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYears ago, a group of us cycled from Brittany to the Mediterranean, and along the way we ate alotof chocolate mousse. Popular, easy to make and happy to sit in the fridge until required, it’s a mainstay of the modest French provincial restaurant and, as we discovered, it’s almost always good. Here’s my favourite version of the little black dress of the dessert trolley.Prep5 minCook20 minChill2 hr+Makes260g at least 70% cocoa chocolate2 medium eggs1 pinchsalt2 tsp sugar, or to tasteView image in fullscreen1 A note on the chocolateYou can use milk or flavoured chocolate here, if you like, but do bear in mind that if it’s quite sweet, you probably won’t need the extra sugar. Unless you’re using uniform chocolate drops designed for melting, roughly chop the chocolate – there’s no need to cut it into very tiny pieces, but they should be fairly even so they melt at the same rate.2 Melt the chocolate over a bain-marieBoil the kettle. Meanwhile, get ready a large heatproof bowl that can sit over a pan holding about 5cm of water without the base of the bowl touching the water. Pour the boiling water into the pan and turn on the heat to medium. Put the chocolate in the bowl, then put the bowl on top of the water pan and turn down the heat so the water is barely simmering. Stir occasionally, until the chocolate is completely melted.3 … or use a microwaveAlternatively, use a microwave, which saves on washing up but carries a greater risk of burning the chocolate if you don’t keep your eye on it. Put the chocolate in a heatproof bowl, microwave for 20 seconds, then stir and carry on microwaving in five-second bursts until completely melted.4 Carefully separate the eggsWhile the chocolate is melting, separate the eggs – it’s important not to get any yolk in the whites or they’ll be tricky to whip up properly. To avoid this possibility, I break the eggs into a glass or metal bowl (plastic will make the job harder), then use a clean hand to scoop the yolks into a fresh bowl.View image in fullscreen5 Beat the egg whitesLeave the chocolate to cool slightly. While it does so, use electric beaters or a large whisk to whip the egg whites and a pinch of salt to soft peaks – that is, to the point when the mix will hold a wave that flops over at the top rather than standing up straight. Add the sugar and carry on whisking until the mix is glossy and holds its shape.View image in fullscreen6 Combine the egg yolks and chocolateMix the egg yolks one at a time into the melted chocolate. If at any point the mixture seizes and turns tight and grainy, don’t worry, it’s not a disaster. Simply add a small splash of boiling water and whisk again until the mix is glossy and pourable again (if that doesn’t work, repeat the process until it does).7 Fold in the egg whitesStir a spoonful of the whipped egg white into the melted chocolate and egg yolk mixture to loosen it up, then add the rest. Use a large metal spoon gently to fold it in, using a D-shaped action so you don’t knock too much air out of the meringue. Stop as soon as everything is uniformly mixed, with no streaks.8 Chill to setSpoon the mousse into a serving bowl or into two separate bowls or glasses (don’t worry if the serving looks ungenerous; this is averyrich dessert). Put in the fridge to chill (covered, if you like, especially if you have any strongly scented ingredients in there), preferably for a couple of hours, so the mousse has a chance to set properly. It will keep well for several days.View image in fullscreen9 Variations on the themeTo ring the changes, when melting the chocolate, stir in the grated zest of a well-scrubbed orange, or two tablespoons of strong coffee, a pinch of cinnamon, nutmeg or chilli flakes, a little more salt, or a splash of vanilla extract or rosewater. Serve as is, or top it with whipped cream, cocoa nibs, orange zest, mint leaves or chopped nuts.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassChocolateDessertFrench food and drinkEggsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep
Content: Rosina, London SW17: ‘An achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced trattoria.’Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRosina, London SW17: ‘An achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced trattoria.’Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewRosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant reviewThe weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weepGrace DentSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 03.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRosinais a serene, heavenly-white neighbourhood Italian restaurant just off Wandsworth Common, on the same stretch as the much-celebratedChez Bruce. It isAdam Byatt’s fifth place – he’s probably best known forTrinity, his Michelin-starred restaurant up the road in Clapham – and, lately, hisvery good, recipe-driven YouTube channelrana Road to Rosina seriesin which he visits suppliers, eats pasta with nonnas and learns peak tiramisu skills from a woman called Pina (more of her tiramisu later). If any neighbourhood can stomach an achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced, candlelit trattoria where the cloakroom tags are actual Amalfi Coast pebbles engraved with numbers, it is Wandsworth Common, land of the hedge fund/interior design power couple who wouldn’t think twice about sipping a basil gimlet with a plate of melon with culatello di Zibello or gnocco fritto with mortadella. Bella Italia in Bolton this is not.Rosina’s cocktail bar leans on art deco shapes, with a pale, marble-topped counter and walls covered inDavid Steen portraits. There’s a small second bar area for those bridging the gap between light dinner and semi-serious drinking, and a larger, linen-tableclothed area for the restaurant proper, with a back room for private dining. Rosina’s intimacy is an optical illusion: the place is as big as a tennis court, and the weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep.View image in fullscreen‘A nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers’: Rosina’s ’nduja strozzapreti.The day-to-day cooking is in the hands ofWill Bee, previously of Michelin-starredLitain Marylebone andPaul Ainsworth at No 6in Padstow, and the menu is hearty, as well as littered with little in-jokes; like all the most promising neighbourhood joints, however, it would take at least five visits before they began to grate. Small plates of fried taleggio,melanzane fritteand smoked sardines on toast give way to a list of pleasingly substantial pastas ranging from caviar linguine at £30 to a staggeringly pocket-friendly cavatelli cacio e pepe at just £8. There is also what’s dubbed as “post-service pasta” (spaghetti with anchovy, chilli and garlic) at £16, which is the first time I’ve seen a restaurant give a glimpse into what its owner eats after hours. More of this, I say. I want cocktail lists that offer “post-service fernet branca plus howling into the abyss about business rates”. Let the light in on the magic.Hugh, my companion, ordered bruschetta of rabbit livers braised in chianti, and ate them withLecter-ish lust. Two plump sardines, coated in breadcrumbs and with their little tails sticking out of one end, resembled something out of a cartoon. Carpaccio of wild sea bass came flecked with chilli and amalfi lemon, and doused in the kind of olive oil you hide from house guests: clean, sharp, precise. It was at this point that something shifted for me, from “this is perfectly pleasant” to “holy god, this is really quite special”. The arrival of the ’nduja strozzapreti only confirmed that: hugely simple, but wonderfully layered, with a rich tomato sauce enveloping a nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers.View image in fullscreen‘A sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop’: Rosina’s ‘wonderful’ risotto bianco.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The GuardianRisotto bianco, made withRiso Buono carnaroli riceand topped with a bold, sunshine-yellow egg yolk, was rich, but it’s meant to be: risotto bianco is for people who laugh in the face of blood sugar spikes. There is nowhere to hide in a white risotto – it is a sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop – and Rosina’s is wonderful. Although, if I want to squander calories willy-nilly on genuine death row delicacies, it is to their fried potatoes that I might turn instead: tiny baby spuds no bigger than fingernails, roasted, crushed and tossed in herbs and oil. Absolutely remarkable. A hugely generous plate of roast summer vegetables came charred from the grill and drizzled with syrupy grape mustsabafrom Modena. We ate those with perfectly cooked roast turbot.Around us, Wandsworth Common conducted its typical Saturday business. The tyranny of school fees. The agony of basement excavations. The management of several homes at once, with only one housekeeper directing all the other housekeepers internationally. The true trials of life. These people deserve a good dessert menu, and Rosina offers an embarrassment of teeth-chattering riches. Dreamy, yesteryear-sounding things: orange riccarelli, marzipan fruits, iced cherries and a sharp, classic amalfi lemon tart with blackcurrant leaf ice-cream, which I demolished. And a bowl of Pina’s tiramisu, too, of course, of which we entertained a rather large amount. My congratulations to Pina: hers is averygood recipe: wet, light and stodgy in all the right places.View image in fullscreen‘Wet, light and stodgy in all the right places’: Rosina’s tiramisu, served family-style.If this rather sumptuous spot needs anything quite as crass as my feedback, Rosina is a surefire hit. If you’re south of the river and on the lookout for an oasis of calm and fanciness at a range of prices, somewhere you can talk and be heard, Rosina is the perfect woman.Rosina35 Bellevue Road, London SW17, 020-8672 5888. Open all week, lunch noon-2.30pm, dinner 5.30-10pm. From about £50 a head à la carte, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsFoodGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsItalian food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The kindness of strangers: On a busy motorway, my child vomited in the car. I was overwhelmed – then a man came with a bucket of water | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: My son was inconsolable and the back seat was an absolute mess. After a few minutes of trying to clean up, a stranger emerged from a nearby house
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: My son was inconsolable and the back seat was an absolute mess. After a few minutes of trying to clean up, a stranger emerged from a nearby house
Content: ‘Ten years have passed, but the memory of this incredible and selfless act still brings a tear to my eye.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Ten years have passed, but the memory of this incredible and selfless act still brings a tear to my eye.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian Design/AlamyKindness of strangersAustralian lifestyleThe kindness of strangers: On a busy motorway, my child vomited in the car. I was overwhelmed – then a man came with a bucket of waterMy son was inconsolable and the back seat was an absolute mess. After a few minutes of trying to clean up, a stranger emerged from a nearby houseRead more inthe kindness of strangers seriesAnonymous, as told toKatie CunninghamSun 13 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKids always get sick at the worst possible time. For instance: the middle of a busy motorway, one hour into a three-hour trip.My husband was away for work and I was driving our two small children to see him, when one vomited in the back seat. I pulled into a slipway just off the motorway to try to clean up as best I could. The kids were too young to be trusted to sit there safely right next to a busy road, so I had to leave them strapped into the car seats while I tried to mop up the vomit with wet wipes. My son was inconsolable and the car was an absolute mess.After a few minutes of trying to clean up, I was feeling utterly overwhelmed, when a man emerged from a nearby house armed with a bucket of water. He sent us over to his wife, who made tea and chatted to me about the kids, while he thoroughly cleaned out the back seat. I apologised for the mess, but the woman told me not to worry.After the cleaning was done, we got in the car and drove back home – admitting defeat on the trip.Ten years have passed, but the memory of this incredible and selfless act still brings a tear to my eye. When I could not cope on my own, this warm and gentle couple swept in and took charge.My marriage later ended, and the love and tenderness I was shown by this couple was something I was so particularly lacking at the time. It remains the single kindest thing anyone has ever done for me.What is the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?Share your experienceWhat's the nicest thing a stranger has ever done for you?From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
