title: This is how we do it: ‘Being in an open relationship means we’re constantly choosing each other’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Michael and Selena have three young kids and practise ethical non-monogamy which helps energise their relationship
Author: Naomi Larsson Piñeda
Headline: Michael and Selena have three young kids and practise ethical non-monogamy which helps energise their relationship
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘Being in an open relationship means we’re constantly choosing each other’Michael and Selena have three young kids and practise ethical non-monogamy which helps energise their relationshipHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toNaomi Larsson PiñedaSun 13 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael, 46double quotation markWhen you come back to your partner, you see the person you fell in love withSelena mentioned wanting to have kids and be non‑monogamous on our third date – I thought she was being very forward, but I was open to both.Our open marriage goes through different phases. We have three children under 10, and when Selena was pregnant and we were in the midst of raising babies there wasn’t much time or appetite for seeing other people.Having children has the potential to accelerate the process that a lot of relationships go through, where things start to become all about logistics, as opposed to connecting as partners. When the babies were young, we fell into the trap of seeing each other as just another person you have to give care to, and that’s not sexy. But having a non-monogamous relationship gives you an opportunity to step away from that. When you are out with someone else, you’re just being yourself, and it helps balance out what can be a very demanding period of raising kids. When you come back to your partner, you see the person you fell in love with.double quotation markAnyone we see always knows that our family is the priorityNeither of us has lots of partners. Typically we’ll find one or two people that we connect with, and then get to know them in the same way as if we were single – dating, which might evolve into a sexual relationship. Anyone we see always knows that our primary relationship and our family is the priority. That’s communicated upfront so there’s a clear understanding that I will always protect my relationship with Selena.We manage it logistically like we’re going out with friends, coordinating and making sure that, for example, if one of us goes out on a Friday, the other will babysit and then go out on the Saturday.Of course there’s jealousy and the feeling that I’m missing out. But ultimately that discomfort snaps you out of complacency. For us, that keeps our sex life and our connection alive. Plus, going out with someone else enables you to put your needs first, which then helps you to be a better parent and partner.Share your experienceTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreSelena, 40double quotation markDating other people was a way for me to come back to my own body after having kidsMy relationship with Michael has been open since the beginning, 14 years ago, but we never did anything about it until our second child was two. After I had been birthing and breastfeeding what felt like continuously for four or five years, I needed to find myself sexually again.Sexhad been tricky during that time because I was exhausted. Looking after babies, cleaning the house, cooking and then having sex with my husband felt like a pile of responsibilities. I felt as if I had no autonomy, which killed my desire.Dating other people was like an electric shock. I still remember this feeling of having sex with someone in a hotel room for the first time. It wasn’t even that great – but walking out, I felt like: “I’m back.” It was a way for me as a woman to come back to my own body after having kids, which was so empowering. I’ve since found that it has played a huge part in awakening me as a sexual being. It has brought more intimacy into our marriage.double quotation markIt’s an injection of fresh energy that you just can’t get after 14 years togetherThis is how we do it: ‘Since having cancer, I’m more open – before I was straight, now I’m queer’Read moreIt was really difficult at the start, and it took many conversations, reading a lot about ethical non-monogamy and listening to podcasts. You have to write the constitution of your own sexual marriage, there is no script to follow. You have to work out every single detail. You have to be comfortable with feelings of jealousy. If Michael tells me he’s got two dates this month, I’m like, “Great, Netflix, ice-cream and quilting, that’s what I’ll be doing.”Ultimately, being open gives an injection of fresh energy that you just can’t get after 14 years together and three children. It’s like Michael and I are constantly choosing each other. You’re going out there, having these potentially wonderful experiences with other people, and then you’re coming home and saying, “I love you. I love being married to you. I love having sex with you.”Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My sister-in-law has published an unfair memoir. Should we cut her off? | Family | The Guardian
description: She should have been much more careful, but everyone has their own version of the ‘truth’. Does your partner want a reconciliation?
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: She should have been much more careful, but everyone has their own version of the ‘truth’. Does your partner want a reconciliation?
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriFamilyMy sister-in-law has published an unfair memoir. Should we cut her off?She should have been much more careful, but everyone has their own version of the ‘truth’. Does your partner want a reconciliation?Annalisa BarbieriSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy sister-in-law wrote and published an emotionally charged “memoir” of familydislocation and trauma, in which she massaged the truth of her family’s past to portraymy partnerasemotionally damaged. (In fact, heis empathetic and was beloved by those he worked with.)Theirs was a complex family story, and there weremany omissions and mistruths, which she failed to factcheck with us.Shetried to de‑identify her brother, but he would berecognisable to anyone with a rudimentary abilityto search the internet. Legal action was considered, but decided against. Who gets to tell a story in these times?Whose story is more“true”?And should we cut off all ties or attempt reconciliation?You have every right to be aggrieved. This sounds upsetting, unfair and also largely avoidable. Unless your partner’s inclusion was an essential and pivotal part of the book (in which case he may have wanted to write the story himself), I wonder why he was included in a way that could identify him, and why she didn’t give you a heads-up.But family members don’t always behave in ways we like, and in families there is usually one person who feels they own the narrative and know all the truths. It may feel as if, by putting her account in a book, your sister-in-law has claimed the definitive, “true” version. But that’s just her side of it. Your question about “who gets to tell a story” is pertinent because not everyone will go on to write a memoir, but many people can and do post a mini version on social media.double quotation markMany families have fallen out over this: whose truth is the actual truth?I spoke to psychologist and psychoanalyst Prof Alessandra Lemma. She wondered who was really asking these questions, you or your partner? Who is the injured party? Before the memoir, did you get on with your sister-in-law, or has this crystallised something that was already there? The strands of grievance may need teasing out.“The core question here,” said Lemma, “is who owns a story? The way we experience the facts is very subjective and individual, and there isn’t a correct account in that strict sense, because versions are filtered through our own internal world. Your letter approaches it as if there is an objective truth, and you and your partner own that, and your sister-in-law is misrepresenting something. Many families have fallen out over this: whose truth is the actual truth?“You first need to have a conversation with your partner to decide who wants what here: does he want to do something about it?My partner’s mother dominates him and it makes me feel helpless | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead more“Everyone has a different version of a situation, and yours may be different even to your partner’s,” said Lemma, “You can’t undo what has happened, so is there a wish to bring the family back together, and does that override the injury of having been treated as you have?”From what you’ve told me, your sister-in-law should absolutely have taken more care when writing about her brother. In your longer letter you said your sister-in-law has been challenged over all this, but you didn’t say by whom. I’m not sure if you’ve all sat down and discussed this, which would be the grownup, decent thing to do. But, your partner would have to want to do that, which is why I go back to my point: what was the relationship like between you all before and is something else being played out here? If all else was relatively OK between you, I would attempt reconciliation.As Lemma also pointed out, though you are aggrieved, it would be a real shame if a book about family dislocation and trauma results in more of the same.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article. Please be aware that there may be a short delay in comments appearing on the site.Explore more on these topicsFamilyAsk Annalisa BarbieriSiblingsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cheap iPhone deal’: warning over scam sites selling latest Apple mobiles | Money | The Guardian
description: Criminals exploit demand for iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo to trick people eager to get their hands on one
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Criminals exploit demand for iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo to trick people eager to get their hands on one
Content: Excitement at the launch of the new iPhone Duo – and it’s the perfect time for scammers to cash in.Photograph: Stan Olszewski/EPAView image in fullscreenExcitement at the launch of the new iPhone Duo – and it’s the perfect time for scammers to cash in.Photograph: Stan Olszewski/EPAScam watchMoney‘Cheap iPhone deal’: warning over scam sites selling latest Apple mobilesCriminals exploit demand for iPhone 18 Pro and foldable Duo to trick people eager to get their hands on oneShane HickeySun 13 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple has just launched a range of new iPhones, including a foldable handset, just as you decide it is time to replace your own ageing mobile. But you balk at the £1,199 price tag for the cheapest of the new options.Searching online for a better price with the words “cheap”, “iPhone” and “deal”, you come across a website which offers an iPhone 18 Pro for a couple of hundred pounds less than theApplesite. You pay for the new phone via a bank transfer and wait for it to arrive.But the website is a fraud - one of hundreds set up in the days before the new Apple phones were announced – and is designed to scam money out of people eager to get their hands on one of the new handsets.Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, the company’s first foldable phone, on Wednesday, as well as two new iPhone 18 Pro models.At the same time, criminals were building up networks of fake sites. Security researchers found a large spike in the number of scam sites registered with “Apple” and “iPhone”, among other keywords, in their domain names.View image in fullscreenExcitement builds at the crowded launch in California of the new iPhones.Photograph: Stan Olszewski/EPAIt is expected that the number will proliferate into the hundreds.Alexandre François, who investigates scams for the intelligence company WhoisXML API, says the days before and after the announcement of the phones typically see a glut of domain names being registered by criminals. Some are then developed into phishing sites in order to dupe people.“Some are flagged as dangerous by dozens of security engines, yet they are still absent from the blocklists that browsers and security tools rely on, so for most people nothing stops the page from loading,” he says.“In each of the last four iPhone launches, domain registrations referencing the new model peaked on ‘keynote day’ – the launch day itself: more than 200 new domains within 24 hours, against zero or one on a normal day.”What it looks likeThe domain names will often include words such as “Apple” and “iPhone 18”. The content of a developed site will look convincingly realistic as fraudsters frequently use AI to mimic genuine retailers.One site found by François, an iPhone Pro Max, in three different colours, was advertised with claims of an “all-day battery”.The release of technical specifications following the launch allows fraudsters to build more convincing websites. François says it then “becomes much easier to convince people that what they are looking at is a real iPhone”.The sites may also claim to offer early access to the devices, as well as cheaper prices. The new iPhone 18 Pro starts at £1,199 officially, while the 18 Pro Max at £1,299, so expect the scam sites to quote prices substantially lower.View image in fullscreenA fraudulent site offering the new iPhone 18 Pro Max.Photograph: WhoisXML APIAs with many scams, fraudsters may give people a deadline to buy – such as a few hours – to encourage them to abandon caution in a bid to land a bargain.The sites will often only take payment via bank transfer to avoid giving people the protections available when you pay with a debit and credit card.What to doRemember what is on sale. So far, the iPhone Duo and the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have been announced – but not the standard iPhone 18. Pages which claim to be selling it now or taking deposits are fakes.François says Apple does not operate lotteries and does not recruit people to test phones.Legitimate websites will offer consumers a variety of ways to pay – debit and credit cards among them. Some fraudulent sites will insist payment is made using cryptocurrency, which should act as an immediate red flag.Apple says its Safari browser has a warning for fraudulent websites that alerts users to phishing or malware sites.If you find you have given out your financial details, contact your bank and Report Fraud. And then change your passwords.Explore more on these topicsMoneyScam watchiPhoneConsumer affairsAppleScamsSmartphonesCybercrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people
Content: The historic ironworks village of Högbo Bruk is now an outdoor recreation destination. All photographs: Emmie Bolmstedt/Visit SwedenView image in fullscreenThe historic ironworks village of Högbo Bruk is now an outdoor recreation destination. All photographs: Emmie Bolmstedt/Visit SwedenSweden holidaysA taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroesChefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its peopleAilsa SheldonSun 13 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses atHögbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food.The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended.“Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home.Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the oldbrukbuildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses.View image in fullscreenA selection of charcuterie at Högbo BrukshotellIngredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work.Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli.double quotation markOver several days, I discover a network of millers,  distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes fromHögbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from.AtGammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby,The Old Millis now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed.View image in fullscreenAppetisers at the Old Mill restaurantAtBergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations.But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon andböckling(hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills.View image in fullscreenThe smokehouse at Bergmans Fisk, run by a seventh-generation fishing familyDriving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsland-hopping in Sweden: an enchanted maze of tiny isles – only a bus ride from GothenburgRead moreAtTeve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930.Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs.At nearbyJärvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.”In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie.View image in fullscreenFood prep at Järvsö Lanthandel country shop and restaurant.Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses.Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb.It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious.It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too.The trip was provided byVisit Sweden. For more information visitgastrikland.seanddestinationhalsingland.se.Högbo Brukshotellhas doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&BExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysFood and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The show choir definitely helped me’: the dos and don’ts of joining student societies | Higher education | The Guardian
description: Signing up for university clubs and societies is a surefire way to meet like-minded people, boosting your social life and your CV at a stroke
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Signing up for university clubs and societies is a surefire way to meet like-minded people, boosting your social life and your CV at a stroke
Content: Culture … music societies are a fulfilling extracurricular activity.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCulture … music societies are a fulfilling extracurricular activity.Photograph: Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Higher education‘The show choir definitely helped me’: the dos and don’ts of joining student societiesSigning up for university clubs and societies is a surefire way to meet like-minded people, boosting your social life and your CV at a strokeAmee Joshi andAlfie PackhamSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClubs and societies are a huge part of student life, though many miss out on them. According toa recent survey by Savanta, 67% of students, particularly those who live at home while studying at university, did not take part in societies, clubs or social activities at least once during term.But if you ask the students and graduates who did benefit from extracurricular activities, they’ll tell you they are well worth the trip. Here are their dos and don’ts.What to doSign up to more than just one.“You’ll probably end up joining more societies than you might be able to keep up throughout your time at university and that’s totally normal,” says Dell*, 25, a graduate of Japanese from Oxford University. “I definitely recommend joining at least two, because it is such a great way to meet people. It can be quite a great escape from when you’re feeling stressed about university work or other situations.”Izzy Clark, 20, an anthropology student at the University of Aberdeen, agrees. “Join maybe three or four and then decide whether or not you like them, because it’s harder to join the societies midway through the semester after they’ve settled into a routine,” she says. “I had no idea whether or not I would enjoy joining the show choir, as I wasn’t a particularly confident person, but I found that it definitely helped me.”Remember, everyone is in the same boat, saysIsabella*, 26, a film-making graduate from the University of Sussex. “I think just realising that can help when you’re going around the freshers’ fair,” she says. “The people running the socs want people to join, so I think it’s good to just go up to their desk and say you’ll join.”View image in fullscreenJoin in … a freshers’ fair at Glasgow University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianPut societies on your CV.Even activities that aren’t directly related to your chosen field can end up making the difference in a future job search, says Alex Frost, 24, a history graduate from the University of Edinburgh. Frost says his experience on the committee of his orchestra was more useful in his current career working at a prison than anything he learned on his degree course. He learned “a lot of skills in how to interact with people and leading projects,” he says. “For example we had someone who needed financial support to buy an instrument and we dealt with that. We also organised a tour to the Lake District. And that’s the sort of stuff that you have to do in a real job. You have to get out of your comfort zone.”Isabella’s time as social secretary of her cheerleading squad gave her leadership and organisation skills, she adds. “I became social sec around the time when people realised you could make a career out of social media – and it was really helpful for me to put on my CV.”Ask for taster sessions first to cut costs.Radhika*, 22, a medicine student at Queen’s University Belfast, advises freshers to first ask for taster sessions before joining any clubs. “Asking if they’ve got any free taster events allows you to see if you’d like to join that one and potentially commit to membership. It just means you’re saving money, especially considering how expensive everything is nowadays.”And try meeting other members online first, saysMartha Page, 23, who graduated from the Lancaster University: “My main advice is to join WhatsApp group chats and connect with people online first.” Page, who is blind and suffers from anxiety, says this helped “take the pressure out” for her when joining a new group felt daunting. “Before the session, that can open some doors so I would advise anyone to do that first.”What not to doView image in fullscreenGood sports … hockey players at the University of Birmingham.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianDon’t ignore sport just because you’re not an athlete,Isabella advises. “As a thoroughly unsporty 18-year-old, I somehow settled on one of the two cheerleading groups at my university,” she says. “I was as coordinated as a newborn foal. We were not a competitive cheer club, and we didn’t have a coach, but we had big sparkly bows and each other.”Don’t feel like you have to drink the whole time.“I definitely think a lot of student culture revolves around drinking,” says Dell, looking back on her slightly underwhelming time at a Marxist society. “Regardless of whether it’s a structured society or not. But I think the less structured societies are more susceptible to just becoming excuses to get really drunk together.”But whatever you do,don’t go without trying any societies at all. As Isabella says: “My only bad experience is I wish I had done even more.”*Surnames withheld on requestExplore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity Guide 2027Student experienceYoung peopleUniversitiesStudentsStudent engagementfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: what have been the most prescient or accurate predictions of the future? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the art of soothsaying, prognostication and futurism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the art of soothsaying, prognostication and futurism
Content: Photograph: zhuyongming/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: zhuyongming/Getty ImagesNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: what have been the most prescient or accurate predictions of the future?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers the art of soothsaying, prognostication and futurismThis week’s question:What would be the most useful superpower?Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Fingertip shopping will be one of the many homemakers’ conveniences. This video console will be channelled into the store of her choice …” I’ve always been fascinated bythis 1967 video(not 1969, as the label says) which accurately foresaw the advent of online shopping, CCTV, fax/email and electronic banking. (It was a little less prescient in its assumption of gender roles – wife shops, husband pays – but we’ll let that slide.) The video, entitled 1999AD, was made by the Philco-Ford company, an American electronics firm that started off in radios and moved into appliances and TVs. I’ve often wished the writer of this short film could see the world as it is in 2026. What are some other predictions that have come spookily close to the truth?Ann, DevonSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyI have a copy of a primary school reading book from the early 1990s that not only predicted online shopping, but that we would also be emailing the local library for research on our homework. The library staff would even be able to fax a reply!AnneTifaHow about Prof James Ephraim Lovelock and hisGaia hypothesis?ANZAC69Kingdom Come by JG Ballard without a doubt. Never read it? Have a look.bricklayersoptionIt wasn’t exactly a prediction, but in Star Trek during my childhood they were using their handheld communicators for the “Beam me up, Scotty” message. These days, everyone has devices like Kirk’s and Spock’s.NerdvanianIt was certainly prescient. Design team members at Apple have actually cited Star Trek’s communicator and Spock’s tricorder when talking about their desire to create a device like the iPhone and iPad. Adults realising their childhood fantasies …FrankieandDexyWhen US shares were going crazy before the 1929 crash, a journalist asked Joseph Kennedy (JFK’s father): “What will happen to the stock market in the future?” Kennedy replied, “It will fluctuate.” Can’t say that he was wrong there.PeteTheBeatMy West Country father-in-law has a similar response to queries about the weather: “It’ll clear up and rain.”SpoilheapSurferGeorge Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.LiveInWonderYes, in part, although I think there’s much more Huxley about in our time. Be quiet and take the “soma” (smartphones, social media), the shallow obsessions with appearance, shiny acquisitions and entertainment, etc.bricklayersoptionReckon Aldous Huxley, with control through entertainment and hedonism as opposed to Orwell’s more directly oppressive alternative, turned out to be pretty close to the mark.SalfordGeoffThe NWRA (The North Will Rise Again) is a track on the album Grotesque (After the Gramme) released by the Fall in 1980. The lyrics by renegade genius Mark E Smith outline the events of a fictional violent uprising by the north of Britain against the south. Two of these events seemed spookily prescient on 15 June 1996. In the morning, an IRA bomb badly damaged the Arndale Centre in Manchester; in the afternoon, Scotland fans gathered in London’s Soho and Trafalgar Square after the match against England at Wembley in Euro 96, and skirmishes with England fans ensued. In the song, Smith had described both the razing of the Arndale Centre, and the streets of Soho which “reverberated with drunken Highland men” (he omitted to mention the drunken English men who also turned up).Matt, AmsterdamWhile it was never intended to depict an imagined future more than a few years ahead of its time, Sinclair Lewis’s 1935 novel It Can’t Happen Here can’t fail but be read during Trump’s second presidency as a sustained act of clairvoyance – if inevitably uneven, it is on the whole remarkably on the money. It isn’t only that Buzz Windrip’s moral character and the strategies he and his supporters deploy in taking and attempting to consolidate power strike repeated resonances – although the parallels here are startling enough. It’s also his prescience (as signalled in the book’s title) about the extent of his more liberal-minded characters’ lack of prescience that makes Sinclair’s novel a truly spooky – as well as salutary – read.fainthopeThe Simpsons predicting Trump’s presidency has to be right up there with the best.ThirdhandlukeNot really a prediction, but I used to have a long commute by train – about 100 minutes each way. I used to think that it would be great if you could watch last night’s TV while you travelled. It only took 20 years or so for that to be a reality.PeteTheBeatPrivate James Frazer of Dad’s Army.We’re doomed.StanEthelThe exposing of Hitler and his socialist veil was enacted by many but, in particular, Otto Strasser. He predicted the rise of fascism, the banning of the left and much else that followed.slojdareThe return of Halley’s comet in 1758. English astronomer Edmond Halley used Newton’s laws of gravity and planetary motions to predict the return of a comet he had observed in 1682. It will return in 2061 on its regular 76-year journey around the sun.Sagarmatha1953In 1912, the Russian futurist poet Velimir Khlebnikov published a short dialogue titled Teacher and Student: A Conversation. In it, he proposed a fantastic mathematical philosophy of history, one of whose rules was that states and empires collapse every 365 (+/-48) years. Hence, Khlebnikov asks in 1912, “In the year 554, the kingdom of the Vandals was subjugated. Should we not expect the fall of the state in 1917?”A few years later, in 1915, Khlebnikov’s partner in Russian futurism, Vladimir Mayakovsky, published his long poem A Cloud in Trousers, one of whose stanzas goes as follows:Where men’s sight falls short,Wearing the revolutions’ thorny crown,Leading at the head of the hungry horde,The year 1916 is coming around.Mayakovsky was one year off; Khlebnikov was spot-on.Roman Vater, CambridgeshireSimon and Garfunkel’sThe Sound of Silence. I’m just waiting for the scribbles to appear on the London tube.PorthosI think the writing team of Frederik Pohl and Cyril M Kornbluth had some outstanding ones (strangely, I’ve never liked the work of either author working alone so much). The Space Merchants, its sequel The Merchants’ Warand the less well-knownGladiator-at-Law all score some really blistering satirical hits – or at least, they were meant to be satirical in an “If this goes on …” kind of way. However, I still think the crown has to go to EM Forster forThe Machine Stops, bearing in mind that it was published in 1909 when most of us in the UK were still lighting our streets with gas.SpoilheapSurferSnow Crash by Neal Stephenson was a pretty accurate prediction of the evolution of the internet, particularly virtual worlds. It’s also a cracking read that stands up today.StumpysheepAmy Hunt predicting she would win four European Athletics golds: 100m, 200m, 4x100m mixed relay, 4x100m relay.Steve4000Generally, only very near-term predictions (less than 50 years) are feasible – often compounded by things like the “Star Trek effect”, where things are less prediction and more inspiration for children to create within their own lifetime the fictional technology they saw. So truly deep historical predictions are incredibly rare, or only very general, and take some generous interpretation by the beholder.The only exception I can think of is Svante August Arrhenius, who in 1896 observed: “If the quantity of carbonic acid increases in geometric progression, the augmentation of the temperature will increase nearly in arithmetic progression.” By using infrared observations of the moon, he then calculated how much of infrared is captured by CO2and water (H2O) vapour in Earth’s atmosphere, leading him to be the first person to correctly conclude that human-caused CO2emissions from burning fossil fuels are large enough to swamp the cooling by orbital variations that precipitate ice ages and so cause long-term global warming. Ironically, he was trying to prove the opposite – that CO2couldonlyexplain the temperature rises ofinter-glacialperiods.He further tried to inform the public in 1906 with his book Världarnas Utveckling (Worlds in the Making), describing his “hot-house” theory of the atmosphere, aimed at a popular audience.Even though Arrhenius’s estimates were very broad and lacked the details of modern techniques, with their many competing heating and cooling drivers, broadly they cancel out and agree surprisingly well with his original estimate that increases of 2.5-3 times of CO2will cause a temperature rise of 8–9C in the Arctic.Maybe mention that next time a troll tries to tell you global warming was “made up” in the last decade or so by the Chinese or some such nonsense.HaveYouFedTheFishExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was hit by an emotional hurricane’: Esther Freud, Deborah Levy and other novelists revisit their childhood homes | Homes | The Guardian
description: Even in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?
Author: Alexei Sayle
Headline: Even in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?
Content: Illustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianHomes‘I was hit by an emotional hurricane’: Esther Freud, Deborah Levy and other novelists revisit their childhood homesEven in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?Julia Samuel,Alexei Sayle,Esther Freud,Deborah Levy, Guy Gunaratne and Chloe AridjisSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘People return to their childhood homes to revisit earlier versions of themselves’Psychotherapist and author Julia SamuelView image in fullscreenJulia Samuel, age six, at the London home she lived in from the age of one until she was 20.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia SamuelI recently took my best friend to see my childhood home inKensington, west London. I lived there with my parents and four siblings from the age of one until I was 20; I have not been inside since I was 23, when it was sold, 43 years ago. Yet it still appears in my dreams. It occupies a place inside me. I wanted to return to help me understand why it still held such power.As we walked through nearby Holland Park, my body remembered before my mind did. A warmth spread through me. I thought of family picnics on the grass, ice-creams on hot afternoons, school sports days and sneaky cigarettes behind bushes as a teenager.The closer we came to my street, the more I noticed what had survived. The backs of the Victorian houses facing the park looked almost unchanged. The trees were taller but familiar. As I turned the corner, my heartbeat quickened. Then I saw it.A large white stucco Victorian house, even bigger than I remembered, as later owners have extended it. The two stone eagles that stood guard at the entrance, which I used to tap every time I ran up the steps, had disappeared. The little coal hole in the front wall was still there. My twin brother and I invented endless games through that opening. I could see us both there, age six, completely absorbed in a world of our own.My friend and I stood on the opposite pavement, looking up at the house, when the family who live there now unlocked the front door and went inside. I felt an unexpected punch in my stomach. For a split second, I wanted to call after them, “I used to live here. Would you mind if I came in?”I immediately changed my mind. I realised I did not want to go inside at all. I wanted to preserve the architecture of my memory. Every room held another version of me.I looked up at the top-floor window on the left. That had been my bedroom. I could picture the desk I persuaded my mother to buy me, where I spent hours writing stories simply for the pleasure of disappearing into another world. I remembered the hall with its black and white tiled floor, the sweeping staircase covered in orange carpet. I recalled lying on the landing with my brother, on guard to see who entered and left. I could see my little legs trying to follow my sisters up the stairs, two steps at a time. My last significant memory is stepping down those stairs in my wedding dress, then standing in the hall beside my husband to welcome our guests.If I walked through those rooms today, they would hold another family’s furniture, another family’s smells, another family’s life. Those memories would become mixed with someone else’s reality.As I stood there, I felt two versions of myself share the same pavement. The woman I am today and the child who knew every creaking stair and every colour in every room of that house. As a psychotherapist, I’ve learned that people rarely return to their childhood homes because they miss the building. They return because they are revisiting earlier versions of themselves.Adolescence lasts into your 30s – so how should parents treat their adult children?Read moreChildren remember the emotional atmosphere of home as much as its architecture. Long before we have language, we absorb the rhythms of family life. We learn whether someone comes when we cry, whether conflict feels frightening or survivable, whether we belong and whether we matter. A stable home creates an inner sense of safety. An unpredictable one leaves us scanning for danger. Those early experiences become the template we carry into future relationships.When parents die and families clear a childhood home, they do far more than sort possessions. Every object carries memory. Every room holds echoes of family life.Another family belongs in my childhood home now, and I hope they fill it with a rich life of their own. I didn’t need to step inside because what mattered had never been contained by bricks and mortar.That house gave me my first experience of rootedness and belonging. Those foundations have steadied me through loss, change and uncertainty.Our childhood homes shape our first understanding of safety, belonging, love and family. We leave them physically, but their emotional architecture stays with us for the rest of our lives.‘Seeing my old home after a decade was a surprisingly gruelling emotional experience’Comedian Alexei SayleView image in fullscreenAlexei Sayle, age two, with his dog Blackie, near his childhood home in Liverpool.Photograph: Courtesy of Alexei SayleThis is not the first time I have returned to my old house on Valley Road in Anfield, Liverpool. I moved out in 1971, aged 19, when I gained a place at Chelsea School of Art. When my mother was still alive, I would visit Liverpool once a month or so, and, although I had bought her a nice semi in the verdant south Liverpool suburb of Aigburth, I would regularly take friends who had come to visit to see our old house. I don’t know why I thought they’d be interested, but they didn’t get a choice.It lies near the top of a street of modest terrace housing, built of yellow brick and distinguished from the most basic of working-class houses by its bay window. The last time I had visited was about a decade ago. At that time, every house in the street had been tastefully done up. Only my former house remained unimproved. Perhaps this was some commentary on how Liverpool viewed my legacy.On this latest visit I assumed I would feel the warm nostalgia I usually experienced. I had no anticipation of the emotional hurricane that assaulted me when I stepped out of the taxi from Lime Street station and stood on the corner of Valley Road and Oakfield Road. I felt like someone who had been kidnapped, had a bag jammed over their head and dumped on some unfamiliar street corner in a rough part of town.My gaze followed the curve of Oakfield Road to a building a few hundred metres away, an edifice of such vastness that it resembled a colossal warship anchored in the harbour of some small town. This is Anfield Stadium, the home of Liverpool FC. It had always been there but seemed to have increased in size exponentially since my last visit, grown fat on TV rights and shirt sales.My old neighbourhood is unusual in that there are times when these streets are crammed with tens of thousands of people, but when the people have gone it feels as if this intermittent frenzy has caused it to lapse into exhaustion.As I walked down Valley Road, I was hit by a range of unexpected emotions, the foremost of which was sadness. I felt a sense of familiarity but also of dislocation. Seeing my old house on an airless summer afternoon aged 74 brought back all sorts of memories of childhood: playing in the street, walking to school and visiting the shops. It all seemed such an impossibly vast time ago that it was hard to believe that I had been alive for so long.When I was little, there was a dairy at the end of Valley Road that actually had cows in it. The building was still there, but it was housing now. When I returned from staring at it, there was a man sitting in a chair outside my old house drinking a can of beer. He said the house belonged to his sister and that she wouldn’t mind me looking around, but it didn’t look like it had changed much from my last visit, so I declined.How I’ve Tried to Change the World by Alexei Sayle review – does protest make a difference?Read moreIn my youth there were so many nearby shops – chandlers, greengrocers, delicatessens – and each was busy, but now 95% of shopfronts are shuttered. Strangely, the only place open was a smart-looking takeaway selling tacos and churros. The twin spectres of economic collapse and incompetent and corrupt redevelopment did for Anfield.On the drive over, I’d asked my cabby how he thought the city had changed in the last few years. He told me that, for a long time, following Thatcher’s economic assault on the city, people were filled with despair, but they were starting, in a modest way, to regain hope.To my mind, the grounds for this hope lie in initiatives such as the Homebaked Cooperative Bakery, which occupies a corner site a little farther along Oakfield Road from my former home. The building had been a bakery for more than 100 years, one that I remember visiting many times as a child, but it closed in 2010. After the Liverpool Biennial art festival used the site as a base, locals worked with the organisation to reopen the bakery in 2013. Now, it is thriving.Perhaps this is where hope lies – not in grand schemes but in a little shop selling pies. Hopefully, other grassroots enterprises will follow and the streets of Anfield will again be teeming with people. I’m not sure if I will visit again. Seeing my childhood home after a decade was a surprisingly gruelling emotional experience. If I make it to 84, it’s hard to imagine what unsettling effect that will have.How I’ve Tried to Change the Worldby Alexei Sayle (W&N, £16.99) is out now.‘I was happy in that house. There were meals around a big old kitchen table, feasts that issued from an Aga’Novelist Esther FreudView image in fullscreenEsther Freud (on right), age 11, with two of her siblings at The Old Laundry, East Sussex.Photograph: Courtesy of Esther FreudThere were a lot of childhood homes. My sister and I counted them once: 16 in two years, but the longest and most defining was a converted laundry in East Sussex where I lived between the ages of eight and 14. The house was owned by an American, the father of three girls. The initial understanding was that my mother, my sister, Bella, and I were renting rooms from him, but it wasn’t long before I discovered my mother’s bed empty when I crept through to her in the middle of the night.My stepfather, as I came to refer to him later, after we’d moved out, had recently divorced, and gained custody of his three young daughters – most unusual in those days. He had bought a derelict laundry on an old estate, which overlooked Ashdown Forest, in a village so small it was termed a hamlet, although there was a pub, a shop and a telephone box, from which we occasionally received calls from our father, pre-arranged by post.The Old Laundry was the last building on the estate to be restored. There was also a coach house and several stable blocks, and the mansion with its Jacobean facade had been turned into flats. Our stepfather had renovated the house himself, adding an extension to the original square brick building. Inside, there was a chimney stack vast enough to heat the water that once washed the estate linen, and this was transformed into a fireplace big enough for us to sit inside on cushions.It seemed at first that our ramshackle family would not be welcome on the Holly Hill estate: our van broke down on the cattle grid; our dog regularly escaped; and a feud developed with the man next door, a retired colonel, who had illegally – according to our stepfather – cut down an ancient tree that blocked his light. The rest of us ignored this quarrel, unwilling to risk our friendship with Margaret, the colonel’s wife, a big‑hearted woman who employed all five of us girls, rewarding us disproportionately for dusting and polishing, or ironing a shirt. Margaret became our ally and would drop round to sample our baking, watch our plays and listen to our recitals.I was happy in that house. There were meals around a big old kitchen table, feasts that issued from an Aga, and occasionally my stepfather would make lasagne, commandeering every surface of the kitchen and allocating jobs. On Sundays he would make pancakes, and on winter evenings we would sit inside the fireplace while he played guitar and sang folk songs. I loved the rituals. I even loved the chores – I was in charge of feeding the chickens and collecting their eggs. And I loved the new baby, a boy, born when I was 10.But there were dark days, too, when one or other of us, most often my stepfather, would lock themselves in the bathroom. When frustrations and jealousies would blacken the mood. Days when my sister would pull me aside and insist the whole setup was a charade: the singing and the pancakes. He didn’t love us or our mum. Charade or not, this house was where much of my character was formed, for better or for worse. The bookshelves, the conversation, the rituals and routines, the idea of family and what, at its best, it could be.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEsther Freud: ‘My parents died within four days of each other. I was engulfed’Read moreI didn’t expect the suddenness with which the household broke apart. I arrived home one day to find a note: my mother had gone. My sister and I were to follow her to Cambridge, she explained, and we would not be going back.My mother, I’m fairly certain, never returned to the house. My sister – absolutely not. But I did, decades later. Finding myself in Sussex, I drove over the cattle grid and into the estate. There were the familiar shrubs and lawns, the Gate House, the Coach House, the steep path that led up to the Old Laundry. I knocked on the door, full of dread – what if there wasn’t any answer? What if there was?The new owners were happy to show me around. The house was smaller, tidier. How had this been the scene of so much joy and anguish? The Aga was still there and the fireplace, but my old downstairs bedroom had been turned into a dining room, and the trees that shaded it had fallen in the storm of 1987, allowing light to flood in. The colonel would be pleased, I thought. As I looked across the fence, I had a yearning to see Margaret, to tell her I still used the button box she had given me, to say how important she was.I was quiet as I drove away. The Old Laundry, mythical receptacle of stories, was nothing but a shell. The real house, the one in which I had learned to read, fallen in love, experienced both triumph and despair, only existed now inside my head.Esther Freud’s most recent novel isMy Sister and Other Lovers(Bloomsbury).‘At its best, a childhood home is a safe place in which solitude can be experienced without anxiety’Writer Deborah LevyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianI do not have to literally knock on the door of my childhood house to enter its domain. It is always inside me – “my first universe”, as the philosopher Gaston Bachelard put it.Yes, in my mind’s eye, the door is ajar at this modest bungalow in Johannesburg, South Africa, 1966. It presents itself to me like a museum. Everything is in place. Nothing has changed since my last visit.Of course, should I visit 11 Iris Road in the suburb of Norwood in real life, everything will have changed, but let’s press a foot into the dust of the past and see what it reveals.Despite the force of the African sun and piercing stretch of blue sky above the tiles of its roof, the interior of the bungalow is dark and cool. Maybe the curtains are drawn in some of the rooms to keep it that way. I can smell floor polish as I glimpse myself, aged seven, with a crooked fringe trimmed by my mother and wearing a sleeveless summer dress, making my way towards the giant sack of oranges propped against the wall in the pantry.Every day after school, I roll one of the oranges under the soles of my feet until it is soft and pulpy. I then make a hole in it with my thumb and suck out the juice, usually while sitting on the steps of the porch outside, reading a book or looking out at the tall uncut grass of the garden, where I am convinced I have dropped one of my Barbie’s pink plastic stilettos. The incredible thing about Barbie is how she never looks sad. In fact, Barbie is still smiling when my friend Leonie twists off her head and throws it at my beloved pogo stick in the hallway.The lounge is where our mother keeps Auntie Molly’s record player, with its speakers made from wood. This sound system will travel with us from Johannesburg to the UK, when I am nine years old. I will inherit it as a teenager and play all my Bowie vinyl on it – but now I’m looking for Mum in the dark, cool bungalow. Yes, she is back from work. I can hear the ice rattling in her glass of brandy, and she has kicked off her shoes, patent leather burgundy kitten heels. My God. My mother is a secretary, and it occurs to my older self that she is like a character from Mad Men, a cross between Peggy and Joan. She tells me all about work. I don’t tell her anything about school. It is a relief not to be asked.My bedroom is located at the back of the bungalow. It is a place of refuge and calm. I can lie in bed and glimpse the bright stars at night through its big windows. At its best, a childhood home is a safe place in which solitude can be experienced without anxiety. Solitude is different from loneliness. It is an invitation to have imaginative adventures, to daydream, to discover something we do not know, to pretend to be someone else for five minutes – perhaps someone braver and happier.My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy review – wonderfully entertainingRead moreMy childhood home represents theturbulent African part of my biography. Sometimes it feels like the child in this house is a ghost child who is not that keen to talk to my English adult self. Yet she haunts every book I have written.The past is literally a foreign country in my case. I can see via Google Earth that the house is still there, but it has been redesigned to conceal its interior. When I was a child there was an iron gate that opened on to the front garden. Now that the garden is closed off to the street with a heavy door and a wall, I do not have a nostalgic longing to unlock its new mystery. If our first home holds “childhood motionless in its arms”, as Bachelard insists, it is also the place my brother and I had to solve the old mystery of where our mother had hidden the family supply of sweets. As it happens, I can tell you they are inside a yellow enamel cup, behind a bag of flour in the pantry.Deborah Levy’s most recent work isMy Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein(Hamish Hamilton).‘For my father, who was part of the first wave of south Asian immigration into the UK, property ownership served as a hedge against future precarity’Novelist and artist Guy GunaratneView image in fullscreenGuy Gunaratne on his eighth birthday at his house on Crest Road in Neasden, London.Photograph: Courtesy of Guy GunaratneBetween the ages of three and nine, I lived with my parents, my brother and my half-sister in a small semi‑detached house on Crest Road, in a suburban part of Neasden, north-west London. The house had a pebbledash exterior, characterful bay windows and a narrow back garden, which, as I recall, extended farther than either of our neighbours’ gardens.As I wander around the area today, not much has changed. There is still a newsagent at the end of the road and a bus stop from where my mother used to catch the no 16 to work. Farther along, a bookie has replaced the charity shop where my mother bought her silverware. There used to be a greengrocer in front of the bus stop. The grocer was a Cypriot man from whom my mother would buy cabbage, leeks and carrots. He wore a white coat and would offer a kindly slap to the cheek whenever I tagged along. The Ox & Gate pub, which the grocer might have patronised after closing time, still stands across the road, although the flash signage and live sports advertising indicate a change in owner.My family moved around often when I was a child, but only ever within a five-mile radius. My mother still lives a few streets away. My father, working as a clerk in Paddington for most of his life, put me and my brother through school and tuition by purchasing modest properties around the area. He would redecorate the houses and sell them on over the years, which meant the family had to relocate every so often.For my father, who was part of the first wave of south Asian immigration into the UK, property ownership was more than a social marker: it served as a hedge against future precarity. He used to tell stories of lodging in overcrowded rooms in the 1960s, shift‑sleeping in shared beds, and fretting over the labour market in the morning. In the 1990s and early 2000s, he had my brother and I help him redecorate these other homes, pasting wallpaper, laying down carpet and mowing the lawn. It was during these weekends that I came to realise that property ownership was never an end in itself but a means to afford a way of life. What mattered was not the high ceilings or the Edwardian bay windows, but whether we could afford the expense of keeping both salted fish and Indian okra in my mother’s kitchen cupboard.I think this is why, as I stand in front of the house on Crest Road today, my memories aren’t so much shaped by its dimensions but by the extended sense of constant migration. I can, of course, locate certain memories in its rooms. I remember watching my brother leave for school from an upstairs window. I can recall the image of suitcases left on the landing when an aunt and uncle came to stay. There is my half-sister, the scent of her hairspray perfuming the hall as she skipped away for a night out. And another, in the narrow back garden, when, aged seven, I found a pigeon lying asleep near the farthest fence. There is an aspect of loss or transition to many of these memories.I often wonder what my father would have made of my now choosing to live in cooperative housing in north London. I live alongside families and artists who both rent and part-own their homes. He would surely have raised an eyebrow at my rent. I also think he would have recognised the same instinct for community and shared shelter.Last September, when my father died, my brother and I plotted a route for the procession that would take in some of the houses he had owned and redecorated. When we slowed down on Crest Road, the last stop before the cemetery, I noticed there were children’s bikes leant against the garden fence, the front door slightly ajar. I imagined other lives looking out at us from behind the net curtains. Somebody was home.‘Everything was animated by our childhood dog, a black labrador retriever named Tarzan, who would pull us through the snow on an orange plastic sled’Novelist Chloe AridjisView image in fullscreenChloe Aridjis, age five, in front of her house with Tarzan the dog.Photograph: Courtesy of Chloe AridjisLatin America has a long and eccentric tradition of appointing its writers to diplomatic posts abroad. Who better, it would seem, to represent your country than a cultural figure, especially if trade and serious geopolitics aren’t too much of a concern. And so it was that in the late 1970s, my father, a long-haired poet in his 30s, was appointed Mexican ambassador to the Netherlands, and our family relocated there. I was five years old when my parents, my sister and I left Switzerland (a previous posting) and moved into the ambassador’s residence in Wassenaar, where we lived for nearly three years. I hadn’t been back since the summer we left.Not until this past April, that is, when I went to visit my childhood friend Victor in Amsterdam. I’d met him aged two in a sandpit in The Hague, and our families have remained friends. On my second day there, his parents, Ad and Ada, were driving me to the Mauritshuis museum when Ad asked whether I’d like to see my old home. We were passing through Wassenaar and had time for a quick detour. I remembered the street name but not the number. We searched for the house until we spotted the Mexican flag in the distance. I rang the buzzer, tried to explain who I was over the intercom. Moments later, a man appeared and introduced himself as the cook. I lived here as a child, I said somewhat timidly, and would love to revisit the grounds. He studied me and my friends and replied that the ambassadress was in a meeting and they couldn’t let anyone in without permission. He tried calling but her phone was switched off.View image in fullscreenChloe Aridjis, c1977, age fivePhotograph: Courtesy of Chloe AridjisIt was tantalising to be so close. I could almost feel a gloved hand keeping my curiosity in check. As we lingered outside, I gazed past the gold-tipped wrought‑iron gates, down the gravel driveway to a corner of the house. I recognised the tall brick chimney and shingled roof. It was by far the largest home I’ve lived in; much of it had remained a mystery. As a child, I had no sense that the space and its furnishings were all borrowed, that the Persian carpets and gilt bedframes had seen family after family come and go. My parents had hung some of their own masks and art on the walls to give character to the rooms. I remember an endless row of cupboards and two staircases, one with red carpeting and the other smaller and more secretive, connecting the kitchen to upstairs – that notion of front and back, the presentable and the hidden, now seems so foreign. On the third floor was the eerie attic, inhabited only by mice.Looking back, the house belonged more to the adults. The garden belonged to me and my sister. It was the highlight of those years, the vagaries of Dutch weather permitting, and most of my memories are from there. There were groves of deciduous trees, a wood of ghostly birch, and a 350-year-old beech at the very end of the grounds. Everything was animated by our childhood dog, a black labrador retriever named Tarzan, who in winter would pull us through the snow on an orange plastic sled. In spring we’d invite our classmates over for Easter egg hunts amid the tulips and daffodils. I remember Hugo, the elderly gardener, always in his olive-green clothes and cap, and the mounds left by moles overnight. The fenced compost heap, the tennis court. After we returned to Mexico, we moved into a normal-sized house – myfamily home to this day – and I went back to being the daughter of a poet, which felt more natural. We were free to explore every space and inhabit every corner and create our own chaos without ever feeling that the house itself was hushing us.The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis review – one of the boldest writers at work in English todayRead moreThat afternoon, after wandering through the Mauritshuis, Ad asked whether I had ever seen the Panorama Mesdag, a vast cylindrical painting from the late 19th century. We could drop by on our way back to Amsterdam. Half an hour later, we stood on the viewing platform as painted scenes from Scheveningen, a beach I’d often visited, wrapped around us. That familiar sea, its ships, dunes and village, all formed part of a great illusion of the past. Yet seeing my old house that day had felt like the greatest illusion of all. Those years seemed so distant, and the impossibility of entering the house only strengthened the sense of remove. Part of me was relieved I hadn’t written over my memories, that the many details from that remarkable time would remain undisturbed, and I feel quite certain I may never return.The Shadow of the Object(Chatto & Windus) by Chloe Aridjis is longlisted for the 2026 Booker prize and is out now.Explore more on these topicsHomesFamilyAlexei SayleDeborah LevyGuy GunaratneChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content
