title: At least six dead and 130 missing after Indonesian ferry capsizes, officials say | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Search and rescue agency says 107 people brought to safety from vessel hit by bad weather in Java Sea
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Search and rescue agency says 107 people brought to safety from vessel hit by bad weather in Java Sea
Content: Survivors recover at the port in Banjarmasin, Indonesia.Photograph: WIWIN/EPAView image in fullscreenSurvivors recover at the port in Banjarmasin, Indonesia.Photograph: WIWIN/EPAIndonesiaAt least six dead and 130 missing after Indonesian ferry capsizes, officials saySearch and rescue agency says 107 people brought to safety from vessel hit by bad weather in Java SeaJon Henleyand agenciesSun 13 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 01.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescue workers in Indonesia said at least six people had died and 130 others were missing on Sunday after a ferry sailing between the islands of Java and Borneo capsized in bad weather.Basarnas, Indonesia’s national search and rescue agency, said 107 people had been rescued from the Virgo ⁠Transport 8 vessel, which set sail on Saturday with 243 ​people onboard, including 30 crew members, ​from ‌the East Java ‌city of Surabaya.The ferry’s last position before it lost contact at 2am on Sunday was in the Java Sea, about 150km (90 miles) from its destination, the city of Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, said Heri Purwanto, the head of the Banjarmasin port authority.Indonesia’s transport minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, said the vessel had capsized. “From the information we received, based on helicopter surveillance … the ship capsized but has not sunk. As of 3pm [local time] it had not sunk yet, but it was capsized,” he said at a news conference in Banjarmasin.Location mapThe local search and rescue chief, I Putu Sudayana, said rescuers were battling waves of up to 2.5 metres (8.2ft) to reach the ferry. “It is extremely risky for vessels. Even our Basarnas vessel, which is 40 metres long, is at great risk,” he said.A Basarnas helicopter had joined the operation, he said, adding that evacuees had been transported ⁠using a number of different ships and some of them would be taken to ​an East Java ​port.View image in fullscreenSurvivors of the ferry accident rest after arriving at a port in Banjarmasin.Photograph: WIWIN/EPAParamedics and ambulances were on standby in Banjarmasin, where dozens of relatives and friends of passengers checked a whiteboard on which the names of the rescued were being updated.Jenah, 26, told Agence France-Presse she had come to the command post for information about her older brother. “I am saddened and very shocked. Until now, I haven’t received any more information,” she said. “He was travelling alone. I hope he survives. I couldn’t contact him since last night.”Indonesia, an ​archipelago of ​more than 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries, with sea routes more affordable and readily available than air travel. However, safety standards are not always rigorously enforced, resulting in a relatively high accident rate.View image in fullscreenPeople look for the names of family members on a passenger list at the rescue command centre in Banjarmasin on Sunday.Photograph: Iman Satria/APOn Monday, a speedboat carrying eight people, including five journalists working for local and international news agencies, went missing near a volcano,Mount Anak Krakatau, in Lampung province.Last month, a fire onboard a ferry killed one person and left five others missing, while 211 were rescued, in the Lombok strait off the island of Bali. The ferry had been heading from Bali to the island of Lombok when it ran into trouble in the early hours of 12 August.In July, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small island south of Sulawesi.Reuters and AgenceFrance-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaWater transportAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: One dead and more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast in rough seas | Vanuatu | The Guardian
description: Prime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continue
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continue
Content: Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office says ‘over 30 people remain missing at sea’ after a ferry sank.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office says ‘over 30 people remain missing at sea’ after a ferry sank.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesVanuatuOne dead and more than 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast in rough seasPrime minister’s office tells families of those missing ‘the nation stands with you’ as search and rescue efforts continueGuardian staff and agenciesSat 12 Sep 2026 22.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 22.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne person has died and more than 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast ofVanuatu, the country’s government says.The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail with more than 40 passengers and crew on Friday from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.“Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones,” Vanuatu prime minister Jotham Napat’s office said in a statement on Sunday.“Search and rescue operations are continuing.”Fifteen of those onboard have been “accounted for alive” and one body has been recovered, the statement said.“Over 30 people remain missing at sea,” it said.“To the survivors, we ⁠pray for your strength and recovery. To the families of ​those ​missing and those we ​have lost, please know that the nation stands ​with you ‌in this time ​of ​grief.”An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.“This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel,” the statement added.The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in New Caledonia said it was assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday morning.The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.Matai Seremaiah, the member of parliament for Luganville who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the south-east coast where currents may have carried survivors.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsVanuatuAsia PacificPacific islandsSouth PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: One Nation vows to cut migration by 750,000, sparking fears for key industries including aged care | One Nation | The Guardian
description: New immigration policy has attracted bipartisan condemnation, with Labor warning it would damage construction, healthcare and agriculture
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: New immigration policy has attracted bipartisan condemnation, with Labor warning it would damage construction, healthcare and agriculture
Content: One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the new migration policy would give ‘illegal migrants’ three months to leave Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenOne Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the new migration policy would give ‘illegal migrants’ three months to leave Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOne NationOne Nation vows to cut migration by 750,000, sparking fears for key industries including aged careNew immigration policy has attracted bipartisan condemnation, with Labor warning it would damage construction, healthcare and agricultureFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorSun 13 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 22.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Nation says it will cut the number of temporary migrants in Australia by more than 750,000 over three years, targeting international students and family members of skilled migrants in a “net-negative” plan.But the business and agriculture sectors have warned the plan would badly hurt the economy and weaken essential services, without lifting living standards for Australians.Labor and theCoalitionsaid One Nation’s plan, announced on Monday morning, would damage regional economies, reduce workers for the construction, healthcare, aged care and disability sectors, and could even spark a recession.The One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, said the new policy would “reset” Australia’s immigration system and help ease pressure on housing and public services.Temporary visa numbers would be returned to 2017 levels, under what Hanson says would represent a net-negative arrivals rate for the first three years. That would mean the net overseas migration (Nom) total would be 130,000 under the One Nation plan.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe announcement comes as Labor and the Coalitionconsider new cuts to overseas arrivals, in an increasingly charged contest before the next federal election. Hanson will hope her plan plays well in the lead-up to the Victorian state election, due in November.“I know Australians are doing it tough,” Hanson said. “Families are competing with hundreds of people for rental accommodation. Patients are stuck in ambulances because there are not enough hospital beds. Young Australians are being locked out of home ownership while wages and infrastructure fail to keep up.”Labor wrestles with migration figures but opponents struggle to find the targetRead moreThe target is to reduce student visa numbers, including visas for accompanying family members, to 350,000 over three years. According toeducation department data, about 680,000 international students studied in Australia between January to May this year.A single student graduate program visa will be created, with numbers capped at 20,000 new visas per year. One Nation’s target is to reduce graduate visa numbers from 270,000 to 40,000.The policy could also drive division within One Nation, with the lower house MP David Farleypreviously expressing concernthat big cuts to immigration could deny his electorate of Farrer the workers needed to care for elderly people and work on farms.Hanson said One Nation would give “illegal migrants” three months to leave, with those who departed voluntarily would be allowed to apply for visas in the future.“Those who remain unlawfully after this period will be subject to immigration enforcement and a lifetime ban from re-entering Australia,” she said.The Pacific labour mobility scheme for agriculture would remain in place under One Nation’s plan but temporary skilled migrants would lose the ability to apply for visas for family members.“We will take back control of who comes here and how many we accept, train more Australians, restore living standards and put the safety and security of Australians first.”The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, have held talks on Labor’s delayed migration package. It is expected to further drive down net overseas migration.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Won’t happen’: One Nation Victoria leader’s comments raise questions about Hanson’s mass deportations policyRead moreBut Labor has struggled to finalise the plan and delayed its announcement by more than a month.One Nation’s policy was widely criticised by business groups.Business Council of Australia boss Bran Black warned One Nation migrants were needed for growth in the economy.“The starting point for any conversation with respect to migration cannot simply have the objective of cutting numbers, it has to be, how do we go about delivering the growth that ultimately locks in and secures our way of life,” he said.Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar said the business community would not support damaging cuts.“Many Australian businesses would be put at risk by major cuts to the migration program. Pubs, cafes, hotels, and accommodation providers desperately need chefs.“Aged care homes and hospitals are short of staff already. Farmers and resources sector businesses continue to face persistent workforce shortages. Housing projects are being held up, while others remain unviable because of lack of workforce and skills shortages.”National Farmers’ Federation boss Hamish McIntyre warned food prices could rise due to worker shortages.“One in seven employees on our farms across regional Australia now are working holidaymakers or backpackers,” he told Channel Nine.“We need these people now.“It’ll prohibit us from planting some of these crops. We rely on these people. We won’t be able to take the risks to spend all the money, we spend up front obviously to produce these crops, so we’re not going to take a risk if we can’t harvest them.”Taylor dismissed the policy as “absolute nonsense”.“I’m interested to know the details of One Nation’s plan. I don’t know what their non-numbers were. A few days ago, their immigration numbers were 130,000. Now it’s something different. Well, what is it, each year over the next three or four years?“What are those numbers? They’re not in their releases. They need to explain it.”The health minister,Mark Butler, warned that One Nation’s cuts would kill critical industries.“Pauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn’t care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business but this is just another level entirely.“This is going to smash industries like construction. It would devastate the health sector and aged care and disability.”Explore more on these topicsOne NationAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian politicsLabor partyCoalitionMigrationAged carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland woman falls to her death at Bali cliff popular with tourists  | Bali | The Guardian
description: Twenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police say
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Twenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police say
Content: The Australian tourist woman was found stuck on the side of the Kelingking beach cliff in Bali on Saturday morning, police said.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Australian tourist woman was found stuck on the side of the Kelingking beach cliff in Bali on Saturday morning, police said.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesBaliQueensland woman falls to her death at Bali cliff popular with touristsTwenty-nine-year-old Queenslander was visiting Kelingking beach on a holiday, Nusa Penida police sayAustralian Associated PressSun 13 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of an Australian woman in a cliff fall at a popularBalitourist destination has been described as “incredibly sad”.Police say the 29-year-old Queenslander was found stuck on the side of Kelingking beach cliff on Saturday morning, local time. Emergency services rushed to the scene but she fell further before they could reach her.“The victim is estimated to have fallen around 9am,” said Nusa Penida’s alert unit coordinator, Cakra Negara.“At the time, she was seeking an independent path toward the edge of the cliff before slipping and falling into the ravine,” he said.“When found, the victim had sustained several fractures; we secured her onto a stretcher to facilitate the evacuation process.”Kelingking beach is one of the most popular destinations forBalitourists, offering panoramic views from the 180-metre-high coastal cliff.Nusa Penida police said the woman was visiting the area on a holiday.View image in fullscreenBali’s police shared imagery of rescue efforts at Kelingking beach in Bali after a woman fell off a cliffA Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade spokesperson confirmed that the government was providing consular assistance to the woman’s family.“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time,” they said. “The family have requested privacy at this difficult time.”Queensland’s premier, David Crisafulli, described the death as “tremendously sad”.Bali and the not-so-great glass elevator: construction on Kelingking beach prompts outrage from localsRead more“To have a life taken away in a heartbeat like that … it’s just incredibly, incredibly sad,” he told reporters on Sunday. “I just express my sympathies to her family and those loved ones with her and back at home.“I think all of Queensland collectively looks at that and just feels ... just a huge degree of sorrow.”Swimming at Kelingking beach, sometimes referred to as T-Rex Bay, is banned year-round due to dangerous currents.The trek down to the beach can take two hours on atreacherouspath.The site gained international notoriety last year after a developer began construction ona giant, 182-metre tall glass elevatorthat was meant to increase tourism to the area and ease the hike down.The project came at the expense of the untouched view and prompted swift outrage from local lawmakers and tourists alike.Bali’s governor said in November he had ordered the company behind it to demolish the structure within six months. But a protracted legal fight continues and a metal skeleton remains attached to the cliff face.Explore more on these topicsBaliQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes counted | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Race too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc win
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Race too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc win
Content: The Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, arrives at the party's election night watch party.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, arrives at the party's election night watch party.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPASwedenSwedish election: centre-left parties lead by just a single seat with most votes countedRace too close to call and may take days to become clear despite early exit polls suggesting left bloc winSweden general election – live updatesMiranda BryantNordic correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith most of the votes counted, Sweden’s national election remained too close to call on Sunday night, with left-wing parties holding a lead of just a single seat according to a partial tally by the election authority.Earlier in the night, exit polls suggested that the country was on course for a brand new left-leaning government. But as the votes were counted, it was apparent it could take days for the outcome to become clear.With 80% of votes counted, there was just one seat between the left and right blocs. The left-leaning opposition parties, led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, had 175 and the rightwing parties, led by the Moderates prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, had 174.At 10:30pm local time, broadcaster SVT predicted there were only 20,000 votes between the blocs.The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday.Kristersson, the incumbent prime minister, said the voters had had their say, but “we still don’t have a final result.”“Which government will lead Sweden in the coming years is still an open question, and we will do everything we can to ensure that this government will be the very best for our country,” Kristersson told supporters.The Social Democrats remain Sweden’s biggest party, but look to have had their worst result in decades. Speaking just before midnight local time, Andersson addressed supporters to say that every vote must be counted.“We will have to wait for the final election results. But my message is clear: we Social Democrats will always be ready to take responsibility for the result. It seems like it will be very even,” she said.“But right now we are leading. If it stands, then Sweden will have a new government. But we have to wait for the final result, so let me end where I began, in democracy, the finest thing we have.”It was also a bad night for the far-right Sweden Democrats, who are hoping to enter government for the first time. They slipped from the country’s second biggest party to third.The deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, of the Christian Democrats, told her supporters that Sweden would be going “to bed with uncertainty” and may have to wait until Wednesday for a result. But she remained adamant that the ruling right-leaning coalition should remain in government.“This is a very clear message for the only unified government alternative in this election campaign,” she said in an upbeat speech. “This will be a real nail-biter, this could be uncertain all the way until Wednesday.”It comes after an unusually heated and polarised campaign punctuated by personal attacks between leaders, accusations of misinformation and Maga-inspired ads. Pollssuggested an extremely tight race, with one showing just 0.3 percentage points between the left and right blocs.Polling stations across the country opened at 8am local time (7am UK time). Enthusiasm among voters appeared to be high. A record 3.6 million voters took part in early voting and there were reports of long queues at some polling stations.Whatever the result, coalition talks are expected to take weeks if not months.2:51‘I hope for a decent period in politics’: views of voters as Sweden goes to the polls – videoThe right-leaning bloc, made up of what are known as the Tidö parties, has been in power for four years. It is formed of the Moderates, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals, with a supporting role for SD, Sweden’s second biggest party.The opposition left-leaning bloc is formed of Sweden’s biggest party, the Social Democrats, the Centre party, the Green party and the Left party.The rightwing coalition broke a longstanding taboo in 2022 by going into partnership with SD, which has neo-Nazi roots.How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden | Martin GelinRead moreSD has attempted to make itself more palatable to the mainstream by toning down its overtly racist rhetoric, while arguing that immigration is responsible for Sweden’s crime problems.After four years in a supporting role for the Moderates-run coalition government, however, during which it hasshifted much of the Swedish establishment to the rightand had a strong influence on policies, SD’s approach to the election has been more brazen. If the right-leaning coalition wins, the party has been promised a prominent role in the government, including key ministerial positions.SD’s campaign slogan of “make Sweden Sweden again” was reminiscent of Donald Trump’s “make America great again”. Its controversial ads on buses – with messages including: “Do you miss Mogadishu? The repatriation grant will help you get home” – were taken down after drivers refused to work in vehicles displaying them.The party leader, Jimmie Åkesson, was accused of sexism after asking the Social Democrats’ leader why she was so angry during a TV debate.View image in fullscreenThe Sweden Democrats leader, Jimmie Åkesson, at a polling station in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, on Saturday.Photograph: Claudio Bresciani/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesAnother leading SD figure, Gustav Gellerbrant, came under national scrutiny after an investigation by the publication Expo connected his partner to Russian state actors and the spread of Russian propaganda. His partner, who is Russian, works as a civil servant for SD in parliament. Gellerbrant said in response that it was “isolated information” intended to raise suspicion about her Russian origins and has since gone on leave.Andersson, who voted on Sunday morning in the Stockholm suburb of Nacka, said the campaign had been “a tale of two sides”.“There have been a lot of lies and bickering, but at the same time there are so many sensible people out there across the country,” she told SVT. “The focus is on winning and setting a new direction for Sweden.”Abba’s Benny Andersson showed his support for the Social Democrats’ leader by performing a reworked version of Mamma Mia to supporters at the party’s headquarters, replacing the words “Mamma Mia” with “Magdalena”.0:31Abba’s Benny Andersson remixes ‘Mamma Mia’ hit at Social Democrat election day rally – videoKristersson, had put considerable focus in the final days of campaigning on the penalty discount applied to criminals convicted of various offences. He accused the Social Democrat leader of not standing up for female rape victims. In response, she accused him of weaponising men’s violence against women.After voting in the town of Strängnäs, west of the capital, Kristersson said “momentum is on our side”. Despite dropping in the latest polls, he said the role of his party was to be “team leaders … uniting for the best of the country”.Voters say the most important election issues are healthcare, law and order, immigration and the economy. But much of the election debate has been focused on personal finance, said Radio Sweden’s senior political correspondent, Fredrik Furtenbach. “The parties have tried to outdo each other with promises of more money. It has been a sort of auction.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenThe far rightEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump doubles down on support for united Ireland | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: US president brushes off Andy Burnham’s opposition to referendum and says he will remove Irish whiskey tariff
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: US president brushes off Andy Burnham’s opposition to referendum and says he will remove Irish whiskey tariff
Content: The US president gestures as he visits his Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenThe US president gestures as he visits his Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPANorthern IrelandDonald Trump doubles down on support for united IrelandUS president brushes off Andy Burnham’s opposition to referendum and says he will remove Irish whiskey tariffRory CarrollIreland correspondentSun 13 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas reiterated his support for Irish unification and brushed off Andy Burnham’s opposition to a referendum.“Everybody says that. Then things happen,” the US president said on Sunday of the British prime minister’s response.“It seems to me that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together,” Trump said of the unification ofNorthern Irelandand the Republic ofIreland.Trump caused consternation on both sides of the Irish Sea on Saturday when, at the start of a two-day visit to Ireland, he said he would“love” to see a united Irelandand “it may as well happen now”.Trump ended his visit on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort in County Clare in exuberant fashion by presenting the Irish Open trophy to Shane Lowry and announcing that he would cut tariffs on Irish whiskey.“Everyone’s been bugging me,” he told the crowd. “They say ‘will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair, could you possibly take the tariffs off Irish whiskey?’ And I said ‘on behalf of the United States of America I’m going to take the tariffs off Irish whiskey’.”Some in the crowd cheered Trump’s name and chanted “USA”.A 10% tariff on Irish whiskey – part of White House measures against EU imports – disadvantaged it against competitors, including scotch andNorthern Irelandwhiskey, which have no tariffs.The decision followed repeated affirmations by Trump that he lovesIreland– and wishes to see the island unified. The avowals undercut the tradition of White House neutrality on the constitutional status of Northern Ireland and prompted responses from London.Downing Street said Burnham still believed there was not the required support for unification to trigger a referendum, as set out in the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement. Two weeks ago, Burnham said a referendum was “off the table”.Irish nationalists welcomed Trump’s remarks, while the Conservative party and Northern Irish unionists condemned them.View image in fullscreenThe taoiseach, Micheál Martin, speaks to reporters at the Irish open, at Trump International Golf Links and Hotel in Doonbeg, County Clare.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAOn SundayTrump expressed delight at the controversy. “Many people agree. I made what I considered to be a fairly routine comment, I have had so much support on that,” he said.Asked about independence forScotland, he reserved opinion. “I won’t talk about Scotland yet, I will save that.”The leaders of Plaid Cymru, the Scottish National party and Sinn Féin are meeting in Cardiff on Monday, where they will discuss ways to strengthen cooperation for constitutional change.Angela Rayner, the UK’s communities secretary, played down the president’s remarks. “Donald Trump isDonald Trump, and the president will say and speak his mind as he sees it,” she told Sky News. The government was serious about the Good Friday agreement and would “continue on that path”, she said.Trump’s comments were awkward for the Irish government, which prefers to discuss cross-border initiatives rather than unification. Last month the taoiseach,Micheál Martin, said that he “goes bananas” when his Fianna Fáil party colleagues call for a border poll.On Sunday, Martin said there had been “overreaction” to Trump’s comments. “He takes a different sort of perspective on things. We know that,” he said. “I think if everyone keeps a calm perspective on things, you know, we will take it from there.”Sinn Féin figures welcomed Trump’s support for Irish unification. “They reflect the broad North American sentiment towards Irish unity and particularly the Irish diaspora towards Irish reunification,” said Gerry Adams, the party’s former leader.Adams accused successive Irish governments of being “incredibly shortsighted” and failing to plan for unification. “There is no excuse for this.”Trump’s comments also proved awkward for Northern Ireland unionists who have supported the president on other topics.“Everyone is allowed a personal opinion even when it’s wrong,” said Ian Paisley Jr, a former Democratic Unionist party MP. “The political, cultural and economic reality is that Northern Ireland and its people are British and wish to remain so,” he said.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandIrelandDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Train carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near border
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Ukrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near border
Content: Firefighters spray water at a burning train carriage hit by a drone strike in Ukraine near the border with Poland.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters spray water at a burning train carriage hit by a drone strike in Ukraine near the border with Poland.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersUkraineTrain carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials sayUkrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near borderAmy HawkinsandCharlotte Higginsin KyivSun 13 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 10.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways.Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described the attack as “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”.Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.The strikes prompted air-raid warnings inPoland, which shares a border with western Ukraine.Ukrainian and Polish authorities said a lorry less than 1km from the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between the two countries was also hit.Katerina Sergatskova, the director of Daily Humanity, an organisation that provides training to people working in high-risk environments, was travelling on aWarsaw-bound train and witnessed the attack.She said passengers were told to evacuate at about 9am as the train approached the Polish border having already been told to disembark for two hours in the middle of the night. “At this point, the mood was different, we were asked to move very fast,” she said. “Then I heard the first drone.“Seeing and hearing Shahed [drones] just a few hundred metres from the border is a very unpleasant experience.”No casualties were reported on the train.View image in fullscreenThe wrecked passenger train hit by a Russian strike.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersA British economist who preferred not to be named, travelling on a night train from Kyiv towards Chelm in Poland, also witnessed the attack. “We spent 10 hours at the border and were evacuated three times. On the third evacuation a missile came over and totalled a locomotive in front of our train.”Railway officials instructed the “grimly focused” passengers to hide in bushes by a lake, said the economist, calling the Ukrainian response “timely and disciplined”. They “gave us good warning of the evacuation and had a plan, which everyone followed”.Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon TisdallRead more“The conductor said when we boarded that there was a high risk that we would be evacuated during the journey. The lady and her eight-year-old son who were in my compartment said they had been travelling back and forth every month to Kyiv from Warsaw since 2022 and they had never been evacuated, or the train attacked, while travelling the route. This is clearly an escalation by Putin and the Russians.”Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries, as well as Johnson, the former British prime minister, and the former CIA chief Petraeus, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” the rail company said.Johnson wrote on X: “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways.”Three people were killed in the eastern Donetsk region, and a 71-year-old woman was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region.Sybiha said the Russian strikes were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders”.“This is Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he wrote on X.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.View image in fullscreenDonald Tusk chairs a special meeting in Warsaw on Sunday after the drone strikes near the border with Ukraine.Photograph: Piotr Nowak/EPAPoland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who visited Kyiv this week, said on X after Sunday morning’s attack: “Putin is escalating.”The Polish interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said: “We treat these events with the utmost seriousness. The situation is being monitored continuously. Russia is the enemy of the free world.”Russia claimed it struck “railway infrastructure” in western Ukraine used to “transport military cargo” from Europe.“Strikes have continued on railway infrastructure in the western regions of Ukraine, which are used to transport military cargo from European countries,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement.Ukraine and Russia have increased attacks oncritical infrastructurein each other’s countries as long-range drones and missiles take the war away from the frontlines.The US president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday that Zelenskyy should “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing shortages.“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said, adding that shortages were caused by the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the US war in the Middle East.In Lithuania, authorities briefly closed the airport in Vilnius, the capital, after a perceived drone sighting. Nato scrambled at least one fighter jet in response to the alert, which turned out to be a flock of birds. The airport reopened within 40 minutes, according to Lithuanian authorities.Explore more on these topicsUkrainePolandRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donor | Spain | The Guardian
description: Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas
Author: Timothy Pratt
Headline: Key government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for Hamas
Content: Fergie Chambers at home in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFergie Chambers at home in Tunis, Tunisia, on 8 February 2024.Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesSpainPressure builds in Spain to deny US extradition request for leftwing donorKey government meeting this month will consider US bid to try James ‘Fergie’ Chambers over alleged support for HamasTimothy PrattSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttorneys for James “Fergie” Chambers, the US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects worldwide who is currently imprisoned in Madrid and sought in extradition, have submitted a brief ahead of a decisive government meeting on the case.Meanwhile, Chambers’ partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, met last week with multiple members of the Spanish parliament to assert his innocence.The legal team’s arguments include that the US government has failed to identify specific acts of violence or damages personally attributable to Chambers and instead is seeking to criminalize acts linked to political protest.They also assert that at least one figure of US law underpinning the request – “conspiracy to commit riot” – has no equivalent in Spanish law, which would also help render the extradition invalid.FBI raided Spanish vacation rental of wealthy leftwing funder James ‘Fergie’ Chambers after his arrestRead moreIt is the first known case of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas.Chambers’ defense has submitted its brief to the government ahead of a meeting by Spain’scouncil of ministersexpected to take place on 22 September. The council can decide whether or not to allow the US extradition request to proceed, based in part on an evaluation of supporting materials the Trump administration supplied to the government on 26 August.Under Spanish law, at this “administrative” stage, the 22-member council has the power to deny the request, before it reaches a “judicial” stage.The US government’s case centers on Chambers allegedly laundering $7.5m that he wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, and allegedly using the money to support the Palestinian group Hamas. The exact details of the indictment against Chambers remain sealed.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators gather at Puerta del Sol in Madrid during a rally demanding the release of the US activist Fergie Chambers and opposing his extradition to the US on 5 September 2026Photograph: Richard Zubelzu/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockChambers’ team say he has been supporting humanitarian aid and other projects. The 41–year-old self-described anti–imperialist’s defense is also asserting that the Trump administration’s additional charges of “international money laundering” don’t hold up because, as heir to one of the richest families in the US, he obtained his personal wealth through legal means. Chambers’ donations have gone to about 100 projects in 20 countries for several years – including theSameer Project,in Gaza.“It would set an alarming precedent in all of Europe if Spain allowed the Trump administration to criminalize offering vital humanitarian aid to the Palestinian people and defending their rights,” saidBaltasar Garzón, the acclaimed human rights lawyer and a member of Chambers’ legal team.“That’s what Fergie has financed: humanitarian aid and support for people in a situation of great need,” said Garzón. “That’s not terrorism, according to Spanish and European legal standards.”Meanwhile, Schnabel has met with members of Sumar and Podemos – progressive political movements vital to the coalition government of the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – and has written a one-page letter to Sánchez asking him to make “the only morally acceptable decision”, that of denying extradition. Sánchez forms part of the council of ministers.Schnabel has not escaped scrutiny since her partner was detained on 10 July in Ibiza. On a recent trip to New York, the FBI pulled her aside at JFK airport and confiscated her phone, she said.Support for Chambers in the lead-up to the 20 September meeting has come from Ione Bellara, leader of Podemos, who opened the party’s quarterly meeting lastSaturdaywith a statement opposing the extradition request, saying that Chambers was “on the right side of history” with his financial support of Palestinians in Gaza.Similarly, Sumar, the leftwing coalition that governs jointly with Sánchez’s Socialist party, filed a statement in Spain’s congress earlier this week urging the government to deny the petition, “given that the goal of the extradition request … is to criminalize, persecute or punish [Chambers] due to his political opinions, his public activity or his participation in political movements – in this case, in support of the Palestinian people”.Irene Montero, member of Podemos and Spanish representative to the European parliament, told the Guardian that “Our laws don’t contemplate the actions he is accused of … [and] we can’t become a subject of the United States.”Activists have held rallies in recent days in at least six cities across Spain in support of Chambers, with plans for more.Other shows of support from farther afield have included a petition delivered to the Spanish government signed by actors, academics, activists and others, including Richard Gere, Greta Thunberg and Angela Davis. In Tunisia, supporters of the Club Africain football team displayed banners and T-shirts at a recent match that read, “Free Fergie”. In Portugal, atFesta do Avante, one of that country’s largest cultural festivals, fans held up a banner saying: “Free Fergie – supporting Palestine isn’t a crime.”Schnabel told the Guardianlast monththat the $7.5m went to support Club Africain. Hamed Mbarek, one of the club’s supporters and an organizer of fans at last Saturday’s match, said Club Africain was “pro-Palestine” and that Chambers and the club had “synchronicity”.Chambers’ money comes from a mid-2023 settlement with his family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications, in which he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m. Members of his family severed contact with him at the time.His views and donations have been extensivelyprofiledin US media. He was interviewed on a TV news station in New Hampshire in late 2023 about a direct action against Elbit Systems, an Israeli defense contractor, staged by a group whose legal fees he paid, then called Palestine Action – a group now proscribed in the UK as a “terrorist organization”.Chambers’ public comments on Israel and Gaza have also brought controversy. A weekafter the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he postedon X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/ There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/ No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/ It’s simply genocide/ Like it has been.”He has also been a staunch critic of the US, tellinga reporterin 2024: “I think the most important thing for the prosperity of humanity is the destruction of the US.”Irene Zugasti helped organize rallies earlier this week and last weekend in support of Chambers in Madrid, Barcelona and several other Spanish cities. She sees the case as bigger than whether he is extradited or not. “If they go after Fergie, they’ll go after anyone … It’s a test – to see until what point European governments feel pressure from the United States.”Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Woman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan Younis
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Woman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan Younis
Content: A destroyed vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City.Photograph: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA destroyed vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of Gaza City.Photograph: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/ShutterstockGazaPregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on GazaWoman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan YounisLorenzo Tondoin Jerusalem andSeham Tanteshin GazaSun 13 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers, as strikes acrossGazakilled at least 10 people in 48 hours.The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the al-Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.‘‘We heard the sound of gunfire while I was praying,’’ Wathfa abu Mashi, Shalouf’s mother-in-law, saidin a video interview with Anadolu. “My daughter asked me, ‘Where is Iman?’ I told her she was in her tent. She went to check on her and found her covered in blood after she was hit by a bullet.”Shalouf’s husband, Ismail abu Mashi, said “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? There is no such thing. There is killing every day. People are dying here every day.”Shalouf was rushed to Nasser hospital, where doctors initially detected her unborn baby’s heartbeat, but she and her unborn baby died a few hours later.According to relatives, Shalouf had already chosen the name Ayoub for the baby, who was due in November.Relatives and community members gathered at the hospital to hold funeral prayers for Shalouf and her child before carrying their bodies for burial in Khan Younis. They were buried side by side.Contacted by the Guardian, the Israel Defense Forces said they were looking into the incident.Despite the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025, violence and the killing of Palestinians continue on a daily basis.The health ministry in Gaza said10 Palestinians had been killed and 56 wounded in Israeli attacks over the previous 48 hours, amid artillery shelling and gunfire in several areas of northern, central and southern Gaza.View image in fullscreenDisplaced Palestinians walk among the ruins of buildings in al-Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood east of Gaza City.Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPAFour members of the same family – Momen Ahmed, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, eight – were killed when their home in Beit Lahiya was struck on Thursday night, according to the ministry. Six other Palestinians were reported killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City on Friday, including a man who died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack.Several other Palestinians were injured in attacks across Gaza. On Friday, two people were reportedly seriously injured in an attack in Beit Lahiya, while three people including a woman six months pregnant and a child were wounded by gunfire in the same city.On Saturday, nine people were injured when a displaced people’s tent in al-Mawasi was shelled, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed and several others injured when a vehicle was struck in Tel al-Hawa in Gaza City, according to the health ministry. The attack also injured people on a passing bus carrying women and children.On 28 August,Unicef said at least four children had been reported killedin the preceding five days and many others wounded, including children who sustained life-changing injuries. On 2 September, it said three other children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours, bringing the number of children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September to seven.“Airstrikes by Israeli forces continue killing and wounding Palestinians,”Médecins Sans Frontières said. “Between September 6 and 9, Israeli forces issued 18 so-called evacuation orders and struck a building less than 250ft from an MSF clinic.”The humanitarian situation remains severe.According tothe UN’s humanitarian office, “most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions”.On 31 August,a temporary halt to desalination in Israelreduced the water available to about a million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid.Several electricity generators at hospitals across the Gaza Strip have stopped working because of shortages of spare parts and fuel, the territory’s health ministry has said.According to the ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the ministry.Explore more on these topicsGazaPalestineIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia
Content: Fighters gather near damaged vehicles in the after what a Houthi-owned TV network says were strikes on pro-government forces in Yemen.Photograph: Al-Masirah Tv/ReutersView image in fullscreenFighters gather near damaged vehicles in the after what a Houthi-owned TV network says were strikes on pro-government forces in Yemen.Photograph: Al-Masirah Tv/ReutersYemenHouthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forcesIran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi ArabiaJon Henleyand agenciesSun 13 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTFirst published on Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHouthi fighters have said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southernSaudi Arabia, as Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government described the rebels’ swift advance along the Red Sea coast as a “painful” development in a new front in the Iran war.The UN said on Sunday that nearly 86,000 people had fledYemen, most of them since early September when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels launched a large-scale offensive that last week resulted in the capture of a key port city and an island on the Bab al-Mandab strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the strait of Hormuz.The overnight attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, theHouthimilitary spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X. The date of the operation was not specified.The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stakeRead moreThe Saudi civil defence force said a projectile had fallen in al-Tawwal governorate near the border with Yemen along the Red Sea, injuring two people and damaging a mosque and several other buildings. The statement blamed theHouthis. It also said sirens had sounded in Sharurah governorate but no damage was reported.Yemeni government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-west of the country.“Air force of the armed forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said on Sunday.View image in fullscreenThe shuttered Saudi embassy in Yemen’s capital Sana’a, with a mural depicting a Houthi fighter stopping a ship.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAA senior government official in Yemen said its forces would return to the Red Sea coast and fight back, after people fleeing the Houthi advance told the Associated Press they had seen forces withdrawing and urging people to run.Sultan al-Arada, a member of the ruling presidential council, described the collapse of government forces in Mocha and elsewhere on Yemen’s west coast as “painful and regrettable”.Al-Arada, who is also the governor of Yemen’s central Marib province, said in a televised interview broadcast late on Saturday night that forces “are currently regrouping and will return to the battle in one form or another”. The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.The US news site Axios reported that the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, twice called Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected. Trump acknowledged the conversation on Saturday but did not say whether Washington would take any action. “Everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy,” he told reporters.The clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the groupcapturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Seacoast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait at the sea’s southern entrance.The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on thestrait of Hormuzin response to the US-Israeli assault on the country.Reuters reported last week that the Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast came with direct guidance from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction.Iranian ship struck near Hormuz, state media saysState-run Iranian media said on Sunday that an Iranian commercial vessel had been struck early in the morning off Qeshm Island, with one person killed and four injured.The state-run IRNA news agency quoted the Qeshm governor as blaming a “terrorist enemy”. There was no immediate comment from the US military, which has struck Iranian-flagged vessels during its blockade of Iranian ports.View image in fullscreenCommercial vessels in the strait of Hormuz off Iran earlier in September.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APSeveral explosions were reported overnight around Qeshm, the largest island in the Hormuz strait. The island, about 14 miles (22km) from the port city of Bandar Abbas, is key to Iran asserting control over the strait.Maritime trackers also received new reports of a separate attack on a ship in the strait on Sunday, adding to concerns about threats to energy supplies after Saudi Arabiashut down a vital oil pipeline.The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said it had ⁠a report of a projectile hitting a ⁠vessel as it moved through the strait, later adding that a fire had broken out and local authorities were evacuating those onboard.The Houthis, mountain fighters who seized the capital, Sana’a, 12 years ago and withstood years of deadly Saudi airstrikes during Yemen’s civil war, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control.View image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemenis rest at a temporary shelter in the Dar Saad district of Aden, Yemen, on Saturday.Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/APYemen’scivil war, which began in 2014, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but reignited in July. Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.The civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes, with the fall of Mocha on Thursday driving many residents to Aden.The UN’s migration agency said on Sunday that more than 2,000 people fleeing Yemen had landed in Djibouti last week.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricaStrait of HormuzInternally displaced peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restoration | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Whist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restoration
Content: Items dating back to the 1800s have been found under the floorboards and in the very fabric of Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenItems dating back to the 1800s have been found under the floorboards and in the very fabric of Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAMonarchyHidden history of royal staff uncovered in Buckingham Palace restorationWhist drive ticket embedded in rock and news article on Great Train Robbers among items discovered during 10-year restorationCaroline DaviesSun 13 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLost or long-discarded items revealing glimpses of the behind-the-scenes life of Buckingham Palace staff over decades have been uncovered during the restoration of the UK monarchy’s HQ.Misplaced belongings, found beneath the floorboards, in other areas of the royal residence and preserved within the fabric of the building, include a ticket to a whist drive run by the royal household’s social club from nearly 80 years ago.View image in fullscreenA packet of Silk Cut cigarettesPhotograph: Aaron Chown/PABlank Littlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957, a pair of battered black hobnail boots and an empty Silk Cut cigarette packet were among the everyday objects unearthed, as well as an almost 140-year-old fragment of the West End theatre listings from the Standard newspaper in 1889.View image in fullscreenLittlewoods football pools betting slips from 1957Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe discoveries were made during the decade-long £370m reservicing of the palace which has included rewiring electrics, upgrading plumbing and heating and overhauling its infrastructure to prevent long-term damage.View image in fullscreenAbout 1.2 miles of Vulcanised Indian Rubber cabling was discovered and removed as a priority.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAElectrical wire covered with Vulcanised Indian Rubber (VIR) cabling, which posed the risk of fire to the building, were also located. The cabling, which becomes brittle with age, was removed as a priority when the project, which is due to be completed next year, began in 2017. About 1.2 miles (2km) of the rubber cabling has been replaced so far.View image in fullscreenThe ticket to the whist drive organised by the staff social club, dated 14 April 1949, was embedded in a lump of rock.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe small whist drive ticket, priced at 6d, a sixpence, and dated 14 April 1949 – during the reign of the king’s grandfather, George VI – was found embedded in a lump of building rock.The pass to the staff social club gathering in the palace reads “Royal Household Social Club – Buckingham Palace: A Whist Drive to be held on” followed by the faded, stamped date “14 APR 1949”.At that time,Queen Elizabeth IIwas still Princess Elizabeth and had been married to Prince Philip for less than 18 months and their eldest son, Charles, was only five months old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPages from the Daily Express in 1966 detailing the prison housing the Great Train Robbers.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAPages from the Daily Express newspaper in 1966 detailed the maximum security prison housing the Great Train Robbers, picturing the inside of Durham prison and reporting that “the men who were found guilty of stealing a fortune in mailbags spend their week stitching them for nine shillings”.View image in fullscreenInstructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenA bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAInstructions for royal household staff for the 1977 Silver Jubilee Diplomatic Corps reception informed them that the queen and other members of the royal family would move round the ballroom in a “clockwise direction”.Aides were to encourage the 350 British guests to mingle with the diplomats at the glittering white tie and tiaras annual gathering, according to the manually typed sheet, which also said that smoking was banned in the certain state rooms and the reception kept to a strict timetable.Other findings included a section of Minton decorative ceramic tiles from a fireplace hearth, with the design dating from around the mid-1800s, an aged Pewter tankard, a bottle of Schweppes still Malvern English spring water, a wooden junction box and a faded box containing six Christmas cards.Explore more on these topicsMonarchyQueen Elizabeth IIKing Charles IIILondonHeritagenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count  | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns
Content: ‘I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact,’ said McNeill.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact,’ said McNeill.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianForeign policy‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid countKirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concernsSupported byAbout this contentHeather StewartEconomics editorSun 13 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending.McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”.But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges.“I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said.Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday.She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño.“It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UNhas warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding.The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending.Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK supportto some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts.At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development.View image in fullscreenMcNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, has served as the minister of state for international development since July.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian“As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said.“I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’”Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources.She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”.“The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added.“That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.”A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries.“Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?”McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party.Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board.“The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourAidManifestos 2024Humanitarian responseDebt reliefnewsShareReuse this
