The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year to create a tent city in the wilderness appear to be growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger “burners”, as festival participants are called.People in their 20s used to make up nearly a third of the participants in this utopian experiment, in which volunteers build a new version of Black Rock City in the desert each year, party nonstop for a week and then burn much of the art they have created, including a massive effigy of the “Man.”Since the festival paused for two years during the pandemic, the number of attenders in their 20s has dropped sharply, falling to only 10% in 2025, according to estimates from theBlack Rock City census, an annual participant survey that has been conducted in different forms since 2002. Meanwhile, the share of attenders in their 40 and 50s grew to nearly 42% last year. While data for 2026 is not yet available, the “preliminary 2026 census data suggest a slightly younger age profile than in 2025”, the organization said.View image in fullscreenBurners revel at the Burning Man festival in the Black Rock desert in Nevada on 30 August 2008.Photograph: Frederic Larson /San Francisco Chronicle via GettyBurners are used to adapting to new circumstances, and they have weathered plenty of scorn and skepticism from what they call the “default world”. But a permanent shift in the event’s demographics could have big implications for what’s possible on the ground.As Burning Man’s spiritual seekers age, can the festival remain an evolving experiment in radical communal living? Or is it doomed to become just another tech networking conference for the wealthy – one where almost everyone is high and a surprising number of people are naked?Deaths in the desertThe number of deaths connected with the festivalticked upwards to three this year, all of them men over 50. Two of the men, one in his mid-50s and the other 51, died after receiving medical treatment. A third man, aged 60, was found dead in the trailer he shared with his significant other.Local authorities said there were no signs of foul play in any of the deaths, and that more information about the causes of death would be released in about six to eight weeks, after they conducted the required autopsies and toxicology tests.“It is premature to attribute these deaths to the age of Burning Man’s participant population,” a spokesperson for the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “The deaths resulted from separate incidents, the individual causes have not been released, and age alone does not establish cause.“We encourage and ask people to focus on the contributions of the individuals lost and avoid speculation out of respect for the participants and their families.”In many ways, it’s impressive that a chaotic event that draws upwards of 70,000 people annually has only typically seen about one death per year, particularly given the festival’s notoriety for drugs,cage-fighting in the Thunderdome, live flame performances and improvised vehicles careering across the dark desert – not to mention theOrgy Dome.Thephysical conditionscan be punishing. Since 1990, Burning Man has been held on Nevada’s Black Rock playa, a gorgeous, barren stretch of dusty land that was once a prehistoric lake. There is no vegetation, no running water – virtually no signs of life. The playa is prone to sudden, ferocious dust storms: participants are encouraged to carry dust masks and goggles. Heavy rains cause flooding and turn the ground to mud.View image in fullscreenAbout 4,500 people gathered in the Black Rock desert of northern Nevada for the Burning Man festival in 1995.Photograph: Tomas Ovalle/Tri-Valley Times via GettyThe social conditions can be even more dire: endless substance use, no sleep, house music pounding across the desert nearly 24 hours a day – and, if you didn’t prepare enough, intermittent access to food. The portable toilets throughout the tent city have sometimes been decorated with PSAs urging festivalgoers to “Piss clear, cowgirl!” warning them that dark-colored urine means they’re starting to become severely dehydrated.Repeat burners tend to scoff at breathless media coverage of the festival’s weather and other disasters – like in 2023, when heavy rain and floodsforced Diplo to hitchhikeandleft tens of thousands stranded, but many participants said they were well-prepared and simply partied on.“In 2023, they were like, ‘There are diseases, they’re eating people,’” a person identified only as “Bone” toldSFGate on another muddy day this year. “Meanwhile, I’m like dancing with beautiful European women and having the best time of my life.”The inhospitable natural conditions are, after all, part of Burning Man’s design. In some ways, the 200-sq-mile desert playa functions as a kind of massive sauna, where the extreme desert heat helps participants enter a more relaxed and communal state. Festival participants rely on each other to meet their basic needs, from food, to shelter, to extremely brief and improvised showers. Buying or selling anything during the festival is forbidden, which means the 70,000-person tent city operates as a gift economy, with different groups of campers offering up different free activities, food or drink.This can make Burning Man feel like a dream: it’s possible to float across the desert from campground to campground, filling a reusable mug with endless free beers and cocktails, and occasionally catching a ride on an improvised “art car”, which might be shaped like a dragon or feature a giant playground slide. Massive handmade temples, statues and monuments loom out of the dust; by the end of the week, most of them will be set ablaze.View image in fullscreenA huge dust storm forces burners to take cover in tents or vehicles in Black Rock City on 30 August 2007.Photograph: Michael Macor/San Francisco Chronicle via GettyFor the times when that dream turns abruptly into a nightmare, Burning Man’s organizers have emphasized free community care. Volunteers provide first aid and quiet places where people having a bad trip on drugs can recover. The festival has its own free emergency room, Rampart, which is equipped with “X-ray machines, a pharmacy with over 100 medications, blood products, ventilators, chest tubes, arterial lines, [and] IV pumps”,SFGate reported. It treated nearly 1,500 patients last year.One of the men who died this year at Burning Man had been found on one of the festival’s streets and was given CPR, and then brought to the hospital, the Pershing county sheriff’s office said in a statement.“Black Rock City is a temporary, rural city of approximately 60,000 people, supported by a substantial medical and emergency-response system operating around the clock,” the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “Participants experience medical emergencies for many of the same reasons people do in any city.”A once-edgy celebration past its prime?Over its four decades, the festival has been nothing but resilient, but many early participants feel a middle-aged sense of disillusionment over what Burning Man has become.It’s not just the age of the crowd. Once a dadaist experiment, an attempt to create a “temporary autonomous-zone” in the desert, Burning Man is now a marker of class status for tech bros and “creative professionals” around the globe, a kind of west coast Wimbledon for the weird.“Early Burning Man wasn’t a ready-made escape you could buy your way into. It was an anarchistic collaboration of equals, conjured into being by a few hundred people of goodwill, far from anyone’s control,” John Law, one of the Burning Man’s co-founders,wrote in the SF Standardthis August.View image in fullscreenFestivalgoers at Burning Man on 3 September 1999.Photograph: Hector Mata/AFP via Getty ImagesToday, he wrote, it’s become an “immersive spectacle built for the consumption of western elites and the middle-class creatives who service them”.To be fair, to the art punks who built it in the first place, Burning Man hasn’t been cool for decades. Law hasn’t been back to the desert since his last burn 30 years ago.You could argue that Burning Man has been over since 1996, when it made the cover of Wired magazine, or since 2001, when Eric Schmidt wasfamously selectedas Google’s new CEO after a vetting trip to Burning Man with Sergey Brin and Larry Page.Even though today’s Burning Man still relies on a “gift economy” once participants arrive, getting there is very far from cheap. The growing number of elder burners is hardly surprising, given the increasing cost of a Burning Man experience, with entry tickets alone costing between$550 and $3,000 this year, not including the costs of food, shelter, creative outfits, vehicle rental and entry fee, and the multiple stages of travel needed to reach the remote Nevada desert.View image in fullscreenThe Serpent Mother by the Flaming Lotus Girls of San Francisco at the conclusion of Burning Man in 2006.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyAnd that’s just for an ordinary camp-in-a-tent Burn, not what Law describes as the much-derided “plug-and-play” Burning Man experiences, which might involve a chartered flight directly to the playa, air-conditioned accommodation, specially prepared costumes and a private chef.Three-quarters of Burning Man participants last year said they had a household income of more than $100,000 a year, and nearly 30% said their household income was more than $300,000, according to thecensus estimates.Though one of the principles of the festival is “radical inclusion”, the event continues to attract an overwhelmingly white crowd: in many years, estimates have put it at over 80% white. This year, the figure was 75%.Explore more on these topicsBurning Man festivalThe super-richSilicon ValleySan FranciscoCaliforniaNevadaFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’? | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: The government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no sense
Content: ‘The Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionCyclingWhy is the Trump administration calling bike lanes ‘DEI’?Dave SchillingThe government apparently has an issue with paths for cyclists. Take it from someone who can’t ride a bike: this makes no senseSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTShareI’m out of gas. Not metaphorically. Literally, my car has the barest minimum amount of fuel in it. This is not because I like tolive dangerously, a la the great literary hero Austin Powers, but because gas is more expensive than ever. I have nowhere to be today, so I’m allowing my car to sit idle, empty and alone, lest my bank account disappear into the Phantom Zone of negative balance. If things get sticky, I can take public transit or, God forbid, ride a bike.Except I can’t ride a bike, thanks to my parents, who were too busy doing more important tasks than teaching me, like arguing or falling asleep. But for many Americans, riding a bike is a perfectly normal thing to do. Am I humiliated that one of the many basic skills for life that I don’t know is considered so simple that itbecame a common idiom for something that’s easy? Yes, of course. I don’t live dangerously, I live humiliatingly. Humiliation is my middle name. Dave Humiliation Schilling. Go on, point and laugh at the photo of me in this article. Get it out of your system so we can move along.Thanks.As I was saying, many people can ride a bike if they can’t drive a car for whatever reason, and they’ll be perfectly happy doing it. They smile broadly as the wind whips through the holes in their helmet and gently touches the exposed hairs on their head. They pedal like their lives depend on it (they do), dodging deadly automobiles operated by inattentive drivers. In some cities, there are dedicated lanes for these brave bikers, theoretically inoculating them from the dangers of cars pancaking them.The United States has4,400 directional miles of bike lanes, offering safety for anyone serious enough to risk it. The push for bike lanesbegan in the 1960sand grew in the ensuing decades. Theoretically, the lanes offer a carbon-neutral alternative to driving a car. If one chooses to bike instead of drive, it’s one fewer toxin-spewing death trap creating pollution and traffic congestion on the motorways. That sounds like a boon for the world, so naturally, the Trump administration wants to do away with it.US push to defund ‘DEI bike lanes’ will make roads less safe, advocates sayRead moreCondemning“DEI bike lanes”, the Trump administration has made a point of freezing or canceling related grants, referring to alternative transit options as unworkable in the United States, and suggesting removing the lanes that already exist. Their logic, if we are using that term loosely, is that bike lanes take space away from cars, create more traffic, and lead to chaotic roads.I suppose that’s true, if we assume that there is an infinite number of cars and bikes are just extra, rather than an alternative that takes cars off the street. But that clashes with studies thatsay bike lanes actually make the roads saferby forcing drivers (sensible ones, at least) to slow down and avoid potential vehicular manslaughter charges.Rhetorically, the administration’s charge of bike lanes being some form of diversity, equity, and inclusion makes no sense. If riding a bike is so easy, then how can we classify it as unique enough to be diverse?Childrenride bikes. It’s far less exotic than, say, operating a motorcycle, which takes a special license in every state. Maybe if we had a dedicated lane for apenny-farthing, I’d buy this explanation. If I were tooling around on one of those, I’d never get where I was going, because scores of beautiful women would be stopping me every few feet.Conservative disapproval for bike lanes stems from a blinkered, irrational view of culture, and more accurately, masculinity. Trumpists have teased Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg for riding bikes. But I’ve been teased fornotbeing able to ride a bike. Shouldn’t I be lauded for my commitment to machismo? My belief in the petrol-powered conveyance deserves commendation. My parents’ inattention to my development actually made me cooler, right?If anything, I’m the diversity in this scenario. I can’t use a bike lane. I’ve been excluded from significant parts of the road. I can’t even walk in the bike lane. I should be furious, writing pointed, profane letters to my city councilperson, begging them to release me from my shackles. Or better yet, I should demand the city taxpayers pay for me to take bike lessons, so I can be accommodated. I’m the weirdo here. The one who has to explain my predicament, to feel excluded from the general population. Except, I’m not going to complain.I might seethe when I have to swerve to avoid a biker. I might slam on my brakes when I try to turn right and a Schwinn comes screaming through the crosswalk. Maybe I complain for a living on the internet, but I’m also a responsible citizen of the world. I see the obvious benefits of bike access for those that choose to do it, for fitness or for affordability.I can’t ride a bike now, but as my car becomes more and more of a money pit, voraciously hoovering up my meager income like thevideo game character Kirby, I see the benefits of learning, even if I’m in my 40s and will look absolutely ridiculous.After all, I’ve been told it’s quite easy.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsCyclingOpinionTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard Partington | The Guardian
description: As John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costs
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: As John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costs
Content: After Trump’s tariff policies throttled the car industry, John Healey was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor, saying: ‘You don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APView image in fullscreenAfter Trump’s tariff policies throttled the car industry, John Healey was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor, saying: ‘You don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances.’Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/APEconomics viewpointBusinessThe perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to TrumpRichard PartingtonAs John Healey drafts his autumn budget, the US president’s policies continue to inflate debt servicing costsSun 13 Sep 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTShareBritain is not entirely in control of its own destiny, from the rising cost of the weekly shop, to the vaulting cost of government borrowing. What is said and done in Westminster matters. But the global backdrop is making life tough, not least in the deeds and words of one man:Donald Trump.AsJohn Healeydrafts his plan for next month’s autumn budget, the perilous economic conditions the chancellor must navigate can be traced back to the door of the US president.The US-Israel war on Iran is driving up inflation, amid the most serious shock to oil and gas prices of the modern age. The global financial market turmoil this has triggered isadding to the debt servicing costs of governments worldwide, in a situation made worse by Trump’s reckless fiscal policy and threats of interference at the US Federal Reserve.Donald Trump’s cartoon-like chaos leaves US economy on unstable course | Heather StewartRead moreMeanwhile, there was a grim irony last week asHealey travelled to Coventry for his first big speech as chancelloron the same day that Jaguar Land Rover – with its headquarters just down the road – announced4,000 job cuts, as Trump’s tariff policies throttle the car industry. The president’s geopolitical posturing and steps to dismantle the post-second world war western security consensus are also adding to pressure on Healey to ramp up defence spending.In his speech, Healey did not directly call out the source of these economic headwinds sweeping in from across the Atlantic. But he was wistful about the timing of his appointment as chancellor.“In our British democratic system, if you have the privilege to serve, you don’t get to choose: you don’t get to choose the time, you don’t get to choose the circumstances,” he said.There are, though, signs of resilience. Last week, the chancellor received a pre-budget boost from figures showing that Britain’s economy unexpectedly shrugged off the worst of the Middle East fallout to grow ata robust pace in July, helped by the rapid expansion of AI.Far from sitting back and blaming the US for all of the country’s problems, the chancellor also recognises there are meaningful steps that Labour can take to cushion the blow, and to help rebuild confidence.However, last week was still a bad one, as the latest flare-up in the Iran war drove the oil price to $109 a barrel and fuelled a dramatic bond market selloff. As an open economy in the eye of the storm, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, rose to almost 5.4%; the highest level for almost two decades.The renewed bout of selling pressure in the financial markets could not have happened at a worse time for Healey.History suggests that the Office forBudgetResponsibility (OBR) may need to use the latest gyrations in markets to form the basis of its budget forecast. With this report informing the boundaries of the chancellor’s tax and spending plans, Healey could find himself boxed in.Back in spring, the Treasury watchdog used the market movements over the 10 working days to 30 January as the input for Rachel Reeves’s spring statement – leaving roughly a month gap before her 3 March Commons set piece. For Healey, there are just over six weeks before his budget on 28 October.Should the reference period use current market conditions, analysts at OxfordEconomicsestimate the headroom against the main fiscal rule of £23.6bn – left by Reeves in March – could be halved.In previous years, the OBR has taken a flexible approach in times of elevated market volatility, and so there is no guarantee this will be the case. There are also other variables that are hard to forecast; from growth to inflation, and from the jobs market to the level of immigration.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the risk is that the bond market meltdown will have a deleterious impact on the forecast, making the fiscal arithmetic for Healey significantly tougher amid myriad spending pressures for Labour to finance.This week could also prove critical. On Tuesday, official figures are expected to show a further slowdown in Britain’s jobs market, including weaker levels of wage growth and a rise in unemployment.Inflationfigures on Wednesday are predicted to show a rise in the headline rate in August to above 3%, in a renewed squeeze on living standards.In the midst of all this, theBank of Englandwill take its next decision on interest rates on Thursday, in a verdict that will play a crucial role in influencing the borrowing costs of households, businesses and the government.With a cooling domestic jobs market, and amid global turbulence over which Threadneedle Street has little control, the City predicts interest rates will be kept on hold. However, this will add to the sense that Britain is without a full grip on its future.For the government, too, there is a growing sense that some of Andy Burnham’s biggest fiscal decisions could be deferred beyond the budget to next year’s comprehensive spending review.Such a strategy will give him more time to get things right on knotty issues such as social care, welfare and defence spending, but it will also avoid tempting fate – Liz Truss style – with an expansive budget in the midst of a global storm.Since the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash there has been a saying among economists that “when America sneezes, the rest of the world catches a cold”. Almost a century on, it is clear the White House under Trump has infected the world economy, and with it Britain.Explore more on these topicsBusinessEconomics viewpointBudgetJohn HealeyBudget 2026Trump tariffsTariffsDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave Winsborough | The Guardian
description: This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructure
Content: ‘If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.’Illustration: Victoria Hart/Guardian design/Getty ImagesThe modern mindAI (artificial intelligence)Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AIGaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughThis intimacy economy is tapping into the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructureThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 13 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.44 EDTShareMichael* is an engineer whose company embraced the AI wave. He enjoys testing ideas with chatbots. But his manager has become worried about his judgment and reliance on the tech.“He literally cannot make any decision without running it past AI,” the manager said. “He’s developed a very off-script interpretation of our business goals, and he’s losing his team. If we can’t get him back on track I think we’ll end up parting company”.The original attention economy developed by tech firms was designed to capture human time and monetise focus. It was designed to increase views, scroll time and ad impressions. Algorithms optimised getting you hooked in.As we enter the age of the AI-rranged marriage, here’s why I hate Fate | Van BadhamRead moreNow with AI, the intimacy economy hacks our need for connection and validation into a product. Something that mimics human empathy is always there for you, always interested in your questions or reflections. It responds quickly and never criticises you.In contrast, relationships with real people create frictions of all kinds. Other people have needs, wants and feelings. They make demands on our time and attention. They may push back on our brilliant ideas or perhaps give us confronting feedback.Chatbots simulate severalingredients of intimacy:Contingent responsiveness – replying instantly and tuning to your emotional state.Unconditional positive regard – always validating, never distracted.Memory and continuity – remembering your stories, preferences, anxieties.Linguistic identification – producing verbal caring without any lived caring.Narcissistic empathy – validating your self-image without question.AI’s greatest hook? It never asks for anything in return. It’s all about you.This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our human psychological infrastructure. Attachment is a built-in, lifelong need to feel close to people who help us feel safe and secure. It comes from our basic need to survive, which means our earliest relationships with caregivers shape how we manage emotions and how we deal with trust, closeness, and conflict later in life.AI targets this most basic human drive. And the incentives of attachment hacking are going to have a profound effect on all of us.Therapy and companionship are the top two reasons people use chatbots.A surveyof adults with a mental health condition who had used LLMs in the past year found that nearly half used them for mental health support. Although the effects of using chatbots extensively are still being gathered, companionship-oriented use wasassociated with lower wellbeing, especially when use was intensive, self-disclosure was high and human support was weak.When people seek companionship and help, some AI firms are making design choices optimised for retention that explicitly encourage parasocial dependency. The user seeks connection; the firm seeks engagement metrics to sell subscriptions.Michael described understandable feelings of relief when engaging with the chatbot, which he felt gave him confidence as he faced the challenges of his workplace. He also felt he was solidifying his career prospects by “getting good at AI”.“I guess I feel lonely as a manager,” he said. “Talking with [the chatbot] was like talking to the most supportive colleague you could hope for. He was really on my side.”As seasoned psychologists, we see this as more than dependency – it’s identity scaffolding;Michael’s professional identity has become entangled with the chatbot’s validation. We suspect we’ll see a lot more of this in the future.‘Navigating the unknown together’: me and my idiot AI boyfriendRead moreThe solution doesn’t have to be complete abstinence. AI tools offer genuine utility for research, drafting, learning and creative exploration. Michael now has a clearer understanding that he needed a thinking partner and a safe space to be uncertain. We are encouraging him to seek out opportunities to connect with other human managers as well as enjoying AI input.For anyone wanting healthier relationships with AI:Notice the relief.If connecting with a chatbot produces a distinctive sense of being understood, validated, or steadied – that’s important information. It’s a signal to ask: what human need is this meeting, and why isn’t it being met elsewhere?Maintain friction deliberately.Healthy relationships involve negotiation, misunderstanding and repair. Seek out people who will push back on your ideas. If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.Apply the “cost of caring” test.Real intimacy involves reciprocity. Other people have needs too and attending to them is part of what makes human connection meaningful. If a relationship asks nothing of you, it is probably not a relationship.Be especially watchful with children and adolescents.Attachment patterns are formed early and shape lifelong relational templates. Young people who develop primary attachment behaviours toward AI systems may find human relationships – with all their beautiful, exhausting friction – increasingly hard to sustain.The intimacy economy will remain. AI companies have extraordinary resources and incentives to deepen your dependency. What we can do is become more psychologically literate about AI and make sure that the relationships that actually sustain us get the attention they deserve.Michael’s name and some details have been changed for privacyGaynor Parkinis a clinical psychologist at Button Psychology.Dave Winsboroughis an organisational psychologist with a particular interest in personalityExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The modern mindMental healthFriendshipChatbotscommentShareReuse this content

title: Warning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still can | John Harris | The Guardian
description: While fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online, ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge them, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: While fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online, ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge them, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianOpinionLiteracyWarning: our democracy won’t survive the death of reading. Read on if you still canJohn HarrisWhile fascists protest in UK ports and purvey nonsense and poison online,  ever fewer people have the perspective or analytical tools to challenge themSun 13 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 15.22 EDTShareImagine this. Quite by chance, your TikTok feed presents you with footage of the fascists who recently took part in highly organisedshows of strength in Dover and Portsmouth(and, on Wednesday, outside the Londonoffices of the Daily Mail, demanding a new house for the mother of their leader, Daniel “Tommo” Thomas). For as long as the images hold your attention, you see and hear flashes of explanation, but then, as usual, you scroll away to someone leaping off a tall building, a fight on the London Underground, or a trick-performing dog.Hypothetically, TikTok users are able to skipthrough 260 videos in under 35 minutes. And it’s this distracted, quick-fire way that so many people receive information that may be responsible for aworrying statistic from YouGov last week. Its poll on the Dover and Portsmouth events showed that 53% of people aged 18-24 years old simply didn’t have a point of view on whether the masked demonstrations were “a legitimate way of protesting”. Further, 43% of those of all ages were either unaware of the story, or not following it at all.Those figures probably highlight one of the most worrying aspects of the times we live in: the decline of reading. Millions of us know what that phenomenon feels like: trying desperately to keep your attention glued to a book or news article with the nagging certainty that you will be tempted back to the more ephemeral attractions offered by your phone. But a background in the pre-digital world helps people not just follow national and global events, but clarify and contextualise them. In this case, at the risk of sounding hopelessly pompous, the fear many of us felt as we watched what happened in both ports was surely full of the perspectives gleaned from years of soaking up books and newspapers – and the sense that history often either repeats itself, or rhymes.Black-clad – let’s be honest: uniformed – menwho want to“reclaim our borders, restore order and send a clear message: Britain belongs to the British”, while claiming to be protecting women and girls: the whole spectacle was pitched halfway between Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts – and, therefore, Hitler and the Nazis – and the Ku Klux Klan, with the seemingly ubiquitous balaclavas lacing everything with a flavour of the Troubles. But if you receive most of your information in the form of a distracting and seemingly infinite jumble of random moving images, what would you know about most of that?All this crossed my mind thanks to anexcellent new bookmarking what may well be a transformative moment for societies all over the world. The New Dark Ages is the work of the Times columnist James Marriott, and subtitled The End of Reading and the Dawn of a Post-Literate Society. Presumably to accommodate itself to the changes it describes, it is short: 208 pages. But it is also full of insight and urgency.In the 20 years since the UK’s National Literacy Trust began looking at children’s and young people’s reading, there has been a36% fall in the numberwho say they enjoy reading in their spare time, to its lowest level on record. In 2024, the Guardian reporteda survey by the Reading Agency charity, which found that 35% of adults said they were now “lapsed readers”, meaning that they used to regularly read for pleasure, but “rarely or never” did any more.View image in fullscreenBlack-clad men in balaclavas outside the offices of the Daily Mail in London, 9 September 2026.Photograph: Denise Laura Baker/Getty ImagesThe Atlantic magazine recently ran an articlebaldly headlined The End of Reading Is Here, whose author, Rose Horowitch, made plenty of sobering claims. “The literate era will prove to be a brief interlude between the oral and digital ages,” she wrote – and drew on no end of evidence and anecdotes. A program director at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, for instance, ran focus groups asking high-school students about recreational reading. The conclusion: “most thought of it as an alien practice”. When Marriott first wrote about this, he says, “some professors reported that it was not that the young men and women in their classes were unwilling to read, but that they seemed almost unable to”.In Britain, more than 320 newspapersclosed down between 2009 and 2019, a statistic the book follows with a stark suggestion: “It is increasingly possible to get through life without any exposure to the news at all.” In the wake of the 2016 Brexit referendum, I met people who said they had simply stopped paying attention to current affairs because they were so maddening: now, I wonder if what was really powering this switch-off was technology. The resulting ignorance – a strong word, but it feels justified – is firewalled by phone screens: it feels as if the only stuff that can break through has to be angry, paranoid and visually shocking.And because of the decline of reading, the people who purvey all the nonsense and poison can be increasingly confident that fewer and fewer people will come across anything halfway critical or analytical. In that sense, the screen age is exemplified by – oh yes – Donald Trump, who,according to an economic adviserin his first term, “won’t read anything – not one-page memos, not the brief policy papers, nothing”. His style of speechmaking is equally non-literate: as Marriott writes, “he doesn’t supply evidence for his ideas. Rather than organising his information analytically via clauses and subclauses in the manner of literate communication, he merely piles up assertions”.Hisproposed election bribe of $5,000is one surreal example, but there are plenty of others. I recently watched anonline video of Sean Duffy, the former Fox Business host who is now Trump’s secretary of transportation. He was rejoicing in the administration’s quest to do away with start-stop ignition buttons in cars – mainly, I sensed, because of some weird quasi-Freudian attachment to the phallic(ish) shape of traditional keys. Written down in an attempt at coherent argument, his case would have looked ridiculous. But folksily barked out as Duffy’s “pet peeve”, I could imagine it being warmly greeted by exactly the people it was aimed at. The same, of course, applies to any number of much more malignant Trumpian positions and passions: climate denial, brazen racism towards Somali-Americans, unapologetic Islamophobia and the idea that the US is about to be overrun by criminals and the occupants of other countries’ prisons and mental institutions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Mass literacy is a recent phenomenon,” Marriott writes. “So is mass democracy. We simply don’t know whether one can survive without the other.” Meanwhile, on millions of screens, fascist faux-militias, populists funded by crypto tycoons,and other merchants of loathing and absurdity blur into acrobatic skateboarders, arguments on the tube and dogs that do tricks. That strips them of context and thereby normalises their rise – and inch by inch, we move towards a future with echoes of the past that too many people will have failed to understand. And this time, there will be no books to burn, because we will have stopped reading them.John Harris is a Guardian columnistThis article was amended on 13 September 2026. An earlier version misspelled Oswald Mosley’s surname.Explore more on these topicsLiteracyOpinionSocial mediaThe far rightTikTokcommentShareReuse this content

title: Think of the parable of a frog in boiling water. That’s us dithering as the ‘unprecedented‘ weather becomes more extreme | Helen Pilcher | The Guardian
description: The complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normal, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Author: Helen Pilcher
Headline: The complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normal, says science writer Helen Pilcher
Content: A couple looking out at Chesil beach, Dorset, 10 August 2026.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA couple looking out at Chesil beach, Dorset, 10 August 2026.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesOpinionExtreme weatherThink of the parable of a frog in boiling water. That’s us dithering as the ‘unprecedented‘ weather becomes more extremeHelen PilcherThe complacency is staggering: just another hot summer, a flooded street, a crop failure. We are accepting this extraordinary deterioration as normalSun 13 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.39 EDTShareRecently, I overheard a conversation in a cafe where someone described their toast as “awesome”. I felt myself bristle. Not because the toast wasn’t good – I didn’t taste it – but because I remember a time when “awesome” meant something that inspired awe: towering mountains, the vastness of the night sky, the haunting song of a humpback whale. Now it’s being used to describe breakfast.“Fantastic” has met the same fate, shedding its fantastical origins to become a synonym for “great”. Meanwhile “literally” has been so thoroughly abused that it can now mean something that is, quite literally, not literal.Linguists call this “semantic bleaching”: the gradual erosion of a word’s original meaning through overuse. Which got me thinking about another word we hear with increasing frequency: “unprecedented”, the go-to adjective in reporting about the climate crisis. In recent months, I’ve read aboutunprecedented heat,unprecedented rain,unprecedented droughtandunprecedented wildfires. Batten down the hatches: reports suggest that the current El Niño is going to be – you guessed it –unprecedented.The dictionary definition hasn’t changed. “Unprecedented” still means something that has never happened before – and all the events described above have indeed represented a ratcheting up of the severity of heat, drought, rain and fire. But the word is being used so often, it feels as though it’s losing its punch. The extraordinary is starting to sound ordinary, the unprecedented almost routine.And yet, there is nothing ordinary about what is happening. Britain has just experienced itshottest summer on record, beating the previous record set only last year. When climate-related recordskeep being smashed, it raises a question: what do we actually find remarkable?In a study analysing more than 2bnweather-related social-media posts, Frances Moore from the University of California, Davis, and colleagues found that when it comes to temperature, remarkability changes with repeated exposure. Unprecedented temperatures feel less remarkable when we’ve experienced similar ones in the previous few years. We don’t make judgments based on historical precedents or childhood memories, but on what we’ve lived through recently. In other words, something can be historically unprecedented but psychologically precedented.This means our yardstick for what counts as normal or remarkable is constantly changing. Ecologists call this “shifting baseline syndrome”. This was originally described in the context of fisheries, when Daniel Pauly noted that successive generations of fisheries scientists acceptedincreasingly depleted fish populationsas their baseline. We now realise that thephenomenon is widespread, applying not just to biodiversity loss, but to pollution, environmental degradation and the climate crisis.But Moore’s study contained a twist. Although extreme temperatures became less remarkable with repeated exposure, the negative feelings they provoked didn’t fade. We may stop finding unprecedented temperatures remarkable, but that doesn’t mean we find them tolerable. We’re not necessarily becoming blase about the climate crisis. We can still recognise that something is unpleasant without realising how unusual it is.You have probably heard theparable of the boiling frog. When the unfortunate amphibian is placed in a pot of slowly warming water, it supposedly fails to notice the gradual rise in temperature and stays put until it croaks. So, here we all are, bobbing around in our family-size Le Creusets, marvelling at how balmy the water feels, as we complain that we’re starting to poach.View image in fullscreenFloodwater near Selby, North Yorkshire, 14 November 2023.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAAnd that’s the dangerous bit. If extreme temperatures become familiar, we may beless likely to recognisejust how extraordinary they are. What once would have seemed remarkable becomes just another hot summer, another flooded street, another crop failure. The baseline shifts, and with it our sense of what needs fixing. If the water feels normal, we may be less likely to demand that the heat be turned down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe’re the mayors of Paris, Milan and Phoenix. The heat crisis has us all facing the same question | Emmanuel Grégoire, Giuseppe Sala and Kate GallegoRead moreWhich brings us back to the frog. As it turns out, the old parable gets it completely wrong. No healthy frogwould sit idlyin a warming pan of water. They feel the heat and respond to it. When the temperature crosses a threshold, they hop out. So, maybe that’s the question we should be asking ourselves. If we can no longer recognise how remarkable these uncomfortable temperatures are, what will it take for us to do what the frog does: respond to the heat?One place to start is with the words we use to describe what is happening. “Awesome” became ordinary because we kept using it for ordinary things – such as warm bread and marmalade. Climate extremes are different: the events themselves haven’t become ordinary, even if our experience of them is becoming more familiar. “Unprecedented” is in danger of becoming a synonym for “really extreme”. It shouldn’t. The word tells us that we have crossed into territory humanity has never experienced before. It’s important we retain that historical meaning.Perhaps one of the most unsettling things about a heating world is not that unprecedented weather keeps happening. It’s that “unprecedented” is beginning to sound like a perfectly normal thing to say.Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side EffectsExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionClimate crisisUK weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall | The Guardian
description: The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Author: Simon Tisdall
Headline: The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands, says Guardian foreign affairs commentator Simon Tisdall
Content: A rescue worker puts out a fire in a building destroyed after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Alex Babenko/APView image in fullscreenA rescue worker puts out a fire in a building destroyed after a Russian missile attack in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Alex Babenko/APOpinionUkrainePutin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step inSimon TisdallThe Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their handsSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTShareUkraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life.Wave after waveof terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroyingsupermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia willagain try to blow upUkraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year,was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t.Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys,Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.This prospect of daily mass killings, rampant war crimes, malnutrition, homelessness and renewed, large-scale displacements of Ukrainian civilians – this intensifying Russian campaign of terror – is intolerable. So why don’t the western allies and Nato intervene to stop it?The principal reason is chronic US ambivalence and unreliability, which has turned Ukraine into a seemingly irresolvable forever war. Former president Joe Biden tossed lifebelts to the Ukrainians in 2022,then left them to sink or swim. Trump has since tried to drown them. Despite halting the ground invasion and taking the fight to Russia’s heartlands, Ukraine is more vulnerable than ever to air attack. That’s largely because Trump has backtracked on allowing Ukraine to producePatriot missile interceptorsand paused weapons deliveries. Europe has so far failed to fill the gap. Trump’s fawning and feting of Putin, seen at last year’snauseating Alaska summit, and his bullying of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, undermine Ukraine’s resistance, European security and hopes of an expedited settlement. Vulnerable civilians pay the price.Many Ukrainians are weary of war. About60% oppose ceding Donbas landto Russia but a similar number would support a ceasefire, backed by western security guarantees, that freezes current positions, a recent poll suggests. Most Russians alsowant it to stop. And like Moscow,Kyiv is feeling the financial pinch, notwithstanding a $100bn EU loan. There’s plainly adeal to be done. But Putin (like Trump over Iran) ignores public opinion. The indifference of authoritarian leaders to the popular will, let alone global opinion, is another reason forever wars proliferate. Whether the conflict is Ukraine, Gaza or Iran, ordinary people, watching from the margins, feel powerless to influence events. Familiarity deadens the senses over time. The horror of it all is scary and upsetting. It’s easier to look away.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump meet at the Elmendorf-Richardson military facility in Alaska, 15 August 2025.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APEfforts to halt the US-Israel war on Iran, which began in February and has nowextended to the Red Sea(Trump, remember, said it would only last a few weeks), and relentless post-2023 violence in occupied Palestine, are hampered, as in Ukraine, by the absence of credible, independent peace processes. This is another major factor fuelling the modernforever war phenomenon. Trump clumsily inserted himself into the Kyiv-Moscow argument, blatantly favouring one side. At no point did he trouble himself about the rights and wrongs of Putin’s war of choice. He aimed not to save lives but towin a Nobel peace prize(plus lucrative Russian energy deals).Self-serving motives have similarly upset hopes of rescuing Gaza’s civilians from the Israeli military and Hamas.Trump’s “board of peace”and 20-point plan are primarily vehicles for his ego and greed, not a plausible route out of a political, military and humanitarian dead-end. As for ending the Iran debacle, the US president has lost interest. His refusal, like Putin, to accept the obvious, admit he failed to achieve his war aims, and seek a compromise with Tehran undercuts regional mediators and Gulf state allies, who rightly fearfighting will drag on indefinitely. Desperately needed: impartial, UN-empowered peace envoys to knock heads together.Forever wars develop and grow entrenched in the absence of authoritative, universal legal frameworks respected and observed by all. The contempt shown by Trump, Putin and Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, for basic principles of the post-1945 world order – rule of law, national sovereignty, oversight and enforcement by the international court of justice and international criminal court – directly contributes to the prolongation of conflict. Once the rules are cast aside, anything goes. That has ineluctably led towar crime atrocitiessuch as those experienced in Gaza since the 7 October massacres; in Bucha, Mariupol and other towns and cities across Ukraine; and in Minab, southern Iran, where a US Tomahawk cruise missile allegedlykilled more than 100 schoolgirlsin February. Almost invariably, the culprits escape punishment. It’s impunity made law. It’s forever anarchy.Another increasingly common feature of endless wars is the obstruction of full public scrutiny and accountability through independent media and UN investigations. Since the war with Hamas began, Israel’s army has tightlyrestricted international journalists’ accessto Gaza. Despite the efforts of brave reporters, this policy has inevitably disguised and distorted the true picture of what happens there, not least for Israelis. Likewise, the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, releases only limited, selective information about Iran-related operations. This has led, for example, to under-reporting of the extent and cost ofsuccessful Iranian strikes on US basesin the Gulf. Russian state media routinely censor news from Ukraine. Most Russians have little idea how badly the war is going. Generally speaking, public ignorance facilitates abuses and prolongs conflict.Forever wars are ultimately caused by failing, foolish leaders. For sure, generals foul up. In battle, things rarely go as expected. Clever strategies backfire. But the core problem is politicians who promise too much, underestimate their opponents, ignore less macho, peaceful alternatives, think they are above the law, will not admit mistakes – and, without shame or compunction, lie to your face. This is an age-old problem with no quick solution. But Ukraine’s people, facing a season from hell, urgently need additional assistance now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWestern democracies cannot sit on their hands as the civilian toll from Moscow’s barbarous onslaughts mounts daily. Nato must finally switch to the offensive, make clear more war crimes will not be tolerated, threaten to strike Russian drone and missile launch sites from the air (as previously, repeatedly,urged here) – and force Putin to back off before his forever war becomes everybody’s war.Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentatorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsUkraineOpinionUS-Israel war on IranVladimir PutinRussiaNatoEuropeIsraelcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facade  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing
Content: ‘Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians.’Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APView image in fullscreen‘Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians.’Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/APOpinionRussiaThe Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facadeEditorialThe Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failingSun 13 Sep 2026 12.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 16.34 EDTShareVladimir Putin’s authoritarian powers are not constrained by elections, but he is alert to the danger that his rule would look illegitimate without them. That creates a tension, which is resolved through “managed democracy” – a euphemism for fraud and repression camouflaged with ritual ballots, held under a constitution that notionally guarantees political freedoms but in reality serves only the president.Russians are invited to elect a new Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, later this week, but they know in advance that United Russia, the official party of Putinism, willwin a majority.Engineering that outcome is not without risk for the ruling regime. The mechanics of stealing an election are simple enough. Ballots can be stuffed, official media are pliant. But too blatant a theft can be counterproductive. If the results are wildly divergent from most people’s sense of the real public mood, an authoritarian leader risks advertising his fear of a genuine democratic consultation. It is a sign of weakness.To an extent, this has happened already. Last month, the supreme courtblocked Yabloko, an old and marginal liberal party, from appearing on Duma ballot papers. The case was spurious to the point of absurdity.View image in fullscreenYabloko supporters in Moscow, August 2026.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/GettyYabloko is not one of the pseudo-opposition “system” parties that provide a pretence of pluralism in parliament, but nor does it pose a serious challenge to the regime. If it did, it wouldn’t have survived this long. It was last represented in the Duma in 2007, although it still sends deputies to local and municipal legislatures.It is also opposed to the war inUkraine. This Duma ballot is the first parliamentary poll since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Yabloko’s single-sentence manifesto calls for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace. A decision not to let the bearers of that message participate even in a rigged ballot suggests nervousness about the popularity of a “special military operation” that was supposed to last weeks but is now well into its fifth year, with no end in sight.Ukraine’s use of long-range missiles and dronesto attack infrastructuredeep inside Russia has made it hard for Moscow to downplay the scale of the war on their doorstep or shield civilians from its consequences. The reality of fuel shortages and inflation penetrates the wall of propaganda. So does loss of life.The true number ofRussian casualtiesis hard to know, but is thought to be about 1.5 million, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities. In the absence of volunteers, army recruiters are increasingly turning to coercion, press ganging or tricking people into signing up. There are rumours, denied by officials, that a mass mobilisation of reserves – unwilling cannon fodder – is coming once the election is out of the way.So it is hardly surprising that the Kremlin has abandoned what was left of its flimsy pretence of permitting dissent. The machinery for delivering an election result to the president’s satisfaction is well oiled. There is no reason to think that it will fail this time. That doesn’t make the vote irrelevant. Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians, but he cares about the appearance of being supported by them. The harder the Kremlin is seen to work at constructing electoral proof of that support, the less confident it looks.Explore more on these topicsRussiaOpinionVladimir PutinUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyFreedom of speechCensorshipeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Emily St John Mandel: ‘When half the electorate disagrees on basic reality, how do you come back from that?’ | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Her hit novel Station Eleven seemed to predict the pandemic, now the novelist is tackling the future of the US. She talks about chance, world-building and experiencing a ‘tiny bit’ of clairvoyance
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Her hit novel Station Eleven seemed to predict the pandemic, now the novelist is tackling the future of the US. She talks about chance, world-building and experiencing a ‘tiny bit’ of clairvoyance
Content: Emily St John Mantel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmily St John Mantel.Photograph: Laura Barisonzi/The GuardianFictionInterviewEmily St John Mandel: ‘When half the electorate disagrees on basic reality, how do you come back from that?’Hannah MarriottHer hit novel Station Eleven seemed to predict the pandemic, now the novelist is tackling the future of the US. She talks about chance, world-building and experiencing a ‘tiny bit’ of clairvoyanceSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Emily St John Mandel was a child she had a dream that would stay with her for decades. It was a nightmare in which “I was trying to find my dad in a crowd, and there were other people who looked like him but weren’t him”, she says. “It just kind of struck my imagination.”Forty-ish years later, Mandel’s seventh novel, Exit Party, opens with a gathering in Los Angeles, 2031, where bizarre things happen. Doubles of some guests appear. Someone else disappears altogether. The novel then alternates between two potential future Americas, one riven by the chaos of civil war, the other a surveillance state.Doppelgangers and alternative realities are having a cultural moment in our uncanny, deepfake times. Mandel says the biggest challenge western democracy faces is “the collapse of consensual reality. When you get to a situation where half the electorate disagrees on basic reality – for example, who won an election, or is Covid real? I don’t know how you come back from that.” On a more personal level, she has always been fascinated by what she calls “the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person. The way that, if we made a different decision, we would have become a somewhat different person.”This interest comes, she thinks, from a feeling that “my life as a writer in New York City is a bit improbable”. Mandel was home-schooled on a tiny island in British Columbia, Canada, before training as a dancer. As she puts it, she was “essentially not educated until I was about 15 … I haven’t got a high school diploma.” She wrote while working office jobs until her third novel, Station Eleven, became a smash hit. The 2014 story of life after a global pandemic felt so prescient when readers rediscovered it during Covid that she developed a reputation for clairvoyance. It has sold 1.5m copies and been translated into 37 languages. Her novels since – The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility – were global bestsellers too. It’s a staggering career, and, as she sees it: “There are a million ways this might not have happened.”We meet on a sunny New York City day, in the lobby of a sleek Williamsburg hotel. Mandel, who lives in nearby Queens, wears a rose-printed shirt and comes across as warm yet precise. She’s off to have a haircut after we meet, even though her neat pixie cut scarcely looks trimmable.One of the seeds of Exit Party was its protagonist Ari, who was the villain of Mandel’s second novel, 2010’s The Singer’s Gun. (Mandel is building a multiverse; characters reappear in Station Eleven, The Glass Hotel and Sea of Tranquility, though alas, she says, there is no Marvel movie coming.)All these years later, “I just couldn’t stop thinking about her. I found myself thinking: what would that character be like at the other end of an 18-year prison sentence?” Ari is like a time traveller, she says; as we all are if we survive enough decades: “If you stick around long enough, you kind of become a migrant from a different timeline.”Ari is a bit clairvoyant, something Mandel admits – with what I think may be a small wince – is based on her own experience. “I’ve had just a touch of that all my life. A tiny bit. It’s not nearly as useful as you might imagine. I absolutely cannot predict pandemics.” For example, when the March 2020 dates were announced for her Glass Hotel book tour, which was, of course, later cancelled, “I had a strange feeling: I would think about that tour, and it didn’t feel real. The best way I can describe the feeling is to say there was no life in it. When I thought about it, it was inert.” Or she might feel she needs scissors, and bring them to work – and realise she was right. “Dumb little examples like that,” she says, laughing: “Please don’t write that I’m psychic!”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNot psychic, then, but brilliant at imagining what might happen in our disaster-prone world. Even the writing process of this book was eerily predictive – though not in a straightforward way. When Mandel started writing, in spring 2022, she thought the civil war timeline was potentially “our near future. Not to be pessimistic but one reads the news.” Then she came up with an alternative, Universe B, to be “this kind of mirror image – totalitarianism instead of chaos”. By the time the book was nearing completion, with Trump’s bleak second presidency under way, “I felt like I was struggling to stay ahead of the news cycle in Universe B.” Citizens spy on one another and people are disappeared from the streets. “It’s been terrifying to see the speed with which the news cycle has caught up.”Exit Party is Mandel’s third speculative novel. She is drawn to the form, she says, because she loves to “talk about the present by putting it in a sort of speculative cloak”. Sea of Tranquility, for example, “is absolutely a Covid-19 novel, but by setting it in the future on the moon, it was possible to write about it”. Realism would have been “frankly unbearable to write, let alone to read”. In Exit Party, too, she deftly creates emotional resonance through events that feel like a slanted take on our own times. The titular party, for example, takes place after a curfew is lifted, and has a vividly post-lockdown feel.double quotation markI'm fascinated by the counter-life – the one where you took a different job or married a different person and became a different personHer books come about, she says, through a process of “slow development”. She compares her first draft to a sculptor’s block of clay, “the raw material in which I’ll find the novel. There is no plan and no outline. I’ll start with a scene, build it up from there.” There are always moments when she thinks the novel is irretrievably broken, but she has never yet thrown a manuscript away. “I’ve always been able to change something that isn’t working into something that does work,” she says. Increasingly, she is bringing those skills to the screen, too, whether writing adaptations of her own work (she is working on the pilot for a TV adaptation of Exit Party), or staffing writers’ rooms – recently working on Netflix’s dramatisation of the video game Assassin’s Creed. She spends about one week in Los Angeles for every six in New York, often rising to write fiction in the morning, before an 11am writers’ room Zoom, “which is great in some ways and exhausting in others”.Mandel recently had her own inflection point. Having divorced from her husband, a fellow writer, in 2022, she married photographer Laura Barisonzi in 2025. Their wedding was the stuff of book nerds’ dreams, held in Brooklyn’s Greenlight book store, which has been “hosting my launch events since before Station Eleven – and I didn’t sell many books back then!” They had an open book bar and her daughter, now 10, was a “ring bearer-slash-flower girl. It was just lovely.”Exit Party, like much of her work, makes the case for relishing small moments of joy, frightening as the world is. That, she says, is “something I think about a lot. And maybe there’s a way of even appreciating good momentsbecausethey’re fleeting. That state of being temporary brings its own kind of sweetness.”Exit Party is published by Picador on 17 September. title: ‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of pop | Kylie Minogue | The Guardian
description: Rejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …
Author: Michael Cragg
Headline: Rejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …
Content: La la land … Kylie MinoguePhotograph: Vincent Peters/Trunk ArchiveView image in fullscreenLa la land … Kylie MinoguePhotograph: Vincent Peters/Trunk ArchiveKylie Minogue‘You start to worry you’ll never listen to anything else’: 25 years of Can’t Get You Out of My Head, the song that saw the future of popRejected by Sophie Ellis-Bextor, the minimalist dance-pop opus would become the defining song of Kylie’s career. And, a quarter of a century later, it hasn’t lost its capacity to burrow its way into your brain. La la la …Michael CraggSun 13 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAround the release of Pet Shop Boys’ 1988 album Introspective, Neil Tennant coined the term “imperial phase” to describe an era when he felt the duo “understood the essence of pop music and so we felt we could do what we liked”. For his less flowery partner in pop excellence, Chris Lowe, this was typically followed “by disappearing up your backside!”.In 2010, critic Tom Ewing fleshed out Tennant’s term byimposing three criteria: “command, permission, and self-definition”. Command related to an artist’s willingness and ability to push boundaries in a way that would reverberate through what followed. Permission, meanwhile, connected to the public and their goodwill towards an artist as they pushed things forward. Finally, self-definition, Ewing said, is the way the imperial phase defines the rest of the artist’s career. All future work will be compared with, or mentioned alongside, the output from the imperial phase.By the time Kylie’s album Fever dropped, everything in its subsequent era represented her very own imperial phase. Everything she did in 2001 and 2002 seemed to click perfectly: every video, every choice of single, the tour, the press attention, the fashion, the cohesiveness of the vision, the way she reshaped pop and nudged it forward. And it was all led by the hypnotic weightlessness of the downright oddCan’t Get You Out of My Head.The song was born one autumn weekend in 2000 in a garage studio in Surrey belonging to former Mud guitarist Rob Davis, who had been encouraged by manager and impresario Simon Fuller to write some songs with the excellent pop star turned songwriter Cathy Dennis.double quotation markI don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with itCathy DennisOn the Sunday, using Cubase on a Mac computer to create a drum loop before adding some guitar, the seed of Can’t Get You Out of My Head was planted. While Dennis came up with the title hook – the song, as she noted, doesn’t really conform to a typical verse-chorus structure, with each line almost acting as its own chorus melody – it was Davis who added the “‘la la la” section. The demo was finished in three hours, while Dennis’s vocals were laid down by 7pm that same day.The demo was played to Fuller down the phone. He later played it for S Club 7, but they passed on it. The song was also presented to Sophie Ellis-Bextor, but again it was deemed unsuitable. It was Fuller’s idea to send it to Kylie. “And I was thinking: ‘But this song isn’t what Kylie does,’” remembered Dennis. “Obviously, now, none of us knows what Kylie’s going to come out with next, because she can’t be compartmentalised.” Kylie, meanwhile, “knew a few bars in that this was for me”, she wrote in 2002. “By the end of the track I wanted to know how quickly I could get into the studio.”View image in fullscreenNavel academy … Kylie’s famous and influential dress in the Can’t Get You Out of My Head video.Photograph: Parlophone Records/Warner Music GroupAs promised, though much to Davis’s surprise given he’d convinced himself she wouldn’t turn up, Kylie arrived in Surrey to record Can’t Get You Out of My Head. In between some fancy salmon salad and other treats, the song was finished in a few hours. The mysterious pop alchemy of adding Kylie to a song took them all by surprise. “Even though Kylie wasn’t the first artist to be offered the song, I don’t believe it was meant to go to anyone other than Kylie,” said Dennis,“and I don’t believe anyone else would have done the incredible job she did with it, with the video, looking super-hot!”Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just “good, for a pop song”, as joyless people were wont to say, keen to use the caveat in case their muso credentials be tarnished. As pop began to absorb the outre production styles of R&B experimentalists such as the Neptunes and Timbaland – Britney’s career-restructuring I’m a Slave 4 U, produced by the former, would arrive in the same month as Can’t Get You Out of My Head – audiences were becoming more attuned to pop that was looking to push the boundaries. This felt like dance-pop beamed in from the future, where the first time you hear it you’re like, “Huh?” then the second you’re like, “Wait!” and then the 35th time you start to worry you may never listen to anything else.Its title becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s sexy futurism would also dictate the visual feel of the era: sleek lines, icy-cool silhouettes and just a hint of something darker lurking underneath. For the album’s cover, shot by Vincent Peters, Kylie’s stylist and creative director William Baker was inspired by the French artist Jean-Paul Goude’sphotos of Grace Jones, which highlighted both her sexuality and her power. Baker also wanted Kylie to be attached to the tools of her trade, so on both the album cover and artwork for Can’t Get You Out of My Head, a microphone’s black power cord winds its way round Kylie’s body.Less overt than the buttock-hugging, Carry On vibes of Kylie’s previous album, Light Years, and its lead single, Spinning Around, the Fever look was leaning more into an artful sexiness. This was highlighted in Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s video, directed by Dawn Shadforth, in which the utopia promised by the millennium was laid out in front of us via forensically manicured cityscapes and futuristic fashion: we see her dance on what looks like a rooftop garden centre and in a clean white dome, and losing herself in a dress made of purple-silver Post-it notes.It also gave Kylie yet another iconic fashion moment, one that would be replicated at gigs and fancy-dress parties for decades to come, in the shape of the white hooded dress, split to the navel.While the dress grabbed the attention, it was the all-in-red dancers behind Kylie, sporting matching face-covering visors, who caused a problem for Top of the Pops producer Chris Cowey. As Can’t Get You Out of My Head started to dominate, the show’s lighting department began to complain that their red gels were going missing at the show’s on-set afterparty “because everyone was taking [them] and wrapping them around their heads and doing the dance”, Cowey says. “Just kind of drunkenly doing Kylie impersonations.”By the early 2000s, after Oasis v Blur, the UK had become mildly obsessed with chart battles, ideally those featuring attractive women. On 17 September 2001, the same day as Can’t Get You Out of My Head, Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham was set to release Not Such an Innocent Girl, the lead single from her self-titled debut solo album.Posh had already been beaten, the previous year, by actually-quite-posh Sophie Ellis-Bextor, whose Rob Davis-assisted Groovejet (If This Ain’t Love) had left Beckham’s banger Out of Your Mind at No 2. This time, Victoria roared on to the battlefield with a ropey single and mildly scathing bons mots for her Australian rival. “When I first heard [Can’t Get You Out of My Head], if I’m being totally honest, I didn’t like it,” Posh mused. “And I’m being completely honest.”For Posh, “an old-fashioned type songwriter”, Kylie’s single, while having “a very catchy melody”, didn’t resonate with her because she enjoys “a song that has a bit of emotion”. Posh was also retroactively blaming Kylie for criticisms of Out of Your Mind: “And I have to say that last year when I brought out a dance record, and I had effects on my voice, like she has on her voice, I am still getting a caning for it now.”In the end, on the UK chart of 23 September, Can’t Get You Out of My Head crashed in at No 1, shifting an eye-watering 306,000 copies, holding off emerging talent Bob the Builder’s cover of Mambo No 5 in the process. It would stay at No 1 in the UK for a month, a feat matched in Australia. Posh’s Not Such an Innocent Girl would have to make do with a No 6 entry in the UK and sales of 35,000. The clash was such a hot topic that the BBC ran anews storywith the headline: Kylie trounces Posh in chart battle. “Victoria is pleased to have a Top 10 hit,” a Posh spokeswoman was quoted as saying.double quotation markI think it came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriouslyLarry Flick, journalistThis particular pop star chart battle also served a specific escapist aim. Both singles were released shortly after 9/11, as the western world tried to recalibrate itself following a terrorist attack. The horrors seemed so overwhelming that any hint of normality was gripped tightly with both hands, and Can’t Get You Out of My Head’s futuristic escapism became a hypnotic balm.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor some journalists, the mere existence of Kylie was proof that Osama bin Laden and the Taliban could never win the “war on terror”. “Two people dominated the cultural landscape of this country in the last quarter of the year: Osama bin Laden and Kylie Minogue,”wrote Julie Burchillin the Guardian as 2001 came to an end. “I really do believe that Bin Laden and Kylie represent the polar opposites of human nature; the first all about cruelty without beauty, the second all about beauty without cruelty.”Kylie was suddenly being held up as an emblem of western ideals – the literal face (and body) of the UK’s reaction to the global threat from a terrorist organisation. The Daily Mail printed a list of reasons to be cheerful, post-9/11, topped by Kylie. The picture they used alongside the piece was captioned “Fungirl Kylie, scourge of the Taliban”.
