Watching from the outside as this narrative unfolded, Kylie was “dumbfounded. I understand the way they’re seeing it as a positive thing, but no! Don’t write things like that!”Actual human Kylie, not the projected superhero being pushed to the frontlines, was being interviewed live on local radio when the attacks took place. One of the DJs asked her on air, “So how does it feel to be a pop star in this situation?” “A two-second silence on live radio seems for ever,” Kylie remembered in the Face magazine. “I said: ‘I can’t believe you just asked me that.’ I think they swiftly cut to a record.”View image in fullscreenKylie contagious … Minogue performs her Can’t Get You Out of My Head/Blue Monday mash-up at the 2002 Brit.Photograph: JMEnternational/GettyAmericans, at first, clung to a very different kind of superstar and song. Enrique Iglesias’s windswept ballad Hero, released on 3 September 2001, was one of the few songs played by New York City DJs after the attacks, but by the time Can’t Get You Out of My Head made its debut on the US charts in January 2002, a shift was happening. People needed something to dance to. “It was definitely at a time when people were gingerly going back [out],” remembers NYC music journalist Larry Flick. “I think [Can’t Get You Out of My Head] came at a time when we just needed Kylie, and an artist that wasn’t going to take it all too seriously. There were a few things, in New York, that got us through 9/11: there was the return of Friends, the return of David Letterman, and the Kylie record.”double quotation markIan McKellen sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching herDavid Russell, Kylie fanFlick remembers the second time he heard it, in the Roxy, New York’s disco roller rink turned hip nightclub, which was famed as a venue that tested out new records. “I ran to the booth and I was like: ‘How about you playing Kylie?’ And the DJ goes: ‘Baby, this is the shit.’ He played it for about 20 minutes and the crowd lost their minds.”Can’t Get You Out of My Head wasn’t just a hit; it was a smash. It didn’t just peak in all the usual places Kylie tended to, but also in places such as Belgium and Romania and Switzerland and Hungary. In the US, it quickly started to climb not just the Dance Club charts, where Kylie had been a regular, but also the main Billboard Hot 100, a chart she hadn’t been in since 1988.“Can’t Get You Out of My Head was inescapable,” remembers US Kylie fan David Russell. “It started to get played on the radio, and then suddenly the video was on MTV. Kylie did Saturday Night Live with Ian McKellen hosting. I begged the publicist and she got me in. McKellen said: ‘You lucky, lucky people, it’s Kylie Minogue!’ He then sat on the side of the stage like a little kid watching her.”Back in the UK, Kylie won twice at the 2002 Brit awards, scooping best international female and best international album for Fever. But it was her award-show performance that would gain instant notoriety, later becoming a mainstay of any homosexual’s post-night-out YouTube binge.Kylie’s 30 greatest singles – ranked!Read morePerforming aspecial mashupof Can’t Get You Out of My Head and New Order’s Blue Monday by then white-hot DJ and producer Erol Alkan, whose Trash club night was London’s hottest ticket, Kylie arrives on stage lying down on a giant CD – her name emblazoned on it in neon pink – seemingly holding on for dear life while wearing a Dolce & Gabbana minidress and knee-high silver boots. As the giant CD is ejected out of the player and lifts up so the crowd can see her for the first time, you’ll believe you can hear God. The performance was a perfect balancing act: audacious, spectacular, camp, sexy and silly in all the right ways.“I feel like I’m on a wave and I actually know how to stand on the board at this point,” Kylie said as Can’t Get You Out of My Head and her imperial era kicked in. “I don’t know where it’s taking me, but everything feels really good.”Can’t Get You Out of My Head: In Search of Kylieby Michael Craggis published on 24 September by Faber.Explore more on these topicsKylie MinoguePop and rockextractsShareReuse this content

title: Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with fun | Movies | The Guardian
description: There’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventure
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: There’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventure
Content: A love story of sorts … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Rediat AbaynehView image in fullscreenA love story of sorts … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Rediat AbaynehMoviesReviewShaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom review – Aardman’s spooky-season caper sparkles with funThere’s trouble afoot when Shaun’s pumpkin-supersizing serum ends up in a balding farmer’s hair growth bottle in this third cinematic adventurePeter BradshawSun 13 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer is over and Halloween is on the way … not for a fair bit, of course, but if all the UK’s Halloween merch and continuing pop culture content is up to the standard of this film, then no one is going to be complaining. This is the third in Aardman’s thoroughly enjoyable and cleverly written Shaun the Sheep stop-motion franchise of what are effectively silent movies, with a few intelligible words. It is the story of gutsy and heroic sheep involved in amazing adventures in the sleepy village of Mossy Bottom, starring characters who first appeared in theWallace and Gromit short film A Close Shave.‘He goes to the dark side’: behind the scenes on the Shaun the Sheep horror movieRead moreThis one is another excellent family film, crammed as ever with top visual gags, great throwaway references and, of course, a homemade Heath Robinson contraption, so often to be found inAardmanfilms. We get nods to The Archers, The Wombles and The Simpsons; there’s a wacky chase worthy of What’s Up, Doc?; a homage to the notorious waxing scene from Judd Apatow’s The 40-Year-Old Virgin; and even what appears to be a brief visual walk-on for George Bernard Shaw as Bigfoot. As ever with Shaun the Sheep and Aardman Animations generally, the standard of writing is extremely high and the script here, from Mark Burton and Giles Pilbrow, sparkles with good-natured fun. One high-street hairdressing salon in the wool-producing district where it’s set is called Barber Black Sheep – and if no real-life shop has stolen this joke yet, they ought to.A klutzy, balding sheep farmer (voiced by John Sparkes), on whose premises Shaun and the gang are to be found, is poignantly in love with a visiting vet (voiced by Nina Sosanya); he longs to invite her to a local country music hoedown, but is shy and moreover ashamed of being follicularly challenged. As for the sheep themselves, they are secretly cultivating a pumpkin patch to harvest a bunch of scary jack-o-lanterns for their forthcoming Halloween frolics. The clumsy big-booted farmer ruins them all, and the resourceful sheep turn to the dark magic of technology and sinister GM techniques (as discovered in a children’s science book) to grow supersized new pumpkins from a rescued seed. But some of their occult new miracle growth-boost liquid finds its way into the farmer’s baldness-cure bottle.The pitchfork-wielding villagers of Mossy Bottom are hilariously stunned at the terrifying appearance of a rampaging, hairy beast who has been spotted in the outlying fields and woodlands at the very moment that the farmer himself has mysteriously disappeared. Has the beast somehow kidnapped or eaten the farmer? It is a nightmarish mystery that will need every ounce of Shaun and his pals’ courage and ingenuity to sort out, not to mention that of the vet, who uses a hi-tech DNA machine to examine the genetic provenance of a piece of the beast’s fur she has managed to snip off.It is a love story of sorts, perhaps a little like that of Beauty and the Beast, but about two people who for most the story’s running time don’t know that they are going to be in love. As for the sheep, their faces convey amazingly distinct expressions and moods with just a few deft movements. It’s sharp, smart, funny and precise; there is nothing woolly about it.Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is out on 17 September in Australia, and on 18 September in the UK and US.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFamily filmsShaun the Sheep MovieAardmanComedy filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Last Night of the Proms review – musical chaos ensues in near four-hour finale | Proms 2026 | The Guardian
description: The evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky Spence
Author: Alexandra Coghlan
Headline: The evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky Spence
Content: On top of his brief … tenor Nicky Spence (centre) with conductor Sakari Oramo (right) on stage with the BBC Symphony Orchestra for the Last Night of the Proms.Photograph: Jennifer Hawthorn /BBCView image in fullscreenOn top of his brief … tenor Nicky Spence (centre) with conductor Sakari Oramo (right) on stage with the BBC Symphony Orchestra for the Last Night of the Proms.Photograph: Jennifer Hawthorn /BBCProms 2026ReviewLast Night of the Proms review – musical chaos ensues in near four-hour finaleRoyal Albert Hall, LondonThe evening features everything from a rendition of an inscrutable Samuel Barber concerto to a celebration of Dolly Parton, but the real star is tartan-clad tenor Nicky SpenceAlexandra CoghlanSun 13 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Richard Strauss’s Ariadne auf Naxos, a wealthy man commissions an evening’s entertainment: a lofty new opera and a comic burlesque. But when time constraints force them to be performed simultaneously, surreal musical chaos ensues. One can only assume that the BBC was taking notes.The Last Night of the Proms is the finale to eight weeks of concerts, and the BBC’s annual identity crisis. Is this the celebratory end to a season of serious music or a standalone party, whose first half is something to be endured before the real fun begins? It’s both, of course. And that’s where the trouble starts.Playing With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworldsRead moreConsider the running time of nearly four hours. That’s longer than Rheingold, pushing into Tristan und Isolde territory: a bloated classical variety performance where all shall have prizes (this year even, perhaps to her heavenly surprise, Dolly Parton) and no music shall be left behind – not even Samuel Barber’s inscrutable, gruffly virtuosic 1962 Piano Concerto. Try waving your flag to that.But try the audience did. There’s a place in musical hell for the person who let off a howling rocket balloon just as the soaring central theme of Holst’s Jupiter began, and again in the ravishing cello solo of Tom Bowling, but you can hardly blame the steady trickle of walkouts during piano megastar Yuja Wang’s stylish, near-superhuman account of the Barber, nor the restless, pre-emptive burst of applause at the not-end of Smetana’s Vltava.View image in fullscreenConductor Sakari Oramo and pianist Yuja Wang.Photograph: Chris Christodoulou/BBC/PAThe conductor, Sakari Oramo, the evening’s ever-genial MC, offered us an alternative definition of AI during his traditional speech: Artistic Integrity. When the night got it right it sang off the stage: in the sardonic dances of Alexander Tsfasman’s Soviet-era Jazz Suite (Wang back as a dazzling blur of a soloist, with a little help from Richard Hosford’s outrageous solo clarinet), in the lightly worn choral excellence of the BBC Singers delivering the world premiere of Anne Dudley’s Iris of Life, and roaring and blazing from tenor Nicky Spence.Has any Last Night soloist better understood the assignment? Whether giving us heartfelt heroism in the Prince’s aria from Rusalka or Broadway pizzazz in Guys and Dolls’ Sit Down, You’re Rocking the Boat (complete with hip flask and New York accent) or a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it tour through his native Scotland’s music that smuggled in the Proclaimers and Yes Sir, I Can Boogie alongside folk songs and an athletic dance-routine, Spence was absolutely himself, absolutely in his element. Sometimes authenticity sounds like a symphony orchestra, sometimes it comes dressed in a Magic Mike­-style pair of breakaway tartan trousers.Available onBBC Soundsuntil 12 October and onBBC iPlayeruntil August 2027.Explore more on these topicsProms 2026Classical musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Burning Man at 40: the once anarchic desert festival faces a midlife crisis | Burning Man festival | The Guardian
description: The subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-rich
Author: Lois Beckett
Headline: The subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-rich
Content: The Burning Man festival on 31 September 2006. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year are growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger ‘burners’.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyView image in fullscreenThe Burning Man festival on 31 September 2006. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year are growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger ‘burners’.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyBurning Man festivalBurning Man at 40: the once anarchic desert festival faces a midlife crisisThe subversive bacchanal for San Francisco’s eccentric underground is ageing out amid an influx of the super-richLois BeckettSun 13 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurning Man, the infamous arts festival in the Nevada desert, turned 40 this year, and it’s showing some distinct signs of middle age.It’s not just the tech billionaires who show up to party, thechartered flightsstraight to the desert or theHBO documentaryaboutbehind-the-scenes power struggles. The tens of thousands of people who assemble each year to create a tent city in the wilderness appear to be growing older, and it doesn’t seem that they’re being replaced by as many younger “burners”, as festival participants are called.People in their 20s used to make up nearly a third of the participants in this utopian experiment, in which volunteers build a new version of Black Rock City in the desert each year, party nonstop for a week and then burn much of the art they have created, including a massive effigy of the “Man.”Since the festival paused for two years during the pandemic, the number of attenders in their 20s has dropped sharply, falling to only 10% in 2025, according to estimates from theBlack Rock City census, an annual participant survey that has been conducted in different forms since 2002. Meanwhile, the share of attenders in their 40 and 50s grew to nearly 42% last year. While data for 2026 is not yet available, the “preliminary 2026 census data suggest a slightly younger age profile than in 2025”, the organization said.View image in fullscreenBurners revel at the Burning Man festival in the Black Rock desert in Nevada on 30 August 2008.Photograph: Frederic Larson /San Francisco Chronicle via GettyBurners are used to adapting to new circumstances, and they have weathered plenty of scorn and skepticism from what they call the “default world”. But a permanent shift in the event’s demographics could have big implications for what’s possible on the ground.As Burning Man’s spiritual seekers age, can the festival remain an evolving experiment in radical communal living? Or is it doomed to become just another tech networking conference for the wealthy – one where almost everyone is high and a surprising number of people are naked?Deaths in the desertThe number of deaths connected with the festivalticked upwards to three this year, all of them men over 50. Two of the men, one in his mid-50s and the other 51, died after receiving medical treatment. A third man, aged 60, was found dead in the trailer he shared with his significant other.Local authorities said there were no signs of foul play in any of the deaths, and that more information about the causes of death would be released in about six to eight weeks, after they conducted the required autopsies and toxicology tests.“It is premature to attribute these deaths to the age of Burning Man’s participant population,” a spokesperson for the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “The deaths resulted from separate incidents, the individual causes have not been released, and age alone does not establish cause.“We encourage and ask people to focus on the contributions of the individuals lost and avoid speculation out of respect for the participants and their families.”In many ways, it’s impressive that a chaotic event that draws upwards of 70,000 people annually has only typically seen about one death per year, particularly given the festival’s notoriety for drugs,cage-fighting in the Thunderdome, live flame performances and improvised vehicles careering across the dark desert – not to mention theOrgy Dome.Thephysical conditionscan be punishing. Since 1990, Burning Man has been held on Nevada’s Black Rock playa, a gorgeous, barren stretch of dusty land that was once a prehistoric lake. There is no vegetation, no running water – virtually no signs of life. The playa is prone to sudden, ferocious dust storms: participants are encouraged to carry dust masks and goggles. Heavy rains cause flooding and turn the ground to mud.View image in fullscreenAbout 4,500 people gathered in the Black Rock desert of northern Nevada for the Burning Man festival in 1995.Photograph: Tomas Ovalle/Tri-Valley Times via GettyThe social conditions can be even more dire: endless substance use, no sleep, house music pounding across the desert nearly 24 hours a day – and, if you didn’t prepare enough, intermittent access to food. The portable toilets throughout the tent city have sometimes been decorated with PSAs urging festivalgoers to “Piss clear, cowgirl!” warning them that dark-colored urine means they’re starting to become severely dehydrated.Repeat burners tend to scoff at breathless media coverage of the festival’s weather and other disasters – like in 2023, when heavy rain and floodsforced Diplo to hitchhikeandleft tens of thousands stranded, but many participants said they were well-prepared and simply partied on.“In 2023, they were like, ‘There are diseases, they’re eating people,’” a person identified only as “Bone” toldSFGate on another muddy day this year. “Meanwhile, I’m like dancing with beautiful European women and having the best time of my life.”The inhospitable natural conditions are, after all, part of Burning Man’s design. In some ways, the 200-sq-mile desert playa functions as a kind of massive sauna, where the extreme desert heat helps participants enter a more relaxed and communal state. Festival participants rely on each other to meet their basic needs, from food, to shelter, to extremely brief and improvised showers. Buying or selling anything during the festival is forbidden, which means the 70,000-person tent city operates as a gift economy, with different groups of campers offering up different free activities, food or drink.This can make Burning Man feel like a dream: it’s possible to float across the desert from campground to campground, filling a reusable mug with endless free beers and cocktails, and occasionally catching a ride on an improvised “art car”, which might be shaped like a dragon or feature a giant playground slide. Massive handmade temples, statues and monuments loom out of the dust; by the end of the week, most of them will be set ablaze.View image in fullscreenA huge dust storm forces burners to take cover in tents or vehicles in Black Rock City on 30 August 2007.Photograph: Michael Macor/San Francisco Chronicle via GettyFor the times when that dream turns abruptly into a nightmare, Burning Man’s organizers have emphasized free community care. Volunteers provide first aid and quiet places where people having a bad trip on drugs can recover. The festival has its own free emergency room, Rampart, which is equipped with “X-ray machines, a pharmacy with over 100 medications, blood products, ventilators, chest tubes, arterial lines, [and] IV pumps”,SFGate reported. It treated nearly 1,500 patients last year.One of the men who died this year at Burning Man had been found on one of the festival’s streets and was given CPR, and then brought to the hospital, the Pershing county sheriff’s office said in a statement.“Black Rock City is a temporary, rural city of approximately 60,000 people, supported by a substantial medical and emergency-response system operating around the clock,” the Burning Man Project said in a statement. “Participants experience medical emergencies for many of the same reasons people do in any city.”A once-edgy celebration past its prime?Over its four decades, the festival has been nothing but resilient, but many early participants feel a middle-aged sense of disillusionment over what Burning Man has become.It’s not just the age of the crowd. Once a dadaist experiment, an attempt to create a “temporary autonomous-zone” in the desert, Burning Man is now a marker of class status for tech bros and “creative professionals” around the globe, a kind of west coast Wimbledon for the weird.“Early Burning Man wasn’t a ready-made escape you could buy your way into. It was an anarchistic collaboration of equals, conjured into being by a few hundred people of goodwill, far from anyone’s control,” John Law, one of the Burning Man’s co-founders,wrote in the SF Standardthis August.View image in fullscreenFestivalgoers at Burning Man on 3 September 1999.Photograph: Hector Mata/AFP via Getty ImagesToday, he wrote, it’s become an “immersive spectacle built for the consumption of western elites and the middle-class creatives who service them”.To be fair, to the art punks who built it in the first place, Burning Man hasn’t been cool for decades. Law hasn’t been back to the desert since his last burn 30 years ago.You could argue that Burning Man has been over since 1996, when it made the cover of Wired magazine, or since 2001, when Eric Schmidt wasfamously selectedas Google’s new CEO after a vetting trip to Burning Man with Sergey Brin and Larry Page.Even though today’s Burning Man still relies on a “gift economy” once participants arrive, getting there is very far from cheap. The growing number of elder burners is hardly surprising, given the increasing cost of a Burning Man experience, with entry tickets alone costing between$550 and $3,000 this year, not including the costs of food, shelter, creative outfits, vehicle rental and entry fee, and the multiple stages of travel needed to reach the remote Nevada desert.View image in fullscreenThe Serpent Mother by the Flaming Lotus Girls of San Francisco at the conclusion of Burning Man in 2006.Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/The San Francisco Chronicle via GettyAnd that’s just for an ordinary camp-in-a-tent Burn, not what Law describes as the much-derided “plug-and-play” Burning Man experiences, which might involve a chartered flight directly to the playa, air-conditioned accommodation, specially prepared costumes and a private chef.Three-quarters of Burning Man participants last year said they had a household income of more than $100,000 a year, and nearly 30% said their household income was more than $300,000, according to thecensus estimates.Though one of the principles of the festival is “radical inclusion”, the event continues to attract an overwhelmingly white crowd: in many years, estimates have put it at over 80% white. This year, the figure was 75%.Explore more on these topicsBurning Man festivalThe super-richSilicon ValleySan FranciscoCaliforniaNevadaFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘He would have been the center of everything’: the art exhibition imagining if Emmett Till lived | Photography | The Guardian
description: Dedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in America
Author: Briana Ellis-Gibbs
Headline: Dedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in America
Content: Emmett Till, a black 14-year-old Chicago boy, who was brutally murdered in Mississippi in 1955 after whistling at a white woman.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenEmmett Till, a black 14-year-old Chicago boy, who was brutally murdered in Mississippi in 1955 after whistling at a white woman.Photograph: APPhotography‘He would have been the center of everything’: the art exhibition imagining if Emmett Till livedDedicated to the boy whose lynching partially ignited the US civil rights movement, the new exhibition celebrates Black creativity and invites audiences to reckon with racism in AmericaBriana Ellis-GibbsSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareSeventy-one years after the brutal murder of Emmett Till, the way that the US as a country honors his memory is still being contested. Markers commemorating his life have beenshot at, stolen and become the site of white supremacist group recruiting events. A new exhibit opening in Chicago asks the country to memorialize his life not only by remembering his death, but by asking America to consider the question: What if Emmett Till Lived?Open now and running until December, the exhibitionIf Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Groundat the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago is an imagined photo library depicting the life Till never got to live. Through the images on display, co-curators of the show, Sarah Elizabeth Lewis, a Harvard professor and founder of the Vision & Justice initiative, and Reverend Wheeler Parker Jr, Emmett Till’s cousin, best friend and last surviving witness to his kidnapping, ask the nation to consider who gets to be remembered on American soil and how the country chooses to see its history.“When I see the exhibition on the walls, it brings to mind the question I’ve always asked myself: “What would he have been?” And knowing him, he would have been the center of everything going on,” Parker Jr said. “He wouldn’t let life pass him by without getting involved. So, you think about what it would have been like. Then I look at the other side, at the laws that were passed and the things that were created because of his death. You’re appreciative and you thank God for that, but he’s still not here. So you have a lot of mixed emotions about him and death.”View image in fullscreenDr Sarah Lewis and Reverend Parker Jr outside the Mississippi barn where Emmett Till was murdered, July 2026.Photograph: Lance Omar ThurmanIn the months leading up to the exhibit’s opening, the state of Illinois officially designated 25 July, Till’s birthday, as Emmett Till Day. Last month, the barn where Emmett Till was murdered was bought by Patrick Weems’s Emmett Till Interpretive Center, with plans to make the space a site of remembrance. And this week, the church where Emmett Till’s funeral was heldunveileda re-creation of the historic neon sign in honor of Till, signaling the exhibition’s opening.“Every American needs to do their part to honor Emmett Till,” Lewis says. “I would not have understood the urgency, though, unless I went toMississippi. When you see the resistance to honoring Emmett Till’s life 70 years later, you start to realize that there’s more to be done. I realized that I not only needed to do my part, but needed to extend the space of the exhibition to constitute a new arena for reimagining society, and that’s what birthed this exhibition.”In the summer of 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black boy fromChicago, was visiting relatives in Mississippi with his cousin, Reverend Parker. While standing outside Bryant’s Grocery & Meat Market, he whistled at a shopkeeper, a white woman. Four days later, the woman’s husband and half-brother kidnapped him and took him to a barn where they tortured, mutilated and killed him. At trial, the woman’s relatives were acquitted but later confessed to the murder in Look magazine.Lewis argues that it is important to remember Till despite efforts to erase his name from American memory. “My hope is that when you reckon with these roadblocks to equity in American democracy and the resistance to honoring Till, you really begin to grasp why bravery is required, why courage is required and why something more than the work of politics and law is required,” she says. “What’s needed is a transformation of how we see each other.”Seventy-one years ago, Mamie Till-Mobley, Till’s mother, set out to change how the nation saw her son and, in turn, how Americans saw each other. On 4 September 1955, she held an open casket funeral at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, for nearly 100,000 attenders.View image in fullscreenMamie Till Mobley weeps at her son’s funeral on 6 September 1955, in Chicago. The mother of Emmett Till insisted that her son’s body be displayed in an open casket, forcing the country to see the brutality directed at Black people in the South at the time.Photograph: AP“We have averted our eyes far too long, turning away from the ugly reality facing us as a nation,” Mamie Till-Mobley is quoted as saying in thebookIf Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Ground, which accompanies the exhibition.Till-Mobley hired photographer David Jackson to photograph Till’s brutalized body at his funeral for Jet magazine. “I wanted the world to see what they did to my baby,” she said in September 1955.“Till-Mobley was prophetic in her understanding that witnessing would be critical for grasping the crucible of American democracy,” Lewis says. With the new show, Lewis and Parker Jr aimed to create “a creative monument” for the nation to see the hopes and possibilities of the life Till did not get to live.The photographers featured are wide-ranging, from Henri Cartier-Bresson, Carrie Mae Weems, Teju Cole and Gordon Parks to relatives of Till, like his cousin, Lance Omar Thurman. Lewis notes that she wanted to include photographs from an extensive range of image makers.View image in fullscreenReverend Wheeler Parker Jr chose this image, Hopscotch, 1952, to show the innocence of children.Photograph: Walter Rosenblum/Extended loan of the Baum Family Collection, Nina and Lisa Rosenblum“I approached the show with the democratic ethos,” she says. “I went into the collection, looking for works, regardless of the name of the artist and their stature. I went looking for works that contained a message and an episode in Emmett Till’s life. And it meant that everyone could be part of the story.”One of the most striking images Lewis chose is the photograph on the book’s cover, taken by Stephen Marc. The photograph is a black-and-white image of a man looking up at a young boy he has thrown into the air, next to a body of water. For Lewis, the image “represents both hope and possibility”.“I think of Marc’s aunt, Dr Carla Hayden, the former librarian of Congress, as a symbol of the power of the archive,” he says. “These images let us recreate the archive we don’t often see, the possibility for lives cut short. Marc’s photograph, with its paradox of possibility and life cut short, became the metaphor for the exhibition. It became a way to see both Till and the Till in all of us as we live.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, from Changing Chicago, 1988. Gelatin silver print.Photograph: Stephen Marc/Gift of Jack A Jaffe, Focus/Infinity FundFor the exhibition, Lewis and Parker Jr asked many notable people, including Dr Chelsea Clinton, Ava DuVernay, Dr Henry Louis Gates Jr, congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, Hank Willis Thomas and others, to select images and write their own reflections on Till’s life.Thomas chose a striking image taken by Dawoud Bey of Barack Obama sitting in a chair, his gaze piercing the camera. In the photograph, the former US president’s facial expression looks present, as if the only thing in the world at that moment is him and the camera. As Thomas notes, the image shows the possibilities that could have come to fruition in Till’s life if he had the opportunity to grow old.“Emmett Till was denied the chance to grow into a man, to be honored, to age into possibility,” Thomas writes in the book If Emmett Till Lived. “This photograph allows us to sit with one version of what history fought to make possible: a Black man looking directly at a camera and into us, with the full force of his humanity intact.”The images in the show are memorials to the life taken from Till. As Lewis writes in If Emmett Till Lived, “sometimes a photograph can be a monument. Sometimes, a photograph has to be a monument when all attempts at making a monument, for decades, have been and are still denied.”View image in fullscreenBarack Obama, 2006Photograph: Dawoud Bey/Columbia College Chicago commissionThe “exhibition is going to help a lot of people”, Parker Jr says. “It helps the cause. As I heard Mamie said, ‘I hope you didn’t die in vain.’”Though the exhibit focuses on honoring the life of Till, Lewis argues that the show also pays tribute to the lives taken from numerous young Black people. “There are many Emmett Tills today,” he says. “Till is a proxy for understanding aNolan Wells. A proxy for understandingBreonna Taylor.”“One of the ways this question of what we do in the face of the visibility of this tragedy is to ask, is witnessing enough? Is witnessing injustice enough to transform the moral imagination? People are seeing the video of George Floyd. Is it enough to let people see? We might have to require people to see, entice them to see and make the invitation to see the truth of American society irresistible.”View image in fullscreenRailroad Yards, South Chicago, 1966. The train route Emmett Till would have taken if he made it home alive.Photograph: David Plowden/Extended loan of the Baum Family Collection.If Emmett Till Lived: Freedom on American Groundis at the Museum of Contemporary Photography, Chicago, until 19 December

title: Céline Dion review – singer’s first live show in years marks a triumphant, emotional return | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description:
Plenitude Arena, Paris
Dion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndrome
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: Plenitude Arena, ParisDion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndrome
Content: Celine Dion walks on stage at the Plenitude Arena, Paris on Saturday night. The show was her first full-length concert in six years.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenCeline Dion walks on stage at the Plenitude Arena, Paris on Saturday night. The show was her first full-length concert in six years.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersCéline DionReviewCéline Dion review – singer’s first live show in years marks a triumphant, emotional returnPlenitude Arena, ParisDion wiped away tears and belted out the notes, giving an astounding performance despite her diagnosis of stiff person syndromeAlim KherajSat 12 Sep 2026 21.47 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2022, when Céline Dion shared that she had been diagnosed with a rare incurable neurological disorder calledstiff person syndrome (SPS),there was no guarantee that the 58-year-old would ever tour again. Her condition, which resulted in muscle spasms so strong thatit left her with broken ribs, had made it impossible to perform, and in a 2024 documentary,I Am: Céline Dion, fans saw how the disease had constricted her once seemingly infallible voice. Through it all, though, Dion was resolute that she would one day return to the stage. “If I can’t run, I’ll walk. If I can’t walk, I’ll crawl,” she said in the film. “But I won’t stop.”‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackRead moreThankfully at the opening night of her sold out five-week residency in Paris, her first full-length concerts in six years, no crawling is needed:Céline Dionis back. She glides on to the stage in a black dress, an enormous diamond necklace clasped around her throat, and launches into On ne change pas. There are tears almost immediately: she struggles through the second verse, her voice cracking as she begins to cry. By the time the strum of Destin has kicked in, though, that emotion is replaced with sheer elation. “I made a promise to be back on stage. Singing for you. Singing for me,” she says. “Singing for life.”View image in fullscreenDion performs during her first concert of a series at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, west of Paris on 12 September.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesThat she does. There is no cure for SPS, but the work Dion has put into managing her condition so she can perform again is astounding. Still, clearly some necessary allowances have been made. Some songs such as Because You Loved Me, The Power of Love and My Heart Will Go On have all been transposed down. It’s understandable given the effect her condition has had on her voice, although, in the case of Because You Loved Me and It’s All Coming Back To Me Now, it does somewhat dampen their melodramatic potency.That is not to say that Dion’s voice is weakened: when she needs to, as she does on the driving Tout l’or des hommes, she can still belt out a note. There’s also some welcome texture to her vocal, too: recently released ballad Dansons sees her embracing her lower register, while Courage, recorded following the death of her late husband René Angélil, is genuinely affecting as Dion allows her voice to get fragile and raspy.For some, Dion’s success – she has sold more than 200m records and is the third most successful female artist of all time – is inexplicable: to them, her music is the apotheosis of saccharin and anodyne adult contemporary. But for the 30,000-plus in the crowd tonight, that contempt is decidedly absent. After all, you don’t attend a Céline Dion show expecting anything avant garde. You’re there to hear Beauty and the Beast, an unexpected highlight.View image in fullscreenDion wipes away tears.Photograph: Samir Hussein/WireImageStill, Dion does have some surprises up her sleeve: the run of J’irai où tu iras, Ne bouge pas and Dans un autre monde provides some rollicking respite from the balladry, Dion strutting up and down the stage while doing vocal acrobatics or fake boxing with backing singer. This is followed by an outlandishly camp disco section, complete with covers of Donna Summer’s I Feel Love (oddly enough, Moroder’s sequenced synths really are a great match), Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) and a chandelier that quickly morphs into a glitter ball. As Dion shimmies about, separating the covers with a souped-up electronic take on That’s The Way It Is, a sly smile reveals that she, too, knows how ridiculous it all is.Most astonishing, though, is a rendition of Ebben? Ne andrò lontana from Alfredo Catalani’s opera La Wally: wearing a pink feathered coat and standing a protruding rock that has just emerged from below the stage, Dion pays homage to Maria Callas as fake snow falls from the ceiling on to the audience below. It is brilliant and ludicrous and purists will loathe it. Nevertheless, the kookiness all feels very Céline.Big hits, massive ballads and titanic emotions: Céline Dion’s greatest songs – ranked!Read moreThe biggest response from the crowd, many of whom have likely been outpractising at one of the many mass karaoke eventscelebrating Dion’s music throughout Paris this week, arrives during Pour que tu m’aimes encore. The singing is so loud it almost drowns Dion out. It is All By Myself, however, that seems like the most significant for Dion. As the piano solo and slide guitar gives way, she glances upwards before unleashing herself on that final chorus. When she realises she hit the big notes, it’s relief – then triumph – that spreads across her face. Given where she has come from, and her performance on stage tonight, it’s a feeling that is clearly well deserved.Explore more on these topicsCéline DionFranceEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a jaw-dropping new end-of-the-world reality show  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Scavenging and squabbling in Apocalypse. Plus: Fatiha El-Ghorri and Lucy Beaumont on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Scavenging and squabbling in Apocalypse. Plus: Fatiha El-Ghorri and Lucy Beaumont on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Pictured: Celia (WEST SIDE) covering mouth in shock.Photograph: channel 4View image in fullscreenPictured: Celia (WEST SIDE) covering mouth in shock.Photograph: channel 4TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a jaw-dropping new end-of-the-world reality showScavenging and squabbling in Apocalypse. Plus: Fatiha El-Ghorri and Lucy Beaumont on The Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Jack Seale,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesSun 13 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 01.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApocalypse9pm, Channel 4Survivor meets The Last of Us in this chilling reality show which dumps two teams of ordinary people in a real ghost town. The groups scavenge for food, find shelter and ultimately aim to survive – but at first they are unaware of each other’s existence. As with all juicy social experiments, the real entertainment starts as dynamics between such different characters begin to form and squabbles erupt into arguments (see jovial content creator Steven and alpha beef farmer Scott). From stealing chickens to pooing in a shared bucket, taking charge of food rationing and – perhaps worst of all – snoring, it’s not long before people turn on each other. How badly can things end for them?Hollie RichardsonThe Great Celebrity Pottery Throw Down 20267.45pm, Channel 4The first ever celebrity version of the pottery competition kicks off with host Liza Tarbuck welcoming five famous faces to “throw down”. Fatiha El-Ghorri is reliably hilarious, Lucy Beaumont is manifesting a new career as a ceramicist, while Paul Merson’s breakfast set, inspired in part by his addiction, is unexpectedly touching.Priya ElanUnmissable Moments at the Proms 20268pm, BBC FourFrom a baking heatwave night of Marvin Gaye’s hot hits to Ladysmith Black Mambazo celebrating the songs of Graceland 40 years on, the Proms have showcased a summer of brilliant live music. Catch up with these highlights and more with this bumper roundup.HRWagging Rights8pm, U&WView image in fullscreenA man’s best friend? … Sara Pascoe and Rhod Gilbert on Wagging Rights on U&W.Photograph: Ollie UptonA bunch of British celebrities training their pooches for dog shows? It’s actually a soothing watch. First up, some heart-tugging stories of how they met: comedian Rhod Gilbert got little Piscen when he was diagnosed with cancer. Then it’s time for an obedience test to earn the first rosette. Sara Pascoe, Harriet Kemsley, Kae Kurd and Vicky Pattison also take part.HRVigil9pm, BBC OneCold and concussed but in possession of hot new information, detectives/life partners Amy and Kirsten (Suranne Jones and Rose Leslie) now have to reassess what they know about an international bioweapon conspiracy. Which of the Arctic Circle’s many similar-looking men in light beards and heavy coats can they trust?Jack SealeTrigger Point9pm, ITV1Series four of this bombastic thriller has been a masterclass in headlong escalation. As the finale looms, the knackered remnants of Vicky McClure’s explosives unit are getting a crash course in handling nuclear material. But will she finally get face-to-face with the shadowy figure behind it all? Concludes Monday.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceRabbit Trap (Bryn Chainey, 2025), 6.50am, 10pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenCreepy … Dev Patel in Rabbit Trap on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyDev Patel stars in this creepy folk horror which combines ASMR atmospherics with the timeless eeriness of Tylwyth Teg fairy-folk legend. It’s 1976 and sound recordist Darcy Davenport (Patel) and his wife, musician Daphne (Rosy McEwen), have relocated to an isolated Welsh cabin, seeking inspiration through immersion in the sounds of nature. But the couple is soon accosted by a nameless child of indeterminate age and gender, who insinuates themself into their home.Ellen E JonesLive sportGreat North Run, 10am, BBC OneAlex Mutiso and Sheila Chepkirui are defending champions.Women’s Super League: Arsenal v Crystal Palace, 2.30pm, BBC TwoAt Emirates Stadium.Premier Leage Football: Man United v Man City, 4pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Monday, Leeds play Newcastle at 6.30pm. On Friday, Brentford play Chelsea at 8pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was hit by an emotional hurricane’: Esther Freud, Deborah Levy and other novelists revisit their childhood homes | Homes | The Guardian
description: Even in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?
Author: Alexei Sayle
Headline: Even in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?
Content: Illustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianHomes‘I was hit by an emotional hurricane’: Esther Freud, Deborah Levy and other novelists revisit their childhood homesEven in adulthood, the place where you grew up never really leaves you. Could paying a return visit help six writers understand its power?Julia Samuel,Alexei Sayle,Esther Freud,Deborah Levy, Guy Gunaratne and Chloe AridjisSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘People return to their childhood homes to revisit earlier versions of themselves’Psychotherapist and author Julia SamuelView image in fullscreenJulia Samuel, age six, at the London home she lived in from the age of one until she was 20.Photograph: Courtesy of Julia SamuelI recently took my best friend to see my childhood home inKensington, west London. I lived there with my parents and four siblings from the age of one until I was 20; I have not been inside since I was 23, when it was sold, 43 years ago. Yet it still appears in my dreams. It occupies a place inside me. I wanted to return to help me understand why it still held such power.As we walked through nearby Holland Park, my body remembered before my mind did. A warmth spread through me. I thought of family picnics on the grass, ice-creams on hot afternoons, school sports days and sneaky cigarettes behind bushes as a teenager.The closer we came to my street, the more I noticed what had survived. The backs of the Victorian houses facing the park looked almost unchanged. The trees were taller but familiar. As I turned the corner, my heartbeat quickened. Then I saw it.A large white stucco Victorian house, even bigger than I remembered, as later owners have extended it. The two stone eagles that stood guard at the entrance, which I used to tap every time I ran up the steps, had disappeared. The little coal hole in the front wall was still there. My twin brother and I invented endless games through that opening. I could see us both there, age six, completely absorbed in a world of our own.My friend and I stood on the opposite pavement, looking up at the house, when the family who live there now unlocked the front door and went inside. I felt an unexpected punch in my stomach. For a split second, I wanted to call after them, “I used to live here. Would you mind if I came in?”I immediately changed my mind. I realised I did not want to go inside at all. I wanted to preserve the architecture of my memory. Every room held another version of me.I looked up at the top-floor window on the left. That had been my bedroom. I could picture the desk I persuaded my mother to buy me, where I spent hours writing stories simply for the pleasure of disappearing into another world. I remembered the hall with its black and white tiled floor, the sweeping staircase covered in orange carpet. I recalled lying on the landing with my brother, on guard to see who entered and left. I could see my little legs trying to follow my sisters up the stairs, two steps at a time. My last significant memory is stepping down those stairs in my wedding dress, then standing in the hall beside my husband to welcome our guests.If I walked through those rooms today, they would hold another family’s furniture, another family’s smells, another family’s life. Those memories would become mixed with someone else’s reality.As I stood there, I felt two versions of myself share the same pavement. The woman I am today and the child who knew every creaking stair and every colour in every room of that house. As a psychotherapist, I’ve learned that people rarely return to their childhood homes because they miss the building. They return because they are revisiting earlier versions of themselves.Adolescence lasts into your 30s – so how should parents treat their adult children?Read moreChildren remember the emotional atmosphere of home as much as its architecture. Long before we have language, we absorb the rhythms of family life. We learn whether someone comes when we cry, whether conflict feels frightening or survivable, whether we belong and whether we matter. A stable home creates an inner sense of safety. An unpredictable one leaves us scanning for danger. Those early experiences become the template we carry into future relationships.When parents die and families clear a childhood home, they do far more than sort possessions. Every object carries memory. Every room holds echoes of family life.Another family belongs in my childhood home now, and I hope they fill it with a rich life of their own. I didn’t need to step inside because what mattered had never been contained by bricks and mortar.That house gave me my first experience of rootedness and belonging. Those foundations have steadied me through loss, change and uncertainty.Our childhood homes shape our first understanding of safety, belonging, love and family. We leave them physically, but their emotional architecture stays with us for the rest of our lives.‘Seeing my old home after a decade was a surprisingly gruelling emotional experience’Comedian Alexei SayleView image in fullscreenAlexei Sayle, age two, with his dog Blackie, near his childhood home in Liverpool.Photograph: Courtesy of Alexei SayleThis is not the first time I have returned to my old house on Valley Road in Anfield, Liverpool. I moved out in 1971, aged 19, when I gained a place at Chelsea School of Art. When my mother was still alive, I would visit Liverpool once a month or so, and, although I had bought her a nice semi in the verdant south Liverpool suburb of Aigburth, I would regularly take friends who had come to visit to see our old house. I don’t know why I thought they’d be interested, but they didn’t get a choice.It lies near the top of a street of modest terrace housing, built of yellow brick and distinguished from the most basic of working-class houses by its bay window. The last time I had visited was about a decade ago. At that time, every house in the street had been tastefully done up. Only my former house remained unimproved. Perhaps this was some commentary on how Liverpool viewed my legacy.On this latest visit I assumed I would feel the warm nostalgia I usually experienced. I had no anticipation of the emotional hurricane that assaulted me when I stepped out of the taxi from Lime Street station and stood on the corner of Valley Road and Oakfield Road. I felt like someone who had been kidnapped, had a bag jammed over their head and dumped on some unfamiliar street corner in a rough part of town.My gaze followed the curve of Oakfield Road to a building a few hundred metres away, an edifice of such vastness that it resembled a colossal warship anchored in the harbour of some small town. This is Anfield Stadium, the home of Liverpool FC. It had always been there but seemed to have increased in size exponentially since my last visit, grown fat on TV rights and shirt sales.My old neighbourhood is unusual in that there are times when these streets are crammed with tens of thousands of people, but when the people have gone it feels as if this intermittent frenzy has caused it to lapse into exhaustion.As I walked down Valley Road, I was hit by a range of unexpected emotions, the foremost of which was sadness. I felt a sense of familiarity but also of dislocation. Seeing my old house on an airless summer afternoon aged 74 brought back all sorts of memories of childhood: playing in the street, walking to school and visiting the shops. It all seemed such an impossibly vast time ago that it was hard to believe that I had been alive for so long.When I was little, there was a dairy at the end of Valley Road that actually had cows in it. The building was still there, but it was housing now. When I returned from staring at it, there was a man sitting in a chair outside my old house drinking a can of beer. He said the house belonged to his sister and that she wouldn’t mind me looking around, but it didn’t look like it had changed much from my last visit, so I declined.How I’ve Tried to Change the World by Alexei Sayle review – does protest make a difference?Read moreIn my youth there were so many nearby shops – chandlers, greengrocers, delicatessens – and each was busy, but now 95% of shopfronts are shuttered. Strangely, the only place open was a smart-looking takeaway selling tacos and churros. The twin spectres of economic collapse and incompetent and corrupt redevelopment did for Anfield.On the drive over, I’d asked my cabby how he thought the city had changed in the last few years. He told me that, for a long time, following Thatcher’s economic assault on the city, people were filled with despair, but they were starting, in a modest way, to regain hope.To my mind, the grounds for this hope lie in initiatives such as the Homebaked Cooperative Bakery, which occupies a corner site a little farther along Oakfield Road from my former home. The building had been a bakery for more than 100 years, one that I remember visiting many times as a child, but it closed in 2010. After the Liverpool Biennial art festival used the site as a base, locals worked with the organisation to reopen the bakery in 2013. Now, it is thriving.Perhaps this is where hope lies – not in grand schemes but in a little shop selling pies. Hopefully, other grassroots enterprises will follow and the streets of Anfield will again be teeming with people. I’m not sure if I will visit again. Seeing my childhood home after a decade was a surprisingly gruelling emotional experience. If I make it to 84, it’s hard to imagine what unsettling effect that will have.How I’ve Tried to Change the Worldby Alexei Sayle (W&N, £16.99) is out now.‘I was happy in that house. There were meals around a big old kitchen table, feasts that issued from an Aga’Novelist Esther FreudView image in fullscreenEsther Freud (on right), age 11, with two of her siblings at The Old Laundry, East Sussex.Photograph: Courtesy of Esther FreudThere were a lot of childhood homes. My sister and I counted them once: 16 in two years, but the longest and most defining was a converted laundry in East Sussex where I lived between the ages of eight and 14. The house was owned by an American, the father of three girls. The initial understanding was that my mother, my sister, Bella, and I were renting rooms from him, but it wasn’t long before I discovered my mother’s bed empty when I crept through to her in the middle of the night.My stepfather, as I came to refer to him later, after we’d moved out, had recently divorced, and gained custody of his three young daughters – most unusual in those days. He had bought a derelict laundry on an old estate, which overlooked Ashdown Forest, in a village so small it was termed a hamlet, although there was a pub, a shop and a telephone box, from which we occasionally received calls from our father, pre-arranged by post.The Old Laundry was the last building on the estate to be restored. There was also a coach house and several stable blocks, and the mansion with its Jacobean facade had been turned into flats. Our stepfather had renovated the house himself, adding an extension to the original square brick building. Inside, there was a chimney stack vast enough to heat the water that once washed the estate linen, and this was transformed into a fireplace big enough for us to sit inside on cushions.It seemed at first that our ramshackle family would not be welcome on the Holly Hill estate: our van broke down on the cattle grid; our dog regularly escaped; and a feud developed with the man next door, a retired colonel, who had illegally – according to our stepfather – cut down an ancient tree that blocked his light. The rest of us ignored this quarrel, unwilling to risk our friendship with Margaret, the colonel’s wife, a big‑hearted woman who employed all five of us girls, rewarding us disproportionately for dusting and polishing, or ironing a shirt. Margaret became our ally and would drop round to sample our baking, watch our plays and listen to our recitals.I was happy in that house. There were meals around a big old kitchen table, feasts that issued from an Aga, and occasionally my stepfather would make lasagne, commandeering every surface of the kitchen and allocating jobs. On Sundays he would make pancakes, and on winter evenings we would sit inside the fireplace while he played guitar and sang folk songs. I loved the rituals. I even loved the chores – I was in charge of feeding the chickens and collecting their eggs. And I loved the new baby, a boy, born when I was 10.But there were dark days, too, when one or other of us, most often my stepfather, would lock themselves in the bathroom. When frustrations and jealousies would blacken the mood. Days when my sister would pull me aside and insist the whole setup was a charade: the singing and the pancakes. He didn’t love us or our mum. Charade or not, this house was where much of my character was formed, for better or for worse. The bookshelves, the conversation, the rituals and routines, the idea of family and what, at its best, it could be.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEsther Freud: ‘My parents died within four days of each other. I was engulfed’Read moreI didn’t expect the suddenness with which the household broke apart. I arrived home one day to find a note: my mother had gone. My sister and I were to follow her to Cambridge, she explained, and we would not be going back.My mother, I’m fairly certain, never returned to the house. My sister – absolutely not. But I did, decades later. Finding myself in Sussex, I drove over the cattle grid and into the estate. There were the familiar shrubs and lawns, the Gate House, the Coach House, the steep path that led up to the Old Laundry. I knocked on the door, full of dread – what if there wasn’t any answer? What if there was?The new owners were happy to show me around. The house was smaller, tidier. How had this been the scene of so much joy and anguish? The Aga was still there and the fireplace, but my old downstairs bedroom had been turned into a dining room, and the trees that shaded it had fallen in the storm of 1987, allowing light to flood in. The colonel would be pleased, I thought. As I looked across the fence, I had a yearning to see Margaret, to tell her I still used the button box she had given me, to say how important she was.I was quiet as I drove away. The Old Laundry, mythical receptacle of stories, was nothing but a shell. The real house, the one in which I had learned to read, fallen in love, experienced both triumph and despair, only existed now inside my head.Esther Freud’s most recent novel isMy Sister and Other Lovers(Bloomsbury).‘At its best, a childhood home is a safe place in which solitude can be experienced without anxiety’Writer Deborah LevyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Paul Blow/The GuardianI do not have to literally knock on the door of my childhood house to enter its domain. It is always inside me – “my first universe”, as the philosopher Gaston Bachelard put it.Yes, in my mind’s eye, the door is ajar at this modest bungalow in Johannesburg, South Africa, 1966. It presents itself to me like a museum. Everything is in place. Nothing has changed since my last visit.Of course, should I visit 11 Iris Road in the suburb of Norwood in real life, everything will have changed, but let’s press a foot into the dust of the past and see what it reveals.Despite the force of the African sun and piercing stretch of blue sky above the tiles of its roof, the interior of the bungalow is dark and cool. Maybe the curtains are drawn in some of the rooms to keep it that way. I can smell floor polish as I glimpse myself, aged seven, with a crooked fringe trimmed by my mother and wearing a sleeveless summer dress, making my way towards the giant sack of oranges propped against the wall in the pantry.Every day after school, I roll one of the oranges under the soles of my feet until it is soft and pulpy. I then make a hole in it with my thumb and suck out the juice, usually while sitting on the steps of the porch outside, reading a book or looking out at the tall uncut grass of the garden, where I am convinced I have dropped one of my Barbie’s pink plastic stilettos. The incredible thing about Barbie is how she never looks sad. In fact, Barbie is still smiling when my friend Leonie twists off her head and throws it at my beloved pogo stick in the hallway.The lounge is where our mother keeps Auntie Molly’s record player, with its speakers made from wood. This sound system will travel with us from Johannesburg to the UK, when I am nine years old. I will inherit it as a teenager and play all my Bowie vinyl on it – but now I’m looking for Mum in the dark, cool bungalow. Yes, she is back from work. I can hear the ice rattling in her glass of brandy, and she has kicked off her shoes, patent leather burgundy kitten heels. My God. My mother is a secretary, and it occurs to my older self that she is like a character from Mad Men, a cross between Peggy and Joan. She tells me all about work. I don’t tell her anything about school. It is a relief not to be asked.My bedroom is located at the back of the bungalow. It is a place of refuge and calm. I can lie in bed and glimpse the bright stars at night through its big windows. At its best, a childhood home is a safe place in which solitude can be experienced without anxiety. Solitude is different from loneliness. It is an invitation to have imaginative adventures, to daydream, to discover something we do not know, to pretend to be someone else for five minutes – perhaps someone braver and happier.My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy review – wonderfully entertainingRead moreMy childhood home represents theturbulent African part of my biography. Sometimes it feels like the child in this house is a ghost child who is not that keen to talk to my English adult self. Yet she haunts every book I have written.The past is literally a foreign country in my case. I can see via Google Earth that the house is still there, but it has been redesigned to conceal its interior. When I was a child there was an iron gate that opened on to the front garden. Now that the garden is closed off to the street with a heavy door and a wall, I do not have a nostalgic longing to unlock its new mystery. If our first home holds “childhood motionless in its arms”, as Bachelard insists, it is also the place my brother and I had to solve the old mystery of where our mother had hidden the family supply of sweets. As it happens, I can tell you they are inside a yellow enamel cup, behind a bag of flour in the pantry.Deborah Levy’s most recent work isMy Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein(Hamish Hamilton).‘For my father, who was part of the first wave of south Asian immigration into the UK, property ownership served as a hedge against future precarity’Novelist and artist Guy GunaratneView image in fullscreenGuy Gunaratne on his eighth birthday at his house on Crest Road in Neasden, London.Photograph: Courtesy of Guy GunaratneBetween the ages of three and nine, I lived with my parents, my brother and my half-sister in a small semi‑detached house on Crest Road, in a suburban part of Neasden, north-west London. The house had a pebbledash exterior, characterful bay windows and a narrow back garden, which, as I recall, extended farther than either of our neighbours’ gardens.As I wander around the area today, not much has changed. There is still a newsagent at the end of the road and a bus stop from where my mother used to catch the no 16 to work. Farther along, a bookie has replaced the charity shop where my mother bought her silverware. There used to be a greengrocer in front of the bus stop. The grocer was a Cypriot man from whom my mother would buy cabbage, leeks and carrots. He wore a white coat and would offer a kindly slap to the cheek whenever I tagged along. The Ox & Gate pub, which the grocer might have patronised after closing time, still stands across the road, although the flash signage and live sports advertising indicate a change in owner.My family moved around often when I was a child, but only ever within a five-mile radius. My mother still lives a few streets away. My father, working as a clerk in Paddington for most of his life, put me and my brother through school and tuition by purchasing modest properties around the area. He would redecorate the houses and sell them on over the years, which meant the family had to relocate every so often.For my father, who was part of the first wave of south Asian immigration into the UK, property ownership was more than a social marker: it served as a hedge against future precarity. He used to tell stories of lodging in overcrowded rooms in the 1960s, shift‑sleeping in shared beds, and fretting over the labour market in the morning. In the 1990s and early 2000s, he had my brother and I help him redecorate these other homes, pasting wallpaper, laying down carpet and mowing the lawn. It was during these weekends that I came to realise that property ownership was never an end in itself but a means to afford a way of life. What mattered was not the high ceilings or the Edwardian bay windows, but whether we could afford the expense of keeping both salted fish and Indian okra in my mother’s kitchen cupboard.I think this is why, as I stand in front of the house on Crest Road today, my memories aren’t so much shaped by its dimensions but by the extended sense of constant migration. I can, of course, locate certain memories in its rooms. I remember watching my brother leave for school from an upstairs window. I can recall the image of suitcases left on the landing when an aunt and uncle came to stay. There is my half-sister, the scent of her hairspray perfuming the hall as she skipped away for a night out. And another, in the narrow back garden, when, aged seven, I found a pigeon lying asleep near the farthest fence. There is an aspect of loss or transition to many of these memories.I often wonder what my father would have made of my now choosing to live in cooperative housing in north London. I live alongside families and artists who both rent and part-own their homes. He would surely have raised an eyebrow at my rent. I also think he would have recognised the same instinct for community and shared shelter.Last September, when my father died, my brother and I plotted a route for the procession that would take in some of the houses he had owned and redecorated. When we slowed down on Crest Road, the last stop before the cemetery, I noticed there were children’s bikes leant against the garden fence, the front door slightly ajar. I imagined other lives looking out at us from behind the net curtains. Somebody was home.‘Everything was animated by our childhood dog, a black labrador retriever named Tarzan, who would pull us through the snow on an orange plastic sled’Novelist Chloe AridjisView image in fullscreenChloe Aridjis, age five, in front of her house with Tarzan the dog.Photograph: Courtesy of Chloe AridjisLatin America has a long and eccentric tradition of appointing its writers to diplomatic posts abroad. Who better, it would seem, to represent your country than a cultural figure, especially if trade and serious geopolitics aren’t too much of a concern. And so it was that in the late 1970s, my father, a long-haired poet in his 30s, was appointed Mexican ambassador to the Netherlands, and our family relocated there. I was five years old when my parents, my sister and I left Switzerland (a previous posting) and moved into the ambassador’s residence in Wassenaar, where we lived for nearly three years. I hadn’t been back since the summer we left.Not until this past April, that is, when I went to visit my childhood friend Victor in Amsterdam. I’d met him aged two in a sandpit in The Hague, and our families have remained friends. On my second day there, his parents, Ad and Ada, were driving me to the Mauritshuis museum when Ad asked whether I’d like to see my old home. We were passing through Wassenaar and had time for a quick detour. I remembered the street name but not the number. We searched for the house until we spotted the Mexican flag in the distance. I rang the buzzer, tried to explain who I was over the intercom. Moments later, a man appeared and introduced himself as the cook. I lived here as a child, I said somewhat timidly, and would love to revisit the grounds. He studied me and my friends and replied that the ambassadress was in a meeting and they couldn’t let anyone in without permission. He tried calling but her phone was switched off.View image in fullscreenChloe Aridjis, c1977, age fivePhotograph: Courtesy of Chloe AridjisIt was tantalising to be so close. I could almost feel a gloved hand keeping my curiosity in check. As we lingered outside, I gazed past the gold-tipped wrought‑iron gates, down the gravel driveway to a corner of the house. I recognised the tall brick chimney and shingled roof. It was by far the largest home I’ve lived in; much of it had remained a mystery. As a child, I had no sense that the space and its furnishings were all borrowed, that the Persian carpets and gilt bedframes had seen family after family come and go. My parents had hung some of their own masks and art on the walls to give character to the rooms. I remember an endless row of cupboards and two staircases, one with red carpeting and the other smaller and more secretive, connecting the kitchen to upstairs – that notion of front and back, the presentable and the hidden, now seems so foreign. On the third floor was the eerie attic, inhabited only by mice.Looking back, the house belonged more to the adults. The garden belonged to me and my sister. It was the highlight of those years, the vagaries of Dutch weather permitting, and most of my memories are from there. There were groves of deciduous trees, a wood of ghostly birch, and a 350-year-old beech at the very end of the grounds. Everything was animated by our childhood dog, a black labrador retriever named Tarzan, who in winter would pull us through the snow on an orange plastic sled. In spring we’d invite our classmates over for Easter egg hunts amid the tulips and daffodils. I remember Hugo, the elderly gardener, always in his olive-green clothes and cap, and the mounds left by moles overnight. The fenced compost heap, the tennis court. After we returned to Mexico, we moved into a normal-sized house – myfamily home to this day – and I went back to being the daughter of a poet, which felt more natural. We were free to explore every space and inhabit every corner and create our own chaos without ever feeling that the house itself was hushing us.The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis review – one of the boldest writers at work in English todayRead moreThat afternoon, after wandering through the Mauritshuis, Ad asked whether I had ever seen the Panorama Mesdag, a vast cylindrical painting from the late 19th century. We could drop by on our way back to Amsterdam. Half an hour later, we stood on the viewing platform as painted scenes from Scheveningen, a beach I’d often visited, wrapped around us. That familiar sea, its ships, dunes and village, all formed part of a great illusion of the past. Yet seeing my old house that day had felt like the greatest illusion of all. Those years seemed so distant, and the impossibility of entering the house only strengthened the sense of remove. Part of me was relieved I hadn’t written over my memories, that the many details from that remarkable time would remain undisturbed, and I feel quite certain I may never return.The Shadow of the Object(Chatto & Windus) by Chloe Aridjis is longlisted for the 2026 Booker prize and is out now.Explore more on these topicsHomesFamilyAlexei SayleDeborah LevyGuy GunaratneChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: Chefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its people
Content: The historic ironworks village of Högbo Bruk is now an outdoor recreation destination. All photographs: Emmie Bolmstedt/Visit SwedenView image in fullscreenThe historic ironworks village of Högbo Bruk is now an outdoor recreation destination. All photographs: Emmie Bolmstedt/Visit SwedenSweden holidaysA taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroesChefs in the east of the country are shunning imported produce for local ingredients, reinforcing how food is intertwined with a region and its peopleAilsa SheldonSun 13 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses atHögbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food.The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended.“Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home.Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the oldbrukbuildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses.View image in fullscreenA selection of charcuterie at Högbo BrukshotellIngredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work.Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli.double quotation markOver several days, I discover a network of millers,  distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes fromHögbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from.AtGammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby,The Old Millis now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed.View image in fullscreenAppetisers at the Old Mill restaurantAtBergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations.But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon andböckling(hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads.
