The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills.View image in fullscreenThe smokehouse at Bergmans Fisk, run by a seventh-generation fishing familyDriving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIsland-hopping in Sweden: an enchanted maze of tiny isles – only a bus ride from GothenburgRead moreAtTeve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930.Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs.At nearbyJärvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.”In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie.View image in fullscreenFood prep at Järvsö Lanthandel country shop and restaurant.Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses.Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb.It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious.It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too.The trip was provided byVisit Sweden. For more information visitgastrikland.seanddestinationhalsingland.se.Högbo Brukshotellhas doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&BExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysFood and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make chocolate mousse – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: The little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classic
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: The little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classic
Content: Felicity Cloake’s chocolate mousse.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s chocolate mousse.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Loïc Parisot.Felicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make chocolate mousse – recipeThe little black dress of desserts, this French staple is quick and easy to make, and almost always delivers. Experiment with flavours and toppings to put your own spin on a classicFelicity CloakeSun 13 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYears ago, a group of us cycled from Brittany to the Mediterranean, and along the way we ate alotof chocolate mousse. Popular, easy to make and happy to sit in the fridge until required, it’s a mainstay of the modest French provincial restaurant and, as we discovered, it’s almost always good. Here’s my favourite version of the little black dress of the dessert trolley.Prep5 minCook20 minChill2 hr+Makes260g at least 70% cocoa chocolate2 medium eggs1 pinchsalt2 tsp sugar, or to tasteView image in fullscreen1 A note on the chocolateYou can use milk or flavoured chocolate here, if you like, but do bear in mind that if it’s quite sweet, you probably won’t need the extra sugar. Unless you’re using uniform chocolate drops designed for melting, roughly chop the chocolate – there’s no need to cut it into very tiny pieces, but they should be fairly even so they melt at the same rate.2 Melt the chocolate over a bain-marieBoil the kettle. Meanwhile, get ready a large heatproof bowl that can sit over a pan holding about 5cm of water without the base of the bowl touching the water. Pour the boiling water into the pan and turn on the heat to medium. Put the chocolate in the bowl, then put the bowl on top of the water pan and turn down the heat so the water is barely simmering. Stir occasionally, until the chocolate is completely melted.3 … or use a microwaveAlternatively, use a microwave, which saves on washing up but carries a greater risk of burning the chocolate if you don’t keep your eye on it. Put the chocolate in a heatproof bowl, microwave for 20 seconds, then stir and carry on microwaving in five-second bursts until completely melted.4 Carefully separate the eggsWhile the chocolate is melting, separate the eggs – it’s important not to get any yolk in the whites or they’ll be tricky to whip up properly. To avoid this possibility, I break the eggs into a glass or metal bowl (plastic will make the job harder), then use a clean hand to scoop the yolks into a fresh bowl.View image in fullscreen5 Beat the egg whitesLeave the chocolate to cool slightly. While it does so, use electric beaters or a large whisk to whip the egg whites and a pinch of salt to soft peaks – that is, to the point when the mix will hold a wave that flops over at the top rather than standing up straight. Add the sugar and carry on whisking until the mix is glossy and holds its shape.View image in fullscreen6 Combine the egg yolks and chocolateMix the egg yolks one at a time into the melted chocolate. If at any point the mixture seizes and turns tight and grainy, don’t worry, it’s not a disaster. Simply add a small splash of boiling water and whisk again until the mix is glossy and pourable again (if that doesn’t work, repeat the process until it does).7 Fold in the egg whitesStir a spoonful of the whipped egg white into the melted chocolate and egg yolk mixture to loosen it up, then add the rest. Use a large metal spoon gently to fold it in, using a D-shaped action so you don’t knock too much air out of the meringue. Stop as soon as everything is uniformly mixed, with no streaks.8 Chill to setSpoon the mousse into a serving bowl or into two separate bowls or glasses (don’t worry if the serving looks ungenerous; this is averyrich dessert). Put in the fridge to chill (covered, if you like, especially if you have any strongly scented ingredients in there), preferably for a couple of hours, so the mousse has a chance to set properly. It will keep well for several days.View image in fullscreen9 Variations on the themeTo ring the changes, when melting the chocolate, stir in the grated zest of a well-scrubbed orange, or two tablespoons of strong coffee, a pinch of cinnamon, nutmeg or chilli flakes, a little more salt, or a splash of vanilla extract or rosewater. Serve as is, or top it with whipped cream, cocoa nibs, orange zest, mint leaves or chopped nuts.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassChocolateDessertFrench food and drinkEggsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant review | Food | The Guardian
description: The weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: The weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep
Content: Rosina, London SW17: ‘An achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced trattoria.’Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenRosina, London SW17: ‘An achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced trattoria.’Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian.Grace Dent on restaurantsFoodReviewRosina, London SW17: ‘Bella Italia in Bolton this is not’ – restaurant reviewThe weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weepGrace DentSun 13 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 03.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRosinais a serene, heavenly-white neighbourhood Italian restaurant just off Wandsworth Common, on the same stretch as the much-celebratedChez Bruce. It isAdam Byatt’s fifth place – he’s probably best known forTrinity, his Michelin-starred restaurant up the road in Clapham – and, lately, hisvery good, recipe-driven YouTube channelrana Road to Rosina seriesin which he visits suppliers, eats pasta with nonnas and learns peak tiramisu skills from a woman called Pina (more of her tiramisu later). If any neighbourhood can stomach an achingly civilised, Emilia Romagna-influenced, candlelit trattoria where the cloakroom tags are actual Amalfi Coast pebbles engraved with numbers, it is Wandsworth Common, land of the hedge fund/interior design power couple who wouldn’t think twice about sipping a basil gimlet with a plate of melon with culatello di Zibello or gnocco fritto with mortadella. Bella Italia in Bolton this is not.Rosina’s cocktail bar leans on art deco shapes, with a pale, marble-topped counter and walls covered inDavid Steen portraits. There’s a small second bar area for those bridging the gap between light dinner and semi-serious drinking, and a larger, linen-tableclothed area for the restaurant proper, with a back room for private dining. Rosina’s intimacy is an optical illusion: the place is as big as a tennis court, and the weekly linen laundry bills alone must make the accountants weep.View image in fullscreen‘A nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers’: Rosina’s ’nduja strozzapreti.The day-to-day cooking is in the hands ofWill Bee, previously of Michelin-starredLitain Marylebone andPaul Ainsworth at No 6in Padstow, and the menu is hearty, as well as littered with little in-jokes; like all the most promising neighbourhood joints, however, it would take at least five visits before they began to grate. Small plates of fried taleggio,melanzane fritteand smoked sardines on toast give way to a list of pleasingly substantial pastas ranging from caviar linguine at £30 to a staggeringly pocket-friendly cavatelli cacio e pepe at just £8. There is also what’s dubbed as “post-service pasta” (spaghetti with anchovy, chilli and garlic) at £16, which is the first time I’ve seen a restaurant give a glimpse into what its owner eats after hours. More of this, I say. I want cocktail lists that offer “post-service fernet branca plus howling into the abyss about business rates”. Let the light in on the magic.Hugh, my companion, ordered bruschetta of rabbit livers braised in chianti, and ate them withLecter-ish lust. Two plump sardines, coated in breadcrumbs and with their little tails sticking out of one end, resembled something out of a cartoon. Carpaccio of wild sea bass came flecked with chilli and amalfi lemon, and doused in the kind of olive oil you hide from house guests: clean, sharp, precise. It was at this point that something shifted for me, from “this is perfectly pleasant” to “holy god, this is really quite special”. The arrival of the ’nduja strozzapreti only confirmed that: hugely simple, but wonderfully layered, with a rich tomato sauce enveloping a nourishing bowl of priest-stranglers.View image in fullscreen‘A sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop’: Rosina’s ‘wonderful’ risotto bianco.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The GuardianRisotto bianco, made withRiso Buono carnaroli riceand topped with a bold, sunshine-yellow egg yolk, was rich, but it’s meant to be: risotto bianco is for people who laugh in the face of blood sugar spikes. There is nowhere to hide in a white risotto – it is a sensory bombardment of unctuous gloop – and Rosina’s is wonderful. Although, if I want to squander calories willy-nilly on genuine death row delicacies, it is to their fried potatoes that I might turn instead: tiny baby spuds no bigger than fingernails, roasted, crushed and tossed in herbs and oil. Absolutely remarkable. A hugely generous plate of roast summer vegetables came charred from the grill and drizzled with syrupy grape mustsabafrom Modena. We ate those with perfectly cooked roast turbot.Around us, Wandsworth Common conducted its typical Saturday business. The tyranny of school fees. The agony of basement excavations. The management of several homes at once, with only one housekeeper directing all the other housekeepers internationally. The true trials of life. These people deserve a good dessert menu, and Rosina offers an embarrassment of teeth-chattering riches. Dreamy, yesteryear-sounding things: orange riccarelli, marzipan fruits, iced cherries and a sharp, classic amalfi lemon tart with blackcurrant leaf ice-cream, which I demolished. And a bowl of Pina’s tiramisu, too, of course, of which we entertained a rather large amount. My congratulations to Pina: hers is averygood recipe: wet, light and stodgy in all the right places.View image in fullscreen‘Wet, light and stodgy in all the right places’: Rosina’s tiramisu, served family-style.If this rather sumptuous spot needs anything quite as crass as my feedback, Rosina is a surefire hit. If you’re south of the river and on the lookout for an oasis of calm and fanciness at a range of prices, somewhere you can talk and be heard, Rosina is the perfect woman.Rosina35 Bellevue Road, London SW17, 020-8672 5888. Open all week, lunch noon-2.30pm, dinner 5.30-10pm.
